22104-the-acorn-planter-a-california-for:
Jack London wrote The Acorn Planter, a California forest play, in 1916, the last year of his life. The stage is a redwood hillside with wide spaces between the great trees. A stream runs from a spring bursting out of the slope. Ferns, brakes, and thickets crowd the forest floor in his opening direction.

London built the play around a Native American planter who sows acorns for a future he will not see. The drama speaks for the redwoods and against waste. It belongs to the Bohemian Grove tradition of outdoor plays written by California authors. Few London works are less known, and few show his love of California land so directly.
22313-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, was Britain's famous comic weekly. Volume 150, dated February 2, 1916, comes from the middle of the First World War. Even wartime issues kept the magazine's dry, teasing voice.

One item mocks Austrians and Hungarians quarreling over occupied Serbian land. Each side, Punch notes, ransacks old history for legal arguments. The joke calls the dispute a purely academic question. Learned men, the piece says, love disputing such points. Readers today get wartime London humor at work: sharp about empires and lawyers, yet printed as light weekly fare for the home front.
22602-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, was Britain's famous humor magazine, and this entry holds its issue of January 5, 1916, from volume 150. The catalog record names no editor. By 1916 Punch had been making fun of public life for seventy-five years, and the Great War now filled its pages alongside the usual jokes.

The sample opens a comic story in a railway compartment. There the narrator finally notices his fellow passenger. The man has wild hair, bright eyes, and a soft hat. The man admits that he writes. Sketches, verses, cartoons, and mock news made up a typical number. Wartime issues mixed laughter with quiet strain. This single weekly number preserves the tone of British humor in the middle of the First World War.
22610-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of January 19, 1916, in this entry from volume 150 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Punch's weekly mix of cartoons, jokes, and light verse had long been a fixture of British middle-class life, and wartime only sharpened its eye.

One sample joke reports, with mock outrage, that the knockers-up of Manchester want a raise. These men, mostly old or disabled, walked the chill morning streets waking workers for threepence a week per head, and now dared ask fourpence. The humor leans on vanished trades and small sums. Read today, the issue preserves everyday wartime Britain: its work, its wages, and its way of laughing under strain.
22612-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of January 26, 1916, from volume 150 of the long-running humor magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Punch lived on topical jokes, and this number turns two look-alike officials, the Postmaster-General and another pea in the pod, into comic copy.

A Welsh paper, the magazine teases, tangled the pair so badly that it reported their doings under a heading about pea soup, salt beef, and three hundred poisoned sailors. That is Punch at work: a real mix-up stretched into absurd news. Verses, sketches, and cartoons fill out the number. Together they show how Britons at war laughed at officialdom while the real headlines stayed grim.
22672-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of January 12, 1916, from volume 150, in the second winter of the Great War. The catalog record names no editor. Wartime Punch joked about recruiting, rationing's first hints, and the small absurdities of a nation in khaki.

One story rides a tram in a northern city, where a wag asks the girl conductor for a ticket to Gallipoli. She charges him for the full journey, rings the bell at a recruiting office, and tells him: you change here, sir, for Gallipoli. The joke lands because Gallipoli was no joke at all that winter. Punch kept such wit weekly, balancing cheek against sorrow. This number preserves the blend exactly as readers took it with breakfast.
22687-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 1, 1916, from volume 150 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. By the war's second spring, Punch treated even distant fronts with its blend of patriotism and gentle mockery of official language.

One item remarks that Russia's capture of Mush, in the Caucasus, deserves more notice than it has had. Mush is, after all, the very town that issued Turkey's official victory reports. The joke punctures enemy communiqués in a single line. Around it stand cartoons, verses, and sketches of home-front life. The number shows how Punch kept morale up by laughing first at the other side's bulletins.
22688-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of March 29, 1916, from volume 150. The catalog record names no editor. This number leans on the magazine's stock in trade: quoting solemn nonsense from the week's speeches and reports, then letting it hang in the air.

A sagacious coroner, Punch reports, observed last week that horses often doze while walking. The magazine recalls the old four-wheeler days, when conversation on breakneck rides was drowned by the snores of the flying steed. Such filler jokes filled columns between cartoons and war sketches. Small as they are, they record the texture of 1916 reading: a public hungry for any laugh that cost nothing.
22697-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of February 23, 1916, from volume 150. The catalog record names no editor. Between war news and jokes, this number finds room to mourn a crocodile, in the deadpan style Punch reserved for its best nonsense.

The magazine regrets to report a sad loss at the Zoo: a much-loved, playful crocodile, dead of tuberculosis. Death was hastened, it reports, by a severe chill. The intelligent reptile caught it after shedding a warm undervest, an elderly admirer's gift, to chase the reptile keeper down a drain. In jest, of course. Such obituaries for animals let Punch be tender and absurd at once. The rest of the number mixes cartoons, verse, and home-front sketches.
22805-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 22, 1916, from volume 150 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Law and the courts supply this number's sample joke, a one-line verdict traded like a music-hall gag.

Bigamy, declares Mr. Justice Low, ranks as low among crimes as drunkenness does. On the other hand, Punch replies, this much favors it: bigamy seldom grows into a habit, as drunkenness does. That is the whole item, and its dryness is the point. Around it, the number gathers cartoons, verses, and sketches of a Britain deep in war, still determined to laugh in short paragraphs. Punch's wartime humor often worked best at this size.
22873-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
London's humor weekly speaks in this single issue of Punch, dated April 5, 1916, from its 150th volume. One joke reports a Lambeth Police Court case. A man convicted of stealing three galvanized iron roofs explained that he had won them at an auction bridge party. The court, Punch notes dryly, rejected the explanation.

War runs under the laughter. By 1916 Punch balanced jokes about courts, food, and fashion against news from the trenches and the home front. Cartoons, verses, and short paragraphs fill the pages in the magazine's settled mix. A single issue like this one works as a time capsule. It shows what Londoners laughed at, and what they worried about, in one spring week.
22941-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Bananas and turnips carry the war news in Punch's issue of May 3, 1916, from volume 150. Six bananas imported last Monday, the magazine jokes, had a dire effect on the digestion of little Percy. Portugal has decided to expel German sympathizers, it adds. Other clubs please copy.

Then comes the week's Zeppelin raid, reported through its strangest casualty. Twenty turnips in the Eastern Counties were completely destroyed, and so, Punch writes, the grim work of starving England goes relentlessly on. Food jokes did real work in 1916, shrinking fear to a size readers could laugh at. The whole number works that way, cartoons and paragraphs together, whistling in a genuine dark.
22988-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
False teeth make war news in Punch's issue of March 15, 1916, from volume 150. Sir Alfred Keogh has ruled out state-funded false teeth for sailors serving at home. Punch replies that the Navy's men will surely keep up its traditions regardless, and gamely stick to their gums.

The pun does the work of a whole cartoon. Around it, the number serves the magazine's wartime mix, jokes about shortages, officials, and the enemy, drawn and written for readers with men at the front. Humor here was a home-front ration, measured out weekly. This issue preserves its flavor exactly, brisk, loyal, and determined to grin at the bureaucracy that war multiplies.
22992-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Staff officers take their leave in Punch's issue of May 10, 1916, from volume 150. Punch hopes one colorful staff habit survives the war. Officers parting with a cheery farewell phrase, it says, should never let the custom die out. So long, Old Tape, it quotes, with real affection for the slang.

Wartime language fills this number, as new phrases poured out of the trenches and offices of 1916. Around the jokes sit cartoons and verses for readers following casualty lists. Punch worked to keep home-front spirits serviceable, one small laugh at a time. The issue's charm is its nearness to the moment. It jokes about the words soldiers actually used, before the dictionaries caught up with them.
22993-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Generals multiply in Punch's issue of March 8, 1916, from volume 150. Answering Sir Arthur Markham in the Commons, Mr. Tennant allowed that a large force of troops in Egypt might make a hundred and seventeen generals necessary. Punch does the sums another way. Even junior generals need armies beneath them, and a hundred and seventeen of them would absorb half a million soldiers.

Arithmetic does the satire's work here. The rest of the number aims its paragraphs and cartoons at wartime officialdom, rationing of news, and the enemy's claims. Readers in 1916 bought Punch for exactly this treatment, respectably rude and reliably brief. The issue survives as a neat gauge of what London found ridiculous in the war's second spring.
23064-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Swedish sardines make diplomacy in Punch's issue of June 7, 1916, from volume 150. Sweden has banned sardine exports in oil, Punch reports. German resentment follows, since German buyers had long smuggled in rubber substitutes soaked in petrol, undetected until now.

Food, blockade, and mockery mix through the whole number, as they had to in the war's second summer. Cartoons and paragraphs treat shortages as sport while the Somme offensive gathers offstage. Punch's readers needed both jokes and news, and the magazine folded them together weekly. This issue preserves that blend at working strength, silly on the surface and quite serious about morale.
al-baladhuri-origins-islamic-state-hitti:
Al-Baladhuri, a scholar at the Abbasid court in the ninth century, wrote the Futuh al-Buldan, the Book of the Conquests of the Lands. Philip Hitti translated the first part into English in 1916 at Columbia. It is the chief early Arabic account of how the caliphate's armies took the Middle East.

Country by country, al-Baladhuri tells how each land fell or made terms: Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Persia, and the islands. He names the treaties, the taxes set, and the men who led the armies. His sources were the records and reports of the caliph's own administration. Scholars start with him for the shape of the early Islamic state.
andreyev-he-who-gets-slapped-1916:
He Who Gets Slapped, Leonid Andreyev's circus play of 1916, came to English in Gregory Zilboorg's translation of 1922. A ruined man of learning joins a provincial circus as the clown He, whose act is to be slapped. Behind the paint he hides his past and watches the ring's small world of riders and acrobats.

He falls in love with the young bareback rider Consuelo, whose father plans to sell her in marriage. Love, poison, and the lion cage bring the hidden sorrows into the open. The Theatre Guild made the play a New York hit in 1922. It remains Andreyev's most performed work in English, a parable of dignity in humiliation.
arxiv-2509-00116:
Akshay K. Jagadish, Mirko Thalmann, Julian Coda-Forno, Marcel Binz, and Eric Schulz present a framework in 2025 that ties human learning to the stats of real-world tasks. Minds are shaped by the settings they grow in, yet whether choices count as fine-tuned adaptation to those stats was open. Their frame, ecologically rational analysis, joins rational analysis with grounding in real settings.

Language models generate realistic cognitive tasks at scale. Meta-learning, which learns how to learn, then yields models tuned for those task worlds. The result, ERMI, takes in the regular patterns of natural problem spaces and adapts to new cases with no hand-built rules. ERMI matches human conduct across fifteen experiments on learning and choice.
arxiv-2509-00216:
Seongmin Kim, Daihui Wu, and Yilong Han study entanglement networks of C-shaped grains in 2025 through experiments and simulations. Highly nonconvex particles, such as staples and metal shavings, can lock together into solid-like masses by geometric entanglement. How the network of those locks is structured was largely unexplored.

Under vibration, links among the C-shaped particles grow over time. Network analysis shows a percolation transition: once links pass a threshold count, a giant cluster spans the system. A continuum percolation model of rings captures the observed transition well. The particle opening angle strongly shapes mechanical bonding and thus the network. Network views could guide granular materials that hold together by shape alone.
arxiv-2509-00616:
Azul Garza and Renee Rosillo introduce TimeCopilot. TimeCopilot is an open-source framework for time series forecasting. Forecasting means predicting future values from past patterns. The framework combines several Time Series Foundation Models with large language models. Foundation models here are large pre-trained forecasters. All parts connect through a single unified interface.

TimeCopilot automates the full forecasting pipeline for its users. It handles feature analysis, model choice, and cross-validation. Cross-validation checks a model on held-out slices of data. It then generates the forecast itself. Users also get explanations in plain language. They can ask direct questions about the future as well. On the GIFT-Eval benchmark, the system reaches top scores. It does so at low cost, the team reports.
arxiv-2509-00816:
J Ovalle, writing alone, gives an exact, purely geometric account of the interior dynamics of Schwarzschild black holes, the simplest black holes, defined only by total mass. The account invokes no specific gravitational theory and adds no charges beyond mass.

Ovalle shows that dynamical evolution generically produces new singularities inside the black hole, features absent in the static case. Resolving those singularities imposes highly restrictive conditions on gravitational collapse, the process by which matter falls inward to form a black hole. The result is presented as a constraint that any theory or collapse model describing regular black hole interiors must respect, narrowing the space of plausible regular models.
arxiv-2509-00916:
Luiz Henrique Prudencio dos Santos leads a team of seven authors on quantum machine learning with Titanic data. The task is a classic supervised one: predict passenger survival. They build hybrid quantum-classical variational classifiers. Such models tune quantum circuit parameters with a classical optimizer. Feature maps come in entangling and non-entangling Pauli forms.

The circuits use a RealAmplitudes ansatz with up to fifty parameters. Training uses the COBYLA optimizer on cross-entropy loss. All runs occur in ideal statevector simulation. Models with the non-entangling map beat those with entangling maps. Their metrics saturate beyond fifteen to twenty parameters. Against a classical support vector classifier, performance is similar. The classical model collapses at one training size, though. That failure mode is absent in the quantum models.
arxiv-2509-01016:
Aishni Parab, with three co-authors, analyzes error sources in LLM-based hypothesis search. The task is few-shot rule induction. This kind of reasoning infers abstract rules from few examples. Humans do this well and apply rules to new cases. The team asks how close machine approaches come.

They compare hypothesis search with direct program generation. The first approach proposes explicit rules and tests them. The second writes programs in one pass instead. The first achieves performance comparable to humans. The second falls notably behind on the same tasks. An error analysis reveals key bottlenecks in generating hypotheses. It also suggests ways to advance program induction. The work shows both the promise and the challenges here.
arxiv-2509-01616:
A test that fails on buggy code and passes after the fix is gold for developers, yet patches are often committed without one. Konstantinos Kitsios, Marco Castelluccio, and Alberto Bacchelli propose BLAST, a tool that generates such issue-reproducing tests automatically from issue and patch pairs. It combines language models with search-based software testing, an optimization approach that evolves tests toward a goal.

Context for the language model is enriched through git history, static analysis, and tests the search component generates. The search side is seeded by a model-generated test, reshaped into a compatible form. On a curated Python benchmark, BLAST produced reproducing tests for about thirty-five percent of issues, beating the prior state of the art at about twenty-four percent. The tool aims to raise confidence that fixes truly close their issues.
arxiv-2509-01716:
Rui Zhao leads four co-authors on a system that turns long privacy policies into clear, machine readable maps of data practice. Few people read these policies, yet they state how sites collect and share personal data. Past tools could check a formal policy but could not build one at scale. The team uses large language models to pull key facts from policy text.

The pipeline builds a knowledge graph tied to a shared privacy word list and covers the top one hundred popular websites. Experts marked up test data so the team could score how well each model did. The graphs can then feed formal rule formats for apps that need consent checks. All data and code are shared for others to reuse and improve.
arxiv-2509-01916:
Jifan Zhang, Michelle M Li, and Elena Zheleva learn causal structure from network data with the help of known interaction maps. Causal disentanglement, pulling apart true cause programs, is possible under set assumptions with both plain and intervened data. Past work ignored the known networks that link measured items, like protein interaction maps. Their model treats pathway membership as an extra view of the hidden causal programs.

A graph neural encoder uses the biology graph and pathway view to sharpen inference. The decoder stays a causal model with soft interventions. Theory shows the method keeps the identifiability guarantees of its base family. Tests on three CRISPR perturbation sets, where genes are edited, show better forecasts of intervention results, even for unseen edit combos.
arxiv-2509-02316:
Aubrey L. Jones and Benjamin C. Bromley wrote a 2025 astrophysics paper on one way supermassive black holes, the giants at galaxy centres, might gain mass. A passing pair of stars can be torn apart by the black hole, which captures one star and later feeds on it.

Their kinematic model, based on motion rather than full dynamics, predicts capture rates from star density, star speeds, the share of paired stars, and black hole mass. Applied to ninety-one galaxies, the model finds only two cases where this channel may drive growth. Nearby, fast stars traced to the Large Magellanic Cloud suggest the same process may be feeding its black hole now, since each ejected star leaves a bound partner behind.
arxiv-2509-02416:
J. L. Alonso and four co-authors wrote a 2025 statistical physics paper building a proper framework for hybrid systems that mix classical and quantum parts. Such mixtures appear in models where a quantum device sits inside an ordinary environment.

The authors apply a maximum entropy principle, choosing the least biased distribution under stated limits, to derive the microcanonical ensemble for hybrids. That ensemble fixes total energy within a narrow band. They show it stays well defined even for very thin energy bands and a continuous range of energies, unlike the purely quantum version. Hybrid systems thus import a classical smoothness into quantum statistics. A weakly coupled reservoir argument links the result to the canonical ensemble, and a toy model illustrates the contrasting behaviours.
arxiv-2509-02516:
Suzana S. A. Silva and ten co-authors wrote a 2025 solar physics paper reporting global oscillations in the Sun's outer corona set off by a coronal mass ejection, a huge eruption of solar plasma. Waves in the low corona are well studied, but the extended corona stayed largely unexplored.

The team studied a July 2012 eruption using white-light images from the SOHO observatory plus a magnetohydrodynamic simulation. A decomposition method separated two signals. One was a directional shock-like wave that faded within hours. The other was a broad circular wavefront lasting much longer and spanning the full field of view, the first detection of its kind. The finding adds a missing piece to how eruptions disturb the space around the Sun.
arxiv-2509-02616:
A. Manas wrote a 2025 solo theoretical computer science paper on sorting when only some pairwise comparisons are allowed. Forbidden pairs form a graph, and the question is how the graph's structure controls the cost of finding the true order.

Algorithms are parameterised by the forbidden graph's clique number and chromatic number, two measures of its density and colouring needs. Results extend to inputs that may not be fully sortable, where only the partial order can be recovered. For random forbidden graphs of Erdős–Rényi type, a simple algorithm always finds the underlying partial order with a modest number of probes. The work links a classic task, comparison sorting, to graph parameters that decide how much information each allowed comparison can yield.
arxiv-2509-02816:
Salini Rajeev and Mayukh Lahiri present a 2025 quantum optics paper on characterising an unknown high-dimensional unitary transformation without ever detecting the particle it acts on. The transformed system is a qudit, a quantum unit with more than two levels, carried by orbital angular momentum states of light.

Reconstruction relies on quantum interference made possible by path identity of undetected photons, a technique where photons that were never measured still shape the observed pattern. The unitary's action is read off from interference data on partner photons. The authors demonstrate the scheme experimentally with light's orbital angular momentum. The trick matters where good detectors for the transformed system do not exist, a common problem at exotic wavelengths or for fragile quantum carriers.
arxiv-2509-02916:
B. Algohi and 85 co-authors reported first results in 2025 from a new ultracold neutron source at TRIUMF in Canada. The source uses a spallation target, where a proton beam knocks neutrons free, plus superfluid helium kept extremely cold. Ultracold neutrons move so slowly that scientists can trap and study them for long stretches.

In an early run, the team counted close to a million such neutrons after a minute of beam time. That tally broadly matched detailed simulations of neutron travel and cooling gear. The source is being built for a precise hunt for the neutron electric dipole moment, a tiny charge imbalance that could reveal new physics. Once a cold moderator system is finished, output should climb far higher.
arxiv-2509-03016:
Yong Yang wrote a 2025 algebra paper on twisted Heisenberg Lie superalgebras in the restricted setting. Lie superalgebras extend ordinary symmetry algebras with two kinds of elements, even and odd. The restricted version applies when the underlying field has prime characteristic, meaning arithmetic that wraps around after a prime number of steps.

Yang works over a field where every polynomial has roots, and first pins down which restricted structures these algebras can carry. He then uses ordinary first and second cohomology, tools that measure how an algebra can be extended, to compute the restricted second cohomology. With those spaces in hand, he classifies the one-dimensional central extensions, the smallest ways of enlarging the algebra by a central piece. The result gives a full account for this family.
arxiv-2509-03116:
Hauke Licht and 6 co-authors evaluated how well large language models can measure graded social science concepts in 2025. Many such concepts, like speech complexity or emotional tone, sit on a continuum rather than in yes-or-no boxes. Models are tempting measuring tools, yet their handling of numbers can be quirky.

The team tested four approaches on political science datasets. Asking a model for a direct score caused bunching around arbitrary values. Comparing items in pairs worked better. Weighting each possible score by how likely the model found it improved results further. Best of all, fine-tuning a smaller model on about a thousand labeled pairs could match or beat the prompted giants. The findings give social scientists a practical recipe for scale measurement.
arxiv-2509-03316:
Fatemeh Azad, Zoran Bosnić, and Matjaž Kukar proposed a 2025 ensemble method for filling missing values in biomedical data. Missing entries plague machine learning in medicine, where tests go unrecorded and samples fail. No single imputation method, which guesses the missing values, wins across all datasets and missingness patterns.

Their method, Meta-Imputation Balanced, learns how to combine several base imputers rather than picking one. It trains on data where values were hidden on purpose, so the true answers are known. From each base method's behavior it predicts the most suitable filled value. The authors present the system as a robust, modular preprocessing step. It is meant to be interpretable as well, so clinicians can see which methods drive each estimate.
arxiv-2509-03416:
Moritz Kade completed a 2025 doctoral thesis on integrable systems, mathematical structures that make certain hard models exactly solvable. His work links models from statistical physics with Feynman diagrams, the picture-like graphs used in quantum field theory. Central cases include the six-vertex and eight-vertex models and the bi-scalar fishnet theory.

Kade reviews known results on free energy and critical coupling, then adds new findings for models that include fermions. He extends the methods to supersymmetric diagrams, using superspace tools to get exact results for anomalous dimensions and expansion coefficients. New boundary setups for the six-vertex model are also proposed. A guessed formula would give its partition function for lattices of any size.
arxiv-2509-03616:
In a 2025 research paper, Rajeev Ranjan Dwivedi and two co-authors focus on removing several biases at once from image recognition models. Real photos carry overlapping shortcuts: textures, watermarks, gendered makeup, or typical object pairings. Models lean on those shortcuts, hurting robustness and fairness, and fixing one bias alone often lets another grow.

Their framework, GMBM, works in two stages and needs group labels only during training. First, separate encoders are trained for each known bias and merged with the main network, forcing the classifier to face those shortcuts openly. Fine-tuning then suppresses the bias directions inside the main network's gradients, leaving one compact model that ignores them. Because older metrics fail when groups are unbalanced, they add a new test-time measure of bias amplification. On three datasets, worst-group accuracy rises and measured bias falls sharply.
arxiv-2509-03816:
In a 2025 research paper, Aman Gupta and seven co-authors focus on fine-tuning a foundation model to build subgrid-scale parameterisations for climate models. Global climate models cannot resolve processes like gravity waves, clouds, or turbulence directly. Stand-ins called parameterisations approximate their effects and lead the uncertainty in the models.

Their case study targets gravity waves, oscillations carrying energy and momentum through the air. An encoder-decoder from a pretrained model, holding a probabilistic picture of how the atmosphere evolves, is fine-tuned for the task. It learns gravity wave fluxes from a reanalysis dataset ten times finer than the target model. Against an attention U-Net baseline trained from scratch, the foundation version predicts better across the atmosphere, where pretraining had no coverage. A distance measure quantifies the gap in its favour. The authors argue reusable foundation models could yield accurate parameterisations for many more processes.
arxiv-2509-04116:
Ioannis Tzortzis and two co-authors tackle remote tracking of systems that switch between modes in a 2025 research paper. Their systems, called Markov jump linear systems, change behavior according to a hidden pattern. A distant estimator must guess the current state from measurements sent over an unreliable network. Noise and missing packets leave doubt about which mode is active, and that doubt is the core problem here.

Their design assumes the true odds sit within a small distance of the guessed odds, then guards against the worst case. The result extends the classic best-estimate solution with extra terms for mode doubt. A practical version built on a standard approximation algorithm is tested in a numerical example.
arxiv-2509-04316:
Chandraniva Guha Ray and three co-authors uncover how every surface of a cell helps shape the hollow spaces inside tissues in a 2025 biology paper. Lumina are fluid-filled cavities wrapped by epithelial sheets, and their shapes emerge from pressure plus cell mechanics. The team studied MDCK cysts, ball-like cell clusters grown in labs, whose inner surfaces destabilize when tight junctions between cells are disturbed. Measurements showed the cysts answering by adjusting tension on their side and bottom surfaces too, not just pressure and the top belt.

A three-dimensional vertex model, which treats cells as interlocking blocks, reproduced the instability quantitatively. Extra sideways tightening acts as the cells' countermeasure, the model reveals. Development biology gains a fuller picture of cavity control.
arxiv-2509-04616:
Methane detection gets a new optical design in a 2025 paper by Shubhanshi Sharma, lead author with four co-authors. Their device combines a silicon nanodisk metasurface, a flat surface patterned at tiny scale, with MXene, a thin material with broad plasmonic response. Loss in MXene is countered using bound states in the continuum.

Both designs reach narrow, strong absorption near a wavelength suited to methane spectroscopy. Simulations report sensitivity to changes in refractive index and to methane concentration when a sensing layer is added. The authors present the design as a compact route toward optical gas sensing.
arxiv-2509-04716:
Answering hard questions from a knowledge graph often fails because retrieval is too narrow. Yushi Sun, lead author with six co-authors, present KERAG, a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, in a 2025 paper. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, offering precise material for question answering.

KERAG retrieves a broader subgraph likely to contain relevant information, then filters and summarises it. Fine-tuned language models reason step by step over those subgraphs, cutting noise. Experiments show gains over leading methods on both simple and complex questions. The authors frame the design as a way to raise coverage without losing answer quality.
arxiv-2509-04916:
Invariant probability measures for geodesic flow can be built as limits of measures sitting on single closed paths. Paul Mella studies that approximation on manifolds of non-positive curvature in a solo-authored 2025 mathematics paper. He introduces weakly regular vectors, defined through how their stable and unstable sets meet a set of non-wandering vectors.

Mella shows every ergodic measure supported on those vectors can be approximated by Dirac measures on periodic orbits. A consequence is that ergodicity is generic among such invariant measures. A classic rank-one example shows the weakly regular set is the largest one with the stated density property.
arxiv-2509-05016:
Measuring how far apart two probability distributions are is a basic task in statistics and computing. Weiming Feng and one co-author study approximating that gap between two Ising models in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Ising models describe interacting binary variables through interaction matrices and external fields.

For a family of chi-alpha divergences, they prove both an algorithm and matching hardness results, so the tractable regime is pinned down. The algorithm extends to many other divergences, including Kullback-Leibler, Rényi, and Jensen-Shannon versions, plus squared Hellinger distance. The work generalises recent results on approximating total variation distance.
arxiv-2509-05116:
Testing rehabilitation robots on patients early in development can be unsafe, so healthy volunteers wear suits that simulate impairments instead. Jialin Chen, lead author with three co-authors, analyse how a hemiplegia simulation suit changes walking in a 2025 paper. Motion capture and muscle and movement sensors record gait under four conditions, with and without suit and rollator.

The data feed a digital twin model used for machine learning analyses. Models detect suit and rollator use and identify turning behaviour. The suit significantly alters movement and muscle activation, prompting more abrupt compensating motions. The authors identify which sensor features capture gait dynamics best.
arxiv-2509-05316:
How training data are sampled can quietly break efforts to make language models forget, Praveen Bushipaka and two co-authors warn in a 2025 machine learning paper. Unlearning aims to remove unwanted knowledge from a forget set while keeping the rest, including facts close to the targets.

Common benchmarks use a single neighbour set, facts linked to the forget targets, plus general knowledge, which the authors find too simple. Standard one-to-one sampling against the retain set also performs poorly and hides trade-offs. Their alternative, modular entity-level unlearning, samples by entity instead of cycling blindly. Combined practices they validate give a clearer, more stable path to forgetting without wrecking general ability.
arxiv-2509-05516:
Spaces of branched covers of a surface, with their branch points kept in a chosen order, are studied by Zachary Himes, Jeremy Miller, and Jennifer C. H. Wilson in a 2025 topology paper. These ordered Hurwitz spaces are moduli spaces, families of geometric objects gathered into one space with its own shape.

The authors ask how the homology of these spaces, a measure of their holes in each dimension, behaves as the number of branch points grows. They prove representation stability, meaning the patterns in that homology settle into a regular form described by symmetry groups. The result answers a question posed by Ellenberg. Stability theorems of this kind turn infinitely many spaces into one predictable pattern.
arxiv-2509-05816:
A 2025 paper by Saptarshi Saha and three co-authors revisits the Unruh effect, where an accelerating atom in empty space warms as if in a heat bath. For one atom, the endpoint is a standard thermal state. The authors ask what changes when many non-interacting atoms accelerate together.

They find a long-lived halfway stage first: the whole system settles into a prethermal generalized Gibbs state, a near-thermal state fixed by extra conserved quantities, before true thermalization. They name this stage Unruh prethermalization. Entanglement measures track how long the stage lasts, matching earlier work. Before reaching it, the atoms can release a burst of radiation like Dicke superradiance, a flash from atoms radiating in step, unlike the plain decay of the single-atom case.
arxiv-2509-05916:
Ground state energies of multipartite p-spin models are bounded in a 2025 paper by Mihailo Stojnic. These models, borrowed from the physics of disordered magnets, split spins into several groups that interact in p-body clusters. Their lowest possible energy is a benchmark quantity that is usually hard to compute exactly.

Stojnic works through partially lifted random duality theory, a technique that turns random optimization problems into tractable dual ones. The machinery produces easy-to-compute lower and upper bounds for any choice of spin sets. For fully spherical spin sets the two bounds meet, giving the exact energy. Numerical evidence hints they may meet for Ising spins as well, and the author poses questions linking that matching to the structure of the spin sets.
arxiv-2509-06016: Haoming Wang studies the martingale problem for a family of Markov generators with a quadratic shape in a 2025 paper. The generators are built from a fixed reference process. Time-dependent weights scale its jump rates and their squares. If the martingale problem for these generators has just one solution, Wang finds exactly when a Girsanov change of measure works. That change rewrites the law of one process in terms of another.
arxiv-2509-06116:
Grouping photos by their look rather than their content helps enhancement software work better, show Giulia Bonino and Luca Alberto Rizzo in a 2025 paper. Their algorithm, CARDIE, clusters images with no labels, by color and brightness, the features enhancement actually changes. Clusters built on meaning, from what a picture shows, turn out to be the wrong neighborhoods for this job.

The authors also introduce a way to measure how an enhancement algorithm shifts brightness spread and local variance. With it, CARDIE's clusters prove more suited to enhancement than semantic ones. Rebuilding enhancement datasets along CARDIE clusters then improves tone mapping and denoising performance. Code is released publicly so others can adopt it and repeat the work.
arxiv-2509-06316:
Quantum error correction tuned to lopsided noise is tested in a 2025 paper by Devon Campbell. Real processors suffer biased noise and faulty readout. Campbell combines two defenses: bias tailoring, which aligns a code's stabilizers with the dominant error type, and single-shot decoding, which uses extra metachecks to spot measurement faults from one noisy round.

Both are implemented in a four-dimensional lifted hypergraph product code built from quasi-cyclic seeds. Simulations show bias tailoring cutting word-error rates by twenty to sixty percent across bias ratios, with the largest gains at moderate bias. One single-shot round recovers over a third of the performance lost to readout noise, and metachecks flag nearly all faulty syndromes. The code family looks promising for hybrid quantum-classical workflows.
arxiv-2509-06616:
Blockchains that run many smart contracts in parallel are redesigned by Anton Paramonov and four co-authors in a 2025 distributed systems paper. Usual blockchains force every transaction into one strict global order through a single consensus process. That design caps speed.

Their system, Mangrove, gives each smart contract its own consensus instance and drops the global order. A mechanism called Parallel Optimistic Agreement lets instances run side by side while blocking conflicting transactions from both being committed. Simple transactions use a lighter broadcast step to cut delay. The protocol is tuned for the optimistic case, where nobody misbehaves and the network is timely. Under those conditions, a transaction can go from creation to execution in two communication steps, a latency the authors highlight as the design's payoff.
arxiv-2509-06716:
Ranking software variants without running every benchmark is the goal of Théo Matricon and three co-authors in a 2025 software engineering paper. Benchmarks compare competing systems or settings of one system, but full runs eat time and computing power. Cutting tests while keeping the ranking stable is the challenge.

Their method, BISS, borrows from test suite optimization. It keeps the most critical benchmark instances and samples the rest with a divide-and-conquer strategy. Experiments span language model leaderboards, SAT solver competitions, and configurable systems used for performance modeling. BISS beat the baselines even when only a subset of variants was available for tuning the selection. On average it cut benchmark cost to well under half, and on more than half the benchmarks the savings reached up to ninety-nine percent, with no loss in ranking stability.
arxiv-2509-06816: How solutions of the Benjamin-Ono equation hold onto their spread over time is studied by Felipe Linares and one co-author in a 2025 analysis paper. The equation models internal waves, and persistence questions ask whether a solution that starts well localized in a weighted sense stays that way. Weighted Sobolev spaces measure both smoothness and decay at infinity. Roughly, below a threshold exponent, a solution stays in the weighted space exactly when its starting data lies there and is regular enough.
arxiv-2509-06916:
Quantum field theory on a curved background with an extra antisymmetric field is examined for consistency by Ioseph L. Buchbinder and two co-authors in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. The extra field is a two-form, an antisymmetric tensor. The question is renormalizability: whether the theory's infinities can be absorbed into its parameters.

The authors argue that renormalizability requires the two-form field to interact nonminimally with quantum fermions and scalars, going beyond the simplest coupling to the background. The situation mirrors the better-known cases of metric and torsion backgrounds. In each setting, the renormalization group flow of the nonminimal coupling parameters shows how the interaction behaves at high energies. General reasoning is backed by one-loop calculations in a concrete gauge model based on the SU(2) group. Such consistency checks decide which curved-space theories can be trusted at short distances.
arxiv-2509-07416:
Eye-tracking signals drift over time, and that drift corrupts gaze estimates in human-robot teamwork. Lianming Hu, Xiaotong Zhang, and Kamal Youcef-Toumi present a de-drifting method in a 2025 research paper. Their method works on electrooculography, which measures eye movement through voltages at the skin. It uses recognized eye-movement features to rebuild the signal baseline.

The approach corrects drift adaptively while keeping the waveform's shape intact. In simulation, the average error fell by more than a third. In real-world recordings, it fell by about a quarter, despite extra unpredictable noise. The method beat conventional de-drifting techniques in both settings. Cleaner eye signals could make gaze control steadier for assistive robots, hands-free interfaces, and performance support tools used by workers.
arxiv-2509-08216:
Textbooks mix prose with charts, diagrams, and algorithms, and ordinary search reads only the prose. Beth Plale, Sai Navya Jyesta, and Sachith Withana test multimodal retrieval in a 2025 research paper. They embedded several thousand digitized computer science textbook pages with a vision-language model. Each page became several vectors capturing both text and visual meaning.

The team stored the embeddings in a vector database and issued a benchmark set of natural language questions. They compared four similarity measures against known correct answers. Cosine similarity retrieved the most semantically and visually relevant pages. The authors also discuss whether such a database is practical for real digital library operations. Their design lessons point toward discovery tools that finally search the pictures and diagrams students actually rely on, not just the words around them.
arxiv-2509-08416:
Language models write decent Python but stumble on Verilog, the language used to describe computer chips, because training examples are scarce. Yan Tan and 3 co-authors present AutoVeriFix in a 2025 research paper. Generated Verilog often parses correctly yet behaves wrongly. AutoVeriFix attacks that functional gap with a two-stage process written in Python.

First, the model writes a high-level Python reference model stating the intended circuit behavior. Automated tests are then built from that reference. The Verilog implementation is simulated against the tests, and every mismatch guides a correction round. Iterating this loop steadily repairs functional errors. Experiments show the method beating existing state-of-the-art approaches for functional correctness. Reliable chip code generation would speed hardware design, where a subtle logic bug can be ruinously expensive.
arxiv-2509-08816:
Simon Pfreundschuh and 19 co-authors present SatRain, a benchmark dataset for satellite estimates of rain, in a 2025 paper. Satellites are the only way to track precipitation across the whole globe. Machine learning helps, but no standard benchmark existed for fair comparison.

SatRain pairs multi-sensor satellite data with high quality radar and gauge reference values. It covers rain, snow, graupel, and hail detection and estimation. A standard evaluation protocol supports robust and repeatable comparisons. Time resolved data from geostationary satellites add extra value. The dataset is meant as a base for next generation AI models for global precipitation.
arxiv-2509-08916:
V. L. Martinez-Consentino and 2 co-authors calculate meson exchange currents in argon-40 for neutrino and electron scattering in a 2025 paper. Two particles are knocked out and two holes remain in the nucleus. Asymmetric nuclei, with unequal protons and neutrons, need care.

Mean field and Fermi gas models use distinct proton and neutron momenta. Results for argon are compared with symmetric calcium-40. Using calcium as a stand-in for argon causes about ten percent systematic error. A new scaling formula estimates responses for other nuclei from carbon-12. Predictions are checked against electron scattering data and neutrino cross sections.
arxiv-2509-09416:
A short-lived meson called psi-prime is a probe of the strong force, and matching theory to collider data for it requires careful corrections. A. A. Prokhorov and 4 co-authors compute next-to-leading-order corrections in a 2025 research paper. They work in non-relativistic quantum chromodynamics combined with high-energy factorization. A matching scheme merges the leading and corrected production amplitudes.

The team extends that scheme to low transverse momenta and forward rapidities, the corners earlier work handled poorly. They then confront all available unpolarized LHC data across the full measurable range. Different models of the proton's gluon distribution are tried. A global fit extracts the long-distance parameters describing how the meson forms. Including the corrections clearly improves the description of the data. Precision strong-force physics advances exactly this way: one corner of phase space at a time, until the global picture holds together.
arxiv-2509-10216:
Noga H. Rotman and 4 co-authors present RFSeek, a tool that turns network protocol documents into pictures, in this 2025 paper. Requests for Comments, the texts that define internet protocols, are long and prose-heavy, which makes their exact logic hard to grasp. RFSeek uses large language models to pull visual summaries of protocol behavior out of the text.

Each diagram stays linked to the passages it came from, so readers can audit it against the source. The tool rebuilt diagrams that some documents already contain, and also found states and steps described in words but missing from those diagrams. Trials on TCP, QUIC, and other protocols show uses from guided study to comparing versions of a standard.
arxiv-2509-11816:
Filip Sondej and Yushi Yang make language model unlearning far more selective in a 2025 paper. Safety training often fails to remove dangerous knowledge. The authors name the cause: unlearning aims at representations that are too general, so it either misses the facts or harms broad skill.

Their method, Collapse of Irrelevant Representations, studies activations and gradients to find subspaces holding common representations. Collapsing those subspaces before computing unlearning updates spares general knowledge. It aims only at fact-specific representations. Tests removed bio- and cyber-hazardous facts from a mid-sized open model. The cut in post-attack accuracy was far greater than the best baseline. Harm to general skill was far smaller, at tiny compute cost per fact.
arxiv-2510-00016:
Ünver studies the infinitesimal dilogarithm, a truncated. Infinitesimal analogue of the classical dilogarithm function used to build regulators and invariants in algebraic K-theory. The ordinary dilogarithm is known to satisfy a functional equation for every period in a cluster pattern, identities coming from cluster algebras. And Ünver asks whether the infinitesimal versions, in characteristic zero and in positive characteristic, obey the same cluster identities in this paper.

The answer is yes on both fronts, proved for the characteristic-zero infinitesimal dilogarithm and for the positive-characteristic version built from Kontsevich's one-and-a-half logarithm. And Ünver goes further to show these cluster identities are actually consequences of the famous pentagon, or five-term, relation. That derivation settles in the infinitesimal world a question still open for the ordinary dilogarithm, where not every relation is yet known to follow from the pentagon identity alone.
arxiv-2510-00216:
Konstantinos Topalakis, Devesh Nandal, and Jonathan Tan published this 2025 astrophysics paper on the first stars and dark matter. Giant black holes exist surprisingly early in cosmic history, so their seeds must have grown fast. The authors test whether dark matter annihilation could power the first protostars. They simulate primordial stars capturing WIMPs, the classic dark matter candidate particles.

Using a one-dimensional stellar evolution code, the team varied the WIMP mass, density, and capture rate. Above clear density and capture thresholds, annihilation heat puffs the young star into a cool, bloated state. That bloated state weakens the star's own disruptive radiation, letting gas keep falling in. Growth can then continue toward roughly one hundred thousand solar masses, a heavy seed indeed. Heavier WIMPs delay the effect, and masses below a few TeV work best in their grid.
arxiv-2510-00416:
Junhyeok Lee, Han Jang, and Kyu Sung Choi published this 2025 paper on Interactive-MEN-RT, a tool for outlining brain tumors before radiotherapy. Meningiomas must be traced precisely so radiation hits tumor and spares nearby healthy tissue. Automated models alone still stumble on these tumors' varied shapes. Interactive segmentation lets a clinician guide the model with quick inputs.

The tool accepts points, bounding boxes, lasso strokes, and freehand scribbles from the clinician. It was built specifically for meningioma planning rather than adapted from generic software. Evaluation used 500 contrast-enhanced MRI scans from the BraTS 2025 meningioma challenge. Overlap scores reached levels the authors describe as substantial improvements over rival methods. Strong results came even from minimal clinician input in many cases. The team argues disease-specific interactive tools fit clinical workflows better than one-size-fits-all segmenters.
arxiv-2510-00916:
Kozyrev and Krivonos, at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, construct new variants of superconformal mechanics in this 2025 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. Superconformal mechanics describes quantum systems with both supersymmetry and conformal symmetry, and it models the near-horizon physics of black holes. The supersymmetric Schwarzian theory hints at which fermionic fields such systems need. Following that hint, the authors add extra fermionic fields to reach maximal symmetry in two cases.

With four added fermions they build an N=3 system carrying the maximal OSp(3|2) superconformal symmetry. With eight, they build an N=4 system with D(1,2;alpha) symmetry, in a new variant where every bosonic subalgebra has a bosonic realization. Both systems contain so(3) currents whose parametrization is left free. That freedom lets the same construction describe different underlying geometries, widening the class of black hole microstate models it could serve.
arxiv-2510-01016:
Seyed Mahmoud, Renner, Khosravani, and Kalidindi calibrate a ductile damage model with sequential Bayesian inference in this 2025 arXiv paper, written for Acta Materialia. The GTN model predicts how metals accumulate voids and fail, but its parameters hide in small, localized features of the response. Specimen-level force-displacement curves dilute those signatures, so the authors add spatially resolved strain fields from digital image correlation. A two-step framework first builds a cheap emulator of the finite element simulator, then samples parameter posteriors with transitional Markov Chain Monte Carlo.

Principal component analysis compresses both data streams into low-dimensional features the sampler can handle. The surprise finding is order: feeding the force-displacement data first and the strain fields second gave sharply better parameter estimates. The reverse order produced broader, less consistent posteriors on the AA6111 aluminium case study. Multimodal assimilation improved identifiability of the damage parameters overall.
arxiv-2510-01116:
Parker, Chan, Zhang, and Ghobadi teach language models to reason step by step about time series in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many real tasks, from medical diagnosis to weather forecasting, need multi-step reasoning over sequences of numbers. Standard time series models cannot show such reasoning, and language models perform poorly on raw numerical streams. Their framework, called COUNTS, is the first to train language models for chain-of-thought time series analysis with reinforcement learning.

A vector-quantized autoencoder first converts each series into discrete tokens that join the model's vocabulary. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the representation, and group relative policy optimization then rewards explicit reasoning on verifiable problems. Across varied time series tasks, the authors report clear gains from the reasoning-driven training. They argue the approach opens complex temporal data to the same careful reasoning that models now apply to maths.
arxiv-2510-01816:
Chen and seven co-authors propose a noise-cutting trick for dark matter searches in this 2025 physics paper. Qubit sensors can register the faint touch of wave-like dark matter as a tiny excitation. Random background excitations mimic that signal and bury it. Earlier enhancement schemes entangled many sensors, but keeping that entanglement alive during data taking is hard.

Their protocol instead projects the sensors onto a collective state called the W state. Dark matter excites the sensors together, so its signal lands inside that collective state. Independent noise mostly excites other states, which the projection discards. The authors show the background can shrink by a factor equal to the sensor count. No entanglement must survive during the accumulation period itself. They also find a ceiling, since the shared state can hold only one excitation at a time.
arxiv-2510-02116:
Daras stabilizes recall control for huge entity-matching jobs in this 2025 paper. Spatial conflation pipelines must hit a recall target precisely across tens of millions of candidate pairs. Standard confidence-interval cuts overshoot the target by several points and swing wildly between runs. His framework replaces the single fragile threshold with a calibrated ensemble.

A bounding-box grid filter and sparse candidate layout first cut the pair count roughly a hundredfold. A small neural ranker, trained on a deterministic hash bootstrap, scores every remaining pair in one pass. Four threshold estimators then vote, weighted by inverse variance, across a stratified calibration set fused from nine subsamples. On two real cadastral datasets, with millions of pairs each, the ensemble hit its recall target within a small error. Redundant manual verifications fell compared with single-method calibration. The whole pipeline runs end to end on one TPU core.
arxiv-2510-02216:
Ye and Chen study how well diffusion transformers can fill gaps in time series data. Their 2025 statistics paper gives theory for a method often used without proof. Real records, from sensors to clinics, often lose values. Diffusion models now fill those gaps with strong results. Why they work, and how sure users can be, stayed unclear. The authors derive bounds on the data needed for accuracy. Their math rests on new approximation results for transformer score functions. They also build tight confidence regions around filled values.

Simulations backed the theory in practice. Results showed that gap patterns strongly shape accuracy. Evenly spread gaps proved easier than clustered ones. The team proposes a mixed masking training trick. The trick teaches the model many gap shapes at once. Users gain both filled values and honest error bars. That pairing supports safer decisions downstream.
arxiv-2510-02816:
Zhang and a large team present a cheaper way to check the reasoning of large language models. One wrong step can spoil the whole chain. Checking the full chain at once is costly and often vague. It rarely shows which step failed. The team's method is called NCV, short for node-wise consistency verification. It needs no extra training.

NCV splits a reasoning chain into linked nodes. Each node gets a simple yes-or-no consistency check. The checks pinpoint the first bad step with care. They also avoid long extra outputs from the model. On public test sets, NCV raised error-finding scores by clear margins over rivals. It used far fewer tokens than chain-based checkers at the same time. Ablation tests show that both the splitting and the checks matter. The method offers a practical path to more trustworthy model output.
arxiv-2510-02916:
Dellali and co-authors generate sound for silent videos. A good track must match both the event and its timing. Rain must sound like rain, and it must start on cue. Their model, SALSA-V, builds long audio tracks of any length. A masked diffusion objective sits at its center. Parts of the track can be hidden during training.

That masking teaches the model to fill gaps and extend audio. It also lets users guide the sound with reference clips. A shortcut loss speeds up generation a great deal. Fine samples emerge in as few as eight steps. No extra fine-tuning is needed for that speed. Tests beat prior top methods on alignment and sync. Human listeners confirmed the gains in a study. Sync held up even as clips grew long. The tool fits pro sound design as well as quick drafts.
arxiv-2510-03016:
Wu and co-authors train diffusion generators on labels that cannot be trusted. Conditional models need a label or caption for each sample. Real data sets carry noisy, vague, or partial labels. Wrong conditions teach the model the wrong matches. Their framework, DMIS, is the first systematic fix for diffusion training. It grows out of a likelihood view of the problem. The objective splits into two cooperating parts.

One part models the messy label distribution itself. The other part is a classifier built from the diffusion model. It infers the odds of each class for a given sample. A smarter sampling of time steps makes that classifier cheap. Trials covered image generation with flawed labels. Weakly supervised learning and noisy data condensation joined in. DMIS kept samples sharp and true to their class throughout. Dirty supervision is the norm in practice, not the exception.
arxiv-2510-03216:
Ahmed, Shaikh, and Mohy-ud-Din design a medical image segmenter light enough for modest hospital hardware. Big segmentation networks demand costly graphics cards and memory. Wave-GMS takes a generative, multi-scale approach instead. A small trainable encoder reads the scan at several resolutions. A frozen tiny variational autoencoder handles the mask side. A compact mapping model links image features to mask codes.

The whole system trains only about two and a half million parameters. Large batches fit on limited-memory cards with room to spare. No giant pretrained vision model needs loading at all. Four public datasets hosted the evaluation trials. Breast ultrasound, endoscopy tools, and skin lesions were among them. The model reached state-of-the-art accuracy on those sets. It also generalized across domains better than rivals. Two-dimensional scans are the current limit of the method.
arxiv-2510-03316:
Demilt, LaHaye, and Tenneson present a 2025 arXiv paper on foundation models that read satellite and Earth data. Such models turn raw sensor readings into compact summaries used for search and mapping tasks. Most are trained on one kind of sensor, then used on others as if sensors matched. The authors ask what happens inside the models when the sensor design changes. Different sensors capture different bands and detail levels, so the mismatch could matter a lot.

Their tests show that the inner summary space shifts strongly with sensor design. The same ground scene can land in quite different spots when seen by different instruments. That drift can quietly weaken search and matching tools built on the summaries. The authors frame the result as a warning for model builders and users alike. Future Earth models should train across sensors or at least report how sensor change bends their inner maps.
arxiv-2510-03716:
Katayama and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper studying hydrocarbon dust around active galactic nuclei using near infrared spectra from the AKARI satellite. Both aromatic and aliphatic dust survive in these galactic centers, and their origin is debated. The team fitted spectra and energy distributions for one hundred two active nuclei. They measured the aromatic and aliphatic feature strengths against each galaxy's infrared light and against the active nucleus's share of that light.

The aromatic share ran systematically lower in active nuclei than in star forming galaxies, where aliphatic features appeared in absorption. The aliphatic to aromatic ratio ran higher in active nuclei and climbed with nuclear activity. Aliphatic emission profiles skewed stronger at longer wavelengths than in star forming galaxies. The authors conclude dust types likely arise near the nucleus. Shattering of carbon grains by outflows could manufacture the aliphatic dust. Budgets for galaxy evolution models need that production channel.
arxiv-2510-03916:
Burgasser and a large team report this 2025 arXiv paper on a chemical surprise in the air of a cool brown dwarf. Brown dwarfs are too small to burn hydrogen like stars, and their atmospheres should hold the molecule phosphine. Earlier observations found far less phosphine than chemistry models predicted. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, the team examined the brown dwarf Wolf 1130C.

The telescope's spectra showed several clear absorption lines from phosphine near a wavelength of about four micrometers. The measured abundance was roughly a tenth of a part per million. That value matches out-of-equilibrium chemistry models that also fit Jupiter and Saturn. It is far higher than the depleted levels reported elsewhere. The authors suggest the dwarf's low heavy-element content may explain the difference. The result sharpens questions about how phosphorus chemistry varies across cold worlds.
arxiv-2510-04116:
Zhang, Wang, and Yao present this 2025 arXiv paper on letting a language model choose its own strategy for reasoning through a problem. Good reasoners monitor themselves: they decompose questions, reflect on shaky steps, and switch approaches when stuck. Earlier systems hard-coded those behaviors into fixed structures like chains or trees. Such skeletons cannot adapt to what a particular query needs.

The authors represent a reasoning skeleton as a directed acyclic graph. Their framework, AutoMR, borrows automated machine learning ideas to search that graph space. A dynamic sampling algorithm grows the skeleton alongside the unfolding reasoning, with minimal extra computation. Experiments on math question answering and general multiple-choice benchmarks beat earlier meta-reasoning methods broadly. Automatic strategy search could make model reasoning less brittle than prompting patterns.
arxiv-2510-04416:
Jonah Gannon and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on galaxies that seem to have failed. Some ultra diffuse galaxies look like the leftovers of galaxies that formed stars fast and then stopped early. No simulated galaxy had matched that story. The team searched the MAGNETICUM cosmology simulations for early galaxies that could grow into such faint systems.

The search found 443 candidate ancestors inside the simulation. The candidates stood out from two control groups in five clear ways. Their dark matter halos were flatter in the center, and their star bodies were more spread out. More of their gas sat in the outer halo, which helps gas escape and end star formation. Their stars held fewer heavy elements, matching what telescopes see in the faint galaxies. Their star formation rates were higher. The team proposes a test: such failed galaxies should grow more common in crowded regions.
arxiv-2510-04516:
Behrooz Farkiani, Fan Liu, and Patrick Crowley wrote this 2025 paper on how web clients should handle rate limits. Services cap how many requests a shared quota allows, and extra requests get rejected with an error. Clients then retry, but blind retries from many clients at once waste money and often fail again. Simple backoff rules make the pileup worse. The team designed client side methods that need no central coordinator.

Their two algorithms infer how congested the service is from minimal feedback signals. One works offline and can run inside a service worker in the browser. The other sharpens its timing with aggregated telemetry shared across clients. Emulations used real world traffic traces and synthetic loads with up to one hundred clients. The methods cut rate limit errors by up to about 97 percent against exponential backoff. Completion time rose only modestly in exchange for that drop.
arxiv-2510-04816:
Junhyung Ahn and Sanghack Lee wrote this 2025 paper on predicting whether a shopper will buy after clicking. Ad systems learn conversion rates from logs of views, clicks, and purchases. Conversions can only be observed for items users clicked. Clicked items are a biased slice of shown items. Models trained on that slice inherit bias. The authors ask a counterfactual question about an unclicked item: would this user have bought it if they had clicked?

 Their system, ESCIM, learns a causal model of how users move through views, clicks, and buys.It imagines the click happening and infers the conversion chance, which becomes training labels for unclicked items. A multi task model trains on real and generated data. Public benchmarks showed gains over rival methods. An online A B test at a service confirmed the lift in practice. The method held up on conversion data, which tests generalization.
arxiv-2510-05016:
Lucas Carrit Delgado Pinheiro and six co-authors put top AI models through an astronomy olympiad in this 2025 arXiv paper. The exam is the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics. It tests deep concepts, long derivations, and analysis of real data. Simple quiz benchmarks cannot measure skills like these.

Five leading models sat theory exams from 2022 to 2025. Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-5 averaged about 85 percent, a gold-medal level. Both ranked in the top two against roughly two to three hundred human contestants. Data analysis exams separated the field more, though GPT-5 still averaged near 89 percent there. Error analysis flagged geometry and spatial visualization as shared weak spots.
arxiv-2510-05116:
Bowen Xu argues that AI hallucination is not a bug to fix but a fact to accept in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models sometimes produce fluent text that is simply false. Engineers usually treat those fabrications as defects. Xu reframes them as a symptom of the generalization problem every learner faces.

The argument turns on two assumptions about the world. Under a closed world, training and test data match, and hallucinations can shrink. Under an open world, the environment is unbounded, and no finite experience covers what comes next. Xu classifies hallucinations into kinds that can be corrected and kinds that cannot. The conclusion urges designing systems that tolerate this structural feature.
arxiv-2510-05316:
James Bartusek and three co-authors build a public proof system for quantum computing in this 2025 arXiv paper. A zero-knowledge argument convinces a verifier while revealing nothing else. For quantum problems in the class QMA, proofs should also let an extractor recover the witness. Prior public systems needed a heavy obfuscated program as their setup.

Their system needs only a uniformly random string for setup, called transparent. Coset state authentication, adapted from recent work, sits at the heart of the construction. A new ZX verifier with strong completeness supports the extraction property. Security first rests on a heuristic use of a post-quantum obfuscator. They then replace the obfuscator with a hash function plus functional encryption, broadening the result.
arxiv-2510-05416:
Xin Gu and five co-authors sharpen private machine learning by correlating its noise across training steps in this 2025 arXiv paper. Differentially private SGD protects training data, but it lags ordinary training in accuracy. Correlating the injected noise lets later steps cancel earlier noise. The authors ask what should guide that correlation.

Their method, NoiseCurve, uses model curvature estimated from public unlabeled data. Curvature information shapes better cross-iteration noise correlations than prior schemes. Across datasets, models, and privacy budgets, accuracy rose consistently over DP-SGD and DP-BandMF. Gains ran about 1 to 4 percentage points at the same privacy cost. Even imperfect curvature from a different public dataset helped, keeping the method practical.
arxiv-2510-05716:
Krabbe extends a convergence result for random recurrence equations used in time series. Such equations drive models like GARCH, a workhorse for volatility in finance. Straumann and Mikosch proved that restarted solutions converge to the stationary one. Their proof assumed the state space was a full Banach space.

Many applications live only on a complete subspace of such a space instead. Krabbe's 2025 note gives slightly different conditions for that weaker setting. Under them, any restarted solution still converges almost surely at an exponential rate. The argument closely follows the original proof, with care at the subspace steps. Bougerol's earlier work supplied the stationary solution's existence and uniqueness. The result supports quasi-maximum-likelihood estimation in conditionally heteroscedastic models. Those models include the GARCH family used across econometrics. Small condition changes can matter when theorems move to leaner spaces.
arxiv-2510-06016:
Gao and Shen revisit the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. In that effect, a charged particle reacts to a magnetic flux even where no field touches its path. The authors study a single Dirac electron confined in a cylindrical cavity around the flux.

They compare two descriptions of the electron, one treating it as a particle and one as a current-carrying field. In the particle picture, only the lowest angular momentum mode keeps a coupling energy as the flux core shrinks, and all higher modes fade away. In the field picture, that same lowest result appears, but higher modes gain an energy shift that grows in even steps with angular momentum. The work recasts a famous nonlocal puzzle as a local, mode-by-mode energy law.
arxiv-2510-07516:
Ananto, Fatin, Ali, and Parvez present CompassLLM, a team of language model agents that answers which route people actually take between two places. Their 2025 paper addresses the popular path query over historical trajectory data. Traditional solvers need training and retuning whenever data updates arrive. CompassLLM splits the job into two stages. In the search stage, agents find the most frequented existing path. When no recorded path exists, a common dead end in sparse data, the generate stage synthesizes a plausible novel route instead of giving up.

Experiments on real and synthetic trajectory sets show superior accuracy in the search stage. Generation stayed competitive with dedicated methods while the whole system remained cost-effective. Performance was particularly strong when historical data ran thin. The authors concede the agents can still propose suboptimal or invalid paths, and model randomness threatens consistency.
arxiv-2510-07716:
Choromanski, Dubey, Sehanobish, and Reid wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on fast graph computation. Graphs model fraud, communities, recommendations, and biology. Kernel functions measure how alike two nodes are, but exact kernels are expensive on big graphs. Graph random features estimate kernels by sampling random walks. The older method struggles with distant node pairs and wastes time on long walks.

The authors refine the method into GRFs++, with two main upgrades. A walk-stitching trick joins several short walks instead of sampling one long walk. Short walks run in parallel and combine through matrix multiplication. The method also generalizes how walk lengths are chosen, which sharpens accuracy at no extra cost. Theory shows the estimates stay unbiased, with concentration guarantees. Experiments across many graph datasets matched the claims. Faster kernels could widen the reach of graph learning in production systems.
arxiv-2510-07816:
Zhang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 nuclear physics paper on the neutron skin of atomic nuclei. In heavy nuclei, neutrons extend slightly farther out than protons. The size of that difference, the neutron skin thickness, is hard to pin down. It matters far beyond the nucleus, since the same physics shapes neutron stars. The authors propose measuring it with extreme shapes of heavy-ion collisions rather than with electron scattering.

One signal counts spectator neutrons when two nuclei collide head-on. Another compares neutrons and protons among participants in glancing collisions. Simulations show both signals respond sensitively to skin thickness in lead-208 and calcium-48. The authors also propose colliding calcium-48 against calcium-40 directly. The forward-backward asymmetry in that pairing isolates the calcium-48 skin especially well. Detectors at RHIC and the LHC can count the needed neutrons, giving experiments an independent handle on a stubborn quantity.
arxiv-2510-08016:
Pawlak, Dubiński, Marczak, and Twardowski wrote this 2025 security paper rethinking backdoor attacks on merged models. Model merging combines fine-tuned models by weight arithmetic, A single poisoned contributor can hide a trigger that controls the merged model's output. The authors isolate the attack itself as a vector. They subtract a clean fine-tuned model's weights from a backdoored twin's weights.

The difference, the Backdoor Vector, measures how attacks resemble each other and how they transfer. Merging several such vectors sparsely produced a stronger combined attack than prior methods. The analysis also exposed the root weakness. Models carry inherent triggers that exploit flaws already present in the base model. Their defense subtracts an injected vector to cancel unknown backdoors, with no assumptions about the attack. It stayed lightweight and general. The framework gives merging pipelines a common language for attack and defense.
arxiv-2510-08216:
Gómez-Ortiz, Bastogne, He, and Ghosez wrote this 2025 condensed matter paper showing that two different orders in an artificial superlattice dictate each other's patterns. The stack alternates lead titanate, hosting polar textures like vortices and skyrmions, with strontium titanate, whose oxygen octahedra rotate. Earlier work mostly ignored the rotations. Through second-principles simulations, the authors found a one-to-one relationship between each polar topology and a specific rotation pattern next door.

The coupling is strain-mediated and fully reciprocal. Freezing the rotations in place is enough to force the associated polar state to appear. Conversely, each polar texture imprints its rotation pattern next door. That overturns the picture of the dielectric layer as a passive spacer. It is an active partner shaping the polarization texture mechanically. The finding suggests a new control knob: engineer the rotations, and the polar texture follows.
arxiv-2510-08816:
Burred and Cella turn sound itself into something musicians can take apart and rebuild, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their tool rests on autoencoders, networks that compress a sound into parts and then rebuild it, with one twist. Every weight inside must stay at zero or above. That rule keeps each part readable as a sound ingredient, with a spectral shape and a time envelope that can be played on its own.

Stacking several layers gives a ladder of detail, from whole note envelopes down to fine texture. The authors add fresh ways to play with the parts. Sounds can borrow components across layers, be pulled apart level by level, or be randomized in ways that steer tone color and event density. Through pictures and rebuilt examples, they show the system working as an open-ended editor for object-based sound design.
arxiv-2510-09016:
Du and a large team scale up singing voice synthesis, software that makes a computer sing written lyrics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems sound expressive but starve for training data, since studio singing is costly to record. The team's pipeline starts small: professional singers record fixed melodies, and language models write varied lyrics for them. Models trained per melody then manufacture the bulk of the data, over five hundred hours of Chinese singing.

On that corpus they train DiTSinger, built on a diffusion transformer, a design that gradually cleans noise into audio.
