They scale it in depth, width, and resolution, with modern positional and normalization tweaks for fidelity. A further mechanism aligns sounds to syllables without the usual hand-labeled timing data, by confining each syllable's attention to its character's span. Experiments confirm the approach delivers scalable, high-fidelity singing that tolerates messy alignment.
arxiv-2510-09316:
Yuanming Zhang, Yan Lin, Arijit Khan, and Huaiyu Wan survey prompt datasets for large language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. A prompt is the text a user feeds a model, and collections of prompts now drive research and product testing. The team catalogues one hundred twenty-nine public datasets holding more than six hundred seventy million prompts in total.

They organise the catalogue into one shared taxonomy and study seven datasets in depth. Their analysis finds word, grammar, and meaning patterns that set prompts apart from ordinary text. A compact set of sixty-three language features, cheap to compute, reached over ninety percent of the sorting quality of heavy GPU embeddings while nearly halving delay. Routing prompts to the right dataset worked far above chance, and some structural features tracked answer quality even after prompt length was accounted for.
arxiv-2510-09416:
Abigail Hayes, Tobias Schumacher, and Markus Strohmaier ask what temporal graph learning models actually learn, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Temporal graphs record links that appear over time, such as messages or transactions, and learning models predict future links from them. Benchmarks report strong scores, yet doubts have grown about evaluation habits and about how well simple heuristics compete.

The team tests eight models on eight basic characteristics of temporal graphs. The traits cover link density, recency effects, and homophily, the tendency of similar nodes to connect. Using both synthetic and real datasets, they check how faithfully each model captures each trait. The picture is mixed: models reproduce some characteristics well and fail on others. The authors argue the gaps matter for practice, and they call for evaluations that probe interpretation, not just leaderboard scores.
arxiv-2510-09616:
Mohammadhossein Homaei, Mehran Tarif, Mar Avila, Pablo Garcia Rodriguez, and Andres Caro propose causal digital twins for guarding water systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Industrial control systems for water distribution and treatment face attacks that exploit both network and physical weaknesses. Detectors based on correlation alone raise many false alarms and explain root causes poorly.

Their framework couples a digital twin, a live simulation of the plant, with causal inference about causes rather than correlations. It supports pattern detection, predicting responses to interventions, and counterfactual analysis of attacks that did not happen. On the SWaT, WADI, and HAI water datasets, the system scored above zero point nine in detection quality on all three. It cut false positives by seventy-four percent and reached about seventy-eight percent root cause accuracy. Counterfactual defences reduced attack success by about seventy-three percent, at a latency of a few milliseconds.
arxiv-2510-10416:
Kannon Hossain, Roger Sidje, and Fahad Mostafa compare ways to test which inputs matter most in models of living chemistry in this 2025 arXiv paper. These stochastic models track random chemical reactions, such as those inside cells. Simulating them exactly is usually infeasible because the number of possible states explodes. The team instead works with moment-based equations, a shortcut that tracks averages and spreads rather than every single state.

Using those moment-based equations, they run both local and global sensitivity analyses. A local analysis nudges one input slightly near a chosen setting, while a global analysis sweeps inputs across wide ranges. Their numerical tests show how changes in each input parameter move the model's output. This lets them identify the key parameters that strongly shape the model's dynamics. The approach gives biochemists a practical way to see which reaction rates deserve the closest measurement and control.
arxiv-2510-10516:
Kanishkha Jaisankar and three co-authors combine spiking neural networks with deep reinforcement learning to control robots, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spiking networks mimic the brain's event driven style of computing and promise low energy use. Motor control for complex robots, though, demands both efficiency and strong performance in continuous, high dimensional tasks. Their framework centers on a Population-coded Spiking Actor Network, called PopSAN, which encodes observations as activity across groups of neurons.

PopSAN learns its policy through gradient based updates, drawing on the robust optimization methods of deep reinforcement learning. The team evaluated the system in the Isaac Gym simulator on PixMC, a benchmark of hard motor control tasks. Their results showed clear gains in energy efficiency and lower latency, meaning faster responses, alongside robust performance in continuous action spaces. They present it as a promising direction for robots on tight power budgets.
arxiv-2510-10616:
Matan Solomon, Ofra Amir, and Omer Ben-Porat ask how users can tell whether an AI update actually helped, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning agents are often revised using human feedback, but updates can be unreliable: misspecified rewards, conflicting preferences, or scarce data may leave a policy unchanged or worse. Policies are hard to inspect directly, so users must judge updates from behavior. The team frames update assessment as a design problem for intelligent interfaces.

In a controlled study, participants gave feedback to an agent in a gridworld, then compared its original and updated policies. The team tested four ways of showing updates, from no demonstration to salient contrast demonstrations that highlight informative differences. Salient contrast displays significantly improved participants' ability to detect when updates helped or harmed. They also reduced the bias toward assuming feedback always helps, and supported better trust calibration across settings.
arxiv-2510-11416:
Open quantum systems, systems leaking information into their environment, evolve under the Lindblad master equation, often on infinite-dimensional state spaces that no computer can hold exactly. Rémi Robin and Pierre Rouchon analyze a classical numerical method for that equation in this 2025 arXiv mathematical physics paper. The method is a Galerkin approximation: project the problem onto a growing sequence of finite-dimensional spaces and solve there.

Using a priori estimates, bounds derived before computing anything, the authors prove the discretized solutions converge to the exact solution. They derive explicit rates for that convergence. Rates matter because they tell a user how large the finite-dimensional truncation must be for a target accuracy. The authors show the method works through examples motivated by autonomous quantum error correction, where a quantum device fixes its own errors continuously without outside intervention.
arxiv-2510-11516:
AI code assistants now sit inside the editor, but watching how programmers use them takes more than counting accepted suggestions. Jeena Javahar and co-authors study developers working with Amazon's CodeWhisperer in this 2025 arXiv human-computer interaction paper. They ran two user studies with ten participants each: the first to learn which interactions mattered, the second to capture fine-grained behavior with a telemetry plugin.

Their mixed-methods analysis identified four recurring behavioral patterns. Programmers refined generated code incrementally in small steps. They steered the tool explicitly by writing natural language comments as instructions. They used suggestions as a baseline structure to build on rather than as finished code. And they integrated the tool with external sources such as documentation and web search. The study offers a clear picture of how a code-generation assistant fits into real problem solving, .
arxiv-2510-11616:
Statistical arbitrage trades one stock against a mimicking portfolio of similar stocks, profiting when their prices briefly diverge and reconverge. Elliot L. Epstein, Rose Wang, Jaewon Choi, and Markus Pelger rebuild that pipeline as a single learning problem in this 2025 arXiv quantitative finance paper. Their Attention Factors are latent factors learned from firm characteristic embeddings, designed to be most useful for arbitrage.

A sequence model reads time-series signals from the residual portfolios of those factors, and factors, signals, and the trading policy are estimated jointly to maximize risk-adjusted performance after trading costs. On the largest United States equities over twenty-four years, the model achieved an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio above four before costs, and a Sharpe ratio of 2.3 net of transaction costs. Weak factors, usually discarded as noise, proved important for arbitrage.
arxiv-2510-11816:
Alfonso Garcia-Soto and Jeremi Niedziela propose turning the LHC's two big general-purpose detectors into neutrino observatories. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies SHIFT, a proposed gas target to be installed inside the LHC tunnel. Protons striking the gas would create neutrinos aimed at the CMS and ATLAS detectors nearby. Dedicated experiments have caught LHC neutrinos before, but never these flagship detectors themselves.

The authors simulate the full chain: proton-gas collisions, hadron travel, and neutrino interactions inside the detectors. With just one percent of the planned Run-4 data, CMS and ATLAS would each record on the order of ten thousand muon-neutrino interactions. About a thousand electron-neutrino interactions would join them, with energies from twenty giga-electronvolts up to one tera-electronvolt. The setup also probes a forward angular range no current LHC detector covers. If built, SHIFT would give atmospheric neutrino experiments a valuable laboratory cross-check.
arxiv-2510-11916:
Silvia Gagliardini and six colleagues forecast two signals from exploding stars wrapped in their own shed gas. Massive stars often dump material months to years before collapsing, forming a dense circumstellar medium. When the supernova blast hits that shell, the collision can glow in ultraviolet light for a long time and may also produce neutrinos. Their paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal and posted on arXiv in 2025, models this shock interaction.

The team first estimates how far away future ultraviolet missions, notably ULTRASAT, could detect such events, and how often. Bright recent supernovae such as SN 2023ixf underline why ultraviolet coverage matters. They then estimate the neutrino output and the rates expected at the IceCube and KM3NeT detectors. Fast blue optical transients may be extreme versions of the same interaction. The study closes by weighing multi-messenger prospects.
arxiv-2510-12116:
Bajian Xiang, Shuaijiang Zhao, Tingwei Guo, and Wei Zou ask why speech models take in less than they read. Large speech language models converse well end-to-end, yet trail pipeline systems on meaning benchmarks. Their 2025 arXiv paper names the deficit the modality gap: after speech-text alignment training, speech inputs fall behind text inputs by more than alignment alone explains.

A close look splits the gap into two shapes. In deeper layers, speech and text embeddings align more and more in direction, cosine likeness rising, while diverging in magnitude, Euclidean distance growing. That likeness strongly predicts the gap's size. At token level, a self-formed alignment pattern emerges, which the authors score with an Alignment Path Score that tracks the gap even more closely. Armed with that finding, they step in on key tokens with angle projection and length normalization, raising correctness for speech inputs.
arxiv-2510-12316:
Damo, Cabrio, and Villata generate fact based counter-speech against hate speech using retrieval augmented generation, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Counter-speech answers harmful content directly, and experts in fact checking and hate speech work rely on it. Pure language model generation can be unreliable and incoherent, while human expert writing does not scale.

Their framework treats counter-speech as knowledge based generation, grounding replies in retrieved documents for eight target groups named in the hate speech literature. They built a knowledge base of nearly thirty three thousand texts from the United Nations Digital Library, EUR-Lex, plus the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights. Using the MultiTarget CONAN dataset, they assessed output quality with standard metrics and human evaluation. The framework outperformed standard language model baselines and a competitive approach on both assessments. The authors present the system and its knowledge base as a foundation for trustworthy counter-speech research.
arxiv-2510-12416:
Ortiz and Rodrigo build a daily dataset linking news based risk measures to sovereign borrowing costs across forty two countries, in a 2025 arXiv economics paper. Their panel combines market data with measures of geopolitical risk, economic policy uncertainty, political sentiment, and trade policy uncertainty, for emerging and rich markets alike. Such daily measures may help forecast sovereign risk beyond standard drivers.

Using credit default swap spreads as the measure of sovereign risk, they race forecast models against each other. Adding the news based measures greatly improved forecast accuracy, and nonlinear machine learning methods, above all random forests, delivered the largest gains. World financial factors remain the top drivers of sovereign risk. Geopolitical risk and policy uncertainty also matter, and their effects amplify through nonlinear links to global conditions. Exposure to shocks differed sharply by region and asset class, with some emerging markets hit hardest.
arxiv-2510-12516:
Ruiz, Peng, Plank, and Schwemmer test whether spending extra computation at answer time helps language models handle tasks where annotators legitimately disagree, in a 2025 arXiv paper from the LeWiDi shared task. Test time scaling techniques, which sample or combine multiple outputs, have succeeded in mathematics and coding, where answers are verifiably right. Annotation disagreement tasks have no single correct answer, so transfer is uncertain.

The team tried three methods: model averaging, majority voting, and a best of N sampling approach that picks the strongest of many candidate answers. The two benchmark methods improved model performance consistently across the LeWiDi tasks. Best of N did not, failing to transfer from mathematics to this setting. The authors analyze why the gap arises, suggesting that without a reliable way to judge which sample is best, extra sampling cannot pick better answers. The paper tempers enthusiasm for scaling test time compute into subjective tasks.
arxiv-2510-13016:
Hannan and colleagues define a new video understanding task and benchmark in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spatio-temporal video action grounding asks a model to find every object matching a spoken description of an action, track it through the video, and mark when the action happens. Existing work handles coarse action recognition or generic tracking, but not this joint, multi-instance challenge.

Their benchmark, SVAG-Bench, contains several hundred videos with close to twenty thousand annotated records spanning more than nine hundred distinct verbs across diverse real-world scenes. They also built SVAGFormer, a baseline adapting leading vision-language models to the joint task, and SVAGEval, a standardized scoring toolkit. Existing models performed poorly, especially in dense or complex scenes, which the authors take as evidence that fine-grained reasoning about object-action interactions in long videos needs substantial improvement.
arxiv-2510-13216:
Kronthaler and Held extend Edgington's method for meta-analysis to prediction in this 2025 arXiv statistics paper, the second part of a series. Meta-analysis pools results across studies, but when true effects vary a lot between studies, inference about the average effect is not enough. Predictive distributions describe what a future study might find, on the plain effect scale.

The authors construct them by combining confidence distributions from Edgington's p-value combination method with a generalized heterogeneity statistic. Simulations showed ninety-five percent prediction intervals usually hitting their nominal coverage when more than three studies existed. They also matched the skewness in effect estimates for samples of twenty or fewer studies. Formulations ignoring uncertainty in the heterogeneity estimate usually failed to reach correct coverage, showing why the adjustment matters.
arxiv-2510-13316:
Abdullahu and Grabner test whether a leading multimodal model finds images interesting for the same reasons humans do in this 2025 arXiv paper. Visual interestingness, whatever captures and holds attention, shapes what people consume online, yet it is deeply subjective. The authors ask how much of that concept a large multimodal model trained on web-scale image and text data has internalized.

Comparing GPT-4o's judgments against human assessments, they found partial alignment, and the model already captured the concept better than state-of-the-art specialized methods. That agreement was consistent enough to label image pairs by their commonly judged interestingness at scale. Those labels became training data to distill the model's knowledge into a learning-to-rank model, transferring the ability into a smaller dedicated system. The authors frame the results as a step toward understanding human interest itself.
arxiv-2510-13416:
Majumdar studies how the placement of active forces shapes the folding of elastic networks. This 2025 arXiv paper uses computer simulations of bead-spring networks, grids of masses joined by springs. Randomly placed pulling or pushing force pairs were already known to cause sharp collapse. Majumdar asks what changes when those forces cluster in patterns instead.

He compares a central patch pattern, a rim band pattern, and a uniform spread of forces. With clustered forces, the network shrinks only partly, even under strong forcing. This spatial rearrangement alone makes the network far more stable mechanically. The rim pattern is most stable at first, but the central patch wins at higher forces. Past a threshold force, deformation turns permanent through crease formation. That threshold shifts with the pattern and drops for clustered layouts. Folding paths also proved highly sensitive to missing bonds in the network.
arxiv-2510-13516:
Feng and Tang develop preconditioned Riemannian gradient methods that minimize the Gross-Pitaevskii energy. Their 2025 arXiv paper computes ground states of rotating Bose-Einstein condensates, clouds of ultra-cold atoms. The energy sits on a curved constraint space, so ordinary gradient methods do not apply directly. Preconditioning reshapes the problem so descent steps move more efficiently.

Their unified framework covers all existing projected Sobolev gradient methods as special cases. For mild assumptions on the preconditioner, they prove energy decrease and global convergence. The local rate is harder, because the energy is unchanged by phase shifts and rotations. Assuming a Morse-Bott structure, they derive a sharp inequality that pins down the local rate. Spectral analysis then yields an optimal preconditioner with the best possible local rate. Tests on rapidly rotating condensates confirm the theory against rival preconditioners.
arxiv-2510-13816:
Walters and co-authors release GQVis, a dataset pairing questions about genomics data with the visualizations that answer them. Their 2025 arXiv paper aims to give AI models a training foundation for genomics graphics. General models handle ordinary statistical plots but stumble on genomics' specialized displays. Researchers need charts that link several views and explain their own design.

The generation framework expands templates using real data from three repositories: 4DN, ENCODE, and Chromoscope. Each item joins a natural question to a chart specification, caption, alt-text, and design justification. Linked follow-up queries come as pairs and longer chains, mimicking real exploration. The release holds 1.14 million single-query items alongside hundreds of thousands of pairs and chains for linked analysis, the team reports. Data and generation code are public for anyone training genomics assistants. The dataset targets a future where plain questions summon the right genome browser view.
arxiv-2510-13916:
Li and co-authors turn Wikipedia text about the chemical elements into number vectors for forecasting unmeasured element traits. Their 2025 arXiv paper, Element2Vec, serves materials design, where many traits resist direct measurement. Only 118 elements exist, so trait data is sparse. Language models offer knowledge, yet make facts up and hide their logic.

From each element's parsed Wikipedia page, the model builds two kinds of vector. A single global vector sums the element up overall for general use. Local vectors instead highlight given traits tied to specific properties. A test-time training method based on self-attention then corrects plain regression errors at use time. The design copes with the clash between plain wiki prose and expert science text. Two data pains drive it: tiny sample counts and patchy trait records. The authors hope text-grounded element vectors will speed AI-driven materials discovery.
arxiv-2510-14016:
Paul Mansanarez, Guillaume Poly, and Yvik Swan sharpen the mathematics of extreme values using a variant of Stein's method, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Extreme value theory predicts that normalized maxima, the largest observations in growing samples, follow one of a few limit laws; the Fréchet law covers heavy-tailed data. Knowing the limit is not enough for practice, since users need to know how close the approximation is at finite sample sizes.

Their version of Stein's method, a technique for bounding distances between probability distributions, compares distributions through ratios of reverse hazard rates, which stay manageable even when density derivatives are not. They bound three standard distance measures on the real line. For extremes, the new discrepancy measures closeness to the Fréchet law through how regularly the underlying distribution's tail varies. They illustrate the approach with explicit computations for maxima of Pareto, Cauchy, and Burr distributions.
arxiv-2510-14416:
Hrishikesh Chakrabarty and Daniele Malafarina propose a single mechanism behind both cosmic inflation, the early universe's explosive expansion, and today's dark energy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their vehicle is the Markov-Mukhanov modification of general relativity's action, in which matter couples to gravity through a scalar function depending only on the matter's energy density.

Assuming the coupling function encodes ultraviolet corrections to standard cosmology, the authors determine its form. That form lets the dark energy component behave dynamically and double as the inflaton field driving early expansion. One field thus plays both roles at opposite ends of cosmic history. Inflation within this model prefers a dark energy equation of state close to, but not exactly, the cosmological-constant value, matching the preference seen in the latest DESI survey data. The authors present the construction as an economical unification of the universe's two accelerated eras.
arxiv-2510-14516:
Ali Kashefi and Tapan Mukerji predict the permeability of porous rock from images using Vision Mamba, a vision model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Permeability, how easily fluid flows through a porous material, governs groundwater and reservoir engineering. Computing it from three-dimensional scans by simulation is slow. These help, but transformer models scale quadratically with image resolution while convolutional networks carry many parameters.

Vision Mamba scales linearly with resolution and needs fewer parameters, making it suited for volumetric data. The authors introduce a Mamba-backed network for predicting it for three-dimensional porous media, and compare it against vision transformer and convolutional baselines across aspects of the task. A study isolates the contribution of the parts. They report the efficiency advantages hold in practice for this task and release the source code. The framework could slot into vision models where Mamba replaces the transformer backbone.
arxiv-2510-14616:
Ying, Li, Qu, and many collaborators ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether reward models can judge writing quality when there is no right answer. Reward models guide language model training by scoring outputs. They shine on tasks with objective errors to catch. The authors built a benchmark of subjective preference, where paired texts are matched for correctness, factual accuracy, and length, so only taste separates them.

The benchmark holds 1,800 human-annotated pairs across eight creative writing genres, in English and Chinese. Standard sequence-based reward models scored only 52.7 percent accuracy on it, barely above chance, and language model judges acting alone scored 53.9 percent in the same tests. Generative reward models that write out reasoning chains reached 81.8 percent, a far stronger result. Scores also swung widely by genre, and bigger models did no better than smaller ones. The authors conclude that current training mostly teaches error detection, not subjective quality.
arxiv-2510-14716:
Lorenzin and Zanasi build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a bridge between discrete and continuous probability inside category theory. Researchers increasingly describe probabilistic programs with string diagrams and algebraic rules. Finite and Gaussian processes are well understood this way. Richer continuous probability resists, because infinite behavior is hard to capture with finite algebraic means.

Their construction adjoins infinite tensor products to a category, letting endless repetition be treated as one object. Applied to FinStoch, the setting of finite sets and stochastic matrices, it yields locally constant Markov kernels. Its objects are finite sets plus the Cantor space, the space of infinite binary sequences. Any probability measure on the real numbers can be reasoned about inside it. The authors also show how to lift known axiom systems through the method, obtaining an axiom-based presentation of continuous probability over countable powers of a two-element set.
arxiv-2510-14916:
Bělík, Chan, and Narayan make a classic compression theorem practical, in a 2025 arXiv paper, for enormous numerical integration rules. Many applications approximate an integral by a set of weighted points, a quadrature rule, wanting positive weights with certain moments preserved. Carathéodory's theorem guarantees a smaller rule with the same moments exists, but naive pruning algorithms need storage growing with the original rule's size, sometimes gigantic.

The authors give a streaming procedure for this Carathéodory-Steinitz pruning. It is built on Givens rotations and on-demand storage of arrays. It prunes very large rules while its memory depends only on the dimension of the function space, not on the original rule's size. That beats the naive method's quadratic runtime and linear storage. They also prove stability: small changes to the input measure, measured in total variation, cannot blow up the pruned rule's quality.
arxiv-2510-15116:
Sarod Yatawatta explores whether radio telescopes built for imaging the sky can also pinpoint where a signal comes from, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Direction of arrival estimation normally needs antenna arrays laid out precisely for one frequency band. Interferometric arrays instead spread antennas to sample data for sharp sky images, with irregular geometry and wide frequency coverage that make direct estimation impractical.

Yatawatta's method skips imaging entirely and works from only a subset of one array's data, using polarization, the orientation of the radio waves, as its clue. Using just a fraction of the collected data keeps the cost low and lets directions be estimated early, before full processing finishes. That suits fleeting transient sources and signals that appear only briefly. The approach also fits naturally after online interference cleanup, giving a quick location for detected interference.
arxiv-2510-15316:
Ashwini Kannan and five colleagues at IIT Madras, IBM, and Northeastern use quantum computing to predict how small proteins fold, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A protein's chain of amino acids folds into a shape that decides what it can do, and misfolding is tied to diseases like Alzheimer's. Mapping the energy landscape of folding is the key step, since the true shape sits at an energy low point.

Their encoding places the chain on a face-centered cubic lattice, a packing that mimics real protein geometry well. The energy score counts hydrophobic collapse, where water-shy parts tuck inward, plus van der Waals and electrostatic forces through a standard potential. A hybrid quantum-classical solver, the variational quantum eigensolver, searched for the lowest-energy folds on IBM's 133-qubit machine. The predicted shapes were checked against experimental structures and against classical methods such as simulated annealing and molecular dynamics.
arxiv-2510-15516:
Giulia Lanzillotta and four colleagues at ETH Zürich find a neglected variable in knowledge distillation, the technique of training a small student model from a large teacher. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that past explanations of why distillation works focus on model size and generalization. Nobody had systematically varied the third factor, the size of the training dataset.

Across many datasets, tasks, and architectures, their experiments show the benefit of distillation not only persists in low-data regimes but grows stronger there. They name this the data efficiency of distillation. Armed with that lens, they retest the leading theories of how distillation works. The results disprove the idea that distillation is merely label smoothing, a kind of softened answer key. They instead support the dark knowledge hypothesis, which credits the teacher's graded opinions about wrong answers.
arxiv-2510-15816:
Chen-Wei Wang and a large collaboration present BREAKFAST in a 2025 paper. It is a framework for running gamma-ray burst monitors as one fleet. Several monitors are now in operation. Teams have begun running them jointly to gain efficiency. The GECAM, HXMT, and SVOM partnership is a proven example. But joint duty burdens the human Burst Advocates. They vet each alert by hand. Trigger counts rise under joint work. Advocates also switch constantly between incompatible mission systems.

BREAKFAST gives joint duty scheduling across monitors. It also gives follow-up guidance. Alert handling becomes standard across instruments. The authors offer it as shared infrastructure. Other constellations can copy the collaboration model. They need not rebuild the operational tooling each time.
arxiv-2510-16116:
Seiji Fujimoto and thirty-nine co-authors map where heavy elements sit inside eighteen normal galaxies from the first billion years of cosmic time. The maps come from the Webb telescope's NIRSpec tool, which takes a spectrum at each point across a galaxy's face. The work sits inside the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST survey of early galaxies.

The team first had to clean the raw data, fixing stray light, stripes, and position errors. Then they read the glow of hot gas in each small region. Galaxy centers show dense, dusty gas and quick bursts of star birth, fed by fresh gas falling in. Yet metal levels stay nearly flat from center to edge, a sign that flows and mergers mix the gas well. Star birth and metal content also track each other more tightly than in galaxies today.
arxiv-2510-16416:
Xiaojun Guo leads ten co-authors in a 2025 study on teaching image-and-text models to use what they see. Such models often lean on word habits and skip the image. Training by trial and reward could fix this, but good rewards are scarce. Their fix, SSL4RL, turns self-teaching tasks into rewards. One such task is to guess how an image was turned.

These tasks give dense, sure scores with no human labels at all. Tests show clear gains on tasks based on sight and on mixed tasks. The team also maps which traits make the trick work best. The same idea gave gains on graph data too. It points to a cheap way to train models well.
arxiv-2510-17316:
Rare decays of kaons, short lived particles made in accelerators, carry clues about the basic forces of nature. Véronique Bernard, together with three co-authors, revisits two such decays in which a kaon turns into a pion plus a pair of lighter particles. Two unknown functions describe these decays, and past work left even the sign of one of them unsettled.

Bernard and her co-authors use the general rules that well behaved physical functions must obey, plus fresh results on kaons decaying into three pions. With only two free numbers left, their formulas reproduce the measured pattern well and fix the sign of the main function without doubt. They also show how one unknown piece of a three pion decay could be pinned down.
arxiv-2510-17716:
Suqiang Ma and nine co-authors study clumps of blood cells that travel through the body. These clusters mix red cells, white cells, and platelets. Doctors link them to clotting, infection, and swelling in tissues. The team works with flow cytometry images, which pair bright views with glowing stains.

Their two-step method first sorts images into cluster and non-cluster groups. It uses a tuned YOLOv11 model, a fast object-spotting network. Next it matches cluster outlines to the stain channels to name each cell type. Tests passed ninety-five percent accuracy on both sorting tasks. The tool may later help study immune and tumor clusters too.
arxiv-2510-17916:
Michael James McCulloch, writing as sole author, presents a working system built on the free energy idea of self-organizing life. The principle says such systems must keep a certain energy-like measure low to persist. Turning that claim into code has been the hard part, and this paper offers a route.

Credit for learning is split three ways: across space, across time, and across structure. A field map guesses which links matter most, and the author reports it tracks true values closely. The system kept most skill after clashes, healed after heavy damage, and learned control tasks with few tries.
arxiv-2510-18016:
Prateek Gothwal, Deeptimaan Banerjee, and Ashis Kumer Biswas judge student engagement from class videos using both face and scene. Online lessons need such feedback to improve outcomes and tailor teaching. Their ViBED-Net reads facial crops and full frames side by side, pulling features with a strong image network.

Two ways of tracking change over time are compared, memory cells and transformer encoders. Extra training data for rare engagement levels helps balance the scores. The memory-cell version led the tested variants on a large e-learning benchmark. Teachers and platform designers get a concrete design for reading attention without asking students directly.
arxiv-2510-18116:
Nahid Binandeh Dehaghani, Rafal Wisniewski, and A Pedro Aguiar solve steering problems for nonlinear systems with help from quantum routines. The classical frame is sequential quadratic programming with a barrier for the constraints. A quantum subroutine handles the hard Schur complement step through block encoding and singular value tools.

The authors bound total time and track how quantum errors shift the outcome. The method settles near the stationary point, with error tied to the barrier setting and solver accuracy. Cost grows very slowly with system size in their analysis. Control engineers get a careful case for quantum help inside a trusted classical loop.
arxiv-2510-18216:
Hua Sun, with Huixiang Chen and Yinhuo Zhang, examines special algebras in a 2025 paper on pure mathematics. The objects are Drinfeld doubles, meaning doubled versions of certain algebras that combine two related structures. Here the starting algebras are pointed rank one Hopf algebras, a narrow family with simple building blocks.

The authors sort all small building-block modules, called indecomposable modules, into a complete list up to sameness. They also spell out Auslander-Reiten sequences, which are standard patterns that link those building blocks together. Their work shows the doubled algebra has tame representation type, meaning its building blocks stay orderly and classifiable. Algebra researchers get a full map of this case.
arxiv-2510-18416:
Pengfei Cai and his eight co-authors introduce SegTune, a system for generating songs with control over each section of the music. Most song generators take one overall prompt, so users cannot ask for a quiet verse and a loud chorus in any detailed way. SegTune accepts separate descriptions for each segment, spreads each description across its time window, and still applies a global prompt to hold the whole song together.

A language model tool predicts how long each lyric line should last and writes out timed lyrics, so words and music line up closely. The team also built a large pipeline for gathering good songs with matched lyrics and prompts, plus fresh measures for checking segment fit. In experiments, SegTune gave stronger control and better musical coherence than the systems it was compared against.
arxiv-2510-18816:
Connor Evans, writing alone, studies vector sequences in Hilbert space. They are built from Blaschke products and an isometry. Blaschke products are special functions from complex analysis. An isometry is an operator that preserves lengths. The central question is redundancy. Which vectors can be deleted from the sequence? The rest must still span the space well. That property makes the sequence a frame. Frames allow reconstruction from measurements.

Evans uses Hilbert space models and the Wold decomposition. That tool splits an isometry into standard parts. With it, he classifies all cases in full. Some frames have no removable vectors at all. Those form a Riesz basis. Some have a few removable vectors. Some are fully insured, so every vector can be removed. The choice of product and isometry decides the case. Model theory thus settles a concrete frame question.
arxiv-2510-18916:
Passimzouwé Dagou, Pagdame Tiebekabe, and Kokou Tchariè study Narayana numbers that can be written as products of four repdigits in a given base. A repdigit is a number made of one repeated digit, and the authors ask which Narayana numbers take this special product form.

For bases from two to twelve, they prove that only finitely many such numbers exist, and they determine all of them. The result closes a narrow but exact counting question in number theory, giving a complete list rather than a bound alone for the bases they cover.
arxiv-2510-19016:
Kwang-Il Seon and four co-authors model the optical colors of galactic cirrus clouds in the Stripe 82 sky region. These thin dust clouds in our own galaxy glow faintly and can be mistaken for dim features in other galaxies, but their colors differ in a way that can separate the two.

The team runs light-transfer models through clouds shaped to mimic turbulence, lit by the surrounding interstellar glow. The modeled cloud density follows patterns known from the space between stars. Comparing results with observed color diagrams shows how cirrus gets its distinct hues, which helps surveys avoid confusing local dust with distant faint galaxies.
arxiv-2510-19716:
Kuai Yu and five co-authors present LyTimeT, a framework for pulling the true state variables of a system out of video. Background motion, occlusions, and texture changes distract naive methods. In the first phase, a transformer autoencoder with global attention locks onto the moving regions that matter. It mutes the rest, giving robust latent states and sharp long-range video forecasts.

In the second phase, the team probes the latent space. They keep the axes that track real physical quantities best. A Lyapunov-based penalty then steadies the learned dynamics. On five synthetic benchmarks and four real systems, some of them chaotic, LyTimeT found the hidden variables most truly and shrugged off background changes.
arxiv-2510-19816:
Veronica Giardini and eight co-authors report a working platform that traps and manipulates single strontium atoms in optical tweezer arrays for quantum simulation. Atoms are first caught in a magneto-optical trap, cooled in two stages to a few microkelvin, then loaded into arrays of tightly focused laser tweezers formed by crossed acousto-optic deflectors. Light-assisted collisions enforce single-atom occupancy about half the time.

Fluorescence imaging detects the trapped atoms with fidelity above ninety-nine percent while keeping most of them alive for the next step. Release-and-recapture measurements put the tweezer temperature near thirteen microkelvin, and the vacuum holds atoms for over seven minutes. The platform supplies the loading, cooling, and detection needed for scalable quantum simulation with alkaline-earth atoms.
arxiv-2510-20016:
Neema Jakisa Owor and seven co-authors build a detection system for traffic cameras that use fisheye lenses. Such cameras see a wide area from one spot, but strong distortion warps objects near the image edges. Standard detectors struggle most in exactly those outer regions, where shapes look degraded and uneven.

Their pipeline adds simple steps before and after detection and combines several trained models through an ensemble, which improves consistency across the whole image. On the 2025 AI City Challenge Track 4 test, the system earned an F1 score near 0.64 and placed eighth among sixty-two teams. The result shows that careful processing can offset much of the distortion penalty.
arxiv-2510-20316: Eduard Feireisl and Wladimir Neves use a live data feed method on the Navier-Stokes-Fourier set for a fluid that can be squeezed, spun, and heat-driven. They prove the track trait of the method: the fed run stays close to the true run. The proof holds when Mach is low and Rossby and Froude are high. Large data are let in through weak solutions.
arxiv-2510-20616:
Aki Rehn and three co-authors ask how to set two knobs in private transfer learning: the clip bound C and the batch size B. The task fine-tunes a pre-trained model on private data with noise added for a privacy proof. Past rules say a strong privacy call wants a small clip bound. Real tests say the large bound wins in that state. The clash comes from shifts in slope spread, they show.

Past batch rules fail when compute is fixed to a set span of rounds. Lumped privacy noise in place of those rules tells when small or large batch sets win. One knob pair for all tasks can cost much, most when privacy or compute swings. Clip acts as a slope re-weight, they note.
arxiv-2510-20716:
Ilya Chevyrev and Massimiliano Gubinelli prove advance bounds for rough differential equations driven by very irregular noise. Such equations appear when a smooth rule is shaken by a jagged input that has no clean derivative, making standard estimates break down.

Their only key demand on the smooth part is a holding property, meaning solutions stay controlled when the noise is switched off. From a local version of that property they lift to a global bound by scaling, for a broad class of equations in time only or in space and time. The bounds hold in small regions and do not depend on edge conditions, reducing hard cases to the simpler setting of small noise.
arxiv-2510-20816:
Sk Asrap Murshed and Bitan Roy study a new pattern in graphene. Graphene is a thin sheet made of carbon atoms. They look at stacks built from one or more layers. Recent tests hinted at order in a quarter metal state.

They identify a valley coherent charge density wave in that state. A charge density wave means charge gathers in a repeating pattern. Valley coherent means two valley states mix in a set way. For some layer counts, the pattern breaks threefold rotational symmetry. Then it forms stripes, as seen in six layer graphene. For other odd layer counts, it keeps that symmetry. They also show how this order can lift a leftover split. It can act together with anomalous Hall order, a sideways electrical effect. Only the Hall order shows a loop in sideways resistance.
arxiv-2510-21616:
Hope Whitelock and fourteen co-authors dissect the magnetism of a rare-earth crystal where erbium ions sit on a triangular lattice, a geometry famous for frustrating simple magnetic order. Working at temperatures near a tenth of a degree above absolute zero, they find the crystal's behavior driven by its single-ion physics as much as by teamwork between ions.

Optical spectroscopy in applied fields tracks how the ground doublet of each erbium ion splits, pinning down the single-ion energy scheme with unusual confidence. That scheme reveals a field-driven crossing of the ground levels, which forces a sudden first-order change of magnetic state. Cooling further, the crystal orders antiferromagnetically on its own below about one hundred ten thousandths of a kelvin, and neutron scattering resolves the pattern. The interplay of the two effects, the authors argue, illuminates insulating rare-earth magnets broadly.
arxiv-2510-21716:
Nicola Webb and four co-authors study what happens to trust when a robot teammate says no. In a simulated firefighting mission, human players worked alongside a robot. At a scripted moment, the robot declined to drop its own task and help immediately. That kind of refusal can poison a human-robot team in real rescue work.

Thirty-eight participants played the interactive game while trust was tracked over time. Refusal cut trust sharply at first. That happened whether or not the robot explained itself. The difference came later. With an explanation, trust climbed back over the mission, largely repairing the damage. Unexplained refusal left the deficit in place. The study argues that robot explanations should be judged by the recovery curve, not the instant reaction.
arxiv-2510-22016:
Pierangelo Lombardo, Antonio Casoli, Cristian Cingolani, Shola Oshodi, and Michele Zanatta argue that classifier scorecards should be built around what mistakes actually cost. Picking a metric shapes which model wins, how it is tuned, and whether it ships, yet no accepted measure directly targets total classification cost. Lopsided classes are often treated as a defect to fix even when fixing them raises real costs.

The team defines Weighted Accuracy, a version of accuracy where each example counts according to its cost. A general reweighting scheme that adapts any cost-style measure or loss to uneven classes without resampling the data. Because results are expressed in cost terms, scores from different datasets become comparable, and gaps between development data and the data a model will really face are handled openly.
arxiv-2510-22216:
Michael Candon, Pier Marzocca, and Earl H. Dowell shrink one of aeronautics' nastiest simulations into a pocket model. In transonic flight, shock waves on a wing can begin to buffet, oscillating violently and shaking the structure. The coupled air-and-structure problem is so nonlinear and unsteady that three-dimensional studies have mostly been out of reach.

Their reduced-order model blends nonlinear oscillator dynamics with Volterra theory, an input-output description of systems with memory. Produces an integro-differential equation whose terms are picked out of data by a sparse matching algorithm. Applied to a standard test airfoil, the compact model reproduces the aeroelastic buffet response that full simulations struggle to deliver. A trustworthy stand-in of this kind lets engineers sweep designs and flight conditions quickly, reserving heavy computation for the cases that deserve it.
arxiv-2510-22616:
Commonsense questions in Persian have lacked a large test set, despite the language's many speakers. Morteza Alikhani, Mohammadtaha Bagherifard, Erfan Zinvandi, and Mehran Sarmadi introduce PerCoR in 2025, a benchmark of multiple choice sentence completions drawn from over forty news and cultural sources.

The set holds about one hundred six thousand problems built with a conjunction based splitting method. Hard wrong options are chosen by an adversarial filter that favors answers most likely to confuse models. Human annotators score eighty nine percent, while the best model tested scores slightly higher. The strongest open model trails, showing Persian commonsense remains difficult.
arxiv-2510-22716:
Lip reading helps speech recognition and assistive tools, but Persian has lacked a large real world dataset. Zahra Taghizadeh, Mohammad Shahverdikondori, Arian Noori, and Alireza Dadgarnia introduce LRW-Persian in 2025, a word level lip reading dataset drawn from television footage.

The set covers hundreds of target words and over four hundred thousand video samples from thousands of hours across many programs. An automated pipeline handles transcription, active speaker finding, and quality filtering. Speaker separate splits, dialect coverage, and per clip details on pose, age, and gender are included. Two known lip reading models are fine tuned to set reference scores.
arxiv-2510-22816:
Many servers hold one data stream, yet sampling must stay global. Honghao Lin leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they solve perfect Lp sampling in that setting. Lp sampling picks an index with chance tied to frequency power. A central coordinator limits communication.

Their algorithm uses communication that is near optimal. Optimality holds up to log factors. They then build robust monitoring protocols. Those protocols estimate frequency moments. Adversaries can adapt inputs in their setting. Their method still gives tight approximations. Sampling is a core primitive for stream tasks. Such tasks include heavy hitter detection and sparse recovery.
arxiv-2510-22916:
Estimating pasture biomass helps farmers set stocking rates well. Qiyu Liao leads a team with ten co-authors. In 2025 they release a dataset for that task. It holds top view pasture images from Australia. Nineteen locations and multiple seasons are covered.

Each image shows a small marked quadrat. Ground measures pair with each image. Biomass is sorted into green, dead, and legume parts. Vegetation height is also recorded. A vegetation index from optical sensors is included. The set holds over a thousand annotated images. It is hosted as a Kaggle competition. The task is biomass estimation from images. Precision grazing management is the target use.
arxiv-2510-23816:
Forouzan Fallah and five co-authors present RareFlow, a generative system that upgrades satellite images from one sensor to look like sharper images from another. The task turns ten-meter Sentinel-2 pictures into two-meter Maxar-like views, in a setting with little training data and a shifted domain. The focus is rare landforms such as retrogressive thaw slumps, which upscalers tend to wash out.

RareFlow guides its flow-matching generation two ways. A gated ControlNet locks in the scene geometry from the low-resolution input, while text-based guidance adds context when the target feature is rare. A loss enforces frequency alignment, perceptual similarity, and color consistency against high-resolution images. The team built a multi-sensor benchmark for rare feature detection and tested on two public sets. Domain experts judged the outputs, backing the claim that the method serves real scientific analysis, not just visual polish.
arxiv-2510-24016:
Aaron Winn and a co-author work out the fluid mechanics of peristalsis when a tube contracts in both directions at once. Peristaltic pumping — a wave of wall contraction squeezing fluid along — drives flows from intestines to engineered devices. Most models impose the radius changes and ignore the length changes that radial squeezing naturally causes in elastic walls, yet net flow depends on those details.

The authors track the fluid in the Lagrangian coordinates of the elastic tube, treating it as flow inside a fixed boundary with a time-dependent metric. The analysis holds even for large contractions, which they confirm against COMSOL simulations. Transverse and longitudinal contractions push flows of the same order but in opposite directions. The wall's Poisson ratio matters: incompressible walls suppress flow by minimizing volume change, while auxetic walls enhance it. Length-driven waves typically produce backflow, though trapping survives at large amplitudes.
arxiv-2510-24316:
Kyeongan Park and four co-authors introduce JADE, a method to estimate the energy distribution of a quantum state from a limited set of moments. The distribution is key to finding a molecule's ground state energy on a quantum computer, but full diagonalization is far too costly for large systems. Rebuilding an accurate distribution from few moments is the core challenge.

JADE is a nonparametric method inspired by quantum mechanics. It reconstructs the characteristic function from the available moments using the Jacobi-Anger expansion, then derives the energy density from it. The authors aim for accuracy with far fewer moments than earlier approaches need, easing ground state estimation for quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2510-24516:
Antonio Condorelli leads a team of four authors on cosmic rays. Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays are particles with extreme energy from space. Their sources stay unknown, a long open problem in astrophysics. The team test two guesses for where the sources live. One guess ties their rate to star birth, the other to stellar mass.

They fit the energy spectrum and mass mix seen by the Auger Observatory. The fit bounds how sources boost particles and what they emit. Sky maps use a catalog of over 400,000 galaxies near us. Galaxy clusters, huge bound systems with magnetized plasma, trap heavy particles. That trapping shapes arrival directions and caps the top energy. Long gamma-ray bursts emerge as the most promising sources.
arxiv-2510-24716:
Simon Schubotz, Eva Bittrich, Holger Merlitz, Quinn A Besford, Petra Uhlmann, Jens-Uwe Sommer, and Gunter K Auernhammer solve a long puzzle on how polymer brushes swell in damp air. Such brushes are dense chains fixed to a base, used in coats and sensors. Past reads said they swell less in steam than in liquid, a gap called the Schroder paradox.

At full damp, their tests show brush swell does match the liquid state. A sharp rise starts once damp passes a high mark just short of full. Their new field model pins the rise on a loop: more swell makes the fluid mix better, which drives yet more swell. The model also nails a wet shift in drop tests.
arxiv-2510-24916:
Fabio Bertolotti, Kyle Myers, and Wei Yang Tham gauge what researchers think their own yield is, and what that says of the market for science. Their way works when counts of output and prices of inputs can not be seen. In their model, how much a researcher will pay for an input shows what yield they think they have.

Fit to a large poll of researchers across the land, the yield spread came out very skewed. A few researchers sit far above the rest in thought yield. Play out tests say a more smart split of the same funds could be worth vast sums. Fresh ways to spot top talent would add much, they find.
arxiv-2510-25216:
Ting-Hsuan Li and Po-Feng Wu ask where the gas came from that woke fresh star birth in near galaxies that had gone quiet. Such wake ups, called rejuvenation, show in zones that began to form stars in the past few spans of years. If fresh gas fell in from out, its chem mix should stand out.

From a large fiber survey, they picked wake zones by two star light marks, then matched their gas chem mix and speeds with plain star zones. Host traits such as gas share and shape were matched with calm and star form hosts as well. No clear odd marks showed in the wake zones. That points to gas that was in the host all along.
arxiv-2510-25316:
Tianbo Chen and Xiaojun Song introduce an asymmetric Huber periodogram. Their 2025 statistics paper generalizes several existing periodograms. A periodogram helps find hidden cycles in time series. The ordinary version uses squared error loss. Quantile and Huber versions offer other trade-offs. Their new method aims for a fuller picture.

They build it through asymmetric Huber regression with trigonometric terms. A special loss replaces the usual squared loss. Scanning an asymmetry parameter shows more data structure. The method can be cheaper than quantile versions. It also resists outliers better than ordinary versions. Chen and Song establish its theoretical properties. They link it to an asymmetric Huber spectrum. They develop confidence intervals and a Fisher-type test. Simulations and two applications show its value. Uses include detecting periodicities and clustering time series.
arxiv-2510-25616:
Nikita Kachaev led four co-authors on vision-language-action models. Mikhail Kolosov, Daniil Zelezetsky, and Alexey K Kovalev helped. Aleksandr I Panov closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper studies visual feature degradation in robots. Vision-language-action models adapt pretrained vision-language models. Those models promise transferable world knowledge for agents. 

They systematically study feature retention during fine-tuning. Naive action fine-tuning leads to visual degradation, they show. Hidden features are probed to characterize effects. Attention maps are studied for feature changes. Targeted tasks contrast action models with vision counterparts. Changes in vision-language capabilities are isolated that way. Strategies for aligning visual features are tested. A simple effective method mitigates the degradation found. It yields better generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios. Trade-offs between action tuning and feature loss are clarified. Useful methods recover inherited vision-language capabilities for agents.
arxiv-2510-25716:
Nadja Vater, Katherine Rossella Foglia, Vittorio Colao, and Alfio Borzi compute Nash equilibria quickly. Their 2025 paper presents a low-rank symplectic gradient method. Two-player Nash games give rise to coupled tuning problems. Symplectic gradient adjustment outperforms plain gradient methods. It includes second-order mixed derivatives at each iterate. That inclusion requires considerably larger computational effort, though.

Their low-rank method approximates mixed derivatives by rank-one updates. Theoretical study gives novel convergence values for both. Setting bounds for the methods are included. Numeric tests complement the theoretical results. Deterministic games with known equilibria test actions. A neural-network training task evaluates computational advantage. The task is inspired by CLIP model training. Low-rank method reaches comparable loss values there. CPU time is lower than exact symplectic method. Game theory and machine learning tuning both benefit.
arxiv-2510-25816:
Tarun Kumar Chawdhury and Jon D. Duke test a method for answering questions from long clinical notes stored in electronic health records. The notes are stored as coded attachments, so search tools often cut them into chunks and miss links between medical facts. The method they test, called CLEAR, retrieves text by clinical entities, meaning named diseases, drugs, and other medical terms.

Chawdhury and Duke built a test platform and ran it on twelve notes that ranged from ten thousand to sixty five thousand tokens. CLEAR won more often than wide context and chunk based methods, matched meaning well, and used far fewer tokens. Gains were largest on the longest notes.
arxiv-2510-26016:
Michael Arntzenius, working alone, links two ideas from computing that seem far apart: fair search in a logic language and efficient database joins. The language miniKanren, a descendant of Prolog, gained fame for a complete yet efficient search that interleaves work fairly between alternatives. It bounds how much work goes to one branch before switching to the next.

Arntzenius shows that the same fairness by bounded work idea gives an elegant way to build worst case optimal joins. The method combines database tables with strong guarantees on running time. His approach uses a seekable iterator interface, where a reader can jump ahead in a sorted stream, and it fits a shallow embedding in functional languages.
arxiv-2510-26416:
Hashir Kuniyil, Asad Ali, and Saif Al-Kuwari study pairs of photons born together in a crystal, a process called spontaneous parametric down-conversion. The sideways links between the two photons support quantum imaging and tests of entanglement, the tight link between quantum particles. The team asks how colour filters placed in the beams change those sideways links.

Kuniyil and his two co-authors give the first full study of filter width in a bulk BBO crystal, for matched and unmatched photon pairs. Far from the crystal, matched pairs ignore the filter, while unmatched pairs spread as it widens. Close in, they find a new dip pattern: the pair width shrinks by about ten percent at a best filter width, then grows again. They also show a handy structural edge along one axis for a classic entanglement test.
arxiv-2510-26716:
Erik J Wasleske, Vivienne F Baldassare, and Christopher M Carroll connect black hole activity in dwarf galaxies to the traits of their hosts. Dwarf galaxies are small, and finding their feeding black holes takes several methods: optical spectra, infrared colours, X-ray brightness, and brightness changes. Different methods pick out different galaxies, which raises the question of whether they catch black holes at different life stages.

Wasleske and his two co-authors use a database that applies all four methods to every galaxy, then estimate host traits with spectral energy distribution models. Infrared-selected active dwarfs stood out most, with the highest star formation rates and lowest stellar masses. Broad-line systems had far higher black hole luminosities, while X-ray and variability picks had higher star formation than optical picks. The patterns may reflect different epochs of accretion.
arxiv-2510-26816:
Rohit Rajendra Dhage reports a hidden pattern in a widely used satellite fire product. The VIIRS active fire product classifies each detection's confidence, and it guides global fire monitoring. Analysing over twenty-one million detections from one year, Dhage finds a complete absence of low-confidence classifications at night.

Of about six million nighttime fires, none were classed low confidence, against roughly seven hundred thousand expected if day and night behaved alike. The pattern holds worldwide, across months and both satellites, and machine learning reverse-engineering points to an algorithmic constraint, not a geophysical cause. Fires cooler than about two hundred ninety-five kelvin at night seem to be dropped entirely rather than flagged. The behaviour touches about twenty-eight percent of all detections. Dhage recommends documenting the constraint in user guides and reprocessing affected analyses.
arxiv-2510-27016:
Jayden Serenari and Stephen Lee present a privacy guard for chats with large language models. Users often paste personal details such as names and addresses into prompts, and that data can leak. Their framework, called LOPSIDED, swaps sensitive entities for realistic stand-ins that fit the surrounding meaning before anything leaves the device.

Once the remote model replies, the stand-ins are swapped back, so the user sees a normal answer. Tests use real shared conversations, expanded and labeled to check whether each entity matters for the reply. The method cuts semantic utility errors fivefold versus baseline techniques while improving privacy. For anyone building chat services, it offers a way to protect users without dulling answers.
arxiv-2510-27216:
Meijie Zhao and Xiao Wen extend a key measure for moving systems in this 2025 paper. The systems are flows, smooth motions that can stall at singular points where speed drops to zero. The measure is pressure, a number that blends chaos and the weight given to paths. Old tools break near stalls, since balls of nearby paths swell or shrink oddly.

The pair define rescaled pressure, built from path balls that adjust for local speed and time shifts. They show several ways of building the balls all give the same pressure. Under mild conditions on the flow, they prove a known formula for pressure still holds. They also link the two rescaled kinds, the space-wide one and the measure-based one, in a partial rule.
arxiv-2510-27416:
Taiyo Nakamura and Kensuke Homma propose using Earth itself as a lens in a telescope for distant axion-like particle sources. Axion-like particles are hypothetical dark matter candidates. A fast unidirectional flux passing through Earth can be gravitationally focused into a distant focal region in space, concentrating the signal where a detector could sample it.

Their method adds stimulated backward reflection: a coherent electromagnetic beam aimed at the focal point induces axion decays that reflect back for detection. Numerical analysis maps the focal region structure for a stream with speed suggested by the observed stellar stream S1, placing the focus billions of meters away. Sensitivity estimates for a conservative distant point source show reach in the electronvolt mass range, outlining a possible general-purpose space-based axion observatory.
arxiv-2510-27516:
Desta Haileselassie Hagos, Legand L. Burge, and three other co-authors make text summarizers handle long documents, in a 2025 paper. Transformer models summarize well, but their attention cost grows with the square of the length. Long reports thus get slow and pricey. Their framework, BiSparse-AAS, cuts that cost three ways at once.

Sparse attention lets each word heed only the most relevant spots. Adaptive spans stretch or shrink that reach as needed. Bilinear attention then models rich word-to-word ties inside the narrowed view. On news and article sets, the system beat top rivals at both extractive and abstractive summarizing. Reported ROUGE gains, a standard overlap score, were large on two news sets. Scores stayed strong on two further corpora, suggesting a practical tool for real work.
arxiv-2511-00016:
Eleonora Maggiorelli, Matteo Negri, and Francesco Vicentini study Gamma convergence for a phase-field cohesive energy used to model fracture. Reproducing fracture under multi-axis stress needs three material inputs: elasticity, strength, and toughness. Strength is the subtle one, being a full surface in stress space rather than a single number, and phase-field models often fail to represent it well.

Their convergence analysis examines whether the phase-field energy methods the meant cohesive fracture model as the regularization length shrinks. Applied mathematics and mechanics readers get rigor for a widely used simulation approach. Gamma convergence is the right notion because it assures minimizers converge, not just energies.
arxiv-2511-00416:
Yiwei Zha, Rui Min, and Shanu Sushmita probe a blind spot in AI text detectors: paraphrasing. Detectors catch direct machine output with high accuracy, yet text that is paraphrased again and again slips past them, even though a machine still wrote its bones. Their analysis finds a laundering zone in between, where meaning shifts but generation patterns survive, enabling two attacks: hiding human authorship and disguising plagiarism.

Their benchmark, PADBen, is the first to test detectors against both attacks in a systematic way. It sorts texts into five types along the path from original to deeply laundered, and sets five detection tasks of rising difficulty. Eleven leading detectors showed a sharp split: they catch plagiarism evasion but fail at authorship hiding. Current methods, the authors conclude, cannot police the laundering zone.
arxiv-2511-01816:
Maryam Bagherian rethinks tensor decomposition, the craft of splitting high-dimensional data into simpler parts. Set methods rebuild the data under a fixed rank. That goal often misses the structures that carry meaning. Her no-rank scheme swaps the goal. It learns by metric learning instead: place points so that gaps between them mirror real semantic and physical links.

Training mixes a triplet loss with diversity and uniformity penalties. Theory backs the scheme, with guarantees on convergence and on the metric's traits. Tests span face datasets, brain connectivity from ABIDE, and simulated galaxies and crystals. Rivals ranged from PCA and UMAP to CP, Tucker, and t-SVD decompositions, plus deep models. The new embeddings kept the meaningful links and clustered well. They stayed readable, and they worked on small datasets where transformers cannot be trained.
arxiv-2511-01916:
P. Daoust and eleven colleagues grow a cleaner home for germanium hole spin qubits. These qubits lose coherence through hyperfine coupling. The coupling is to the nuclear spins of silicon-29 and germanium-73 atoms in their own crystal. The remedy is a layered structure built only from spin-free isotopes. It is a germanium-70 quantum well, between silicon-28 and germanium-70 layers.

The team demonstrates epitaxial growth of these nuclear spin-free structures on industrial silicon-germanium buffered wafers, while economizing on the expensive purified source gases. Atom probe tomography showed isotopic purity above 99.99 percent, with carbon and oxygen below detection. Magnetotransport on gated Hall bars confirmed clean gate control of hole density. Densities were consistent between Hall and Shubnikov-de Haas analyses. Charge motion was fast. Together, these mark the material as a platform for longer-coherence quantum chips.
arxiv-2511-02016:
Patrick Cheridito, Jean-Loup Dupret, and Zhexin Wu build a trading laboratory where liquidity is made by the players, not assumed. Classical optimal execution theory tells a trader how to work a large order against a pre-specified price impact. But when market makers adapt by design, that assumption fails structurally: execution becomes a finite-horizon stochastic game among mixed agents.

Their framework, ABIDES-MARL, extends the ABIDES-Gym market simulator to many reinforcement learning agents with synchronized decision periods that preserve proper information flow and market microstructure. The framework is validated in an extended Kyle setting. There, multiple learning agents recover gradual price discovery. The simulations show a sharp contrast. Strategies learned under adaptive liquidity differ at root from fixed-impact benchmarks. Strategies optimized against exogenous impact perform poorly once market makers adapt, especially when information is unbalanced, because the makers exploit predictable execution flow.
arxiv-2511-02116:
Mary Thomas and six colleagues at the San Diego Supercomputer Center describe a service that lets researchers run Jupyter notebooks on high-performance computers without opening security holes. Notebook servers on shared supercomputers expose both the system and its users to risk if reached directly. The Satellite Proxy Service answers with a token-authenticated secure reverse proxy.

Through the proxy, each user reaches their notebook server over an encrypted connection using a single web address they can paste into a browser. The short paper explains how the service is put together and why the design addresses the main security concerns of notebook access on HPC systems. It is a practical report aimed at other computing centres facing the same problem.
arxiv-2511-02216:
Hyemin Yu and Hong-Chuan Yang design a relay system for wireless traffic that cannot afford to be late or lost. Ultra-reliable low-latency communication serves mission-critical uses. A two-hop relay link makes the guarantees harder: each hop must choose its own settings, from the time structure of transmissions to the coding scheme, within a strict delay budget.

The authors model each hop's configuration choices as a Markov decision process and train two reinforcement learning agents, one per hop, to cooperate on latency-aware policies. Their algorithm, DRL-CoLA, learns in a distributed way rather than from a central controller. Simulations show the learned policies reach near-optimal reliability while respecting the strict latency limits, which the authors offer as a design route for next-generation wireless services.
arxiv-2511-02316:
Guangshuo Zhou, Zechun Hu, and Renming Song study the most-visited spots of a wandering particle. A one-dimensional simple random walk steps left or right at random, here with a bias making the two directions unequal. A favourite site is whichever location the walk has visited most often up to that moment. Such sites are natural records of the walk's history, and their behaviour over long times is a delicate probabilistic question.

The authors prove that, with probability one, having exactly r favourite sites at once happens infinitely often, for every fixed whole number r. In other words, ties for the most-visited location, of any prescribed size, recur forever rather than eventually resolving. They also determine how fast the total number of favourite sites grows as time goes on, giving the asymptotic growth rate for this biased walk.
arxiv-2511-02716:
Krzysztof Pachucki and Michal Silkowski refine predicted transition rates in the hydrogen molecule. Their 2025 paper handles electric quadrupole transitions, a faint kind of light emission and absorption. Simple theory treats the two nuclei as fixed, but real molecules wobble, and that motion adds corrections called nonadiabatic effects.

The authors derive formulas for those corrections, built around a curve that tracks the molecule's quadrupole moment as the nuclei move apart. The curve parallels the classic one Wolniewicz derived for the fixed-nuclei case. Their numbers shift rates in the fundamental band by amounts from 0.4 percent to 12 percent, depending on how fast the molecule spins. Precise spectra of hydrogen, in labs and in space, depend on such fine details.
arxiv-2511-02916: Lin Chen, Yuchen Fu, Dennis Gaitsgory, and David Yang prove a structural result about loop groups, groups of maps from a circle into a group. Categorical representations of such a group form a 2-category, one level up from ordinary representation theory. Their 2025 paper shows this 2-category embeds fully faithfully into another: factorization module categories over the affine Grassmannian. The embedding loses nothing, so tools from the factorization side apply to loop group representations.
arxiv-2511-03016:
Iffat Gheyas, Muhammad Rizwan Asghar, Steve Schneider, and Alan Woodward review how platforms decide which crowdsourced data to trust. Crowds feed live decisions in maps, wikis, social media, phone sensing, and review sites, but they also carry misinformation, errors, and a few voices with outsized power. Their 2025 study sorts platforms into five types and compares how each manages trust.

Strengths included automatic moderation and community checking. Weak points were fast data floods, thin oversight in niche corners, hidden trust scores, and dominance by elites. The authors propose sharper AI tools, open reputation metrics, decentralized moderation, and structured community roles. A soft power strategy, spreading decision authority more evenly, ties the package together in their account.
arxiv-2511-03216:
Md Ashad Alam presents RKUM, a software package for the R language that makes kernel methods tougher against dirty data. Kernel tools compare data through a hidden mapping and power many pattern methods. RKUM swaps the usual squared loss for gentler losses when it estimates spread and cross-spread, so a few bad points do less harm.

Alongside robust versions of a two-view method called kernel canonical correlation, the package adds a tool that measures how much each point sways the result. Tests on made-up two-view and multi-view data show that tool can flag odd, high-impact points well. The package aims to give analysts a ready way to run robust kernel checks without building them from scratch.
arxiv-2511-03416:
Nikolai Herrmann and colleagues automate the task of turning embryo scans into a standard pose for fair comparison. Aligned three-dimensional ultrasound views help doctors track growth, find standard planes, and spot landmarks. Starting from an outline mask of the embryo, a classic axis method yields four candidate poses.

Three choosers then pick the standard pose: a shape-based rule, matching against an atlas image, and a forest classifier, alone or combined. Testing used more than two thousand scans from over a thousand pregnancies in a Rotterdam cohort study. A combined ensemble proved most robust across that large set. Reliable alignment can cut manual fiddling and make growth charts more trustworthy across visits and clinics.
arxiv-2511-03616:
Iason Chrysomallis and Georgios Chalkiadakis teach agents to learn from watch-only expert data and then surpass the expert. Classic imitation needs full records of states paired with the expert's actions, and it caps the student at the expert's level. Real settings often give only observations, and experts are frequently flawed.

Their method infers the missing actions through online exploration, guided by a confidence dial that shifts weight between expert hints and self-directed learning. The main algorithm folds that inference into a deep value network. Agents can thus start from silent films of good play and improve past them. Robotics and game settings with video-only demonstrations stand to benefit first.
arxiv-2511-04016:
Mahmoud Soliman, Islam Osman, Mohamed S Shehata, and Rasika Rajapakshe present MedDChest, a foundation vision transformer pretrained specifically for thoracic imaging rather than adapted from natural images. Fine-tuning backbones trained on everyday photos leaves a domain gap that limits medical performance, the team argue.

Pretraining from scratch used over one point two million chest images, X-ray and computed tomography, gathered from ten public sources. A guided cropping strategy biases training samples toward anatomically relevant regions instead of random crops. Fine-tuned on varied diagnostic tasks, MedDChest beat strong publicly available ImageNet-pretrained models clearly. Large in-domain pretraining with domain-aware augmentation gives a better starting point for chest imaging work.
arxiv-2511-04216:
Wen-Yuan Ai, Bjorn Garbrecht, and Carlos Tamarit reply to a critique of their claimed resolution of the strong CP problem, the puzzle of why quantum chromodynamics conserves CP symmetry so precisely. Catalog evidence gave only a report number as title; the arXiv record gives the reply title used here, and their stance is reported as their argument, not settled fact.

One objection used a quantum rotor analogue to claim a vanishing topological susceptibility, which would clash with the observed eta-prime mass. The susceptibility, they answer, is fixed by a canonical commutation relation independent of the disputed limit order. A second objection from low-energy theory alone assumes coupling choices that already build in violation, they argue.
arxiv-2511-04316:
