Tim Beyer, Jonas Dornbusch, Jakob Steimle, Moritz Ladenburger, Leo Schwinn, and Stephan Gunnemann introduce AdversariaLLM, a unified toolbox for studying how language models resist jailbreak attacks. Safety research has splintered across fragmented, often buggy code, datasets, and scoring methods, making results hard to redo or compare fairly.

Twelve attack algorithms and seven benchmark datasets covering harmfulness, over-refusal, and utility sit inside one framework, with access to many open-weight models. Compute tracking, deterministic results, and distributional evaluation support fair scoring. A companion judging package can also stand alone. The goal is a sturdy base for open, reproducible robustness research rather than another single attack.
arxiv-2511-04616:
Elvis Agbenyega and his co-author rethink safety stock sizing for hardware makers. Safety stock shields supply chains when demand or supply wobbles. Standard formulas assume demand follows a normal curve and ignore how demand spread changes.

Real factory demand is often skewed, intermittent, and far from normal, they note. Their data-driven method drops the normality assumption entirely. Each item's demand distribution is worked out from its own data instead. Hardware makers powering the digital economy face sharp swings, so sizing buffers from real demand shapes could cut both shortages and waste.
arxiv-2511-05416:
The Pierre Auger Collaboration reports on the time gap between rings of elves, brief light rings high above storms, seen at its observatory in Argentina. A past idea blamed the gap on the storm's pulse bouncing off the ground.

With a time sharpness of one hundred nanoseconds, the fluorescence detector caught many multi-ring elves, about a fifth to a quarter of events. The team traced seventy double and twenty-four triple elves from four storms at varied ranges. Their data show the gap stays near constant, which rules out the ground bounce as its cause.
arxiv-2511-05616:
Connor Dunlop, Matthew Zheng, Kavana Venkatesh, and Pinar Yanardag present a method for editing images to suit one person's taste. Text-to-image models are generic by design. They cannot learn that one user likes moody light while another wants bright color, so edits often miss the mark.

Their framework, Collaborative Direct Preference Optimization, places each user in a graph of people with like tastes. A small graph network learns user embeddings, and those embeddings steer the diffusion model's editing objective. The aim is edits that fit the person and stay coherent with their taste neighbors. In benchmarks and user studies, the method beat baselines at matching what each user preferred.
arxiv-2511-06116:
A Acharyya leads the Fermi-LAT and VERITAS collaboration authors testing whether cosmic rays from a blazar make the neutrinos and gamma rays seen from it. In 2017 the IceCube observatory caught a high-energy neutrino tied to a flare from the blazar TXS 0506+056. Escaped cosmic rays can hit background light on their way to Earth, spawning pions that decay into neutrinos and cascades of gamma rays.

The team searched for that cascade glow by combining Fermi space telescope and VERITAS ground telescope data. They fit the gamma-ray spectrum as the blazar's own light plus a cascade part, using simulations to set the cosmic-ray spectrum. The data fit a proton spectrum with a stated slope and cutoff, and they bound how much power escapes as protons.
arxiv-2511-06216:
Yanan Zhao and colleagues rethink how graph learning creates the multiple views it needs for contrastive training. Graph contrastive learning teaches representations by comparing different views of one graph, but most methods rely on two fixed, hand-made views. That habit limits the range of structure the model can notice, from local detail to global shape.

Their framework builds views from fractional-order diffusion, where a single adjustable order sweeps from local to global behavior. The order itself is learned, so the data decides which diffusion scales are informative, with no manual augmentation. Experiments on standard benchmarks produced stronger, more robust embeddings than leading graph contrastive baselines.
arxiv-2511-06416:
Dian Jin and Jeremy Coulson learn system models online from streaming data when the true complexity is unknown or drifting. Subspace methods summarize a dynamical system by the directions its behavior spans, but classical versions assume fixed linear systems with known order. Their framework tracks a nested family of subspaces on a flag manifold instead.

New data recursively updates the whole ensemble of subspaces, so the model adapts as dimensions change with no advance knowledge of order. The method generalizes an earlier Grassmannian tracking algorithm. Plugged into a data-driven simulator, the adaptive predictor handled sudden changes in system behavior and outperformed several baselines in the case study.
arxiv-2511-07416:
Generated videos look convincing, yet copying their pixel motion can teach robots the wrong moves. Jiageng Mao and colleagues introduce PhysWorld to fix that gap. Their framework pairs video generation with a rebuilt model of the physical scene behind the video.

Starting from one image and a task command, the system generates a demonstration video and reconstructs the objects and surfaces in it. Motions are then grounded through object-focused reinforcement learning inside that physical model. Tests suggest the grounded actions transfer to real robot tasks more reliably. The work links generative video to physics-aware robot training.
arxiv-2511-07516:
Christine Hao and colleagues ask where a galaxy cluster stops shaping its galaxies. Far inside a cluster, environment rules; far outside, galaxies evolve alone. The border between cluster and field members marks a transition zone worth mapping precisely.

Neural networks trained on the IllustrisTNG simulation learn to sort galaxies by inner traits alone. Applying that classifier across space yields the first quantitative, probability-based map of the transition region. The zone proves broad rather than sharp. Clusters studied exceed ten trillion solar masses at the present day. The map helps observers interpret galaxy change without relying only on distance cuts.
arxiv-2511-07716:
Jian-Min Wang and colleagues caught a quasar echo arriving before its trigger, or so it seems. In active galaxies, broad emission lines normally lag the brightening continuum, and that delay maps the gas region and weighs the central black hole. The lag usually grows with the square root of luminosity.

Eight years of monitoring the quasar PHL 1092 found hydrogen line changes leading the continuum by roughly seventeen to fifty seven days. Leading delays break the standard structure picture of broad-line regions. Either geometry, driving light curves, or measurement assumptions need rethinking. Surprises like this keep reverberation mapping honest about black hole weighing.
arxiv-2511-07816:
Jarett Dewbury, Chi-en Amy Tai, and Alexander Wong sharpen prostate cancer maps with a synthetic imaging channel. Deep learning segmentation of lesions stalls at low overlap scores in large patient groups. Synthetic correlated diffusion imaging adds information beyond standard diffusion scans, and the team tests whether it lifts performance.

Six leading segmentation architectures run on two hundred patients with aligned synthetic, diffusion-weighted, and coefficient maps. Adding the synthetic channel improved or preserved results in nearly all configurations, with some architectures gaining strongly. Better lesion outlines support biopsy targeting and treatment planning. Multimodal gains from a computed channel cost no extra scan time.
arxiv-2511-07916:
Narendra Singh Yadav and Pavan Kumar Perepu analyze a humble step that decides whether machines can read text in photos. Before recognition, images are binarized, and binarization needs polarity: is the text darker or lighter than its background? Guessing wrong inverts the page and breaks everything downstream.

Power-law transformation, the gamma adjustment familiar from image editing, gets a theoretical treatment for polarity detection. License plates, captchas, and handwriting all pass through this gate. A principled account of when the transform reveals polarity correctly turns a folk preprocessing trick into engineering knowledge that recognition pipelines can rely on.
arxiv-2511-08116: Alexander Kolesnik models surface soil pollution spreading from a fixed source as a random flight in the plane with finite speed and random lifetime. Particles move symmetrically, then stop after a lifetime drawn from a chosen distribution, a framework also called the planar Markov random flight. The arXiv record credits Kolesnik alone, while the evidence creator field was blank.
arxiv-2511-08216:
Thomas Maullin-Sapey and Fabian Telschow build spatial trust regions for data processes that are ongoing in pieces rather than smoothly differentiable. Fields such as neuroimaging, climatology, and cosmology study peak sets, the regions where an image rises above a threshold. Trust statements about overlaps or unions of such sets across settings were only recently introduced, under a smoothness assumption that excludes many real settings.

Requiring only continuity widens the reach considerably. A new settling notion for piecewise ongoing functions over finite partitions supports the theory and yields settling results for maxima over changing sets. For the first time, trust regions become ready for hard cases like symmetric differences of peak sets.
arxiv-2511-08516:
Devesh Nandal and Sunmyon Chon model how metal enriched supermassive stars grow through accretion and collisions, using the GENEC stellar evolution code. Supermassive stars are candidate seeds for massive black holes and may explain odd abundance patterns in early galaxies and globular clusters. Simulations now show they can form at modest metal content, not only in metal free gas, so growth histories across a range of enrichment levels are needed.

Final masses fall steeply as metal content rises, from tens of thousands of solar masses at the lowest enrichment to a few thousand at the highest. The main growth channel switches from collisions to accretion across a narrow enrichment range. Lifetimes stay near two million years, and collisions alone cannot rejuvenate the star enough to drive runaway collapse.
arxiv-2511-08616:
Kelvin Koa and four co-authors teach language models to do technical analysis, the chart-based reading of past prices that traders use. Earlier model forecasters read company text but ignored price history, partly because prices live in numbers while reasoning lives in words.

Their framework, Verbal Technical Analysis, turns price series into written annotations and trains the reasoning trace with a reward tied to forecast error. A time-series backbone then converts the reasoned attributes back into numeric forecasts. Across stock datasets from the United States, China, and Europe, the method posts the best accuracy the authors compare against. Industry experts also rated the written reasoning traces highly, which matters for trust in trading tools.
arxiv-2511-08716:
Ce Sui and four co-authors bring information theory to a practical cosmology question: which summary statistics of a cosmic field actually carry the information, and which merely repeat each other? Their yardstick is mutual information, which measures how much one quantity reveals about another.

Two test cases show the method at work. For the cosmic microwave background, the power spectrum extracts nearly everything, as expected for a Gaussian random field. For the twenty-one centimeter brightness temperature map, the scattering transform captures the most non-Gaussian information, yet it still complements the power spectrum and bispectrum rather than replacing them. The authors propose mutual information as a sturdy foundation for judging and improving the summaries cosmologists rely on.
arxiv-2511-08816:
M. Volz and eight co-authors compare two young stars whose planet-forming disks look alike on paper yet smell chemically different. Both GM Aur and the star called J1615 host transitional disks with inner cavities, and the Webb telescope's mid-infrared spectrometer read the molecular emission from each one.

J1615 glows with water, hydrogen cyanide, acetylene, carbon dioxide in two isotopic forms, hydroxyl, and a rare labeled acetylene, while GM Aur shows only water and hydroxyl lines. J1615 also accretes more slowly and holds larger, more processed dust grains with more crystalline silicates. The authors suggest that combination lets carbon-rich gas persist in the inner disk where telescopes can see it. The result widens the known chemical diversity of planet-forming environments around Sun-like stars.
arxiv-2511-09316:
Zhuoqun Huang, Neil G. Marchant, Olga Ohrimenko, and Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein certify that sequence classifiers stay correct under small edits to their input. Randomized smoothing proves such robustness by randomly deleting parts of the input and checking the prediction holds. Fixed deletion rates, though, fit poorly when inputs vary in length, like sentences.

Their AdaptDel methods adjust the deletion rate to each input's properties. They extend the smoothing theory to variable rates while keeping certification sound against edit-distance attacks. On natural language tasks, the certified regions grow dramatically. The median size improves by up to thirty orders of magnitude over earlier certifications, they report. That leap makes certified text classification far more practical.
arxiv-2511-09616:
Matthew Dodelson, Cristoforo Iossa, and Robin Karlsson propose how string theory smooths a famous black hole singularity signature. In holography, a thermal two-point function diverges at one complex-time point, tracing a light ray that bounces off the singularity. At finite coupling, stringy corrections cannot be ignored, and the bouncing ray's fate was open.

The authors propose the divergence shifts slightly into the complex plane, becoming a finite-size bump instead of an infinite spike. They demonstrate the smoothing explicitly in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model at infinite temperature, where the correlator is analytically controlled. The picture suggests bulk duals of planar theories at finite coupling are stringy black holes with softened singularities.
arxiv-2511-10316:
Yu Deng, Baozhu Zhao, Junyan Su, Xiaohan Zhang, and Qi Liu improve 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes where near and far regions fight each other. Distant areas get inaccurate depth, while close-range structure degrades, because supervision signals conflict across the depth range. Their framework attacks both problems by unifying the physics of camera defocus with multi-view geometric constraints.

A monocular depth estimator supplies scale-recovered depth priors, and defocus convolution synthesizes physically accurate blurred images, tied together by a new depth-of-field loss. Separately, semi-dense feature matching across views feeds a least-squares step that enforces depth consistency on reliable matches. On the Waymo Open Dataset the method improved peak signal-to-noise ratio by just under one decibel over the previous best.
arxiv-2511-10416:
Francisco Cunha, Yves Lepage, Miguel Couceiro, and Zied Bouraoui revisit analogical inference. That is the pattern of reasoning that says: if a is to b, then c is to some unknown d. Formal theory for this pattern existed mainly for yes-or-no, Boolean domains, where it is provably sound for a narrow family of functions. Regression and continuous domains were left out.

The authors first show, by counterexample, that old generalization bounds fail even in the Boolean case. They then build a unified framework using parameterized analogies based on generalized means, covering classification and regression together. Within it they characterize which functions preserve analogies and prove worst-case and average-case error bounds under smoothness assumptions.
arxiv-2511-10916:
Long Wei and Liheng Hao study reasoning with statements that use words like most and all. They look at broad forms of the classic syllogism, the short proof that links two claims to reach a third. Their focus is on which of these forms hold up and how nested talk that mixes them should be judged.

The authors give formal forms for these claims and prove one key broad syllogism. From it they derive many more valid forms, both plain and modal, plus valid classic forms. They argue the work gives a base for computer handling of English and a method for studying like systems.
arxiv-2511-11016:
Davide Pradovera, Alessandro Borghi, and their colleagues study a spectral problem that sits at the heart of probing hidden materials with waves. The problem links a material's inner makeup to a set of special values, and those values guide methods that image what cannot be seen directly. In theory the values shift smoothly as the material changes.

In practice, the authors show, the map from material to values can kink or split into branches. They give conditions for that rough behavior and study round cases in finer detail. A tracking solver follows the value paths as inputs vary, and tests confirm the predicted splits and reveal new rough effects.
arxiv-2511-11216:
Kebin Wu and Fatima Albreiki investigate positional bias in multimodal embedding models, the tendency to favor content at certain spots in an input regardless of what it says. Such bias is well studied in text generators but barely explored in representation models, and even less in models that join images and text. The authors study the bias in image-text retrieval tasks.

They first separate true content importance from pure position effects, then measure bias across models and data sets. Bias proved widespread but split by modality: text encoders favored the start, while image encoders favored both the start and the end. Encoding scheme, training loss, and paired training all feed the effect.
arxiv-2511-11316:
Vincenzo Amato, Rosa Barbato, and their colleagues prove a quantitative form of the Talenti comparison principle. The setting is the Poisson equation with Robin boundary conditions. Robin conditions mix fixed values and flow at the edge. The classic principle compares a solution on a general domain with one on a ball. It gives no rate, though. A quantitative form says how close the two must sit. The gap is measured through the domain's asymmetry.

The proof tracks how asymmetry spreads. It spreads through the level sets of solutions. As byproducts, the authors give a new proof of a quantitative Saint-Venant bound for Robin torsion. In the plane, they also prove a quantitative Faber-Krahn bound. That bound concerns the first Robin eigenvalue. A rigidity frame for these results is also completed.
arxiv-2511-11816:
Andrea Brunello and four co-authors re-benchmark how well large language models translate natural language into first-order logic, a precise formalism used to specify and verify system properties. Reports on this skill conflict, with some studies praising and others panning the models.

A close audit finds flaws in existing datasets and evaluation protocols, and a new benchmarking strategy is proposed to measure translation more honestly. Under cleaner measurement, strengths hidden by faulty tests come into view. The broader lesson travels: before declaring a capability weak, check whether the ruler is bent. Reliable language-to-logic translation would make formal verification accessible to far more users.
arxiv-2511-11916:
Sinan Urgun and Seçkin Arı benchmark how the scaffolding around a language model changes its abstract visual reasoning, using the RAVEN-FAIR dataset of matrix-style puzzles. Four models, from GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama families, are each wrapped in four reasoning architectures: single-shot answering, embedding-controlled repetition, self-reflection, and multi-agent debate.

Model drawings pass through extraction, reasoning, and tool stages, then are scored with image similarity metrics alongside chain-of-thought quality and error types such as semantic hallucination and numeric misperception. One model led across all architectures. The systematic grid separates raw model skill from architecture gains, a distinction buyers of reasoning systems rarely get to see cleanly.
arxiv-2511-12016:
Youwu Lin and four co-authors unify outlier detection and multi-class classification under label shift. Their method is called MMDCP, and it is distribution-free. When training and test distributions differ, many conformal methods lean on resampling. They grow expensive, and their prediction sets turn wide and unstable on small samples.

Class-specific Mahalanobis-style distances feed a full conformal score. The result is adaptive prediction sets with coverage guarantees. False discovery control is layered on top. One frame thus flags strangers and classifies familiars, with honest uncertainty for both. The coverage promise holds without trusting a model of the data's source.
arxiv-2511-12116:
Piotr Pęzik and six co-authors introduce LLMLagBench, a benchmark for finding where a large language model's knowledge stops in time. Models learn from text up to a cutoff date, and beyond it they cannot know events without outside sources. Worse, they may blend old facts with general knowledge and sound sure while being wrong.

The benchmark tests knowledge of recent events to estimate the earliest likely boundary of a model's training data. The authors apply it to many models, some with stated cutoffs and some without. They check the method by hand validation and by comparing it with public facts about how the models were trained.
arxiv-2511-12316:
Zhijun Zeng, Junqing Chen and Zuoqiang Shi tackle an inverse problem where the times of observations are unknown. For stochastic and quantum systems, they receive only unordered density snapshots, taken at random unknown times. From the spread of those snapshots they must recover the parameters that govern how the system evolves.

Their method, BlinDNO, learns a neural operator that maps a distribution of densities to a function, using an architecture that does not depend on snapshot order. A multiscale encoder and an attention mixer form its core. Tests across many systems, including a protein-folding reconstruction tied to cryo-electron microscopy, show reliable recovery and wins over prior neural inverse methods.
arxiv-2511-12416:
Zack Hassman and four co-authors present ExtraFerm, an open-source quantum circuit simulator tailored to chemistry problems. It computes the chances of measurement outcomes for circuits built from particle-number-conserving matchgates plus controlled-phase gates. Ordinary state vector methods cannot reach some of the systems this class covers.

ExtraFerm supports both exact calculation and an approximate mode. In that mode the cost grows only with the size of the controlled-phase angles. The team demonstrates it on a cluster-based wavefunction method combined with sample-based diagonalization, improving molecular ground-state energy estimates at negligible extra cost. Against tensor network and state vector simulators, they report far better memory scaling in its target regime.
arxiv-2511-12716:
Joanna M. Rankin and eleven co-authors measure emission heights in the pulsar PSR B1237+25 across an unusually wide range of radio wavelengths. This bright pulsar has a classic core and double-cone beam profile that stays clean down to very low frequencies. The team gathered more than a dozen high-quality profiles, from 30 megahertz to 5 gigahertz, from six observatories. Then fitted the components to catch small asymmetries caused by aberration and retardation, effects that reveal how high above the star the radio waves originate.

Their fits give a consistent offset of about half a degree of longitude, pointing to emission heights of a few hundred kilometers at all wavelengths. That flat result challenges radius-to-frequency mapping, the widely used idea that lower frequencies come from higher up. They also find no height difference between the inner and outer cones. The study narrows how pulsar beams can be modeled.
arxiv-2511-12816:
Gregory J. Gilbert and five co-authors ask where giant planets end and brown dwarfs begin. Convention draws the line at the deuterium-burning mass, about thirteen Jupiter masses, but that boundary reflects no formation process. Earlier work hinted at a crossover somewhere between one and ten Jupiter masses. The team studies seventy sub-stellar companions found by Doppler surveys in the California Legacy Survey, orbiting beyond the water ice line. Tracks how their rates, host star chemistry, and orbital shapes change with mass.

Every trend changes gradually across the whole mass range. That smoothness suggests the two formation routes, planets building up from cores and brown dwarfs collapsing from gas, produce objects that overlap in mass. The eccentric orbits could reflect those mixed origins or later gravitational jostling between heavy companions. The study argues the planet to brown dwarf transition is a slope, not a cliff.
arxiv-2511-13016:
Subramanyam Sahoo compares ways of scoring a language model's homework during training. Reinforcement learning from human feedback steers models with rewards, and the reward can be hard, a simple right or wrong, continuous, a graded score, or hybrid. Sahoo builds a unified framework for the three styles and tests them fine-tuning Qwen3-4B with LoRA on GSM8K math problems, with reward signals combining correctness, perplexity, reasoning quality, and consistency.

His adaptive hybrid scheduler shifts between discrete and continuous signals during training, balancing exploration against stability. The hybrid structures converged faster and trained more stably than purely hard or purely continuous rewards. Reward design is often treated as an afterthought in alignment work, tuned by feel. A controlled comparison on a standard reasoning benchmark gives practitioners evidence for a concrete choice: blend the signals, and schedule the blend, rather than committing to one kind of feedback.
arxiv-2511-13716:
Benjamin K. Capistrant and Jason Dittmann catalog stellar flares in TESS light curves of planet-hosting M dwarfs. Cool M dwarfs flare often, and flare rates track age, mass, and spin, while the bursts also complicate the search for planets around them. The survey covers a known active population plus every M dwarf within fifteen parsecs.

Flares were found in just over half the nearby sample, and each star's flare frequency pattern was fit with a power law. The power law slope barely changed between quiet and highly active stars, suggesting the flare distribution holds its shape as activity fades. For stars with Webb atmosphere follow-up, flare levels matched the wider nearby sample.
arxiv-2511-14016:
Rubén Oncala and Joan Soto update the predicted spectrum of hybrid mesons, exotic particles that carry active gluonic degrees of freedom alongside quarks. Interest has grown as experiments keep finding new XYZ mesons that do not fit the standard quark model. Working in Born-Oppenheimer effective field theory, the authors feed in the latest lattice QCD results for hybrid static potentials.

They refine earlier mass calculations for heavy hybrids in the charmonium and bottomonium families and analyze which decays into ordinary quarkonia are allowed, both spin-conserved and spin-flip. A full error analysis accompanies the numbers. Comparing with Particle Data Group data, they assign hybrid or quarkonium readings to nearly all observed heavy isospin-zero mesons.
arxiv-2511-14216:
YunLiang Zheng, Xiaohu Yang, Teng Liu, and ten co-authors ask what actually shines in X-rays inside galaxy groups. Is it hot gas spread through the group, or the active black hole in its central galaxy? Using the first eROSITA all-sky survey, they sort groups by halo mass and redshift. They identify central active nuclei with X-ray, radio, and DESI spectroscopic catalogs, then stack images for statistical power.

Groups with X-ray-bright central engines top the luminosity ranking, followed by quasar, radio, and line-diagnosed active hosts. Below a halo mass threshold the central engine dominates the X-rays, while extended gas takes over in heavier groups. Where the engine dominates, the gas signal stays hard to isolate.
arxiv-2511-14316:
Hua-Lin Huang, Haoran Miao, and Yu Ye solve the Waring problem for complex binary forms. The problem asks how a homogeneous polynomial can be written as a sum of powers of linear forms, and how few powers suffice. For forms in two variables over the complex numbers, the authors give a complete solution using only basic tools from algebra and analysis.

Their treatment includes elementary presentations of the Apolarity Lemma and of Sylvester's 1851 theorem, the classical pillars of the subject. Keeping the proofs accessible is deliberate: the binary case becomes a model approach the authors hope to extend to forms in more variables, where the Waring problem remains substantially harder.
arxiv-2511-14516:
Hao Qian, Shikui Tu, and Lei Xu present PepBFN, a generative model for designing peptide binders at full atom detail. Peptides are short protein chains that can bind target molecules. Past diffusion models mix discrete residue types with smooth atom motion in awkward ways. They also assume side chain angles follow a single peak, which misses real multi peak behavior.

PepBFN works wholly in continuous space by learning distributions over parameters. Residue types and structure then update together in a smooth Bayesian flow. A mixture model captures the multi peak nature of side chain angles. The aim is more accurate full atom peptide designs for drug and biology work.
arxiv-2511-14616:
Lei Chen and Weiyan Chen determine the normal closure of a homological genus zero bounding pair map in mapping class groups. Recent work with Justin Lanier settled the same question for higher genus. The subgroup involved links to the Chillingworth subgroup and the Casson-Morita map. Genus zero remained open until this paper.

The authors show the kernel of that map equals a key commutator subgroup. That kernel is generated by a single bounding pair map of the stated type. They also build one element that normally generates the whole Chillingworth subgroup. The results complete the genus picture for these subgroups and give strikingly small generating sets.
arxiv-2511-14716:
Xiyuan Wang and Muhan Zhang unify latent diffusion into a single end to end trainable network. Standard latent diffusion splits work among an encoder, a decoder, and a diffusion network trained in stages. That split wastes compute and blocks single network designs common in vision foundation models. Naive joint training fails through latent collapse.

The authors trace the collapse to interference between diffusion and representation learning. They draw a novel analogy to self distillation in unsupervised learning. Guided by that analogy, they propose Diffusion as Self-Distillation with key changes to the training objective. The changes stabilize joint training. The result is one model that learns representation and generation together.
arxiv-2511-14916:
Aysha Aamer and 23 co-authors dissect one of the most luminous stellar explosions ever recorded, the superluminous supernova SN 2023taz. Events of this class are the brightest deaths of stars known, and this one sits near the top of the list in peak brightness and total radiated energy. A spinning magnetized neutron star left behind by the blast is the favored engine.

Fits to that magnetar picture give mostly ordinary values, but an odd mix of weak field, low ejected mass, and fast spin explains the extreme output. Around peak light the glow is very hot, yet the ultraviolet share is strangely low compared with similar events. That mismatch challenges simple models of how these explosions shine.
arxiv-2511-15116:
Chung-Yang Wang, Zeming Sun, and three co-authors peer into superconducting films with a microscope that sniffs out the birth of tiny magnetic whirlpools. The films, made of niobium tin, coat the cavities that accelerate particles, and whirlpools nucleated at defects waste energy as heat. The microscope presses a local radio-frequency field onto the surface and listens to a harmonic signal that betrays each nucleation event.

Two films made by different routes, vapor diffusion and electrochemical plating with annealing, are compared. Both show defect-linked nucleation signatures below a certain temperature. The plated film shows extra structures at higher temperatures that the vapor film lacks, a fingerprint of its different defect landscape.
arxiv-2511-15416:
Davide Tornielli Bellini, Dario Tagliaferri, Pietro Grassi, Davide Scazzoli, Stefano Tebaldini, and Umberto Spagnolini show how a future 6G base station could image objects hidden around a corner. Seeing what is not in a direct line of sight is a hard task for systems that mix sensing with communication. Earlier fixes needed a full map of the site or special reflectors placed in the scene.

Their setup uses a plain modular reflector during the normal first link-up, when the station sweeps a narrow beam to find users. Extra beam patterns plus the reflector let the station build a sharp image from echoes. Formulas, simulations, and a real test support the method, including tracking moving targets.
arxiv-2511-15516:
Federico Settimo, Kimmo Luoma, Dariusz Chruściński, Bassano Vacchini, Andrea Smirne, and Jyrki Piilo widen a simulation tool for open quantum systems, which lose energy or information to their surroundings. Stochastic unravelings follow random sample paths instead of a full average, which can be far cheaper to compute. Until now they were largely limited to equations that keep total probability fixed.

Their framework handles general equations that do not preserve that total, needing only basic positivity and symmetry. Sample paths can vanish or multiply to match falling or rising totals. Special cases cover dynamics viewed from the operator side and counting statistics, where the method yields moments of the full outcome distribution.
arxiv-2511-15616:
Aravind Asok, Jean Fasel, and Samuel Lerbet ask when a vector bundle over a real algebraic variety splits off a simple free piece. A variety is a shape defined by polynomial equations, and a vector bundle attaches a vector space to each point in a consistent way. Splitting off a rank-one free summand is a basic structural question with a celebrated answer over complex numbers tied to a top Chern class.

For real varieties, they treat two near-complete cases. In one, the obstructions turn out to be purely topological beyond that class, proved with motivic methods that blend algebra and topology. In the other, several natural guesses for a real analogue of the complex theorem fail, showing the real case is more complicated.
arxiv-2511-15716:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg presents MACIE, a tool that explains how groups of learning agents act as a team. Such multi-agent systems are used in safety-critical work. Old explanation tools fail to credit outcomes to each agent. They also fail to measure emergent team behavior, or capture how agents affect each other.

MACIE mixes causal models, what-if interventions, and Shapley values from game theory. It answers three questions. What did each agent cause? What team-level effects go beyond single agents? And how can the findings be told in plain words? Across four scenarios, from cooperative to competitive, it credited outcomes well, found positive emergence in team tasks, and ran in under a second per data set.
arxiv-2511-16116:
Tan-Dat Khuu, Trung-Hieu Huynh, and Hoang-Hung Vo prove Liouville-type results for a class of degenerate elliptic equations. The driver is a fractional infinity Laplacian. Liouville results say only trivial solutions exist under stated growth terms, ruling out surprise global solutions. Their equation adds a Hamiltonian term based on the solution and its gradient, plus a Hardy-Hénon term that weights position and size.

They extend theory from the classical infinity Laplacian with a new weighted comparison rule and sharp local Lipschitz estimates for viscosity solutions. For power-type terms, precise growth terms give full conclusions. The exponential case is strongly supercritical. There, only partial conclusions hold, under growth assumptions at infinity.
arxiv-2511-16216:
Zhen Hao Wong, Jingwen Deng, and seven co-authors present FlipVQA, a system that mines textbooks to build training data for multimodal models at scale. Textbooks hold rich, human-verified reasoning. But complex layouts, cross-page splits of questions and answers, and interleaved figures make automated extraction hard. Other routes either synthesize data from scratch with no real context, or rely on costly expert notes that cannot scale.

Their mining pipeline resolves long-range links and cross-page breaks in OCR-parsed documents. It recovers question, answer, and figure links even when answers sit in companion volumes. A curation pipeline turns the raw take into AI-ready supervision. The data set spans eleven disciplines at large cost savings over manual work, and fine-tuned models gained in reasoning and cross-domain generalization.
arxiv-2511-16316:
Musa Furkan Keskin and seven co-authors map multi domain security challenges for integrated sensing and communication in 6G transportation. Sixth generation networks will fuse sensing and communication into one system for vehicles. That fusion creates attack points absent from separate systems. Manipulation can mislead perception and control, signals can be spoofed over the air, and protocols cannot detect lower layer attacks alone.

The article organizes threats across cyber physical, physical layer, and protocol domains. An integrated framework unifies protection across those domains. Existing sensing and communication measurements enable lightweight cross checks between layers. Transportation is the motivating setting, where failures carry safety stakes. The vision argues security must be designed across domains from the start of 6G.
arxiv-2511-16716:
Maurizio Atzori and five co-authors present SODA ADVANCE, a tool that judges password strength using what people expose about themselves on social networks and other public sources. Users pick memorable passwords, often built from personal facts, and traditional strength meters ignore how guessable those facts are.

The system reconstructs user data from multiple public sources to test whether a password can be derived from its owner's profile. The authors also probe large language models on both sides of the problem. Models proved able to generate strong yet personalized passwords matched to user profiles, and effective at evaluating password strength, especially when given profile data. Tests with a hundred real users ground the claims, and the discussion flags the risks of the same capabilities in attacker hands.
arxiv-2511-16816:
Lekha Patel and six co-authors estimate the yield of the 2020 Beirut explosion by fusing wildly different evidence streams. The data itself decides how much each stream deserves to be trusted. Seismic waves, crater dimensions, radar imagery, and vision-language model readings of ground-level photographs each carry partial, differently biased information.

Their Bayesian fractional posterior framework learns trust weights for each modality through a Dirichlet prior, automatically weighting each stream's content. The fused estimate lands at roughly a third to a half of a kiloton of TNT equivalent, about twelve to seventeen percent of the theoretical maximum from the stored ammonium nitrate. Uncertainty estimates beat single-modality estimates and stays robust against systematic bias, offering a template for explosion monitoring, disaster response, and forensic analysis.
arxiv-2511-17116:
Yijun Xu and eight co-authors present PEGS, a framework for reconstructing fast rigid motion in three dimensions from blurry video. Large-scale motion defeats standard reconstruction: blur erases detail, and purely visual fits can violate physics. PEGS builds on 3D Gaussian splatting, a fast scene representation, and adds event camera data, which records brightness changes with very fine timing.

Three layers of supervision keep the reconstruction honest: an acceleration constraint enforces physical plausibility, the event stream guides timing, and a Kalman regularizer merges the evidence sources. A motion-aware annealing schedule adapts training to the object's real-time kinematics. The team also contributes the first paired color and event dataset for natural fast rigid motion. Experiments show clearer, more faithful reconstructions than mainstream dynamic methods.
arxiv-2511-17216:
Jureeporn Yuennan, Farruh Atamurotov, and Phongpichit Channuie test an inflation model against a shift in the cosmological data. New measurements from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, combined with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument data, favor a slightly larger scalar spectral index than the Planck satellite reported. That strains standard models of the universe's first instant. The authors study a squared-quartic hilltop potential, modified by a non-minimal coupling between the inflaton field and gravity.

They derive formulas for the slow-roll parameters and the two key observables, the spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, in both weak and strong coupling regimes. In each regime, suitable parameters land on a spectral index near 0.974 with a small tensor ratio, matching the joint constraints from Planck, the Atacama telescope, and DESI. The implied inflationary energy scale stays in the expected high range.
arxiv-2511-17516:
Rohit Chouhan evaluates dynamic window managers, desktop systems that tile application windows on their own instead of letting them float and overlap. Mainstream systems leave users dragging and resizing windows by hand, which wastes time on small laptop screens. Dynamic managers arrange windows into non-overlapping layouts and support multiple workspaces, but they remain niche, mostly on Linux. Chouhan built a prototype with custom layouts and workspace management to test the idea properly.

Heuristic evaluation and statistical testing compared the prototype against floating management. In multi-window workflows, the dynamic manager cut task completion time by nearly 38 percent. The study combines cognitive heuristics with measured performance, giving human-computer interaction research rare controlled evidence for a tool its users swear by. Chouhan argues dynamic window management deserves a place in the mainstream.
arxiv-2511-17616:
Alexander Strunk and Roland Assam introduce Tensor Gauge Flow Models, a new family of generative models that enriches flow-based generation with higher-order gauge structure. Generative flow models transport a simple distribution into the data distribution along a learned flow. Gauge flow variants already dress that flow in gauge fields borrowed from physics; this work goes further, incorporating higher-order tensor gauge fields into the flow equation itself.

The added structure lets the model encode richer geometric and gauge-theoretic patterns in the data, producing more expressive flow dynamics. Experiments used Gaussian mixture models, a standard testbed where the true structure is known. On them, the tensor gauge models achieved improved generative performance over both ordinary flow baselines and the earlier gauge flow models. The paper is a compact proposal, offering the construction and first evidence rather than a large-scale benchmark campaign.
arxiv-2511-18616:
Joseph Malone, Rachith Aiyappa, Byunghwee Lee, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An, and Yong-Yeol Ahn ask what helps a language model guess a person's beliefs: who they are, or what else they hold. Beliefs form a web, tied by logic, habit, and group life. Model skill at that web bears on privacy, tailored persuasion, and stereotype risk.

With data from an online debate platform, the team test off the shelf open weight models at belief forecasts for named users. They vary the clues: traits of the person, past stances, or both. Results weigh which clue drives the forecast and how the two mix. The study maps how models read the belief web that shapes how people reason and talk.
arxiv-2511-18816:
Nimeshika Udayangani, Sarah Erfani, and Christopher Leckie localize odd regions in street scenes with geometry guided scores. Pixel level out of distribution detection marks the parts of a segmentation map that fit no known class. Past ports of image level scores, like energy or entropy, inherit a flaw: overconfidence on strange inputs.

SupLID steers those classifier scores with the shape of the sense space. A local intrinsic dimension gauge reads how data spread near each point, which exposes zones where the space folds oddly. Score and shape checks combine for sharper maps of the unknown. Self driving stacks need such maps to slow for the unseen. Geometry, the team argue, steadies confidence.
arxiv-2511-19016:
E. Quintin and 14 co-authors present a gallery of overlooked optical transients found in the Zwicky Transient Facility archive, many of them tidal disruption events. In such an event a star strays too close to a black hole and is torn apart, flaring for months to years. The events are rare, so each new case grows a thin sample.

The finds came while the team built an early detection tool for the Fink alert broker and ran its classifier on past data. For each transient they gather optical and infrared records from three surveys and check the host galaxy's past nuclear activity. Light curves are fit by both a descriptive and a physical model. The set previews what future surveys must handle.
arxiv-2511-19116:
Young-Pil Choi, Seungchan Lee, and Sihyun Song improve a popular optimization method that works like a crowd reaching agreement. In consensus-based optimization, many particles wander and drift toward a shared point that should sit near the best answer. The classic version needs cutoffs and extra assumptions to stay stable.

A regularized Gibbs weight in their model steadies the shared point and removes those workarounds. The authors prove that particles settle together exponentially fast when the drift is strong enough. They also prove uniform-in-time propagation of chaos, meaning the particle crowd tracks its mean-field limit closely, with bounds that do not grow with dimension.
arxiv-2511-19316:
Xincheng Wang and ten co-authors benchmark dataset watermarking, a defense for image collections used to fine-tune diffusion models. Hidden marks in training images should survive fine-tuning and appear in generated outputs, proving where a model got its style or faces. No shared yardstick existed to judge these methods.

The team sets a threat model and grades methods on universality, transmissibility, and robustness. Current tools do well on the first two and resist common image edits, but fail under realistic attacks. The authors then show a removal method that strips the marks fully without harming fine-tuning, marking a clear challenge for future defenses.
arxiv-2511-19716:
Mitchell Scott and six co-authors set design rules for tools that rescale the steps of stochastic gradient descent. Training slows when the loss surface curves unevenly and when gradient noise piles up. A rescaling tool, called a preconditioner, reshapes the space to fight both effects.

In the space set by the tool itself, the speed of training and the noise floor both come out tied to matching condition numbers. For nonconvex problems, a stability result bounds the chance of leaving a well-behaved region. The rules cover simple and curvature-aware choices, and matter most for science-based machine learning.
arxiv-2511-20016:
Fumin Wang introduces Kernelized Decoded Quantum Interferometry, a noise-toughened version of a quantum optimization method. Decoded Quantum Interferometry promises large speedups on structured problems, but hardware noise and spectral spread make it fragile in practice. Wang's idea is to shape the problem's energy landscape inside the circuit itself.

A unitary kernel placed before the interference step concentrates solution weight into a low-frequency head that the decoder can handle. A new metric, the noise-weighted head mass, measures this effect, and a monotonic improvement theorem ties raising it to higher decoding success under local depolarizing noise. Explicit circuits using chirp and linear canonical transform kernels give clear signal gains on test problems with little extra depth.
arxiv-2511-20216:
Seong, Kim, Kim, and colleagues grade delivery robots by profit, not just success. Their 2025 paper introduces CostNav, a navigation benchmark with economics built in. Existing benchmarks count successes, collisions, and path lengths. Commercial deployment lives or dies on money instead.

CostNav models the full economic life of a delivery robot. Hardware, training, energy, and maintenance costs all enter. Delivery revenue follows service-level agreements with customers. Parameters come from real industry data sources. A learning-based baseline was projected to realistic scale. It met service agreements only forty-three percent of the time. Each run lost about thirty dollars overall. No break-even point exists at that performance. Collision-driven maintenance swamps the cost structure. It makes up 99.7 percent of per-run costs. Upfront hardware and training ran near twenty-eight thousand dollars. Avoiding collisions matters more than saving energy.
arxiv-2511-20316:
Prando and Speziali build lattices from Fermat curves that beat a trusted distance bound. Their 2025 paper constructs function field lattices of growing rank. Lattices from curves inherit a distance floor from gonality. Known examples usually sit exactly on that floor. Elliptic and Hermitian curves supply most of them.

For every n at least four, a new family appears. The Fermat function field supplies the curve. Its 3n total inflection points anchor the construction. The lattices have rank 3n minus one. Their shortest distance grows like the square root of 2n. That exceeds the classical bound tied to gonality. The kissing number, counting nearest neighbors, stays fixed. Second-shortest vectors get a structural analysis too. These are the first explicit families beating the bound at any rank. Coding theory and cryptography both watch lattice geometry. Arbitrarily large ranks join the counterexample club. Geometric intuition about function fields needs updating.
arxiv-2511-20516:
Laing and Orvieto argue a standard piece of Adam can be dropped. Their 2025 workshop paper examines bias correction in Adam, deep learning's default optimizer. Adam rescales its moment estimates early in training to fix startup bias. That correction is included almost everywhere by default. Its actual contribution was poorly understood.

Systematic ablations covered vision and language modeling tasks. With well-tuned hyperparameters, bias correction gave no final performance gain. Without proper learning rate scheduling, it sometimes hurt results. The authors reinterpret correction as a hidden learning rate schedule. Its behavior depends strongly on the two smoothing constants chosen. In effect it acts as a clumsy implicit warm-up. Explicit warm-up plus cosine schedules made it fully redundant. Vision tests used ResNet models on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet. Language pretraining reached identical validation scores without it. Removing it simplifies code and theory alike.
arxiv-2511-20616:
Shen, Pean, Dunson, and Berchuck map where hospital readmission risk runs hot after bone surgery. Their 2025 paper builds a Bayesian model for elderly patients with upper limb fractures. Many such patients die before any readmission can happen. That competing risk distorts simpler analyses badly. Where a patient lives may shape the risk too.

Gaussian processes let risk intercepts and slopes vary smoothly over space. A Hilbert space low-rank trick keeps computation feasible at scale. Baseline hazard curves are modeled as piecewise constant steps. A multiplicative gamma prior shrinks and smooths those curves. Clustering the spatial effects then flags high-risk regions. Readmission costs ran 12.4 percent above first admissions in 2020 figures. National readmission spending topped fifty billion dollars in 2018. Simulations plus Duke Hospital records validated the method. Inference sharpened compared with non-spatial rivals. The maps give policymakers concrete places to intervene.
arxiv-2511-21116:
Lachlan McGinness and colleagues evaluate in 2025 Particle Builder, a board game that teaches the Standard Model of particle physics to secondary students. Particle physics entered many school curricula over the last decade, yet its particles are abstract. The game, built in 2016 by teachers from several countries, turns them into cards listing each particle's charge, spin, mass, and lifetime, drawn from Particle Data Group values.

Players build particles from quarks across seven levels of rising difficulty, reaching exchange particles, colour charge, and neutrino oscillations. The physical game has been viewed over 11,000 times and downloaded more than 2,000 times from CERN's Zenodo archive; a browser version pits students against a simple AI. In trials with 281 Australian high school students, 225 completed pre- and post-tests. Their average learning gain was 0.16 after a one-to-two-hour game session, comparable to the 0.17 gain from a week and a half of traditional instruction.
arxiv-2511-21516:
Linbo Wang, Thomas Richardson, and James Robins compare the three great dialects of causal inference in a 2025 survey aimed at working researchers. Science's central question, what happens if we intervene, has been formalized three ways. They are directed acyclic graphs, the arrow diagrams of cause and effect, structural equation models, and the potential outcomes framework. Each speaks its own language and carries its own philosophical baggage. Practitioners often must translate between them.

Wang and his coauthors clarify how the frameworks connect, where each is strongest, and where each misleads. Worked contrasts make the differences tangible. In their coin-flip wager, guessing heads over tails changes nothing in intervention terms. The counterfactual effect, judged after you guessed heads and lost, is the full prize. The paper is a conceptual map for graduate students and researchers who want to combine the frameworks in real analyses rather than pledge allegiance to one.
arxiv-2511-21616:
Umberto Pappalettera and Francesco Triggiano construct wild but physically disciplined solutions to the equations of an ideal fluid buffeted by noise, in 2025. The three-dimensional Euler equations describe frictionless flow, and random forcing makes their solution theory delicate. Smooth flows may not exist globally, and convex integration work has shown they can be badly non-unique. The question is what extra conditions restore order.

The pair build probabilistically strong solutions, defined on the given probability space, not an invented one. The flows are almost surely continuous in time and Hölder continuous in space. Crucially, they satisfy the local energy inequality, the rule that energy may drain away but never appear from nothing, up to any chosen stopping time. That discipline makes the flows dissipative rather than arbitrary: among many wild solutions, the energy rule singles out the admissible ones.
arxiv-2511-21716:
Anshuman, Ayush Chaurasia, Bogar Prathmesh Balaji, and Shabbir Khuzem Anees hunt computer-written fake reviews with an optimized ensemble, in 2025. Machine-generated reviews now mimic human writing closely enough to poison shoppers' trust at scale. Their system combines heavy text preprocessing and feature extraction with Harris Hawks Optimization, a bio-inspired search that selects the features worth keeping.

On a public dataset of 40,432 original and computer-generated reviews, the optimizer cut 13,539 candidate features down to 1,368, a reduction of 89.9 percent with the signal intact. A stacking ensemble classifier trained on those features reached 95.40 percent accuracy, with precision of 92.81 percent and recall of 95.01 percent, plus an F1 score of 93.90 percent in the reported tests. The authors argue the pairing of ensemble learning with bio-inspired feature selection is what makes machine-generated text recognizable, and note privacy-preserving handling matters when such analytics run in the cloud.
arxiv-2511-21816:
Kawabe and colleagues describe B4R, a new 2 millimetre receiver for the 50 metre Large Millimeter Telescope in Mexico. The receiver uses mixer technology developed for the ALMA observatory and a fast digital spectrometer. Its main job is finding distances to dusty, star-forming galaxies in the early universe by detecting several carbon monoxide spectral lines at once.

During commissioning tests in 2018 and 2019 the team mapped the Orion Molecular Cloud and observed dusty galaxies on the sky, confirming that the system met all of its design specifications. They also measured the telescope's aperture efficiency across the full 130 to 160 gigahertz range of the receiver and found it roughly matched expectations for the dish's surface accuracy. The band also carries lines from deuterated molecules and shock tracers, widening the telescope's chemistry work.
arxiv-2511-21916:
Mejia and Schweitzer study the D(t) form factor of proton and neutron, describing how energy and internal forces are distributed inside them. With strong forces alone, models and lattice calculations agree it is negative and finite. Adding electromagnetism changes the proton's version dramatically at small momentum transfer, flipping its sign and making it diverge, because the proton's long-range Coulomb field reaches far out.

Their neutron analogue of a classical proton model accurately explains the electromagnetic proton-neutron mass difference. After rescaling the residual nuclear forces, their model reproduces lattice data up to momentum transfers of about 1 GeV squared, including the electromagnetic effects. Their headline result is that proton and neutron D(t) stay practically indistinguishable down to momentum transfers near ten to the minus four GeV squared, far below experimental reach. Coincide within a tenth of a percent in the model after regularization.
arxiv-2511-22016:
Le Beux, Audu, Ankeli, and colleagues introduce AfriStereo, the first open dataset and evaluation framework for stereotypical bias in large language models grounded in African contexts. Existing bias benchmarks mostly reflect Western perspectives, so stereotypes affecting African users go unmeasured. Working with communities in Senegal, Kenya, and Nigeria, the team collected 1,163 stereotypes spanning gender, ethnicity, religion, age, and profession, then expanded them with human-checked prompting into over 5,000 stereotype–antistereotype pairs.

Entries passed semantic clustering plus manual review by culturally informed annotators. Testing eleven language models on the pairs, nine showed statistically significant bias, with bias preference ratios from 0.63 to 0.78 favoring stereotypes over antistereotypes, concentrated in age, profession, and gender. Newer models were no fairer than older ones, while domain-specific models looked somewhat less biased. The authors release everything openly to support culturally grounded bias testing and mitigation beyond Western benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-22116:
Zhou, Bouadjenek, and Aryal, data scientists, fill in missing values in messy real-world tables with IVGAE, a variational graph autoencoder designed for heterogeneous data mixing numbers and categories. Imputation methods often assume data are missing completely at random and mangle categorical variables with one-hot encodings. IVGAE builds a bipartite graph linking samples to features, learns the structural dependencies on that graph, and uses two decoders, one reconstructing feature embeddings and one modeling the missingness pattern itself.

A transformer-based embedding module handles categorical variables without exploding dimensionality. Across 16 real-world datasets, at 30 percent missing values, IVGAE consistently improves reconstruction error and downstream classification F1 over competing methods. The tests cover all three standard missingness mechanisms: completely at random, at random, and not at random. Code and data are publicly available, making the approach easy to test on new incomplete tables.
arxiv-2511-22216:
Panov, a statistical physicist at Ural Federal University, solves a class of one-dimensional spin models exactly by an unusually direct route. Many spin and pseudospin chains, Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and decorated variants, admit a transfer matrix, which quietly maps the model onto a Markov chain. Panov writes the free energy in terms of bond concentrations, frequencies of neighboring spin pairs, so the exact solution drops out of minimizing over them.

As the worked example, he treats a dilute Ising chain with interacting impurities. A simple chain with a frustrated ground state where the method reproduces the exact thermodynamics. The paper positions the minimization approach as a complement to the standard largest-eigenvalue machinery. It exposes ground-state phase structure through the same bond statistics and gives a variational handle useful for testing concepts that higher-dimensional models can only approach numerically.
arxiv-2511-22516:
Schack, Krighaar, Lenander, and Lefmann add magnetic samples to the neutron simulation package McStas. Neutron scattering reveals a material's magnetic excitations, the spin waves rippling through its ordered moments, but beam time is scarce. Experiments are planned with ray-tracing simulations. McStas, a widely used package, had no samples for inelastic magnetic scattering, limiting the virtual experiments researchers could run.

Their new component, SpinWave_BCO, simulates scattering from ferro-, antiferro-, and altermagnetic excitations in a body-centred orthorhombic crystal, computing the spin wave energies and intensities from linear spin wave theory. Data from a simulated ultra-high-resolution triple-axis spectrometer matched theory directly and agreed with the SpinW package, tested on the antiferromagnet MnF2 as an example. The authors present it as a proof of concept for a general spin wave component, with wider crystal geometries, more magnetic ions, and neutron polarisation left as future work.
arxiv-2511-22716:
Bassler and colleagues propose a cleaner yardstick for comparing radiotherapy techniques. Spatially fractionated radiotherapy delivers deliberately uneven dose, peaks and valleys across the tumour. Ordinary metrics such as peak dose or equivalent uniform dose give inconsistent verdicts on whether the therapeutic window widened. Their Biologically Effective Particle Number Ratio sidesteps dose averaging: the ratio of total particle numbers, proportional to machine monitor units, needed to reach specified tumour control and normal tissue complication probabilities.

Comparing modalities through the relative BPNR grounds verdicts in measurable endpoints. In their test case, proton minibeam therapy against conventional proton therapy, no normal tissue complications appeared in the minibeam arm even at maximum output, yielding a relative BPNR of at least 1.4 in the reported ratio, favouring minibeams. The framework needs no radiobiological assumptions and applies in principle to other modalities, including FLASH and high-LET radiation.
arxiv-2511-23216:
Sekulovski and colleagues run a preregistered head-to-head of 28 established methods for choosing predictors and handling model uncertainty in logistic regression, the workhorse model for yes-no outcomes. Rather than inventing data, they built simulations on 11 real empirical datasets spanning different sample sizes and predictor counts. They scored every method twice, in ordinary cases and in the separated cases where a predictor perfectly splits the outcomes.

Without separation, Bayesian model averaging with g-priors performed best overall, especially the version setting the prior scale to the larger of the sample size and the squared predictor count. Penalized likelihood methods, above all the LASSO, were the most stable once separation appeared. The local empirical Bayes averaging prior proved the most robust single choice across both regimes, balancing accuracy, stability, and computing cost. This gives applied researchers a concrete default.
arxiv-2512-00016:
Mubarek Mohammed keeps an architect in the loop of AI-driven hardware design and verification. Hardware design keeps growing more complex, demanding better methods. Generative AI can now draft hardware code and testbenches for small components with a few leaf parts.

Scaling that automation to real designs still needs human judgment at key points. The approach pairs model generation with architect oversight, rather than full automation. That balance aims for speed without surrendering correctness on safety-critical chips. Leaf-level components are where current generators succeed, which is exactly why architect oversight is kept for larger assemblies.
arxiv-2512-00316:
Ranking institutions from samples is common, but sample noise makes the ranks themselves uncertain. Onrina Chandra and Min-ge Xie build finite-sample valid rank confidence sets in 2025, covering a broad class of statistical and machine learning models. A confidence set lists the ranks a population might truly hold.

Uncertainty quantification becomes crucial when latent characteristics are poorly separated and many estimated ranks may be wrongly ordered. Finite-sample validity means the guarantees hold at the actual sample size, not just asymptotically. Honest rank sets could keep league tables in education, health, and research from overstating small differences. Rank confidence sets answer with a set of plausible ranks instead of one fragile ordering.
arxiv-2512-00416:
Some operator algebras hide clean combinatorial patterns inside their product rules. Abdelhay Benmoussa investigates normal ordering in the algebra generated by multiplication by x and an integration operator in 2025. The two generators obey a simple commutation relation that drives the whole study.

Normal ordering rewrites products of operators in a standard form, and the numbers that appear often count objects. His work leads to a broader version of the Bessel numbers, one that blends algebra with counting. Such bridges link algebra with counting, and they draw in both operator theorists and fans of integer sequences. Normal ordering is where operator algebra meets the art of counting. The commutation relation is simple, which makes the resulting patterns worth exhibiting. For a reader who likes links, the charm is the bridge. Rules for how marks swap places give rise to counts that no one put in by hand at the start.
arxiv-2512-01516:
Sung Rak Choi and co-authors develop the theory of Morrison-Kawamata dream spaces. These spaces axiomatize varieties that obey a cone conjecture. The class is broader than Calabi-Yau types alone. Cones in the theory encode how divisors and curves can move.

Using the theory, they prove generic deformation invariance for several cones. They apply that to boundedness tasks for varieties. Boundedness asks if varieties of a type form a finite family. Progress there is a core goal in algebraic geometry, with links to moduli theory. Cone invariance under deformation means those cones are traits of the family, not accidents of one chosen member's special form.
arxiv-2512-01616:
Chainesh Gautam and Raghuram Diddigi align language and policy traits for task transfer. Deep reinforcement agents must now solve many tasks in one world. Tasks often come with language labels. Those labels hold sense that could guide transfer.

Their method, CLIP-RL, pulls policy traits toward language traits. Shared traits let a skill learned for one task aid a new one. The agent can use a task's words to set its acts. Better transfer cuts training time when new tasks are added to a robot or game agent. Language grounding also eases human oversight, since a task can be changed by editing its words rather than retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2512-01716:
Louis Lacoste, Pierre Barbillon, and Sophie Donnet find shared structure across bipartite networks. Such networks link two kinds of nodes, like plants and pollinators. Comparing organization across many such networks is a first step to grasp how environment shapes communities.

Past methods study one network at a time. Shared patterns across a collection are missed. Their method hunts for common blocks across the whole set. Pollination systems are the test case. Shared blocks could reveal which interaction patterns persist across sites and seasons. Collections, not single webs, are the unit here, which matches how ecologists actually store years of field surveys across many meadows.
arxiv-2512-02316:
Estimating the trace of a huge matrix, the sum of its diagonal, is a basic task in computing that randomized algorithms now handle by probing the matrix with random vectors. Eric Hallman studies in 2025 two possible modifications of XTrace, a 2024 randomized trace estimator, aiming to sharpen its accuracy.

The first change is a variance reduction step, averaging the algorithm's output after rotating its test vectors by random orthogonal matrices. Trace estimation feeds into log-determinants, uncertainty estimates, and machine learning diagnostics on matrices too large to read fully. Small variance gains matter, because every probe of a giant matrix costs real computation.
arxiv-2512-02416:
Blending many voters' ranked lists into one joint order is prone to clashes. Karen Sargsyan gives a 2025 graph-based frame built on discrete sheaves. It does more than flag a clash. It points to the exact voter links that break the blend.

Older smoothing tools, like HodgeRank, turn ranked lists into scores. In the act, they lose just that local clue. Keeping the discrete form of each ranked list lets the block be traced on the graph. To fix a joint choice, one must first know where it breaks. That holds for votes and for ranked feeds alike.
arxiv-2512-02616:
Sebastian Harris, Volker Schomerus, and Takashi Tsuda study interfaces between two copies of a toy quantum theory. Symmetric product orbifolds are controlled settings for probing gauge theory and holography. Their tractability comes from covering maps, which describe the gauge structure fully in complex terms.

The authors introduce generalized covering maps that define a universal family of interfaces. An interface joins two theories while letting signals pass in a structured way. New interface families give theorists fresh probes of how quantum theories connect, a step toward understanding more realistic holographic systems. Fresh maps of this sort give peers new doors to try in their own work on linked quantum fields and their dual forms in gravity.
arxiv-2512-02716:
Tianyi Zhang and nine co-authors build a small language model for spotting mental health risk on a phone. Mental illness affects hundreds of millions of people, yet early detection stays limited. Large models show promise here, but their size blocks use on everyday devices.

Small models offer a lighter path, though their use for social media based prediction is barely explored. Menta is designed to run on device, keeping data local and costs low. Private, phone based screening could help flag risk earlier, while sending fewer personal posts to distant servers. On phone checks keep the posts on the phone, a plus for teens and folks in small towns alike.
arxiv-2512-02916:
Ayana Ghosh and three co-authors probe how to flip electric polarization in a family of layered materials. Hybrid improper ferroelectrics could serve electronic and spintronic devices, if their polarization can switch reliably. Switching grows from coupled rotations and tilts of oxygen octahedra, a mechanism now well established.

What sets the switching barrier, though, has stayed elusive. The study uses causal reasoning to uncover which factors truly control that barrier. Knowing the levers lets material designers lower switching energy, a step toward low power memory and logic. Low cost flips are the gate to real use. A cell that needs a hard push per flip will lose to plain chips each time.
arxiv-2512-03016:
Debojoti Kuzur and Kamal Krishna Nath ask what a thin topological shell inside a neutron star would do to the star. Neutron stars pack more than a Sun's mass into a city sized sphere. The authors insert a distributional density profile: a massless shell at an chosen radius inside the star.

They build equilibrium sequences for several realistic equations of state with the shell included. Oscillations and gravitational wave signatures shift with the shell's presence. If future detectors hear such shifts, an exotic internal layer could explain data that standard star models miss. Thin shells leave thin marks, but marks are all we get from such far fires. Each mark that can be told from the norm is worth the hunt.
arxiv-2512-03216:
Materials that flash when hit by radiation help detect particles. Alex Bocchieri, John Mamish, David Appleyard, and Andreas Velten present a new imaging idea in this 2025 work. These materials, called scintillators, turn high-energy hits into visible light.

Most current methods use fast single-pixel detectors to time each flash. The authors propose an event imaging approach with a kaleidoscopic design. Better imaging of each flash could sharpen where and when a particle struck. That helps in medical scans, security checks, and physics experiments. Event imaging could also cut the blur that limits current scintillation cameras.
arxiv-2512-03416:
Serving language models to many users needs smart scaling. Ruiqi Lai and co-authors present TokenScale in this 2025 work. Modern serving splits prefill and decode stages, which improves use of hardware but struggles with bursty demand.

Older autoscaling policies rely on lagging signals like GPU use or rough request counts. TokenScale uses token velocity, a timely signal tied to real work. Faster, more accurate scaling keeps response times low without wasting machines. That balance saves cost for firms running large AI services. Token velocity reacts at once to load, unlike utilization gauges that lag behind bursts.
arxiv-2512-03616:
Christian Ewert and co-authors design a compact chip engine for the SHA-3 family of hash functions, hardened against its own faults. Post-quantum schemes lean heavily on these hashes, and small devices need them cheap and trustworthy. Their 2025 architecture unifies SHA-3 and the SHAKE variants in one byte-wise engine.

A two-dimensional parity scheme watches the Keccak state, the algorithm's cube-shaped working memory. It caught every triple fault in testing and nearly all larger fault storms. The protected engine shrank dramatically against prior art while covering every standard configuration. Dropped into a RISC-V system, the safety machinery cost under eight percent extra area.
arxiv-2512-03716:
Some exploding stars eject matter so fast that their spectral lines smear into broad features. Stritzinger and a large team caught one such supernova, named 2020lao, within two days of its explosion. Their 2025 preprint combines early light curves from the TESS and ZTF surveys with spectra, radio, and X-ray observations.

The star rose to peak brightness in under nine days, at a level typical for its class. Light-curve fitting suggests it forged about a fifth of a solar mass of nickel. It threw off a few solar masses of material with unusually high energy per unit mass. The progenitor looks like a compact Wolf-Rayet star with no extended envelope. No radio or X-ray afterglow appeared. The light curve showed no extra glow. If a jet existed, the authors conclude, it pointed far from Earth or choked before escaping.
arxiv-2512-03916:
Dynamic programming solves hard combinatorial problems by stitching together answers to smaller ones, and semiring algebras give that stitching a flexible language. Ambroise Baril, Miguel Couceiro, and Victor Lagerkvist widen the language in a 2025 preprint. Swapping the semiring can turn a decision problem into a cost or counting problem, without raising complexity.

The authors define a semiring extension for any problem with a sensible notion of certificate, making no special assumptions about the algebra itself. A new operation they introduce, the delta-product, lets algorithms count how many solutions achieve minimal cost, an overlooked question they highlight. They test the framework on two very different hard problems: connected dominating sets and constraint satisfaction. For both, they prove fixed-parameter tractability under clique-width and tree-width.
arxiv-2512-04216:
Simulating a quantum circuit is essential while real quantum machines stay small and noisy, but the toolbox has fragmented. Oriol Bertomeu and colleagues present Maestro in a 2025 quantum computing preprint: one interface over simulation methods, choosing among them automatically. Users face a barrier: picking a backend before knowing which fits.

Maestro unifies six simulator families under a single API: state vector, tensor network and matrix product state methods, stabilizer simulation, GPU acceleration, and p-block approaches. A predictive runtime model inspects circuit structure and available hardware, then selects the backend it expects to run fastest. Backend-specific optimisations, from multiprocessing to improved sampling, run behind the scenes. Benchmarks across workloads show Maestro beating individual simulators, for single circuits and large batches alike, especially on high-performance computing systems. The authors position it as an extensible platform for algorithm research and hybrid workflows.
arxiv-2512-04316:
Haoze Guo built ConsentDiff, a tool that tracks how web privacy works in practice over time, and reported the first large run in this 2025 arXiv paper. Privacy on the web shows up in two places: the words of a site's policy, and the clicks a visitor must make in its consent box. Past checks looked at one point in time, so no one could see how the two change together.

The tool saves copies of sites each month, lines up policy clauses to spot edits, and sorts consent boxes by kind using page code and screen images. A new score links what a policy claims to what a visitor can truly do. The run found steady churn in policy text, a shift away from high-friction banner designs, and far better match where the reject choice is clear and easy to reach.
arxiv-2512-04416:
Zhou Liu and co-authors introduce DataGovBench, a benchmark that grades language model agents on real data governance work. Governance keeps data clean, safe, and lawful through shared rules. Language models promise to automate much of it by turning plain requests into data-cleaning code. Older benchmarks test code snippets or chart work, not whether the data itself ends up right. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds tasks from actual governance cases.

The bench holds a wide set of tasks drawn from real practice. A reversed-objective method plants realistic noise into clean data to make the tests fair.
