Strict metrics then grade the whole pipeline end to end. Early runs on leading models expose weak spots in reliability. The authors map where agents drop errors and where they hold up. Such a bench gives teams a honest check before trusting agents with production data.
arxiv-2512-04516:
Damon Beveridge, Alistair McLeod, Linqing Wen, and co-authors built a hybrid search that pairs matched filtering with deep learning to find merging black holes in LIGO data. Gravitational wave hunts scan detector noise for the faint chirp of two black holes spiraling together. Matched filtering is the classic tool, but it strains on odd or weak signals. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the hybrid on the third observing run of Advanced LIGO.

First, fake signals were injected into real noise to grade sensitivity. The hybrid matched standard pipelines for heavier systems above a set chirp mass. Below that mass, its reach faded for the weakest signals. The search also flagged genuine candidate events in the run data for follow-up. Independent pipelines matter because each catches events the others miss. A hybrid that blends both styles widens the net for rare mergers.
arxiv-2512-04716:
Haodong Feng, Lugang Ye, and Dixia Fan propose an AI Fluid Scientist, a framework that runs the full experimental cycle in fluid mechanics on its own. Most AI in the field helps with simulations or data fitting. Bench experiments, with real water and moving parts, stayed human work. Their 2025 arXiv paper closes the loop: the system forms hypotheses, designs tests, drives robots, analyzes data, and drafts manuscripts.

The test bed is a computer-controlled water tunnel whose flow speed, cylinder position, and shaking settings answer to code. Sensors record displacement, force, and torque. The team validated the setup on vortex-induced vibration, where flow makes cylinders sing, and on paired cylinders that disturb each other. Automated runs reproduced classic literature benchmarks. A tireless lab agent could screen far more flow conditions than a human crew, hunting patterns in wakes and vibrations around the clock.
arxiv-2512-04916:
Roger Lidón, Darío Martínez, and Patrick Morris study when a random set of integers is forced to contain a same-colored product triple. Schur's theorem guarantees that in any finite coloring of a long enough row of integers, three numbers of one color satisfy a simple product relation. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how sparse a random subset can be before that guarantee fades, in the two-color case.

The threshold density sits in a narrow band between two close negative powers of the row length, which the authors pin down from both sides. Analogous questions for linear equations are well understood, with settled thresholds and standard proofs. The product setting behaves differently on both counts, demanding fresh methods. Mapping this nonlinear frontier sharpens Ramsey theory's picture of how structure emerges from randomness.
arxiv-2512-05316:
El Mahdi Mouloua and Essaid Mohamed write lecture notes that introduce information theory with an eye toward algebraic coding theory. Information theory, founded by Shannon, quantifies uncertainty and the capacity of channels to carry messages; coding theory builds the error-correcting codes that let real channels approach those limits. The notes develop the mathematical foundations connecting the two, aimed at students and researchers who want the bridge in one place.

The exposition builds from entropy through conditional entropy and mutual information to the noisy channel model, illustrated with the binary symmetric channel, the simplest channel that flips bits. It then presents maximum likelihood decoding — how a receiver should guess what was sent — and Shannon's noisy channel coding theorem, which fixes the theoretical limit of reliable communication. The notes position the probabilistic framework of information theory as the natural partner of the algebraic techniques used in modern coding.
arxiv-2512-05616:
Kati Asikainen leads a large team studying a single layer of iridium telluride. Left alone, this crystal likes to settle into striped patterns at low temperature. Making sheets one layer thick is hard, so the team uses a gold surface to peel off sheets as wide as a few millimeters. Does resting on gold change the material itself, or does the sheet keep the traits it would have on its own?

Using a light based probe that maps how electrons move, backed by first principles sums, they find the low energy behavior looks much like a free standing layer in its simple form. The gold does leave a mark. Bonding between sheet and metal locks in that simple phase and blocks the striped patterns, while strain matters less. The work shows the surface under a thin material can act as a tool, steering which structure the sheet takes.
arxiv-2512-05816:
Robb Calder and four co-authors ask whether the most common known planets are seas of lava. Sub-Neptunes top the exoplanet census, but their sizes and masses fit several interiors. One option is the gas dwarf: rock and iron under a light hydrogen atmosphere. All such planets are born molten. The question is which ones stay that way, since a magma ocean touching the atmosphere would leave fingerprints telescopes could spot.

Using a coupled interior and climate model, the team maps a solidification shoreline separating molten from frozen gas dwarfs. Nearly every detected sub-Neptune, about ninety eight in a hundred, falls on the molten side, if gas dwarfs at all. Mantle chemistry shifts the cooling, but the cases that freeze easily tend to leave the gas dwarf class anyway. The verdict: expect permanent magma oceans, and hunt signs of rock and air in contact.
arxiv-2512-06016:
Clara Tourbez, Cyrille Chevalier, and Claude Semay put a popular shortcut in baryon physics on trial. A baryon contains three quarks, and three body problems are hard. The quark-diquark approximation cuts the work in two: first bind two quarks into a diquark, then bind the diquark to the third quark. The trick is used everywhere, but its accuracy is rarely measured against the real thing. The authors run both calculations with the same semi-relativistic interaction: masses and distances, approximation against full model.

They also present a new procedure for building the potential. The headline result is liberating: a diquark does not need to be compact, a tight little sub-particle, for the approximation to yield good baryon masses. Knowing where it errs tells builders how far to trust it. Such audits convert a habit into a measured tool.
arxiv-2512-06416:
Zhe Li, Lijuan Li, Mengxue Guan, and Sheng Meng find a looser route to a prized magnetic state in stacked crystal sheets. The state, altermagnetism, mixes traits of the two classic magnetic orders and draws interest for fast, dense memory. Past recipes for making it in two sheet stacks of a certain antiferromagnetic type demanded strict symmetry and exact stacking, which real labs can rarely hold.

The team shows that shining circularly polarized light on the stack breaks a key symmetry for them, lifting those strict demands. Their symmetry study finds stacks that keep the state even when one sheet slides, and when the light comes in from varied angles. In a case study on a manganese bismuth telluride stack, the light held distinct forms of the state, and sliding flipped its parity in set ways. Light becomes a tuning knob for designing such magnets.
arxiv-2512-06616:
Rasam Dorri and Rami Zwick name a power gap growing inside human ties with AI: one side forgets, the other side remembers everything. Human bonds rest on mutual forgetting, which makes room for forgiveness, fresh starts, and changed identities. An AI system, often run by a firm, can record, store, and recombine the whole history of its dealings with a person, and deploy that history at will.

The authors call this Memory Power Asymmetry and map it along four dimensions. Those cover how long records persist, how accurate they are, how easily they can be pulled up, and how fully they can be joined. They trace four ways the gap turns into power, from strategic use of the past to growing dependence and vulnerability. Consequences are drawn at the level of the person, the relationship, and society at large, with conditions that blunt or sharpen the effect.
arxiv-2512-06816:
S A Bondarenko and V V Strelkov study how a model atom answers an intense, short laser pulse, and where simple theory starts to fail. For weak fields, step-by-step approximation methods describe the response well. Past a certain strength, though, their answers turn poor no matter how many correction steps are added. The authors instead solve the full time-dependent Schrödinger equation on a computer and track the atom's shifting charge.

To capture strong-field behavior, they fit the computer results with a special ratio-based expansion that stays accurate well beyond the weak-field range. That fit then feeds a simpler oscillator model for other light effects. The model tracks how third and fifth harmonics grow as the laser gets stronger, and how a two-color field produces rectified light. It falls short on one related quantity, the nonlinear refractive index, which the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2512-07216:
Bin Wu and co-authors from an industrial team describe MUSE, a recommender framework that remembers a shopper's whole history rather than a recent slice. Lifelong interest modeling matters in online stores, yet most systems lean on product ID codes, which generalize poorly to rare items and say little about meaning. Pictures and text about products could enrich the picture, and rivals have used them for the first rough retrieval stage while neglecting the fine stage that ranks the finalists.

Their study of both stages reaches opposite conclusions for each. In the rough stage, plain similarity over good multimodal embeddings beats elaborate retrieval machinery. In the fine stage, rich sequence modeling that truly fuses IDs with multimodal signals pays off. MUSE is built on those lessons and now runs in a major shopping platform's display advertising, reading behavior sequences of enormous length with negligible added delay.
arxiv-2512-07316:
Gianpietro Battocletti, Dimitris Boskos, and Bart De Schutter make two robot boats dock with each other as partners rather than as mover and target. Uncrewed surface vehicles swarm harbors and waterways for shared jobs, and sometimes they must link up mid-task. Earlier methods park one vessel and send the other in, wasting the parked boat's ability to help. Here both vessels move, meeting at a location they agree on.

A centralized model predictive controller plans their paths, looking ahead through a model of the boats' motion to keep every constraint satisfied. Because the controller reasons from a physical model, it can anticipate slow disturbances like water currents and cancel them before they push the boats off course. In simulations the cooperative scheme docks the pair faster and more efficiently than the one-mover approaches.
arxiv-2512-07416:
Pınar Akkanat and Levent Kargın, two mathematicians, wrote this 2025 paper on special families of polynomials in pure mathematics. Their subject is the harmonic geometric polynomials, a class built from the familiar harmonic numbers. An older attempt by Keller had posed the problem but left the needed coefficients unsettled.

The authors show how each harmonic geometric polynomial can be written out fully in terms of simpler geometric polynomials. They give several clear formulas for that conversion, then put one of them to work. From it they gain a broader version of a classic identity for harmonic numbers. They also work out integrals that involve these polynomials alone and in pairs. Those integral results lead to fresh formulas for the Bernoulli numbers. Recurrence relations and a finite sum with harmonic numbers round out the findings. Readers in number theory and combinatorics will find new tools for sums and integrals here.
arxiv-2512-07616:
Simon Friederich wrote this 2025 paper on the foundations of quantum physics. It tackles the measurement problem: why quantum math gives averages that lack a plain story. In classical physics, an average is a weighted sum over a map of positions and motions.

Quantum averages are normally computed through inner products in an abstract space. Friederich shows that a tool called Anti-Wick quantization changes that picture. It links each physical quantity to an operator in a way that restores the classical form. The averages then read as true weighted averages over phase space. The result leans on the Segal-Bargmann space, where key operators act as simple steps. A function named the Husimi Q-function becomes a genuine probability density there. Unlike Bohmian mechanics, the approach keeps the standard operator rules intact. It offers a classical-style reading of quantum statistics without new hidden machinery.
arxiv-2512-07716:
Alicia Kendall and fifty-two co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on distant giant planets. Beyond ten-day orbits, transiting gas giants are strangely scarce in catalogs. Farther from their stars, such planets keep cleaner records of how they formed.

The team reports three of them: one Neptune and two Saturns. Each first appeared as a lone transit in the TESS space telescope's data. Ground telescopes NGTS and ASTEP caught the repeat transits that pinned their periods. Two spectrographs, CORALIE and HARPS, weighed the planets by their stars' wobble. The Neptune, NGTS-34b, circles in about forty-three days. It ranks among the longest-period well-measured transiting Neptunes known. Its bright host suits later air studies. The two Saturns each take about twenty-five days per orbit. All three worlds are cool by giant-planet standards.
arxiv-2512-07816:
David Kogan wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on approximate message passing, an algorithm family for inference. AMP iterates its estimates through a matrix again and again. State evolution formulas predict how those iterates should behave on average.

Universality asks whether the predictions survive beyond tidy Gaussian matrices. Kogan proves they do for symmetric matrices with sub-Gaussian entries. His setting allows polynomial nonlinearities inside the iteration. The proof is combinatorial rather than analytic in flavor. Each iterate is rewritten as a sum over tree structures. A Wick pairing algebra then counts the valid pairings of tree edges. That count matches the trees' contribution to the state evolution formulas. Extra trees, the ones outside the pairing scheme, are the danger. Explicit counting bounds show their contribution vanishes as size grows. Moments of the iterates match the predictions for a stated number of rounds.
arxiv-2512-08016:
Jiyoon Pyo, Yuankun Jiao, Dongwon Jung, and a large team of computer vision researchers posted a benchmark paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their benchmark, called FRIEDA, tests whether vision language models can truly reason with maps. Map reading means aligning legends, scales, compass directions, labels, and shapes across one or more map images, a skill needed in disaster response and urban planning.

FRIEDA draws real maps from documents and reports across many regions and fields. Its questions cover topological, distance, and direction relations, and every question needs several reasoning steps. The team tested eleven leading models in two settings, one giving the right maps and one forcing the model to find them first. Even the strongest models scored far below human readers. The gap shows how much spatial reasoning in these models still has to grow.
arxiv-2512-08316:
Kilian H Scheutwinkel, Will Handley, Christoph Weniger, and Eloy de Lera Acedo, astrophysicists and statisticians, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their software, PolySwyft, does simulation based inference for problems where the likelihood cannot be written down, but a simulator can generate fake data. Nested sampling and neural ratio estimation each handle part of that problem well, and this work unites them.

PolySwyft nests rounds of neural ratio estimation inside nested sampling exploration, with a principled rule for when to stop. On toy problems with known answers, it recovered every mode and credible region while calling the simulator fewer times than the leading alternative. It also stays rigorously Bayesian, which matters when results feed real decisions. As a real test, the team inferred cosmological parameters from cosmic microwave background power spectra using a fast emulator. The software is open source, aimed at astrophysics and beyond.
arxiv-2512-08516:
Ainna Yue Moreno Locubiche and Josep Vidal, wireless engineers in Spain, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces are panels that steer radio waves by adjusting many small elements, and a newer beyond diagonal design links those elements together for extra control. The authors test what that buys in a millimeter wave MIMO downlink, where signals travel mostly by line of sight.

They compare two transmission styles: focused beamforming, and full capacity transmission with water filling power allocation. No closed form exists for the best surface settings in either case, so they optimize with a gradient based method that is cheaper than an earlier published solution. In simulations, the beyond diagonal surface beat the conventional diagonal one clearly on spectral efficiency and coverage. The gain matters for dense urban links, where every bit of reflected signal helps.
arxiv-2512-08616:
Fa Peng Huang, a particle cosmologist in China, posted a conference contribution on arXiv in December 2025, written for the TAUP 2025 meeting on astroparticle physics. It asks how dark matter was made in the early universe, if the standard story is wrong. Thermal freeze out has dominated model building for decades, but non thermal production routes are drawing growing attention.

Huang explores several fresh channels for heavy dark matter candidates. They include pseudo Nambu Goldstone bosons, Q balls, and filtered dark matter, arising from dramatic early universe events. The possible engines are evaporating primordial black holes, superradiance, and first order phase transitions. The key point is that these mechanisms naturally produce gravitational waves as a byproduct. Future observatories, from space based LISA to the ground based Cosmic Explorer, could hear those signals. Dark matter might reveal its origin not underground, but in the sky.
arxiv-2512-08716:
Anagha Nitindala and coauthors present the first optical polarization measurements of a black hole X ray binary during a major outburst in recent years. The source, Swift J1727, was watched as it moved from a hard state to a soft state and back to a decaying hard state. On most nights the team detects clear polarization at about the percent level, part of which comes from interstellar material.

A clear change in polarization lines up in time with discrete radio ejections from the source. Its direction differs from angles seen in X rays, radio, and the resolved jet. After removing the interstellar part, the intrinsic level stays roughly steady through the hard intermediate state. The authors argue the signal most likely comes from scattering in a thin disk wind. Its angle offset hints that black hole spin and orbital axis are misaligned.
arxiv-2512-09016:
Haiqian Han and coauthors present the first systematic framework for removing lens flare from event camera data. Event cameras offer high time resolution and wide dynamic range, yet they remain vulnerable to lens flare, an optical artifact. In event streams, flare forms a complex distortion across space and time that had been largely overlooked.

The team first derives a physics based forward model of the nonlinear suppression mechanism behind the artifact. That model enables a benchmark with a large simulated training set and the first paired real world test set, captured with a novel optical system. Their network, E DeflareNet, achieves leading restoration performance on that benchmark. Extensive experiments validate the approach and show clear benefits for downstream vision tasks. Code and data sets are made publicly available. The work opens a new restoration problem for event based vision.
arxiv-2512-09216:
Guangzong Cai and colleagues study a quiet problem in software maintenance: bug reports change priority while they wait to be fixed. In the JIRA tracking system, each report gets a priority level showing urgency. When that level changes, it signals that the bug's importance has been rejudged, and manual rejudging is slow and subjective.

The authors propose predicting priority changes in two phases, one at report time and one during fixing, using features drawn from how the bug's handling evolves. They also handle the imbalance in the data, where most bugs never change priority. Tested on bugs from thirty-two Apache projects, their models scored well in both phases. Performance varied a lot between projects, though it stayed decent overall and held up across priority levels. The work is an early step toward automated triage of changing bug priorities.
arxiv-2512-09516:
Ginés R. Pérez Teruel builds a common language for modified theories of gravity that go beyond Einstein's Riemannian picture by letting the connection, the rule linking directions at points, stand alone. Non-Riemannian branches include metric-affine theories using curvature invariants, Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity, and symmetric teleparallel theories built on non-metricity.

For the first class, the connection equations admit a matrix solution whose square-root form expands into a convergent series in powers of stress-energy content. The Born-Infeld theory likewise solves its connection algebraically, producing a parallel expansion. Both can then be rewritten as a working Einstein equation with corrections grouped by density scale, forming what the author calls a dual effective field theory. He proves a convergence criterion and extends the framework to teleparallel gravity, matching its coefficients and a background case. The result is one shared language for all three families.
arxiv-2512-09716:
Vinod N. Rao leads a team showing quantum random number generation aboard the SPOQC space mission, using its continuous-variable payload. Random numbers are needed for simulation and cryptography, and quantum processes can certify randomness from physics rather than algorithms. The payload's homodyne setup, which measures light's quadratures using its own laser, doubles as the randomness source.

The team quantifies how much randomness can be extracted from homodyne measurements of the vacuum state, bounding the min-entropy, a cautious measure of unpredictability. The extracted numbers were tested against the NIST statistical test suite. From a raw key of about a megabit collected during a single satellite pass, they obtained nineteen and a half kilobits of certified random numbers through the payload's twelve-bit converter. The demonstration shows an in-orbit quantum random number generator, with the same hardware serving as a detector in an uplink scenario.
arxiv-2512-10616:
Sagar Malhotra and a large team weigh the stars of open clusters and count their hidden companions. Unresolved binaries, two stars blended into one point of light, bias mass estimates for both stars and clusters. Using Gaia's third data release for distances plus photometry in several bands, the authors infer each star's mass and, for pairs, the mass ratio between the partners.

Their simulation-based inference fits cluster properties alongside the stars, and tests on fake clusters show that adding infrared photometry sharply improves the catch of lopsided pairs. Applied to forty-two well-populated clusters, the method produced masses and mass ratios for more than twenty-seven thousand stars, with small uncertainties. Two famous clusters, M67 and NGC 2360, get detailed treatment. The high mass-ratio binary share tracks cluster age strongly, and the catalogue sets up population studies of how multiplicity shapes cluster life.
arxiv-2512-10916:
Haidar Esseili and Graham Kribs study a light vector boson, a possible new particle that could link to dark matter ideas. Their particle can couple to ordinary matter through a mix of two currents, with the dark photon as one special case. They work out which experiments and observations already limit such a particle.

The key case is a chargephobic version whose links to electrons and protons are very weak, so beam dumps and colliders barely test it. Neutrino scattering, supernova emission, and early universe data give the strongest limits instead. The authors also point to future experiments, such as SHiP, that could probe the still open regions.
arxiv-2512-11116:
Z. Li and the nEXO collaboration test a custom chip designed to read out signals inside a huge tank of liquid xenon. The proposed nEXO experiment will search for an extremely rare nuclear decay that could reveal whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles. Its detector needs electronics that work while submerged at cryogenic temperatures to keep noise low.

The chip, called CRYO ASIC, sits on fused silica tiles that collect charge from particle events. Tests in a cold chamber and in a liquid xenon stand show stable gain over a full day and reliable built in calibration. Heat from the chip caused boiling in the liquid, but raising the pressure a little controlled it. Noise in the liquid matched simulations and met the design target, supporting the chip as a viable readout solution.
arxiv-2512-11216:
Chihiro Matsui, Thomas Quella, and Naoto Tsuji extend a prized idea in quantum physics, symmetry protected topology, from a system's lowest energy state to special excited states. Most quantum systems thermalise, but a few exceptional states called quantum many body scars stay non thermal and isolated. The authors ask whether a whole family of such scar states can carry topological character.

They define a symmetry protected topological scar subspace, held together by a restricted algebra that generates the scars while symmetries guard its properties. Individual scars may break the protecting symmetries, yet the subspace they form together keeps them. In the well studied AKLT spin chain, the scar subspace built from paired magnons mirrors the ground state's topology, showing the expected string order and responses. Scars could thus offer an experimentally reachable window on topological physics beyond ground states.
arxiv-2512-11416:
Xueming Liu and colleagues devise a better way to dismantle directed networks by removing their most critical nodes. Cutting a network's core apart can stop rumours, block harmful sentiment, or slow epidemics, but most dismantling research assumes links run both ways. Real systems like the web and world trade are directed, and their function depends on the giant strongly connected component, where every node can reach every other.

The authors propose a new importance measure called network incoherence centrality, built on trophic analysis, which ranks nodes by how much their position sustains coherent flow. Removing nodes in that order shrank the strongly connected core faster than leading existing methods across synthetic networks and fifteen real directed networks. The method also triggered the largest avalanches during removal, a sign it finds genuinely load bearing nodes. The findings inform how to build directed systems that resist attack.
arxiv-2512-11616:
Javier Fumanal-Idocin and co-authors present a fast way to grow fuzzy decision trees that people can still read. Fuzzy systems decide with word based rules, like warm or high, which makes them clear. Many older methods, though, give huge rule sets or take far too long to train.

Their method adapts the classic greedy tree split to fuzzy rules. On standard table data tests it matched the accuracy of top fuzzy systems. It ran far faster than slow evolution based methods. Its rule sets also stayed small and used clean word based splits. That mix of speed, accuracy, and clarity suits cases where users must trust and check each choice.
arxiv-2512-11716:
Yaling Ke studies what a trapped light field does to chemical bonds at a metal contact. The setup is a molecule on an electrode, pushed out of balance by a voltage, with a strong vacuum light field confined in a cavity nearby. Such junctions can snap bonds at high bias, a known failure point.

Ke models the linked electron, vibration, and photon system with exact quantum dynamics. The bond follows a Morse curve, so stretching and breaking are built in. When the cavity tone matches a rung of the vibration ladder, reaction rates drop sharply. A multi tone cavity can then drain vibration energy step by step. That cooling trick could shield junctions from voltage damage.
arxiv-2512-11816:
Enes Özeren and Matthias Aßenmacher test whether reinforcement learning can teach language models to think in silent vectors instead of words. Word by word chain of thought wastes tokens on grammar, not logic. Latent space thinking reasons in raw number vectors, but the leading recipe, Coconut, proved touchy and weak on hard math.

The pair try GRPO, a popular reinforcement method, and craft a Latent RL method that rewards the hidden thinking steps directly. Even so, the trained models still trail plain word based reasoning on math tasks. The honest negative result, with public code, maps a real limit and warns builders that latent thought needs more than a reward tweak.
arxiv-2512-11916:
Nicholas J Daras gives two simple algorithms that reshape data sets while keeping every angle intact. One shrinks a data set into fewer dimensions, the other lifts it into more. Both work on any data set, whether or not it has a hidden low dimension.

The methods chain conformal maps, which preserve angles by design. The image data set keeps all pairwise angles exactly, so local shapes survive untouched. Global size and shape do bend away from a chosen center point. Such angle true reshaping could help visualization, where local pattern matters most, and feature building, where raising dimension can expose structure. Daras stresses the low complexity of both methods.
arxiv-2512-12016:
Mevan Wijewardena, Kamiar Asgari, and Michael J Neely study rate picking for a single server queue where the channel quality is unknown. Each time slot, a transmitter picks a rate. The send works only if the rate stays under the hidden channel capacity. Only a success or failure signal comes back.

Their phased algorithm keeps refining a grid over the rate range and never needs to know the slack between arrivals and capacity. It guarantees average queue size growing like log factors over slack cubed. A converse proof shows no method can beat slack squared in the worst case. If the slack is known, a simple UCB policy matches that bound, closing the gap.
arxiv-2512-12116:
Muhammad Bilal Shahid and co-authors pair learned forecasters with a corrector that cleans up their drift. Any learned time series model, continuous or discrete, piles up error over multi step forecasts. Their predictor corrector frame lets the first model forecast freely, then fixes the result.

The corrector is a neural controlled differential equation, built to handle unevenly sampled series. It pairs with both continuous and discrete time predictors. Two regularization tricks sharpen its reach beyond the training range and speed its training. Stability and convergence guarantees back the design. Across synthetic, physics, and real data, forecasts improved for every predictor tried, from neural ODEs to DLinear.
arxiv-2512-12216:
Yiqi Zhu, Apurva Gandhi, and Graham Neubig present SWE-Playground in a 2025 paper on training coding agents. Past training used tasks built from real GitHub issues and their tests. That ties training to old projects and mostly to fixing issues, a narrow slice of what software engineers do.

SWE-Playground builds projects and tasks from scratch with strong language models and agents. It can teach wider jobs, like writing tests that reproduce a bug or building a library from nothing. Tests on three benchmarks show its training paths carry dense signal. Agents reached matching scores with far fewer training paths than older methods needed.
arxiv-2512-12316:
Edoardo Sernesi studies nodal plane curves and their Hodge structures in a 2025 math paper. A nodal curve has simple crossing points called nodes. The Severi variety gathers all irreducible plane curves of a given degree with a set number of nodes, and Sernesi asks how their inner geometry shifts as the curve moves.

He proves the infinitesimal variation of Hodge structure is maximal for every such curve of degree at least 4. That means the curve's period data moves as freely as possible within the family. A first result covers families of curves mapping onto a fixed curve. Maximal variation holds there exactly when the target curve has genus zero.
arxiv-2512-12616:
Siddhant Manna, Shantanu Desai, and Roman A Krivonos search for hard X-ray and soft gamma ray emission from a merging galaxy cluster in a 2025 paper. The cluster SPT-CL J2012-5649, also called Abell 3667, sits at redshift 0.0556 and hosts radio relics from merger shocks. Those shocks imply relativistic electrons that should emit inverse Compton light at higher energies.

Using archival INTEGRAL/ISGRI data in the 30 to 300 keV band, with 2817 seconds of effective exposure, they detected no significant emission. The spectrum matched pure background. They set a 3 sigma upper limit of 3.63 times 10 to the minus 10 erg per square centimeter per second, the strictest soft gamma ray constraint on this system so far.
arxiv-2512-12816:
Hasan Burhan Beytur, Haris Vikalo, Kevin S Chan, and Gustavo de Veciana study how to split resources between training and deploying machine learning models as data patterns drift in a 2025 paper. A model provider ships models to many clients whose devices can run inference but cannot retrain, so the provider carries the upkeep burden under a limited budget. When to retrain and when to redeploy are linked choices.

Their model agnostic framework captures how allocation, drift dynamics, and deployment timing interact. Optimal training policies hinge on the aging properties of concept durations: under sudden changes, they derive optimal policies for decreasing mean residual life settings and show intuitive heuristics fail under increasing ones. The deployment problem is quasi-convex under mild conditions, and a randomized schedule gets near optimal client performance.
arxiv-2512-13016:
K. U. Can and co-authors, for the QCDSF team, work to pin down the pion's electromagnetic form factor at large momentum transfer. This quantity describes how the pion, a light particle made of quarks, responds to electric probes. Lattice simulations struggle here because noise grows and the boosted pion is hard to isolate.

They apply the Feynman-Hellmann theorem plus two noise cutting tricks: all-mode averaging and momentum smearing adapted to back-to-back momentum states. Each trick helped on its own at the same computing cost. Combined, they gave a strong early improvement in the form factor value at a momentum transfer squared of 6.6 GeV squared.
arxiv-2512-13316:
Mayank Gulati, Benedikt Gross, and Gerhard Wunder present ALIGN-FL, a federated learning method for clients whose data barely overlap. Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw data. Standard versions swap full model weights, which fails when clients use different architectures or hold disjoint data.

ALIGN-FL instead shares only generative components, so clients pass capabilities rather than parameters, and the server trains on synthetic samples. Two privacy tools, adaptive clipped DP-SGD and a regularized variational decoder, map sensitive outliers toward typical points. Tests on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST held up in extreme non-IID settings, including heterogeneous client architectures working together.
arxiv-2512-13616:
Laurenz Kremeyer, Bradley J. Siwick, and Samuel Huberman study heat flow that departs from simple diffusion in crystals. For low-conductivity materials with large cells or strong anharmonicity, the Boltzmann view misses tunneling between overlapping phonon bands. The Wigner Transport Equation includes that effect.

The authors solve that equation to track phonon populations and coherences under any heat source. They apply the method to CsPbBr3 and La2Zr2O7, using first-principles data. They predict large gaps from bulk conductivity at scales of hundreds of nanometers to a few microns at room temperature. Those scales sit within reach of current lab tests, so the forecasts can be checked directly.
arxiv-2512-13716:
Yitong Luo and co-authors introduce ValuePilot, a two-phase framework for AI decisions that match a person's values. Personalized choices matter as AI agents act in the real world, yet most systems chase task success or group alignment. Human values offer stable signals that can transfer across settings.

ValuePilot pairs a dataset generation toolkit with a decision-making module. The toolkit builds varied, value-annotated scenarios through a human and LLM pipeline. The module learns to judge actions by personal value preferences, giving context-sensitive choices. On unseen scenarios, it beat strong baselines including GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2-flash, and Llama-3.1-70b at matching human choices. The authors frame value-driven choice as a path to interpretable, personal agents.
arxiv-2512-13816:
Zhaoyu Bai and co-authors re-examine whether neutron star superradiance can probe ultralight bosons such as axions and dark photons. Stellar cooling already limits how strongly such particles couple to matter. Superradiance is a distinct process: bound boson modes grow by taking rotational energy from the star.

Cooling probes boson emission at thermal wavelengths, while superradiance modes have wavelengths near the star's size. Past work linked lab-scale absorption rates directly to superradiant growth, giving rates near pulsar spindown times. The authors show that naive link fails in dense nuclear matter. Repeated nucleon collisions, a collective effect, change the low-energy absorption felt by the bound state. That strongly suppresses the rate relevant for superradiance, especially the naive vector field rates.
arxiv-2512-14416:
Björn Liljegren-Sailer addresses a bottleneck in model order reduction, where a large simulation is replaced by a much smaller model that behaves the same. For nonlinear systems the small model still needs its nonlinear terms approximated, and empirical quadrature does that job well. Its training step, though, works on a matrix that grows with both the number of snapshots and the model size.

Compressing the training data in a structured way before training shrinks that matrix itself, rather than just processing it faster. Offline cost and memory dropped by roughly a factor of ten in his tests. Error analysis and numerical examples indicate accuracy is preserved.
arxiv-2512-14616:
Survey answers about program participation are sometimes simply wrong, and that misclassification can distort economic estimates. A partial remedy exists when one answer category can be checked: follow-up questions can validate one category, while the other category stays unverified.

Two economists study how to estimate binary choice models under exactly this partial validation setup. Their setting matches real surveys on program take-up, where confirming one kind of answer is feasible but checking every answer is not. Sound methods here matter because participation estimates drive policy judgments about who a program reaches. The paper gives researchers a firmer way to use imperfect survey data.
arxiv-2512-15116:
Runze Li and six coauthors fill gaps in multivariate time series by teaching a diffusion model to think in frequencies. Missing values plague sensor data in health care, traffic, and biology, thanks to failures and irregular sampling. Transformer and diffusion imputers work well, but they mostly model time directly and miss the rhythm in the data.

Their framework, FADTI, adds a Fourier Bias Projection module that injects learnable, frequency aware bias during denoising. It works from hidden states rather than from masked raw input, and comes in DFT, STFT, and FSST variants for global cycles, local time frequency shifts, and wobbly oscillations. Self attention and gated convolution complete the design. On several benchmarks, including a new biological one, FADTI improved accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and sampling speed, above all when missing rates were high.
arxiv-2512-15616:
Fabio Guglietta, Diego Taglienti, and Mauro Sbragaglia extend a droplet deformation model to include interfacial viscosity in a 2025 paper. A droplet in shear flow stretches from a sphere into an ellipsoid, and surface tension pulls it back. Real interfaces can also resist shearing and stretching themselves, which older simple models ignore.

The extended Maffettone Minale model adds interfacial shear and dilatational viscosities through two Boussinesq numbers. The authors map where the simple model stays realistic as the capillary number and those numbers vary. They check model predictions against fully resolved numerical simulations. The result is a cheap tool with a known range of trust for droplet studies.
arxiv-2512-16116:
Li Guo and three co-authors connect several algebraic structures in their arXiv mathematics paper, posted in 2025. Braces are algebraic systems that produce solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation, a famous equation from physics and knot theory. Rota-Baxter operators, borrowed from integrable systems and Lie group factorization, are another classic tool.

The authors define relative Rota-Baxter operators on braces and on post-braces, a newer variant. They show each such operator on a brace creates a post-brace, and every post-brace comes back from an operator on a smaller brace. Each post-brace yields two equivalent solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. For a special enhanced class, they prove a factorization theorem and give examples, including one from the three-dimensional Heisenberg Lie algebra.
arxiv-2512-16416:
Vincent Van Eylen leads a very large author list in their 2025 white paper, submitted to a UK Space Agency program on the future of space science. Its subject is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, NASA's planned flagship telescope of the 2040s, designed to search for life on other planets and to transform broad areas of astrophysics.

The paper argues the United Kingdom is well placed to lead the design and construction of the observatory's High Resolution Imager, its main camera. That instrument is likely to produce the mission's most visible public impact. Early participation, the authors contend, would return investment to UK industry and secure generational leadership for the UK in space science, technology, and astrophysics. The document is a strategic case for involvement rather than a research report.
arxiv-2512-16716:
Sanjeeb Poudel, Sanghyun Lee, and Lin Mu build a pressure-robust enriched Galerkin method for flows where heat drives motion, the Boussinesq regime that covers air and water with mild heat gaps. Standard methods can let pressure errors spoil the flow field.

Their scheme pairs smooth Lagrange elements with a small extra vector per cell for speed, and a flat pressure per cell, all inside standard software frames. Rebuilt velocity fields that are exactly divergence-free keep the method robust, even on badly warped grids. Tests with Picard steps and Anderson speed-up show steady, fast results at high Rayleigh numbers, where heat-driven flow turns fierce.
arxiv-2512-16916:
Juno C. L. Chan and coauthors reanalyze GW231123, the most promising case yet for gravitational wave lensing, where a cosmic mass bends waves from a black hole merger. Lensed waves could map dark matter clumps, but proving lensing takes huge simulation counts.

A deep learning tool, DINGO-lensing, cuts inference from days of CPU time to minutes. With over 200,000 simulations across three waveform models, the team finds the lensing signal sits below four sigma, too weak to claim. About 8 percent of unlensed look-alikes favor lensing, a warning about short signals. Waveform choice only lowers the score, yet the speed shows the hunt for a true lensed event is within reach.
arxiv-2512-17316:
Michael Merry, Pat Riddle, and Jim Warren propose a test for whether an AI model is truly explainable by design. The field calls that gold standard inherent explainability, yet no shared test exists; most work leans on gut feeling. Their test turns gut feeling into something a regulator could check.

A model passes if it can be split, using graph theory, into small parts that each carry a clear local explanation. Those local notes must then join back into one global account, in a hypothesis-and-evidence form others can verify. The team works the test in full on PREDICT, a heart risk model used in New Zealand clinics. A large tangled model, they argue, would fail where a sparse network passes.
arxiv-2512-17416:
Martin Krebs and three co-authors speed up the explanations behind an AI that flags prostate cancer in tissue images. Doctors will not trust a bare verdict; they want a map showing which areas drove it. The standard way to draw that map, hiding one patch at a time, is so slow that it stalls daily work with pathologists.

With no agreed way to compare explanation methods, the team first set fair criteria and measures. Their tests picked a rival method that matched the old map's quality while running at least ten times faster. Near-instant explanations let doctors probe the model live and argue with it. The same selection recipe, they suggest, can guide other medical imaging teams.
arxiv-2512-17616:
Vinícius Francisco da Silva, Heitor Leite, and Fernando Magno Quintão Pereira grow fake computer programs the way a botanist grows fake trees. L-systems, invented to model branching plants, rewrite a short seed pattern again and again into sprawling structures. Pointed at code instead of branches, the same trick yields huge, tangled programs in C, C++, Julia, and Go.

Such grown programs make honest stopwatches for compilers, which bug-hunting fuzzers were never built to be. The team times clang against gcc, tracks gcc's code quality across its history, and probes how profile-guided tuning shifts speed. They also race the four languages against each other and dissect a common library's data structures. Controllable, realistic benchmarks are the deliverable.
arxiv-2512-18116:
Satyaki Sikdar leads a nine author team mapping cyberbullying on Instagram as a web of roles. Past work mostly counted nasty words. Their study uses human marked data from over 400 posts to build session graphs, where each user is a node tagged as bully, victim, or defender, and comments form the links.

Two scores sum up each session: net malice from bullies, and net support reaching victims. In most sessions attacks outweighed support for victims, while bullies faced slightly less pushback than they dished out. Small repeating patterns showed defenders present again and again, a sign that pushback is a built in part of these fights, not a rare rescue.
arxiv-2512-18416:
Jiangqi Dai, Mohsen Ghaffari, and Julian Portmann work on fast algorithms for huge graphs. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, estimates a graph's arboricity, a number that measures how dense the graph is in terms of overlapping forests. Older methods could only pin it down within a factor that grew with the graph's size, even when allowed near-optimal time.

The authors give a randomized algorithm that reaches a constant-factor estimate while asking only about n over lambda adjacency queries, where n is the number of nodes and lambda the arboricity. That query count is nearly the best possible. The trick is to run many recursive samplings in parallel under a careful schedule, so bad runs cannot slow the whole search. The result settles an open question from a 2022 paper.
arxiv-2512-18516: James M. Cline wrote this two-page comment, posted to arXiv in December 2025, on a recent paper about spontaneous baryosynthesis. That process, driven by a rolling phase field in the early universe, may explain why matter came to outweigh antimatter. The commented paper (arXiv:2512.11011) tried to improve on 1994 work by Dolgov and Freese. It dropped their small-angle approximation. Cline points out a serious technical shortcoming in the new derivation. That flaw puts the paper's claimed improvement in doubt.
arxiv-2512-18716:
Chenyu Wang, Wanjian Yin, and Ke Zhou ask what happens to water squeezed into a layer one molecule thick. Water's habit of splitting into H3O+ and OH- ions underlies acid-base chemistry and life itself. Using first-principles calculations and machine-learning-driven molecular dynamics, their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, finds confinement rewrites that chemistry.

Monolayer water splits into ions far more easily than ordinary bulk water. Confinement rearranges both the bonds inside each molecule and the hydrogen-bond network between them, while flat dipolar correlations amplify dielectric fluctuations. The authors suggest such two-dimensional water could act as a superdielectric and show superionic behavior, matching recent experiments. The findings matter for earth chemistry, cell biology, and nanofluidic devices, anywhere water works in tight spaces.
arxiv-2512-19016:
Liming Lu and three co-authors present DREAM, a red-teaming framework that attacks AI agents across many digital settings. Most safety tests use one short exchange, which misses attacks that build over many steps. DREAM instead keeps a graph of known weaknesses that spans different environments.

A search method uses that graph to chain small attack steps into long plans, drawn from nearly two thousand actions in hundreds of settings. Against twelve leading agents, the chains worked in over seventy percent of cases for most models. The failures point to weak tracking of harmful intent over time, and defenses based on a first prompt helped little.
arxiv-2512-19116:
Chaoyang Hu, Mingyong Jing, Zongkai Liu, and Shaoxin Yuan image microwave fields without disturbing them, using a probe built on Rydberg atoms. Metal probes scatter the very near fields they measure, which ruins accuracy close to a source. Their probe is a compact, fiber-linked device designed to leave the field nearly untouched.

Working in the reactive near field, the probe reached a resolution of one fifty-sixth of a wavelength. Its maps matched full-wave simulations almost exactly. The team frames the result as the first reactive near-field imaging of this kind with a Rydberg probe. Uses include antenna checks, circuit diagnostics, and biomedical imaging.
arxiv-2512-19216:
J. I. Opadara and M. E. Egwe study frames of band-limited functions on Dirichlet spaces of homogeneous type. Such frames act like flexible building blocks that can rebuild signals and functions from local pieces. The setting is broad: spaces with a doubling measure and a scale-invariant Poincaré inequality, where heat kernels come with Gaussian bounds.

The authors show the localized frames exist in that full generality, and give non-zero descriptions of natural spaces such as Besov spaces. Frames also arise on homogeneous Lie groups with polynomial volume growth, and on manifolds with curvature bounded below. Their build-up makes many function spaces easier to use in harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2512-19316:
Marica Muffoletto and four co-authors rebuild three-dimensional heart shapes from only a few clinical image slices. Sparse scans are routine, yet patient-specific heart models need full anatomy. Their method first maps each case into Neural Implicit Heart Coordinates, a shared frame based on universal ventricular coordinates.

A network predicts those coordinates from a handful of two-dimensional segmentations. A decoder then expands them into dense three-dimensional segmentations and meshes at any chosen resolution. Trained on five thousand heart meshes, the model kept surface errors near two and a half millimeters in a large diseased group. It stayed reliable even with severe slice gaps and noisy outlines.
arxiv-2512-19416:
Mamoru Saita and Yutaka Hori join droplet microfluidics with machine learning to learn how temperature steers reaction speed. Temperature bends chemical and biochemical kinetics in nonlinear ways. Most data-driven work, though, models only final yields from sparse runs, not the full time course of a reaction.

The platform holds thousands of droplets still for long time-lapse imaging while a thermal gradient sweeps across them. That yields parallel, time-resolved data under many temperatures at once, exactly the feed that kinetic models need. Learning from such traces aims to capture transient behavior directly from experiment. The authors present the setup as the missing end-to-end link for thermal kinetics.
arxiv-2512-20016:
Areg Danagoulian proposes using cosmic radiation to police a treaty. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons in orbit. It has 117 parties, with all major space powers among them. Yet it has no verification scheme. Fresh official worries make that gap concrete. They concern a possible Russian nuclear-armed anti-satellite device. A blast in low Earth orbit would wreck most satellites there.

His concept listens for neutrons. GeV protons in the inner Van Allen belts knock neutrons loose inside a satellite. A hidden thermonuclear weapon would betray itself by that neutron mark. The sums say a 9U CubeSat detector could spot such a weapon. It would do so from four kilometers away, in about a week of watching. The feasibility study aims to seed real verification platforms.
arxiv-2512-20316:
Tushar Singh, Gyanendra K Verma, and Shiv Datt Kumar extend classic ring theory by relativizing it to a chosen subset. Fix a multiplicatively closed set S inside a ring R. Notions such as integral domain and field then get S-versions, where the usual requirements are only enforced after interaction with elements of S.

The authors prove an S-version of the Krull intersection theorem and carry several integral-domain results into the S-setting. They show that localizing an S-field at S yields a field in the corresponding relativized sense over the localized ring, with the converse holding when S is finite. A neat consequence is that every finite S-integral domain is automatically an S-field. Examples throughout illustrate why the new notions are genuinely broader.
arxiv-2512-20616:
Javier de Cruz Pérez, Adrià Gómez-Valent, and Joan Solà Peracaula line up a crowd of dark energy models and ask the newest data to judge them. Contenders include the running vacuum family in several variants, a recently proposed hybrid model, the standard cosmological constant picture, and the popular two-parameter evolving equation of state.

Two supernova compilations, Pantheon+ and the DES five-year sample, are each combined with baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI and cosmic microwave background data from Planck. No structure-formation data or local distance-ladder calibration is used. Even so, the flipped running vacuum model, and to a lesser degree its cousins, show significant evidence for dynamical dark energy, most visibly with the DES sample. Interacting vacuum models hint the same way, more weakly.
arxiv-2512-20716:
Sondre Vik Furuseth and Guillaume Aulanier watch a solar flux rope assemble itself in a simulation. Flux ropes, twisted bundles of magnetic field, are the pre-eruptive structures behind coronal mass ejections, so predicting space weather starts with understanding their birth. The question is whether photospheric flux cancellation alone can build them from sheared arcades.

A three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulation with the Bifrost code supplies convection for free; no external forcing is imposed after a sheared field is inserted. Over two and a half hours, a rope forms with footpoints up to twelve megametres apart. Slipping reconnection, loop emergence, and tether-cutting reconnection all contribute, and not every cancellation helps. Formation is messier than the smooth textbook model, yet the verdict stands: flux cancellation works.
arxiv-2512-20816:
Philip Korman and Dieter S. Schmidt study resonant oscillation problems posed as partial differential equations on balls and rectangles. Resonance, where a driving term matches a natural frequency, often makes such problems tricky or hopeless. Earlier results often needed the first harmonic of the forcing term to vanish or stay small.

The pair remove that restriction. They prove countless solutions exist for a whole class of these problems and describe the full set of solutions as a whole. They also derive formulas that approximate large solutions using their first harmonic. Worked examples show the formulas hold up well. The work widens the range of resonant systems where solutions are sure to exist.
arxiv-2512-20916:
Haoyu Wang, Yitong Wang, and Jining Wang recommend the next item in a user's history using pictures, text, and keywords. Multimodal models understand products richly, but earlier systems either hid that understanding in opaque embeddings, paid huge computing costs, or ignored what similar users did.

Their framework, MMSRARec, first has the model summarize each item into short keywords. A reward balances brevity against lost information, teaching good summary habits. Signals from similar users become keywords too, added as retrieved context. Multi-task fine-tuning then aligns everything with the recommendation job. Tests on common datasets showed accurate, efficient recommendations that a human can read and audit.
arxiv-2512-21016:
Giacomo Graziani counts, with algebraic geometry, how hard it is to fit the simplest neural network. The Euclidean distance degree of a model measures how many critical points arise when fitting it to data, a proxy for the hardness of the optimization landscape. For shallow networks with two neurons, quadratic activation, and scalar output, the model's parameter space is matched with a classical object, the second secant variety of a quadratic Veronese embedding.

Graziani defines a virtual version of the degree from polar classes and reduces its counting, through intersection theory and Kempf's resolution, to concrete intersection numbers on a Grassmannian. Equivariant localization then proves the count grows as a stable polynomial in the input dimension. Homotopy-continuation tests show how the count shifts with the choice of metric, telling the generic case apart from special ones such as Bombieri-Weyl.
arxiv-2512-21316:
Ali Merali treats language models like capital equipment and asks what another year of progress buys a working professional. In a preregistered experiment, over five hundred consultants, data analysts, and managers performed real professional tasks, each assisted by one of thirteen language models spanning the recent capability range. Regressing task time against the models' training compute yields an economic scaling law.

Each year of model progress cut task completion time by about eight percent. Decomposed, fifty-six percent of the gains trace to larger training compute and forty-four percent to algorithmic improvement. The gains were unevenly shared: straightforward analytical work sped up far more than agentic workflows that demand tool use and multi-step execution. Extrapolated, continued scaling could lift United States productivity by roughly twenty percent within a decade. For executives and forecasters, the study converts AI hype into a measurable depreciation schedule for knowledge work.
arxiv-2512-21416:
A large collaboration led by Google Quantum AI reports an experiment where disorder, usually the enemy of quantum order, creates a superfluid. The work used a superconducting quantum processor whose units act as qutrits, systems with three usable energy levels instead of the usual two.

In a clean system the particles form a Mott insulator, an incompressible state with particles locked in place. Adding disorder normally destroys coherence, but with three levels per site it can open resonances that restore mobility. Measurements map the insulator and the compressible phases around it, some showing glassy, non-ergodic behavior. Other measurements find regions with a nonzero condensate fraction, the signature of a superfluid. The team also images a phonon mode that appears even after disorder is added to the clean insulator. Together, they give strong evidence for disorder-induced superfluidity.
arxiv-2512-21616:
Rongpei Hong, Jian Lang, Ting Zhong, Yong Wang, and Fan Zhou study personalization for multimodal language models over long conversations. Personalization means the assistant remembers a concept, such as the user's own pet, and refers to it correctly. Existing methods and benchmarks test simple identification and name replacement, ignoring how concepts change across a dialogue history.

The authors introduce LCMP, a benchmark for long-context multimodal personalization. It tests whether a model notices variations in a personalized concept and answers in ways that reflect those changes. Their baseline system, TAME, needs no training and keeps two kinds of memory per concept, separating passing variations from persistent ones. A retrieve-then-align step filters memories down to what fits the current question. On LCMP, TAME performed best among the systems tested. The work reframes personalization as a state-aware conversation skill rather than a one-time labeling trick.
arxiv-2512-21716:
Shengminjie Chen, Xiaoming Sun, and their co-authors design quantum algorithms for combinatorial optimization with proofs about solution quality. Quantum optimizers are usually heuristics: they often work well, but their approximation ratio, the guaranteed fraction of the optimal value, is rarely known in advance. The obstacle is that the optimum itself is unknown.

Their method builds a Lyapunov function, an energy-like quantity designed never to decrease. Enforcing that monotonicity produces a controlled Schrödinger evolution, a quantum dynamics that a quantum device can simulate. The second ingredient bounds the unknown optimum using the current quantum state, which closes the loop and yields approximation guarantees. They apply the method to Max-Cut, turning it into an adaptive variational algorithm with a Hamiltonian ansatz. The algorithm avoids assumptions about the ansatz and the graph, and replaces training with a tunable function driven by measurement feedback.
arxiv-2512-22116:
Yue Wu, Meng-Yuan Li, Chengshu Li, and Hui Zhai present a general recipe for building quantum error-correcting codes out of several classic codes at once. The known hypergraph product construction uses two classic codes. Their recipe works for any number D of input codes, stays inside the stabilizer formalism, and nearly exhausts what such product constructions can produce.

Setting D equal to two recovers the hypergraph product, while D equal to three yields four distinct construction types, one of them earlier known. Fed with simple repetition codes, the three-code versions unify several 3D lattice models, including the 3D toric code and a fracton model. Two types let builders trade code distance against code dimension by adjusting input code lengths.
arxiv-2512-22516:
Xiangyu Wang proves a nearly sharp mapping estimate for a class of oscillatory integral operators. These operators, central to harmonic analysis, average functions against rapidly oscillating phases. The ones treated here satisfy the cinematic curvature condition, a geometric premise borrowed from the study of variable-coefficient wave equations that has driven major progress on restriction and local smoothing problems.

The theorem gives an almost optimal bound on how the operator maps functions from one Lebesgue space to another. Wang's proof combines Wolff's two-ends reduction, a geometric split that part clustered from spread-out wave packets, with refined decoupling bounds. Results of this kind feed directly into Fourier restriction theory and the analysis of dispersive equations.
arxiv-2512-22616:
Mojtaba Eshghie, Melissa Mazura, and Alexandre Bartel present Raven, a system that learns from Ethereum transactions that failed on purpose. Smart contracts contain guard statements, requires, asserts, and revert statements, that block transactions violating safety invariants. A reverted transaction is therefore evidence of an on-chain defense working, yet these defensive patterns had never been mined in bulk.

Raven aligns each reverted transaction with the exact invariant that stopped it, embeds the invariants with a fine-tuned BERT model, and clusters them by semantic intent. On a sample of twenty thousand reverted transactions, the clusters were cohesive. Expert review of 19 clusters found six defensive categories missing from current catalogs. These included replay prevention and caller-provided slippage thresholds. A case study used one new category as a fuzzing oracle.
arxiv-2512-22816:
Grigorios Giotopoulos and Hisham Sati continue a series rebuilding field theory on higher-geometric groundwork. The first installment set out bosonic variational field theory using smooth sets, spaces described by how smooth probes map into them. This second part moves to thickened smooth sets, where spaces carry a slight fuzz, so notions like an infinitesimal neighborhood of a field configuration become literal objects.

The authors first present the Cahiers topos, the home of these thickened sets, in a simplified yet fully rigorous algebra setting meant to welcome both physicists and mathematicians to synthetic differential geometry. Local Lagrangian field theory is then built inside it, with jet bundles and off-shell and on-shell field spaces treated directly. The variational principle becomes an intersection of thickened sets, and perturbation theory emerges as restriction to a tiny neighborhood. Notably, none of this uses infinite-dimensional manifolds or functional analysis of mapping spaces.
arxiv-2512-22916:
Z. Kepuladze and J. Jejelava explore whether the masses of short-lived bosons measured at colliders can betray a failure of Lorentz invariance. That symmetry, the rule that physics looks the same for all fast-moving observers, is basic, yet its possible breakdown is a popular window to physics beyond the Standard Model. Strong limits exist for light and strongly interacting particles, while the weak sector, above all unstable bosons, remains largely untested.

Focusing on the Z boson, the authors trace how a violation would alter its dispersion relation and shift the resonance seen in Drell-Yan production at colliders. They argue precision mass measurements could rival cosmic-ray bounds. A key subtlety is gauge invariance: only some violation operators produce real physical effects. The discussion extends to the W boson and sketches measurement strategies for current and future collider experiments.
arxiv-2512-23316:
E. P. Csirmaz and L. Csirmaz push at an open frontier of information theory: the entropy region for five random variables. For a set of distributed variables, every subcollection has a Shannon entropy, and the set of all achievable entropy vectors forms a region whose boundary is cut out by entropy inequalities. With four or more variables the structure is mostly unknown, and the hard part is finding the non-Shannon inequalities that simple rules miss.

Their tool is a maximum entropy variant that adds copies of variables in successive generations. Symmetry arguments and reductions tamed the computation enough to extract every five-variable non-Shannon inequality the method yields in its nine generations. From those results the authors define two infinite families of inequalities and prove them valid. They then develop an algorithm enumerating the extremal ones. They conjecture the set characterizes what their method can produce.
arxiv-2512-23416:
Sandeep Kumar Mondal, Shubham Kishore, Alok Gupta, and Gwenael Giacinti search for a clock ticking inside the gamma-ray flare of the blazar OP 313. Quasi-periodic oscillations, regular pulses in a light curve, would point to structured motion in the jet or the accretion flow. The team analyzed nearly seventeen years of Fermi-LAT satellite data, compressing the light curve into monthly bins with a Bayesian block method and isolating four high-flux states.

Inside the fourth bright state, two timing tools, a weighted wavelet transform and a Lomb-Scargle periodogram, hint at a month-scale oscillation. The authors are careful: with only a few cycles observed, the detection significance stays limited. They frame the result as tentative evidence whose confirmation needs a longer data set. Exploring explanations, they find a curved-jet model, where our viewing angle of the jet sweeps periodically, can reproduce the observed behavior.
arxiv-2512-23616:
Christoph Willibald, Lugh Martensen, Thomas Eiband, and Dongheui Lee want factory robots programmed by the people who use them, not only by robotics experts. Long, expert-heavy setup is why collaborative robots are rarely used for surface finishing in small workshops, where products vary and batches are small. Their answer is a mixed reality interface organized around the finishing task itself.

Through the interface, a user marks regions of a workpiece for processing, guided by a new segmentation algorithm that folds human input into its surface model. Continuous visual feedback lets the user refine the segmentation, after which the robot's path over the chosen area is generated automatically. In two user studies, the chosen design cut workload and improved usability, letting even inexperienced users program finishing tasks effectively.
arxiv-2512-23816:
Wenqian Weng, Yi He, and Xingyu Zhou study aligning language models when the preference data are both private and partly corrupted. Alignment learns from human comparisons, but those labels may involve sensitive information and may include adversarial or noisy entries. Earlier theory handled privacy or corruption separately, and often pessimistically. This paper treats the two together, in the order privacy-then-corruption and corruption-then-privacy, in both offline and online settings.

For privacy alone, they show that log loss with a maximum-likelihood-style algorithm achieves near-optimal suboptimality rates, contrary to conventional wisdom. For the joint setting, existing offline algorithms turn out to carry stronger guarantees than previously proved, in corruption level and privacy parameters simultaneously, which also sharpens the corruption-only bounds. The first results for private and robust online alignment complete the paper, all resting on new uniform convergence guarantees for log and square losses.
arxiv-2512-24116:
Amedeo Chiefa, Luigi Del Debbio, and Richard Kenway build theory to explain how parton distribution functions get fitted. These functions describe the momentum carried by quarks and gluons inside protons, and nearly every collider prediction depends on them. The NNPDF collaboration fits them with neural networks trained on experimental data, a flexible approach whose inner workings can be hard to audit.

The authors analyze that training through the neural tangent kernel, a tool that yields an analytical picture of how a network evolves while learning. Under stated assumptions they can describe the training trajectory and track how the spread of the network's outputs, which encodes uncertainty, flows from data to fitted function. The framework clarifies how architecture choices and data each shape the result. It is not a replacement for fitting, they stress, but a diagnostic for judging the robustness of current methods.
arxiv-2512-24216:
Masatoshi Noumi and Takashi Takebe revisit the base of a classic theory. The theory covers integrable hierarchies, chains of equations that can be solved exactly. Its Zakharov-Shabat equations are usually built from Lax operators. The Lax data come first. The equations follow from them. The dependence seems to run one way only.

The authors reverse the flow. They show the equations alone can rebuild the Lax operators. A fitting change of variables makes this work. Two hierarchies serve as test cases. One is the KP hierarchy. The other is its modified cousin, in matrix form. The result tightens the logic of the whole subject. Objects once treated as inputs become outputs of the equations. Readers in integrable systems gain a cleaner base for both hierarchies.
arxiv-2512-25016:
Gabriel Siqueira, Alexsandro Oliveira Alexandrino, and Zanoni Dias study genome rearrangement distance with flips, swaps, and inserts or cuts, weighted by expected rate and enriched with intergenic region lengths. Genomes are modeled as signed gene series with at most one copy of each gene, and gaps between genes are shown by their DNA unit counts.

Approximation results for that weighted distance problem are the goal, since exact computation is hard. Computational biology readers get distance measures that respect both gene order and the DNA between genes. Including intergenic lengths makes evolution-based distance estimates more real-world than gene order alone.
arxiv-2601-00916:
Chanatip Sujsuntinukul and Christophe Chesneau wrote a 2026 math paper on a named inequality and its wider family. The Damascus inequality, set out in 2016, bounds a sum of fractions built from powers of positive numbers. It holds when the numbers multiply to one. The pair ask which choices of two whole-number dials keep such a bound true. One dial counts the terms, and the other sets the power.

They sort the dial pairs into those that work and those that fail. Their tools are a form of convexity for geometric means and a classic root-counting method. For the failing pairs, they study the shape of the set of counterexamples. Work of this kind maps the exact reach of a pretty inequality. It also shows where a tempting generalization breaks. The result is a full census for this family, of use to analysts who test bounds.
arxiv-2601-01016:
Ata Akbari Asanjan and three co-authors study, in 2026, how a wave-based twist improves AI models that flag odd flight data. The models are autoencoders, which learn to rebuild their input and flag what they cannot rebuild. The twist is a random Fourier step, which re-codes data with waves before the model sees it. The team ask what that step does to learning.

With the step, models learn low and high wave rates at the same time. Plain models learn the low rates first, and may never reach the high ones. The authors also try a trained form of the step, tuned by the model's maths. The main test was Dashlink, an aviation safety set. Wave-based models beat the plain ones at spotting odd flights. Whether the trained step beats the random one stayed unclear. The work matters for safety checks that must catch rare faults.
arxiv-2601-01416:
Five authors led by Yue Zhou build AirSpatialBot, an aerial agent that can find and describe vehicles in drone imagery by their fine traits. Remote sensing vision-language models are weak at spatial understanding: where things are, and how views relate. The team attacks that gap with data first, building the AirSpatial set with more than two hundred thousand instructions.

The set adds two new tasks, spatial grounding and spatial question answering, and is the first remote sensing grounding set to include three-dimensional bounding boxes. Training runs in two stages, first general image understanding, then spatial fine-tuning. The resulting agent plans tasks and mixes image reading, spatial reasoning, and execution to answer varied queries. Tests confirm the approach works and expose how far current models lag on spatial skill. Model, code, and data are slated for public release.
arxiv-2601-01616:
Rifat and 4 co-authors build a real-time power monitoring system for textile cutting machines in Bangladesh. Textile work uses much energy, yet many factories still track use with outdated methods, raising costs. Their approach, called non-intrusive load monitoring, reads one combined power signal and tries to tell which machine is running.

Sensors, a microcontroller board, and a wireless module gather data from three matching induction motors plus extra loads, making a data set of more than 180,000 samples. Total energy estimates were fairly accurate, but telling apart matching machines running at once proved hard. A phone app gave remote access, showing both promise and limits.
arxiv-2601-02016:
Some information is available while training a detector but never at deployment: exact masks, saliency maps, depth cues. Matthias Bartolo and six co-authors show how to exploit that privileged information through a teacher-student setup that works with any detector architecture.

The teacher learns with the extra descriptive inputs, and the student, which sees only ordinary images, absorbs the benefit during training while staying the same size and speed at inference. Across five state-of-the-art detectors and benchmarks including drone-based litter detection and Pascal VOC 2012, the students consistently beat their baselines, with the largest gains on medium and large objects. Careful weighting of the teacher's guidance mattered, making privileged training a practical upgrade rather than a research curiosity.
arxiv-2601-02316:
DatologyAI and co authors argue that the tests used to grade vision language models are themselves in poor shape. Good tests, they say, should be faithful to the real task, able to separate strong models from weak ones, and cheap enough to run often. Many current benchmarks fail on all three counts, which distorts claims about model progress.

They document concrete faults. Multiple choice formats reward guessing, many questions can be answered without looking at the image at all. Up to seventy percent in some tests, and mislabeled or ambiguous items reach high shares in certain data sets. Evaluation also eats a large share of development computing. Their response, DatBench, rebuilds evaluation around the three requirements so scores track real capability more honestly.
arxiv-2601-02416:
G. G. L. Nashed and A. Eid study how primordial black holes could form in a modified gravity theory where Einstein's action gains a squared curvature term. They expand the theory around general relativity to first order in the small strength of the extra term. For a collapsing ball of dust described by a flat expanding universe interior, they compute corrections to the scale factor, the star's radius, and the time when a horizon forms.

Those corrections suggest how the collapse threshold for making a black hole should trend, rather than fixing its value directly. In a radiation filled background the first order correction vanishes, so any change there must come from stronger, non perturbative effects. A second part of the study takes up that non perturbative side, giving qualitative guidance on how curvature corrections shape collapse.
arxiv-2601-03116:
Mohit Thakre and five co-authors examine an anisotropic model of the universe inside a modified theory of gravity. The setting is a Bianchi type-I universe, which can expand at different rates in different directions, under an f(R,T) style gravity with a scalar field.
