It also transfers with no retraining to an unseen hand with fifteen degrees of freedom. Skills learned on one hand can carry to the next.
arxiv-2606-15616:
Liu and Yu build a high-order solver in 2026 for waves scattering off an endless impedance cylinder hit at an oblique angle. Splitting off the axial phase leaves two coupled Helmholtz equations for the electric and magnetic parts. The surface condition ties them through tangential derivatives, so the integral system on the boundary mixes logarithmic kernels with principal-value terms.

Their Nyström scheme splits the logarithmic kernel Kress-style, uses periodic product quadrature, and takes the tangential terms by Fourier differentiation. A block diagonal preconditioner from the scalar subproblem keeps iteration cheap. Given uniqueness of the continuous problem and uniform stability of the discretization, density and far-field errors follow the accuracy of the quadrature. Tests on round and smooth non-round cylinders converge fast to round-off, and a variable-impedance example shows the solver cutting scattering width in a chosen backward sector.
arxiv-2606-15816:
Di Nezza, Guedj, and Lu study the Kähler-Ricci flow on compact Kähler manifolds in 2026, asking what the flow does to singular geometric data over time. A positive closed current is a generalised notion of a Kähler metric, allowed to be singular. Earlier work showed the flow smoothes such a current at once when its Lelong numbers all vanish. The harder case, with divisorial singularities along hypersurfaces, is the subject here.

The flow does not erase these singularities at once. Instead, it gradually replaces them by Poincaré-type singularities, the cusp-like kind carried by complete metrics near a divisor. On the remaining Zariski open set, the flow approximates the initial current by complete Kähler metrics with bounded curvature. The result extends the flow's regularising power to genuinely divisorial data, a smoothing tool for singular metrics in complex geometry.
arxiv-2606-15916:
Masoero and Shapiro count the solutions of a generalised Stieltjes system in 2026, where each of N distinct complex numbers feels the others through inverse-distance terms balanced by a polynomial source Q. With Q constant after translation, this is the classical Stieltjes problem: solutions are the zeros of a Hermite polynomial, an equilibrium of logarithmic charges. Here Q is any monic polynomial of degree M+1, counted modulo permutations.

They prove the number of solutions is at most the binomial coefficient 'N+M choose N'. The coefficient equations have intersection multiplicity exactly that number. So the bound is attained for every Q in a non-empty Zariski open set: generically, the count is exact. They describe the regime when Q's linear coefficient is large, where the system splits into M+1 coupled Stieltjes systems, one near each zero of Q. The binomial appears because the roots distribute themselves among those clusters.
arxiv-2606-16416:
Bagaglini and co-authors show in 2026 that twisting stacked layers of molybdenum disulfide switches on new channels of light-driven current. The bulk photovoltaic effect generates current in materials without a center of symmetry. Its shift current part is prized because it follows the geometry of electronic wavefunctions and can run large. Moiré supercells from twisting are far too big for standard first-principles calculations, though.

The team builds a Slater-Koster tight-binding model fitted to first-principles data, and validates it against density functional theory and Wannier-based results for one, two, and three layers. The model reproduces the band-edge electronic structure and the main features of the shift current spectrum. Twisting then breaks the crystal symmetry and activates additional conductivity tensor components that stay dark in untwisted stacks. In multilayer systems, the shift current magnitude also grows with the number of layers, driven by interlayer hybridization.
arxiv-2606-16516:
Federl and co-authors shrink neural network weights for small FPGAs in 2026 by storing differences instead of values, and training the network to tolerate the compression. Embedded deployments are starved of memory, and full-precision weights do not fit. Delta-aware training stores weights as low-bitwidth deltas and lets training adapt the network to the resulting errors. Two schemes compete: deltas between consecutive weights, and deltas against one fixed reference value.

Evaluated on FashionMNIST with a multilayer perceptron, the fixed-reference scheme wins clearly. With 4-bit weight deltas it reaches about 78.6 percent validation accuracy, a loss of roughly 8.3 percent against an 8-bit fixed-point network. A specialized hardware accelerator with a delta-compressed multiply-and-accumulate operator compresses weights by nearly 50 percent. It achieves a maximum throughput of about 7.99 million multiply-accumulates per second on an AMD Spartan-7 S15 chip.
arxiv-2606-16816:
Choi gives a faster fairness check in a 2026 algorithms paper on dividing indivisible goods. When items cannot be split, fairness is often judged by stochastic dominance envy-freeness: no agent's bundle looks worse than another's when ranked items are counted from the top down. A relaxed version allows envy that one removed good would fix.

Verifying either property used to take time quadratic in the number of agents times the number of goods. Choi's algorithm checks each agent with a single pass over prefix-dominance conditions, using lazy initialization to avoid wasted setup work. Total time drops to agents times goods, exactly the size of the preference table that forms the input. No algorithm can beat that bound in general, since every entry may need reading. The result makes fairness audits of proposed allocations cheap enough to run routinely, even for large groups and many goods.
arxiv-2606-16916:
Asad Ali and colleagues derive exact benchmarks for turning coherence into entanglement under noise in a 2026 quantum information paper. A CNOT gate can convert one qubit's superposition into a two-qubit entangled resource. Real hardware then degrades that resource, and designers need formulas, not just simulations, to judge how much survives.

For the minimal setup, a coherent qubit plus a blank partner, the authors prove the noiseless law linking output entanglement, measured by negativity, to half the input coherence. They then solve four standard noise channels exactly. Phase damping shrinks entanglement by one simple factor and never kills it outright. Global depolarizing noise does kill it, past a threshold that depends on input coherence, with more coherent inputs proving hardier. Amplitude damping adds a penalty tied to excited population. Local depolarizing noise is the most destructive of all at equal strength. Each channel's first decay slope acts as a fingerprint.
arxiv-2606-17116: Mircea Bejan and colleagues improve surface codes, the leading scheme for protecting quantum computers from errors, using ideas from random-matrix theory. By projecting logical ensembles with tools borrowed from quantum dot physics, they get better estimates of error thresholds. The cross-pollination yields practical guidance for building fault-tolerant qubits.
arxiv-2606-17216:
Shedlezki and Agmon, both of Bar-Ilan University, present a 2026 arXiv paper on when two selfish agents on a graph will cooperate, if only at certain meeting points along their routes. Each agent heads for its own target, and joining forces at specific nodes can cut both travel times. Cooperation is fragile, though, since either agent may deviate at any point when doing so pays better alone.

Modelled as a two-player shortest-path game, the problem yields a tight description of which joint strategies form a pure Nash equilibrium. Stable cooperation must follow a highly constrained form, and at least one equilibrium exists in every instance of the problem. A polynomial-time algorithm enumerates all relevant equilibria for the agents to choose among. When several equilibria arise, bargaining-based selection ideas are compared on travel times and social welfare in experiments.
arxiv-2606-17316:
Prabhu, Schwiegelshohn, and Shyam present a 2026 arXiv paper on coresets, small weighted summaries that let clustering algorithms run on a sketch of a huge data set. Theory promises certain sizes, yet in practice far smaller coresets often work, and this paper explains why. The key is that users only need the costs of good solutions preserved well, not the costs of every possible solution a strong coreset must handle faithfully.

The authors define approximation-preserving coresets, which sit between strong coresets, covering all solutions, and weak ones, covering only the optimum. They give constructions achieving the smaller sizes seen in practice under this weaker guarantee. A matching lower bound shows even a tiny slack in the approximation factor cannot admit coresets of that size in general. The gap between practice and theory is thus pinned on the guarantee, not the analysis.
arxiv-2606-17516:
Blöbaum, Balasubramanian, and Kasiviswanathan present a 2026 arXiv paper on FoundCause, a model that reads a data set and outputs a causal graph in one forward pass, hidden confounders included. Causal discovery from observations alone is hard, and classic methods search slowly without any way to intervene. FoundCause is trained entirely on synthetic data from simulated causal models, learning statistical patterns that transfer to real data sets it has never seen during its single training run.

Its design bakes in causal instincts: attention alternates over samples and variables, and classical asymmetry statistics steer the attention itself. A split decoder handles edge existence and edge direction separately, while a refinement module reasons over chains and colliders. Learnable latent tokens stand in for hidden common causes, a first for this amortised family. It beat classical and rival amortised methods on real data sets.
arxiv-2606-17616:
Monica Gonzalez-Machorro and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on predicting speech impairment in German-speaking people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that often weakens speech through bulbar damage. Speech scores used in clinic are the targets, and the team tests two modelling styles: one across speakers at a single time, and one personalised within each speaker over time. They also ask which everyday speech tasks carry the most signal for future standardised collection.

The cohort held dozens of speakers with the disease, recorded on common tasks such as syllable repetition. Simple repetition tasks gave the best cross-sectional predictions of a quality-of-life score for dysarthric speakers. The within-speaker models scored far higher still, showing how much a personal baseline helps track decline. The authors present the work as a first step toward automated speech checks that support, not replace, clinical judgement.
arxiv-2606-17716:
Zink, Ihle, and Menth present a 2026 arXiv paper on DPDS, a fast network link emulator built for the hundred-gigabit era of protocol testing. Emulators inject delay, jitter, and loss so researchers can watch protocols cope, but adding varying delay is treacherous: a packet delayed longer than its successor distorts the average and scrambles order. Their adaptive delay correlation method gives neighbouring packets positively linked delays, holding the target mean and spread while taming those artefacts. A half-life knob steers how fast the delay wanders over time.

Implemented on the DPDK framework, the emulator sustained zero-loss throughput far beyond the widely used NetEm tool and a recent rival. Rates stayed high with spacing enabled, and even while deliberately reordering packets for tests. Loss models and policing are built in as well. The authors close with concrete guidance on setting the half-life for realistic runs.
arxiv-2606-17816:
Tran and colleagues chart the hidden constants of neural network training in a 2026 theory paper. As gradient descent trains a model, some quantities never change, and these conservation laws reveal the built-in bias that steers training toward certain solutions. Such laws were well mapped for plain linear and ReLU networks, but modern designs had largely escaped the analysis.

The team builds one framework covering today's building blocks: feedforward layers with GELU, SiLU, and SwiGLU activations, multihead attention with sinusoidal and rotary position codes, and mixture-of-experts designs under several gating styles. For each case they derive the quantities that training must preserve, and experiments confirm the predicted invariants hold in practice. The catalogue gives researchers a firmer grip on why over-parameterized models generalize, by exposing the geometry that training can never leave.
arxiv-2606-18616:
Bonča and the team show a proposed photoemission method can reveal whether electrons in a quantum material are paired. The work is a 2026 condensed matter paper. The technique fires two photons in and catches two electrons out, in coincidence. Pairing underlies superconductivity. But the standard single-electron version senses correlations only indirectly, through subtle distortions that need heavy modeling to interpret.

The authors set this out on general grounds, and confirm it with large-scale simulations of strongly correlated models with paired and unpaired ground states. The two electrons' energies separate cleanly in a 2D energy plane. Electrons from the same pair sit in one region, and electrons from other pairs sit in another. That split follows from energy conservation alone. The spectrum also yields the pair binding energy, the size of the pairs, and the energy of the boson gluing them together.
arxiv-2606-18716:
Paimann, Valarini, and Juhl study what makes business users' experience with autonomous AI agents positive, in a 2026 human-computer interaction study. As agents move into business processes, planning multi-step actions and chatting, conventional user experience practice built for set, human-run tools no longer fits. No tested framework of design principles for agent interaction yet exists.

The authors combine qualitative and quantitative study of user hopes with a survey experiment, ending in a conjoint study testing design parts. Higher levels of the three human-control criteria all strongly raised user choice. Agent transparency had the strongest impact of all: the ability to follow the agent's logic, task status, next steps, and data sources. Users also preferred a low-confidence indicator paired with a warning message and accountability signal, over a bare note. A stop and pause mechanism reached only weaker weight.
arxiv-2606-18816:
Siddhad and Meena design a brain-computer interface classifier small enough for low-power embedded hardware, in a 2026 neural engineering paper. Hybrid interfaces mixing motor imagery and steady-state visual evoked potentials decode richer commands than either paradigm alone. But the deep models usually exceed what assistive devices can run.

SwitchBraidNet has three stages. A dual-path temporal braid extracts multiscale oscillatory features. An adaptive squeeze-and-excitation spatial switch gates electrodes. And a log-variance readout encodes band power. Trained with quantization-aware training, and tested on the OpenBMI dataset against four baselines, it reached motor imagery accuracy near seventy percent. Visual-evoked accuracy was above ninety-three percent. The hybrid information transfer rate was around sixty-five bits per minute. Its fully quantized footprint is only about three kilobytes, with negligible accuracy loss. That supports deployment on low-power embedded interfaces.
arxiv-2606-18916:
Akoramurthy and colleagues introduce a 2026 quantum computing method for systems whose energy rules are non-Hermitian, meaning they gain or lose energy to their surroundings. Standard variational solvers assume ordinary Hermitian rules, so they cannot track the special exceptional points where states merge. The new Biorthogonal Variational Quantum Eigensolver uses two separate circuits, one for each side of the biorthogonal description, to follow those points on noisy near-term hardware.

Tests cover a non-Hermitian Hubbard chain, a spin chain with quantum many-body scars, and a two-dimensional model with a Fermi skin effect. Across all three, energy errors stay very small and the detector module locates exceptional points closely against exact checks. An added geometric readout separates state topology from band topology, while importance sampling keeps the cost growing only polynomially. The work fills a clear gap for mapping non-Hermitian phase diagrams on current devices.
arxiv-2606-19016:
Hansen and colleagues demonstrate coherent microwave control of donor qubits in zinc oxide in 2026. Shallow donors in this material offer optical transitions and the promise of long spin coherence in a pure host. That mix suits spin-photon quantum technology. Until now, though, control was limited to small-angle rotations from ultrafast optical pulses, a gap this work closes with microwaves.

The team implants indium donors and uses resonant optical pumping to set and read the electron spin. Pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance resolves ten hyperfine transitions tied to the coupled nuclear spin, and reveals nuclear polarization from optical pumping. Clear Rabi oscillations show full coherent control on a nanosecond scale. Ramsey, echo, and dynamical decoupling tests then gauge coherence. Surprisingly, coherence is much shorter than earlier optical studies at high field suggested. Control tests rule out simple causes like microwave heating.
arxiv-2606-19116:
Bandara and colleagues argue in 2026 that the web must be redesigned for AI agents, not just human visitors. For three decades the web assumed a human reader. Its access rules, ad-based economics, and page design all target human attention. Agents now browse, summarize, and act for people at scale, yet sites block them with blanket bans and CAPTCHA walls that treat agent access as theft.

Changes are proposed across three linked layers. At the access layer, agents acting for humans should inherit those humans' access rights, governed by rate limits and standard agent identity data in requests rather than blanket blocking. Content and economic layers are reworked on the same principle. The aim is a web where legitimate agent use is named, metered, and priced fairly. That shift could end the current arms race between agent builders and site defenses.
arxiv-2606-19216:
Richards and colleagues study how developer problem-solving styles shape needs in chat with GitHub Copilot in 2026. Programming assistants help in many ways, but developers differ widely in what they need from them. Some groups hit challenges others never face. The study explores how cognitive diversity drives those differences, using a mixed-methods think-aloud design with professional developers and students working through real tasks.

The team characterizes five distinct interaction modes and ten underlying needs in developer chats with the assistant. A conceptual model links those modes and needs to problem-solving styles and experience profiles. Some developers probe and verify each step, while others delegate broadly and check at the end. Experience shifts which mode dominates. The authors give design and research recommendations for assistants that adapt to diverse styles. One-size interaction design, they argue, underserves large parts of the developer population in systematic ways.
arxiv-2606-19316:
Bao and colleagues present NeuMesh++ in 2026, a neural mesh-based representation for versatile three-dimensional editing. Neural implicit rendering has advanced novel view synthesis and scene reconstruction rapidly. Editing support in existing methods is narrow, though, often limited to rigid transforms or category-specific changes. The new scheme encodes a neural field with separate geometry, texture, and meaning codes on mesh vertices, which unlocks broader editing.

That disentangling supports mesh-guided geometry editing, designated texture editing with swapping, filling and painting, and semantic-guided editing in one system. Several techniques back it up. A local space scheme improves rendering quality and stable training. A learnable color on vertices raises texture editing quality, and a spatial-aware strategy makes edits precise. Label-guided region choice eases editing work. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show superiority in both representation quality and editing ability over prior approaches.
arxiv-2606-19416:
Toles and colleagues present MortarBench in 2026, a benchmark for mortgage loan origination agents. Origination runs from application and underwriting through approval and funding. It judges applicant eligibility and risk, and mistakes carry legal and financial consequences. Firms have begun using language model agents to augment loan officers, yet no public benchmark existed.

MortarBench generates examples with a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline. The cases match real-world distributions with broad edge case coverage. State-of-the-art models perform poorly. Closed-source models reach at most about seventy-seven percent exact match accuracy on the tasks. The study also finds systematic bias in how models perceive foreignness tied to non-English names. The team answers with CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. It raises accuracy to about eighty percent while improving risk steering and reducing the name bias. The benchmark gives the industry its first shared yardstick.
arxiv-2606-19516:
Virginie Ehrlacher, Rodrigue Lelotte, and Luca Nenna reframe a classic optimal transport result in 2026. Optimal transport finds the cheapest plan for moving mass between two distributions. Its hallmark test, c-cyclical monotonicity, has long marked optimal plans.

The trio show that property boils down to a zeroth-order optimality condition. Optimality equals the transport cost staying non-negative on the cone of allowed perturbations. That viewpoint extends the property to weak optimal transport, a relaxed modern variant. There it matches the first-order condition, the linearised cost staying non-negative near the optimiser. Under suitable assumptions the property marks optimal plans in both settings. Classical results return with fresh, unified proofs along the way. The reframing ties a geometric test to plain calculus of variations, clarifying why the property decides optimality.
arxiv-2606-19916:
Andrés Rodríguez-Galán and three colleagues explain a sideways drift of charged microparticles in microchannels in 2026. Experiments mixing electrophoresis with pressure-driven flow show particles migrating across the electric field direction. Fluid inertia was a suspect, but it runs far too weak in these regimes.

The missing mechanism is concentration polarization, the field's reshaping of ion density around a dielectric particle. A particle with surface conductance sits in both an electric field and a shear flow. Shear breaks the ion cloud's symmetry across the field direction. That broken symmetry drives the lateral migration. The velocity splits into electrophoretic and diffusiophoretic parts. An explicit formula ties its size to zeta potential and the Dukhin number. Typical speeds land near a micrometre per second, and the direction flips for Dukhin numbers near one.
arxiv-2606-20116:
Jānis Užulis and Andris Gulans establish a route to the Hartree-Fock limit for energies in solids and molecules inside the linearized augmented plane wave method, a workhorse of electronic structure theory. Their 2026 paper removes a known weakness. Radial basis functions and core orbitals were usually built from simpler local potentials. The nonlocal exchange defining Hartree-Fock therefore entered only halfway, leaving energies slightly off the true limit.

By building the radial basis and core states directly from the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian, the authors reach total energies precise to a few microhartree, and publish reference values for fourteen semiconductors and insulators. Reassuringly, the cheaper standard approach still proves highly accurate for relative energies chemists use, including formation energies and a silicon defect case. The benchmarks give developers a strict yardstick, and open a path to X-ray spectroscopy built on hybrid-functional core states.
arxiv-2606-20216:
Moman Ul Haque Khan and Samira Sadaoui survey and evaluate methods for detecting concept drift, the moment a data stream's underlying pattern changes and a learned model starts to go stale. Their 2026 paper focuses on learner-based detection, where the model's own performance signals trouble. Drift haunts fraud detection, intrusion monitoring, health tracking, and predictive maintenance, because a detector that misses a change keeps making confident, wrong calls. The study first examines drift theory: what kinds of change occur, and how fast.

The authors then compare numerous detection algorithms across several families, including statistical process control, windowing, and ensemble methods, on synthetic and real-world streams with abrupt and gradual drift. Results show how detector behavior shifts with drift type and transition speed, and where each method fits best. Practitioners gain a grounded way to choose a detector for their stream.
arxiv-2606-20416:
José Chávez challenges a basic design habit of diffusion models: telling the network what time it is. His 2026 paper examines timestep embeddings, the signals that tune denoising across noise scales in U-Net and diffusion transformer architectures. Removing them, he finds surprising robustness. Theory shows that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the training objective can be reached with no explicit timestep conditioning. The architectures can infer the noise scale from the corrupted input itself.

Ablation studies on CelebA and CIFAR-10 back the theory. Time-agnostic models stayed sharp and faithful, and even surpassed their conditioned rivals on FID, precision, and recall. The information, it turns out, is already inside the input, readable by the network under stated assumptions. If that signal is redundant, future designs can drop a component and focus capacity on structure instead of clocks.
arxiv-2606-20616:
Ivan Chajda and Helmut Länger examine residuated mappings in posets in their 2026 mathematics paper, extending ideas first studied for lattices. A poset is a set with a partial order, where some pairs may not compare. A residuated mapping links two maps by an order condition that mimics implication. The authors define operator-residuated mappings for posets and show how they differ from the usual definition.

Chajda and Länger also adapt the idea of a lattice homomorphism, a structure-preserving map, for settings where suprema, or least upper bounds, need not exist. They connect that notion to residuated mappings and to induced ideals, which are special downward-closed subsets. Several examples are given, with ways to construct them. The work clarifies which lattice results survive under a weaker order.
arxiv-2606-20716:
Andrea Fagnani and three colleagues measure the emissivity of oxidizing titanium in simulated space entry flows in 2026. Emissivity is how well a surface radiates heat. Titanium parts on returning space debris heat fast and oxidize in dissociated oxygen. That changes surface heat balance and how the part breaks up. Data in the literature do not capture the full dynamic change.

Samples of Grade 2 and Grade 5 titanium are exposed in the Plasmatron facility at the von Karman Institute. Infrared emissivity is tracked over time across five wavelength bands. Results show a sharp drop tied to a sudden surface temperature jump. Microscopy after testing reveals varied oxide layers at small scale. Plasma tunnels reproduce only part of real entry. Still, better emissivity data can improve models of debris demise, which matters for predicting what survives re-entry and where risk falls.
arxiv-2606-20816:
Steven Miller and Arman Rysmakhanov analyze the spectrum of dense Barabási-Albert graphs in 2026, a model of networks that grow by preferential attachment. In such graphs, well-connected nodes attract more edges. Degree distributions become highly uneven, like many real networks. Spectra, the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, let graph questions be studied through matrix tools. The dense case adds edges in proportion to final size.

The authors compute the large-size limit of the expected adjacency matrix. It is described by a rank-one limiting kernel, a continuous analogue of the matrix. After centering and scaling, fluctuations form a random matrix with a computable variance profile. A quadratic vector equation yields the limiting bulk spectral distribution. The leading eigenvalue location is also determined. Spectral results can predict how dense preferential networks behave, from influence spread to the stability of dynamics running on them.
arxiv-2606-20916:
Yuecheng Cai and Jasmin Jelovica propose a physics-guided graph neural network in 2026 to predict full-field stress and displacement in stiffened panels. Fast, accurate field prediction supports iterative design of large structures. Finite element analysis is accurate but costly. Neural surrogates often struggle with new topologies and boundary conditions. Their network works on panel-level graph representations that are heterogeneous, with several node and edge types.

Physics-guided edge states start from edge type, spatial data, and boundary motion. Dual-stream message passing separates lengthwise and crosswise structural information, while allowing exchange. Geometry and load effects enter through feature-wise modulation and spectral convolutions. Fields are rebuilt with a low-rank readout. Tests use box beams made of stiffened panels. A fast surrogate that respects physics could let engineers screen many designs before paying for full simulation.
arxiv-2606-21316:
Shaikh Saad presents bsm_agent in 2026, an open-source framework that lets particle physicists build models beyond the Standard Model through a chat interface. Model building needs exact symbolic work: writing the Lagrangian, checking gauge anomalies, and deriving particle masses. The framework pairs a deterministic Python physics backend with a language model that only handles conversation, confirmations, and tool calls, never the math itself.

Starting from the Standard Model's fields plus user-specified new scalars or fermions, the backend builds the renormalizable Lagrangian, expands operators into component fields, and derives symmetry-breaking conditions and tree-level mass matrices. Local, self-hosted, and commercial model providers are all supported. Keeping computation deterministic while the language model orchestrates keeps results repeatable and makes model building far more convenient.
arxiv-2606-21516:
Mikael Bisgaard Dahlsen-Jensen, Laure Petrucci, and Jaco van de Pol bring stronger state-space abstractions in 2026 to parametric timed games, where a controller must beat an adversary under uncertain timing constants. Checking such games symbolically explodes in size, and only mild zone inclusion checks were in use. Methods that worked for timed automata or non-parametric games, such as double inclusion, zone merging, and hull and location variants, had never been carried into the parametric game setting.

The authors define one general framework, place each technique inside it, and prove the framework preserves correct parameter synthesis and winning strategies. On a production cell benchmark and a new adversarial Internet-of-Things case study, the shortcuts greatly improve scale. Instances that defeated existing tools become solvable.
arxiv-2606-21616:
Shalom Lappin compares in 2026 how large language models and humans represent knowledge, focusing on two domains: language itself, and real-world reasoning and planning. Models often match or beat human scores and sound fluent, which fuels claims on both sides of the debate about their cognitive standing. Lappin reviews recent experimental work task by task rather than arguing from headline performance.

On linguistic knowledge, models rate sentence acceptability and handle subject-verb agreement under hierarchical structure in ways that diverge from human processing, even when final answers agree. On reasoning and planning tasks, they are mostly less efficient learners than humans, needing far more exposure to generalize. Fluency, the review concludes, should not be mistaken for human-like representation, and efficiency gaps remain a central contrast.
arxiv-2606-21816:
Chau and Han prove a bound on Bartnik mass in 2026, a quantity from general relativity that measures the smallest possible total mass of a space matching given boundary data. The data here are a metric and a positive mean curvature function on a two-sphere, describing a surface with constant mean curvature. Earlier bounds usually required the surface's Gauss curvature to be nonnegative everywhere, a strong restriction.

Their condition is spectral instead: the first eigenvalue of a natural operator built from the Laplacian and the Gauss curvature must be nonnegative. That assumption allows the curvature to dip below zero in places, even with the area fixed, so it genuinely extends earlier results. Under it, the Bartnik mass is bounded above by a quantity set by the surface's area alone. The proof therefore widens the class of boundary data for which a clean mass ceiling is known.
arxiv-2606-21916:
Freese and Theunissen investigate data pruning in 2026, the practice of shrinking a training set by deleting samples while keeping model performance. Pruning promises cheaper training and cleaner data, and two popular methods work well on tidy benchmarks. The authors test what happens when labels are noisy, a common condition in real datasets that benchmarks often hide.

Empirically, both methods failed in the presence of significant label noise, losing the performance they were meant to preserve. The investigation separates three factors that decide whether pruning succeeds. Redundancy means some samples repeat information others carry. Problematic samples, such as mislabelled or out-of-distribution items, actively mislead training. Interdependence means a sample's value depends on which others remain, so scores computed one by one mislead. The findings held across common classification datasets, network architectures, data distributions, and training protocols, giving practitioners a checklist before trusting a pruned dataset.
arxiv-2606-22016:
Zhang and colleagues study, in 2026, how helper variables should be used in multiple imputation when the goal is estimating an average causal effect from data with missing values. Multiple imputation fills gaps repeatedly with plausible values, and extra measures not used in the final analysis can be added to help. Earlier work mostly asked whether such helpers improve precision, not whether the causal effect can be identified at all.

The authors separate auxiliary variables into mediators, which lie on the causal pathway, and non-mediators, and examine typical missingness patterns drawn as missingness directed acyclic graphs. For each setting they derive recoverability results, stating when the effect can in principle be recovered. Simulation studies then compare imputation strategies and complete-case analysis under correctly specified g-computation. The practical guidance is sharp: treating mediators and non-mediators differently matters for avoiding bias, as do compatible, flexible imputation models.
arxiv-2606-22116:
Yang and colleagues introduce DeformX in 2026, a simulation framework for deformable linear objects such as wires, cables, and ropes that robots must manipulate. Visual simulators draw such objects with procedural shapes that bend unrealistically, while physics engines usually approximate them as rigid-link chains or generic soft bodies. Neither captures the bending, twisting, and shear of slender elastic structures well enough for robot learning.

DeformX couples a dedicated Cosserat rod physics engine, which models a slender rod's full deformation mechanics, with NVIDIA Isaac Sim for rendering and robotics workflows. The engine handles self-collisions and contact with free-form meshes, while mesh skinning maps rod deformation onto CAD models for realistic visuals. The authors demonstrate it on synthetic data generation and policy learning. Comparisons with real-world experiments validate its visual and physical fidelity.
arxiv-2606-22416:
Prajwal Gatti, Simon Jenni, Fabian Caba Heilbron, and Dima Damen address skewed training data for video action recognition in this 2026 paper. Video collections are long-tailed: a few actions have many clips, while most have very few. Models trained on such data perform poorly on the rare actions.

Their method, Gen2Balance, uses a text-to-video generative model to create clips for the underrepresented actions. Prompts draw on action profiles and real examples, turning the set into a balanced mix of real and generated video. A two-stage strategy then limits harm from the gap between synthetic and real footage. On long-tailed versions of two benchmarks, the method beat the strongest prior approaches by about five and seven percent. On RareAct, a dataset of scarce actions, the gain was far larger. Partial balancing delivered seventy-nine percent of the gains at twenty-seven percent of the compute cost.
arxiv-2606-22516:
Yuhang Jiang questions a standard trick in adversarial machine learning in this 2026 paper. Transfer attacks craft misleading inputs on a local surrogate model and hope they fool unseen targets. Input diversity, randomly resizing and padding the input at each step, is a near-default ingredient because it supposedly improves transfer.

Holding the attack fixed and varying only the surrogate, Jiang finds the effect splits by surrogate type. For standard surrogates, more input diversity raises transfer success, but for robustly trained ones it lowers success, so the two curves separate like scissors. On ImageNet the harm averaged about ten percent of attack success across four target families and ten attacks. A controlled sweep of surrogate robustness shows the harm is graded, appearing already at little robustness. Decomposing the transform attributes roughly two-thirds of the harm to resizing itself. A single probe, local gradient consistency, cleanly separates the two regimes.
arxiv-2606-22716:
Jungseob Lee and five colleagues stabilize efficiency training for reasoning models in this 2026 paper. Teaching language models to reason briefly usually adds length penalties to Group Relative Policy Optimization. In practice that often triggers reward collapse, badly damaging the reasoning the training meant to keep.

By testing many reward configurations, the team pinpoints the mechanism. Group normalization creates divergent advantages when wrong answers receive steady length penalties, so penalizing their length is structurally prone to collapse. Penalizing only correct answers avoids that failure but invites a random collapse from over-compression. Their method, Acoer, gives brevity bonuses only to correct completions, isolating the penalty loop entirely. A dynamic budget rule and control-loop penalty tweaks guard against that failure. Across math reasoning benchmarks, Acoer improved accuracy over the base model while cutting token generation by more than sixty percent. They present it as a stable route to efficiency-aware training.
arxiv-2606-23416:
Bacem Etteib, Daniele Lunghi, and Tégawendé Bissyandé detect malicious agent skills in the wild in a 2026 security paper. Deployed at scale, the detector flags skills with high precision, most confirmed malicious by hand.

babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-16:
The second part of Tract Sanhedrin fills volume sixteen of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud, printed in 1902. Part one built the court and its trials. The debate now turns to the crimes themselves and to the fate of the soul.

The rabbis list the offenses that carry death, and argue over idolatry, blasphemy, and the stubborn son. A famous passage weighs who is shut out of the world to come, naming kings and commoners alike. Other pages picture the age of the Messiah and the judgment to come. The volume blends criminal law with the Talmud's boldest theology.
barrow-geometrical-lectures-child-1916:
Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher at Cambridge, gave his Geometrical Lectures in the years before Newton rose. J. M. Child translated the Latin Lectiones geometricae for Open Court in 1916. Barrow treats curves, tangents, and areas with pure geometry. Along the way he comes close to the fundamental theorem of calculus.

That theorem links tangents and areas as inverse operations, the core of calculus. Barrow states a form of it in geometric dress. Child's notes help readers track the proofs and their later echoes. The lectures show calculus in the moment before its birth. Newton learned from the man who wrote them. Historians of math prize the text highly.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-5-:
The fifth and last volume of Maudslay's Bernal Díaz, from 1916, closes The True History of the Conquest of New Spain. Díaz's chronicle, written in 1568 and printed in 1632, ends with the campaigns that followed the fall of Mexico. Appendices and an index complete the Hakluyt Society edition.

An old soldier's memory governs the whole work, and its last pages keep his plain, stubborn voice. Díaz never stops insisting that common men, not only Cortés, won New Spain. Paired with Cortés's own letters, his history lets readers judge the conquest from two sides of the same camp. The set remains the fullest soldier's account of that world-changing war.
blasco-four-horsemen-1916:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez published The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse in 1916, a Spanish novel set during the First World War. The Desnoyers family has roots in both France and Argentina. Julio Desnoyers lives idly in Paris before the war. His cousins in Argentina have grown rich and partly German in sympathy.

War splits the family, as sons end up on opposite sides. Julio enlists and faces the horror of the trenches in France. The four horsemen of the Bible's Book of Revelation stand for war, conquest, famine, and death. The novel became a worldwide bestseller. A famous silent film later carried its fame still further.
boas-tsimshian-mythology-1916:
Franz Boas, the founder of modern American anthropology, built this 1916 study from texts dictated by Henry Tate, a Tsimshian man of the northern Northwest Coast. Boas printed the myths as Tate told them, with close translation, in a Bureau of American Ethnology report.

The tales include the Raven cycle, in which the trickster steals light and shapes the world, and crest myths that families treated as treasured property. Boas added analysis showing how the stories link to Tsimshian social rank and custom. The book is a landmark of text-based fieldwork, preserving a people's own telling of their traditions.
boutroux-contingency-laws-nature-1916:
French thinker Emile Boutroux published De la contingence des lois de la nature in 1874, early in his career. Fred Rothwell's English translation followed in 1916. The short work attacks a belief most scientists of the day took for granted. It holds that the laws of nature had to be as they are.

Boutroux argues the opposite: those laws are contingent, meaning they could have been otherwise. Each level of nature, from matter to life to mind, brings something new that lower levels cannot predict. His case gave French spiritualism one of its founding texts. It still frames debate on chance, freedom, and natural order.
breasted-ancient-times-1916:
James Henry Breasted built Chicago's Oriental Institute and wrote the first great popular history of the early world. Ancient Times, printed in 1916, sweeps from the first farmers to the fall of Rome. Breasted was a working dig scholar, not an armchair teller of tales.

Egypt, the Near East, Greece, and Rome pass in one clear line of growth. Breasted ties trade, war, law, and faith to the rise of each land. His schools text taught two generations how the ancient world hung together. The book set a new bar: deep learning in prose any reader could follow.
chekhov-plays-second-series-west-1916:
Anton Chekhov wrote the plays in this second series, and Julius West made them English in 1916. The volume holds The Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard in early English dress. West's versions helped seed the deep English love of Chekhov that still thrives on stage.

Three sisters, stuck in a province town, dream of a return to Moscow in vain. Soldiers, work, and dull marriages drain their hopes across four slow, rich acts of talk. In The Cherry Orchard, a family loses its estate and orchard to a merchant's axe. Chekhov mixes grief and farce so deftly that directors still argue his true tone. His people talk past each other, and whole lives slip away between the lines.
chymische-hochzeit-1616: Chymische Hochzeit, 1616. The Chemical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz. This book preserves that Rosicrucian classic. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-0000009716:
Low Pathet Lao morale, the local economy, propaganda work, and prison matters share one wide CIA paper from October 1971. The heading shortens the Pathet Lao to PL and stacks four subjects in a single report. Such bundles often came from one source's broad debriefing in Laos.

Mixed reports show intelligence gathering as it really happened: whatever a source knew, taken down together. Morale and food prices could matter as much as prison news for judging the enemy's strength. Analysts sorted the bundle into files afterward. This entry preserves the bundle whole, a snapshot of everyday reporting from the secret war.
cia-0000009916:
Four American pilots were held at a cave at Hang Long, east of Sam Neua in Houa Phan province, an October 1967 item states. Hang Long's caves lie in the same limestone belt as the Pathet Lao's wartime cave capital. Four men in one cave made a sizable group for Laos.

A group in a fixed cave could be watched, in principle, far better than men in shifting camps. In practice, the cave country stayed closed to outsiders for years. The report at least fixed the men's place in the autumn of 1967. Later files on Sam Neua prisoners build on points like this.
cia-0000012416:
September 30, 1961: meeting number thirty-six closes the month's intensive Paris run. The month's debriefings had been relentless by any standard. Session followed session through the early autumn, and the handlers' notebooks filled accordingly. Their source stayed willing, his memory stayed exact, and the questions stayed ahead of the answers by design.

The record tallies September in the series' plain numbering. It closes a month that proved Paris could carry the case as London had. For readers, the page marks a season's end inside an operation that still had no way to know its own.
cia-0000013616:
Uruguay's growing troubles fill a CIA paper from May 1965 on the situation there. The small republic had long been South America's calm exception: prosperous, democratic, and dull in the best sense. By 1965 the old calm was fraying. Prices rose, strikes spread, and a city guerrilla movement, the Tupamaros, was just beginning to stir in the capital's streets.

The paper senses the turn early. It weighs the economy, the parties, and the first signs of armed revolt together. For readers, it keeps the watch on a model republic at the moment its luck began to run out.
cia-0000013916: How North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces treated American and South Vietnamese captives fills a CIA report dated November 5, 1967. The report spans both the northern army and the southern Viet Cong. It also spans both sets of prisoners, U.S. and Saigon government men. Broad treatment reports like this set the base line for judging single camp claims.
cia-0000015316: A letter to Lawrence Tacker from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated May 3, 1958. Strong enclosed the letter the office had received, per the title. Routing a writer's own letter back with a fresh cover was a standard move. The file keeps the paper loop of the saucer debate turning one more time.
cia-0000015416: Major Donald E. Keyhoe, the best-known saucer writer of his day, sent an inquiry that the CIA logged on January 4, 1959. Part of the record was cut before release. Keyhoe led a civilian group that pressed the government for candor on flying objects. His questions forced officials to answer in writing, and those exchanges fill many files from the late nineteen fifties.
cia-0000020316: Two bullets tied to the killing of Castillo Armas were definitely the same caliber, an untitled CIA record dated in 1957 notes. Carlos Castillo Armas was president of Guatemala when he was shot that year. A caliber match is a small hard fact in a case full of rumor. The note shows field reporting carrying forensic detail back to headquarters.
cia-0000022316: Gary Powers' trial would be public, and American policy was on trial too, a CIA record dated in 1960 argues in its heading. Moscow staged the August 1960 trial before the world press. Powers faced espionage charges after his U-2 fell in Soviet land. The heading's claim rang true for many watchers, since Washington's spy flights stood judged beside the pilot.
cia-0000044016:
Rosa Chavez commented on the Jesuits' killing, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. Chavez spoke from inside El Salvador's church community. Church workers lived close to the war's daily violence and loss.

Inside, her comments on the murders are preserved as she gave them. A voice like hers carried the grief of a working parish. It lacked the polish of a president's statement, and gained force from that. The file holds one woman's witness beside the generals and ministers, and hers may be the voice that best shows what the killings meant at ground level.
cia-0000044116: An unidentified flying object report survives in a CIA record dated November 2, 1968, with the title noting that the publication date is estimated. Saucer reports reached the agency in large numbers during the 1950s and 1960s, and each one was logged in the same plain way. This record's own dating is part of its interest, since even the file could not fix when its report first appeared. It stands as a routine page from the long official file on things seen in the sky and never explained.
cia-0000045216:
A bishop predicted a wave of reprisals, in a CIA record dated September 6, 1985. Reprisals were the war's habit: each blow answered by another. A bishop's warning carried the voice of the church into the crisis.

Inside, the forecast of revenge attacks is preserved as he made it. Warnings from the pulpit reached people no communique could reach. They also named the cycle that kept the war feeding itself. The file holds the prediction from that September, spoken by a churchman who had watched reprisal follow reprisal for years and saw no reason it would stop.
cia-0000049016: A CIA item from 1981 traces responsibility for a death squad run by businessman Ricardo Sol Mesa in El Salvador. Private money behind public murder was one of the war's worst features, and this item names a funder. It survives in the Truth Commission files, where the money trails mattered as much as the trigger men.
cia-0000049216: A partly blacked-out file on Colonel Jose Chavez Caceres survives in a CIA item from 1992, kept with the Truth Commission records. By 1992 the peace accords had ended the war, and files on its officers passed to history's keeping. What the redactions still guard sits inside the document, for the next reader.
cia-0000096716: Prominent author Pa Chin singled out for struggle by a Shanghai rebel faction is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000096716, dated June 3, 1968. The heading names the writer and the faction's act. The brief file records a cultural figure targeted in Shanghai, preserved as a short item on the human cost of factional campaigns.
cia-0000104916:
India: A Growing Role in Technology Transfer is a CIA memorandum released as declassified document 0000104916, dated May 5, 1985 in the catalog. The sample memorandum is dated June 7, 1985, a month later. It came from the Office of Near East and South Asia Analysis in the Directorate of Intelligence.

The summary says Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi had introduced sweeping economic reforms. Those reforms promised to encourage imports of sophisticated western technology. They also promised to boost India's ability to manufacture its own high-tech products. As a result, India would offer a more attractive target for Soviet science and technology collectors.
cia-0000119216:
Dated November 3, 1967, this CIA document covers the detention of American prisoners of war in Hanoi. By then, North Vietnam's capital held many captured American airmen in its prisons. The best known of those prisons was later nicknamed the Hanoi Hilton by the men held there.

The document records what the agency knew about how and where the prisoners were confined. Such reporting fed decisions in Washington about protests, talks, and public pressure over prisoner treatment. It also forms part of the wartime record of a captivity that lasted years for many men, written while their fate was still unknown to their families.
cia-0000119716:
Dated September 1956, this CIA paper examines probable developments in Eastern Europe and what they would mean for Soviet policy. Poland and Hungary were both in turmoil that autumn. Moscow's hold on its allies suddenly looked less certain than it had in years.

The paper steps back from single countries to the empire as a whole. It asks how unrest at the edges might force choices at the center: reform, concession, or force. That framing gives the paper lasting interest. Written weeks before the Hungarian Revolution, it shows analysts thinking through the Soviet dilemma that the uprising would soon pose in its sharpest form.
cia-0000132416: Cuban developments return as item 15 in the CIA's Latin America series, dated November 1, 1959. The numbered format shows Cuba becoming a standing item on the agency's agenda. Two months had passed since the last general survey in the file. The short item updates the picture, tracking the new regime's latest moves for readers who followed the series as a running watch.
cia-0000132516:
Paired with a same-day companion, this CIA paper on Cuba is dated April 4, 1961. Intelligence was flowing to the White House daily by then. The Bay of Pigs landing, planned in secret, was thirteen days away.

Two papers on one day, so close to the operation, show the tempo of the final countdown. Each fed the pre-invasion picture that planners relied on: conditions on the island as the exile force readied itself. Read together with its companion, the briefing helps reconstruct what Washington thought it knew in April 1961. The pair of papers is preserved together in this record.
cia-0000132616: The situation in Cuba fills item 2 of the CIA's Latin America series, dated July 4, 1960. Eighteen months into the revolution, that situation was the standing question before the agency. By the middle of 1960 the answer grew darker with each passing month. The short item gives the current picture as analysts summed it up for their readers that summer.
cia-0000135616: One of the Spanish-language records of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 5 February 1961. The brigade of Cuban exiles, trained and supplied by the CIA, landed in Cuba two months later. February found it in final training. The catalog gives this item no subject heading. It is described only by date, language, and provenance. The piece is part of the brigade's declassified paperwork, preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135816: Dated 2 May 1954, a declassified CIA document deals with an operational report with five attachments, its key names blank or deleted in the heading. coleridge-christabel-kubla-khan-1816:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge published this slim volume in 1816, pushed by friends and by Lord Byron's praise. It gathers three poems he had kept back for years. Two of them, Christabel and Kubla Khan, were unfinished, and Coleridge knew it.

Christabel tells of an innocent young woman and a mysterious lady guest whose spell works by night. Kubla Khan, which Coleridge said came to him in a dream, builds a pleasure palace in flashing images. The Pains of Sleep adds a darker note of addiction and dread. Unfinished or not, these are among the most haunting poems of the Romantic age.
collingwood-religion-philosophy-1916:
Religion and Philosophy, published in 1916, is R. G. Collingwood's early study of how religious faith and philosophical reason relate. He wrote it while a young Oxford tutor, before the work on history that made his name.

Collingwood argues that religion and philosophy are not rivals but overlapping forms of thought, each expressing man's attempt to grasp his world whole. Where they conflict, he seeks the common ground of experience beneath doctrine and system. The book is earnest and exploratory, a young thinker's first map. Readers of his later work will find the seeds of his philosophy of history here.
commons-principles-labor-legislation-191:
Commons and John Andrews published Principles of Labor Legislation in 1916, a handbook for the reform movement. Both men worked at the center of the campaign for better labor law in the Progressive Era. The book argues the case for public rules on work, state by state and topic by topic.

Chapters take up hours of labor, workplace safety, child labor, and the new idea of social insurance against sickness, accidents, and old age. The authors compare the laws of American states with those of Europe and judge what works. Their manual gave legislators and activists a shared program and a shared evidence base. Much of the labor law of the next generation, state and federal, grew from the agenda set out in these pages.

coomaraswamy-buddha-gospel-buddhism-1916:
Ananda Coomaraswamy, the Ceylon-born art historian, published Buddha and the Gospel of Buddhism in 1916. The book expounds Buddhism as a whole: its founder's life, its doctrine, and its art. Coomaraswamy wrote with a convert's sympathy and a scholar's range.

He sets out the Four Noble Truths, the doctrine of no-self, and the monastic path in clear, ordered chapters. Images of the Buddha in stone and bronze appear as theology made visible, not mere decoration. The synthesis helped Western readers take Buddhism seriously as both a faith and a civilization. He writes the Buddha's life and teaching before turning to the art he loved.
cotta-triall-of-witch-craft-english-1616:
John Cotta, a doctor of Northampton, published The Triall of Witch-craft in 1616. Rather than defend the accused, Cotta attacks the tests used to find witches. His method is a physician's skepticism, turned on the whole business of witch-finding in Jacobean England.

Swimming a suspect, hunting for devil's marks, and watching for familiars all fail his scrutiny. Such proofs, he argues, can brand the innocent as surely as the guilty. Cotta accepts that witchcraft exists, but demands evidence worthy of a court. His book is medicine enlisted against superstition. Doctors would cite it whenever weak tests sent neighbors to the gallows.
crawford-reality-psychic-phenomena-1916:
William Crawford brings scales and rods to the seance in The Reality of Psychic Phenomena, out in 1916. Crawford taught the craft of machines in Belfast. A kin ring there, the Golighers, drew his tests. Chairs rose with guests on them. Crawford claims stiff rods of strange stuff, thrust from the seer's frame, did the lift like levers of a crane in his test room.

He weighs, draws, and prints each test with a craft man's care. Peers were split: awe, doubt, and scorn in kind. The book is the lab's most bold claim. Its plates still startle.
der-entlarvte-adeptus-realis-oder-treuhe: Der entlarvte Adeptus realis, 1716. The unmasked adept. This book preserves that warning. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
dewey-democracy-education-1916:
John Dewey published Democracy and Education in 1916, his most complete work on schooling and society. Dewey argues that education is the reconstruction of experience, not the pouring in of facts. A democratic society needs schools that grow free, shared inquiry. Learning by doing stands at the center of his method.

He treats aims, play, work, subjects, and morals as parts of one problem. Growth itself, he says, is the only moral end of education. The book became the summa of progressive education. Teachers and philosophers have argued with it for a century. Few works on education match its scope and influence.
diderot-early-philosophical-works-jourda:
Denis Diderot, before the great Encyclopédie made his name, wrote the bold little works gathered here. Margaret Jourdain's translation, issued by Open Court in 1916, holds the Philosophic Thoughts of 1746 and the Letter on the Blind of 1749, with its later Addition. The Letter on the Deaf and Dumb of 1751 completes the set.

The Thoughts are sharp sparks on God, nature, and the passions, in the manner of Shaftesbury. The Letter on the Blind asks how a man born blind builds a world, and lands its author in prison for his answers. In the Letter on the Deaf and Dumb, Diderot turns to language and gesture. Together they show a first-rate mind finding its weapons.
dunsany-last-book-of-wonder-1916:
Dunsany closed his great early run of tales in 1916 with Tales of Wonder. In America the book bore that name; in Britain it was The Last Book of Wonder. The title tells the truth: a first manner ends in these pages.

The tales still cross to the edge of the world and the courts of the gods. But war was on, and Dunsany's voice would change with his years at the front. The book is a farewell to the dream world of Pegana and its kin. It ends the run that began in 1905 in fine form.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-16: The sixteenth volume finds Montaigne in a mellow mood. He writes of conversation, solitude, and the quiet pleasures of the mind. The essays feel like evening talk with an old friend. Gentle wisdom from the tower study.
europmc-pmc10154216:
Dejanovic and co-workers show that astrocytes and microglia remove synapses in Alzheimer's mouse models through a complement protein, in a 2022 study. Synapses are the contact points where nerve cells pass signals. Their loss tracks closely with memory decline in Alzheimer's disease.

Using combined molecular analyses, the team found that a protein called C1q drives the removal of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Brain support cells carried out the pruning as the mice aged. The work points to a shared mechanism behind synapse loss. It also names a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc10623016:
Sender and co-authors counted every immune cell in the human body in 2023. No full census of this kind had been pulled into one view. The team pooled past measures of cell counts by tissue and type. Their aim was a single tally of number, mass, and spread.

An average body holds about 1.8 trillion immune cells, Sender reports. Their total mass comes to roughly 1.2 kilograms. Lymphocytes, a key defence type, make up 40% of the cell count but just 15% of the mass. Neutrophils hold like shares of both. Macrophages are 10% of cells yet near half the mass, due to their large size. The census gives model builders a firm base.
europmc-pmc11006616:
Jamali and co-authors built an AI tool that reads frozen microscope maps of proteins on its own in this 2024 paper. Cryo-EM is a method that images flash-frozen samples to reveal protein shapes. Turning those maps into atom-level models takes expert labour by hand. The team asked whether a neural network could do the job as well.

Their tool, ModelAngelo, fuses the map with protein sequence and shape data in one network. Its protein models matched the quality of expert-built ones, the authors report. For DNA and RNA parts, its backbones matched human accuracy too. When fed unknown proteins, its residue guesses powered database searches that beat human experts at naming the protein. The authors say the tool removes a bottleneck and adds objectivity to the process.
europmc-pmc13191116:
Wong and a very large team released IQ-TREE 3, software for evolutionary trees, in 2026. The tool infers family trees from DNA by maximum likelihood. It is open source and widely used. Version 3 extends version 2 with major features.

New mixture models replace some partitioned model uses. Concordance factors now quantify disagreement between genomic regions. Divergence time estimation is integrated into the package. A full sequence simulator was added for testing methods. Wong keeps the tool current for phylogenomic data at scale. Source code is posted on the project GitHub page. As open source code, it stays free for labs anywhere to use and adapt.
europmc-pmc1323316:
Choi and Pak catalogued biases in health questionnaires in 2005. Survey data drive public health decisions, so accuracy matters. Bias can creep in at design or delivery stages. Their review of the literature sorted every bias type found.

Forty-eight distinct bias types were identified and categorized. Each type comes with an example in the catalogue. Three sources organize the list: question design, whole-form design, and administration. Mechanisms behind each bias are explained in plain terms. Choi supplies a pre-use checklist for spotting bias early. It appeared in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2005.
europmc-pmc1420316:
Brain cells grown in a dish do not sit quiet. Wagenaar and co-authors recorded 58 cultures of rat cortex cells for five weeks in 2006. The cells grew on grids of tiny sensors that pick up their electric spikes. Cultures ranged from sparse to dense.

Dense cultures began firing in bursts sooner than sparse ones. After two weeks, most cultures fired in waves that swept the whole dish. Burst styles varied a great deal, with gaps from one second to five minutes. Some bursts came in tight packs with a set inner shape. Wagenaar shows dish networks stay rich and changeable far longer than past reports claimed.
europmc-pmc1479816:
Drugs that block acetylcholine, a nerve signal, open airways in lung disease. Gosens and co-authors reviewed in 2006 whether the signal does more than tighten airway muscle. In asthma and COPD, airway swelling raises nerve tone and acetylcholine release. The signal also drives mucus output.

Fresh work links the signal to airway wall thickening, a lasting change called remodeling. Many airway cells, not just nerves, make acetylcholine and bear its receptors. Gosens notes one blocking drug slows lung decline in COPD, hinting at wider action. The review argues these drugs may help beyond quick relief of tight airways.
europmc-pmc1481516:
The prostate gland makes huge amounts of citrate, a fruit acid, and stores zinc to do it. Costello and Franklin reviewed in 2006 how that odd chemistry flips in prostate cancer. Healthy gland cells hoard zinc, which blocks citrate burning. Cancer cells lose that hoarding skill.

Without zinc, the cells burn citrate for energy instead. A gene for a zinc intake pump, Zip1, fades in cancer cells. Costello frames zinc as a tumor suppressor, a brake on growth. The review ties lab and clinical proof into one story. It urges more heed to metabolism, long ignored in prostate cancer work.
europmc-pmc1586216:
Evolutionary studies drown in sequence and structure data held apart. Roberts, Eargle, Wright, and Luthey-Schulten built MultiSeq in 2006 to unify them. Public databases then held over 3 million sequences and 35,000 structures.

MultiSeq organizes, aligns, and displays both data kinds for proteins and nucleic acids in one space. It carries standard classifications that users can adjust in an electronic notebook. A new algorithm builds clean evolutionary profiles for families of distant kin, stripping redundancy from alignments. Roberts frames the tool around evolution, but built it flexible enough for other patterns of use.
europmc-pmc1592316:
Leaf pores close when a drought hormone sounds the alarm. Mori and co-authors traced that signal in 2006 to two calcium-sensing proteins in Arabidopsis guard cells, the cells that work the pores. The hormone, abscisic acid, was thought to use calcium, but the sensors were unproven.

Plants missing the two kinases, CPK3 and CPK6, showed impaired channel responses. The hormone could no longer open calcium channels or fully trigger anion channels. Stomata closed only partly. Fast anion channels still worked, hinting at a branched signal path. Mori offers genetic proof that these sensors relay the calcium message.
europmc-pmc1693916:
Plant oils can kill germs, and cinnamon oil leads the pack. Prabuseenivasan, Jayakumar, and Ignacimuthu screened 21 oils in 2006 against six bacterial species, four Gram-negative and two Gram-positive kinds, at four dilutions.

Nineteen oils beat at least one strain. Strong effects came from cinnamon and clove oils, and also from geranium, lemon, lime, orange, and rosemary. Cinnamon worked even at low strength. Aniseed, eucalyptus, and camphor oils were weakest. One soil germ was the most sensitive; a lung germ was the least. The team names cinnamon, clove, and lime oils as broad agents hitting both germ classes.
europmc-pmc1779816:
Colizza and colleagues modeled in 2007 how a new flu pandemic could spread around the world. Their concern was the H5N1 bird flu virus then spreading in Southeast Asia and parts of Europe. They asked how fast a human pandemic strain might travel, and what could slow it.

Their computer model used real air travel flows between 3,100 urban areas in 220 countries. They varied how infectious the virus was, plus where and in which season an outbreak began. Leaving air travel out badly understated the risk of a global outbreak. Wide use of antiviral drugs in every hit country could blunt a pandemic. Sharing even a small part of rich-country drug stocks worldwide worked better than hoarding supplies at home.
europmc-pmc1971116:
Schrettl, Haas and co-authors separated in 2007 the jobs of the iron-grabbing molecules a lethal mold uses during infection. Aspergillus fumigatus needs siderophores, small molecules that capture iron, to be virulent, and humans make none, making the pathway a tempting drug target. The fungus secretes two siderophores to scavenge iron and stores iron inside with a third.

The team mapped the making of both classes and found a fourth siderophore, hydroxyferricrocin, used to stock spores with iron. Knocking out the builder enzyme SidC removed the internal siderophores. The mutant then failed at spore germination, spore formation, oxidative stress defense, and virulence. Restoring spore iron stores partly rescued a fully siderophore-free mutant's virulence, proving spore iron matters at infection's start. Cutting off the external scavengers separately also crippled the fungus.
