gao-gaoreports-gao-07-216: The federal tech worker swap got a status check in 2007, and GAO's report reviews the employee exchange program's progress and hurdles. The findings grade the swap. The report shows the talent trade needed better tracking. The exchange had to pay off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-316: A terror attack on a gas tanker would be catastrophic in 2007, and GAO's report spells out the public-safety consequences of an LNG strike. The findings do the grim math. The report warns that the floating bombs in the harbors needed guarding like the threat they were.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-516: Congress's own carbon footprint got an audit in 2007 — GAO's report says energy checkups were the key to cutting the legislative branch's greenhouse gases. The findings start the cleanup at home on Capitol Hill. The report's nudge is pointed: lawmakers should green their own house before preaching to others.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-716: The derivatives paper jam broke in 2007 — GAO's report says the confirmation backlogs that had scared the dealers got worked down at last. The findings credit the cleanup effort. The report reads as a rare good-news chapter from the pre-crisis derivatives world.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-816: Black children lingered in foster care in 2007 — GAO's report says states needed more federal help to shrink the disparity. The findings put numbers to a painful imbalance. The report's demand is moral arithmetic: every child deserves the same shot at a permanent home.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-116: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on convicted Sex Offenders: Factors That Could Affect the Successful Implementation of Driver's License-Related Processes to Encourage Registration and Enhance Mon. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-16: In 2007, the Government Accountability Office published this report on DOD Travel Improper Payments: Fiscal Year 2006 Reporting Was Incomplete and Planned Improvement Efforts Face Challenges. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-416: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at financial Audit: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Funds' 2007 and 2006 Financial Statements. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-516: GAO published its findings on space Acquisitions: DOD Is Making Progress to Rapidly Deliver Low Cost Space Capabilities, but Challenges Remain in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gogol-mantle-and-other-stories-1916:
Claud Field gave Gogol's tales English dress in The Mantle, and Other Stories in 1916. Nikolai Gogol was the great Russian scribe of the odd and the grim. Field picks four tales that show his range at its best. The set is a sound door into Gogol's world.

The Viy is a tale of a priest's son kept three nights with a dead witch. The Nose tells of a nose that leaves its man's face and gains rank in town. Memoirs of a Madman and A May Night round out the set. Gogol's blend of laughs and dread still marks all Russian tales since.
gorky-in-the-world-1916:
In the World, the second volume of Gorky's autobiography, appeared in Russian in 1916 and in Gertrude M. Foakes's English in 1917. His grandmother's ruin sends young Alexey out to earn his bread. He serves in a shoe shop, a draughtsman's office, an icon workshop, and a Volga steamer's scullery.

Each place teaches him how Russia worked, and how it cheated the poor. Books, begged and borrowed, become his secret school against that world. A cook on the steamer first puts serious reading into his hands. The volume covers his teens among cooks, clerks, and outcasts. It stands as one of the great records of a self-made education.
grant-passing-great-race-1916:
Madison Grant published The Passing of the Great Race in 1916 in New York. Grant, a conservationist and museum trustee, wrote a treatise claiming that a Nordic race had built European civilization. He warned that immigration and lower birth rates among the old stock were destroying that inheritance.

Grant sorted Europeans into Nordic, Alpine, and Mediterranean races and ranked them in worth. He urged eugenic laws, limits on immigration, and bars on race mixing to save the group he favored. The book influenced American immigration restriction in the 1920s and was praised by Hitler. Scholars now cite it as a primary source in histories of eugenics and American nativism.
hd-sea-garden-1916:
H. D. published Sea Garden in 1916, her first collection of poems, under the initials Hilda Doolittle used. Hard, clear images of sea, wind, and rock mark Imagism at its most exact. Pound had championed her in London, printing her first poems as H. D., Imagiste, in Poetry magazine.

Greek gods and shores haunt lyrics of storm-beaten fruit, cliffs, and the heat of noon on Aegean rock and sand. Oread, her five-line whirl of pines and sea, became the textbook instance of an Imagist poem. The verse is pared to the bone, each image cut like the shells and stones she celebrates in the poems. Behind the Greek mask stands a young American woman remaking herself as a poet in wartime London. The book founded a career that ran to epics, novels, and memoirs of Freud.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume sixteen: the Silesian Wars, and Maria Theresa's doomed struggle to recover her stolen province. Carlyle narrates campaigns with a soldier's eye and a prophet's voice. The making of Prussia as a great power, told at immense length. For the historically hardy.
homer-iliad-chapman-1616:
Homer's Iliad reached English readers in full in George Chapman's version of 1616. Chapman's was the first complete English Iliad, in fourteen-syllable rhymed couplets of great speed. Keats later praised it in a famous sonnet on first looking into its pages.

The poem sings the wrath of Achilles in the last weeks of the Trojan War. Quarrels, duels, and godly meddling fill the camps of Greeks and Trojans at Troy. Hector's death at Achilles' hands and Priam's plea for his son's body close the arc. Chapman drives the verse with a rough music all his own in English poetry. His Homer shaped how England heard Greek epic for the next two centuries.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-16:
Huronia in 1639 stands at its high point in Volume 16, from 1898. Sainte-Marie among the Hurons rises as a walled mission headquarters. Thwaites prints the reports of a work that seems to have arrived.

Sainte-Marie was the most bold building project in New France then. Stores, chapels, and safe walls serve priests, workers, and guests. The fathers write like men who trust the future is theirs. Yet success and death march toward them hand in hand. Readers who know the end feel the height before the fall. Pride in the work rings through each letter home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyra-nicolas-de:
Nicolas de Lyra, a French Franciscan Bible scholar, is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia for his debt to Jewish learning. Born at Lyre in Normandy about 1270, he entered the Franciscan order in 1291. He took his doctorate at Paris and taught at the Sorbonne. He died at Paris on October 23, 1340.

The article explains his turn to the literal sense of Scripture. Among the four medieval methods of reading, Lyra ranked the plain meaning first. His great commentary, the Postillae, covered the whole Bible between 1322 and 1330. He worked from the original Hebrew and Greek rather than corrupt Latin copies. For Jewish tradition he drew on Rashi, often copying him almost word for word. The entry shows why medieval Christians prized Lyra: his sound scholarship carried Jewish exegesis into the heart of church learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makre-dardeke-1:
Makre Dardeke, meaning teacher of children, names a kind of Hebrew glossary explained in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Such glossaries served medieval students of the Bible. The first and most notable was printed at Naples in 1488. Its author, Perez Trevot, had composed it in 1395 in southern Italy.

The article explains the book's design and purpose. Every Hebrew word in it carries a translation into Italian and Arabic, plus a short Hebrew explanation. It sometimes quotes the French glosses of Rashi and Kimhi. Trevot aimed to rebuild Bible study among Italian Jews, who had drifted toward Talmud alone. Better knowledge would help them answer Christian and Muslim attacks on Judaism. The book also preserves fourteenth-century Italian of real value to scholars. Later versions in other lands swapped in French, German, or Spanish. The entry shows a schoolbook doing cultural work on several fronts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mariampol-polis:
Mariampol, a town in the Suwalki government of Russian Poland, is given a community entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The town and its Jewish community are both fairly recent. At first the community depended on neighboring Kalvariya for its affairs. Its first rabbi, Hayyim Shershaver, was elected in 1780.

The article notes the new community's poverty and its war years. The town was too poor to build a synagogue, so the rabbi toured other towns collecting for one. During the Polish revolution of 1831 a Polish regiment seized four Jewish elders loyal to Russia. They were left bound in the forest. That same year, townspeople locked all the Jews inside the synagogue during a battle. Only one Jew was killed in the encounter. By 1897 Mariampol held 6,298 people, over two thousand of them Jews. The entry preserves a young community's rough start.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-moritz-10:
Moritz Mayer, a German rabbi transplanted to America, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch. Born at Dürckheim on December 16, 1821, he studied law at Munich and practiced in his home town until the revolution of 1848 forced him to flee. In New York he taught at Dr. Lilienthal's school, then served as rabbi at Charleston, South Carolina, from 1851 to 1856, when ill health and quarrels over his radical views drove him out. He died at New York on August 28, 1867.

After a brief Albany pulpit, Mayer settled into the secretaryship of the Grand Lodge of B'nai B'rith, which he held from 1863 until his death. The entry also honors his translator's work: he carried Geiger's lectures on Jewish history, Samuel Adler's catechism, and Fanny Neuda's "Hours of Devotion" from German into English for American readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memphis-10616:
Memphis, the great city of ancient Egypt, stood about ten miles south of modern Cairo. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Müller trace it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name is Greek for the Egyptian "Menfe," which the Bible gives as "Mof" and, corrupted, "Nof." Prophets mention it as Egypt's capital. Jeremiah places a colony of Jews there. They were refugees from the Babylonian war.

The article digs into the name itself. The city's sacred title was "Temple of Ptah." It probably gave the whole country the name Egypt. Its civil name came from King Pepi I's pyramid, "Men-nofer," the good resting-place. From the sixth dynasty to the Arab conquest, Memphis stood first or second among Egypt's cities, and often ruled it. Then Arab builders founded new capitals nearby. They quarried its ruins so thoroughly that only traces near Mitrahineh and the desert necropolises remain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-k:
Meshullam ben Kalonymus ben Todros was a French scholar of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries who served as nasi of Narbonne. His entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 was written by Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn. He entered the fierce dispute over the writings of Maimonides that divided Jewish scholars of his day.

Meshullam sided with Judah al-Fakhkhar in attacking Maimonides and the philosophers, the article reports. Yet he also blamed Al-Fakhkhar for the excessive heat of his attacks, noting that many great and pious Jews stood on the other side. In a letter he asked his friend to spare David Ḳimḥi, and Al-Fakhkhar agreed to write nothing against him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morgenstern-lin:
Lina Morgenstern, née Bauer, was born at Breslau on November 25, 1830. She was the German author and communal worker who put kindergartens and people's kitchens on the national map. The Jewish Encyclopedia tells her story in 1906. The Revolution of 1848 woke her social conscience. Marriage in 1854 to Theodor Morgenstern of Kalisz took her to Berlin.

In 1860 she published Das Paradies der Kindheit. It was the first German textbook of Froebel's kindergarten method, and it ran to five editions. She presided over a society supporting eight kindergartens. In 1866 she left to found the popular kitchens. Their system became a model in Germany and abroad. In 1904 she still directed them as honorary president.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-kohen-: Moses ha-Kohen was rabbi of Salonica in the first half of the eighteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn give him a two-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is known for one book, a collection of responsa called Kehunnat Olam, printed at Constantinople in 1740. It was followed by his novellae on the Tur Yoreh De'ah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munich-11216:
Munich, capital of Bavaria, counted eight thousand seven hundred thirty-nine Jews in 1904. Gotthard Deutsch and Siegmund Salfeld wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia's long history of its Jews. The first firm record is a Jew of Munich witnessing a house sale at Ratisbon in 1229. A synagogue was allowed in 1210 and a cemetery in 1225.

The article is a record of favor and fire. In 1285 a blood accusation brought a mob that burned the synagogue with one hundred eighty Jews inside. King Rudolph's inquiry found the charge false, and the Jews returned. Expulsions still came: in 1442 Duke Albert drove them from Munich and forty other towns. The seized synagogue became a church, and later decrees barred Jews from Bavaria altogether.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-hirz-b: Naphtali Hirz ben Jacob Goslar was an eighteenth-century German rabbi and philosopher. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia notice. He served as dayyan at Halberstadt, then settled at Amsterdam and took up philosophy. His two books both appeared at Amsterdam in 1762: Talmudic novellae, and an attack on primeval matter and natural religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nezikin-injurie:
Nezikin is the Mishnah order on injuries and damages. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Talmud itself uses the name Nezikin for it. Several of its treatises deal with claims for harm. It is also called Yeshu'ot in one source.

Nezikin stands fourth among the Mishnah's six orders. It holds ten treatises and seventy-three chapters in all. The three Babas open it: Kamma, Mezi'a, and Batra. Sanhedrin, Makkot, and Shebu'ot follow in the list. Eduyot, Abodah Zarah, Abot, and Horayot complete it. Abot has no Tosefta and no Gemara at all. Eduyot likewise lacks a Gemara in both Talmuds. The order's core is civil law and the courts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-opet-otto-11716: Otto Opet was a German man of law and a judge. Isidore Singer wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin on April 1, 1866. He taught law at Bern, in Switzerland, in his early years. By 1904 he was a judge and law teacher at Kiel. His books treat the rights of women in old folk law. They also treat court forms, stage law, and kin law in the new German code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-gius:
Giuseppe Ottolenghi was an Italian general from Lombardy. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sabbionetta on December 26, 1838. He died at Turin on November 2, 1904. He began the study of law at Turin in youth.

Giuseppe then entered the war school of that city. In 1859 he joined the war as a man who chose to serve. He rose in rank through the wars that followed fast. He was the first Jew to join the staff corps. In 1863 he was made a captain in the host. He fought the brigands of Basilicata in 1864. He won the silver medal for worth in war there. In 1902 he was made the kingdom's minister of war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parody-11916:
Parody is a work that turns a grave work to mirth. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Davidson wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It may be made in verse or in plain prose form. It is built close on an old work or a class of works. Its trick is to make the grave sense look absurd.

Two near forms are travesty and the mock heroic style. One way to make a parody needs no change of words. A man just uses a known line in a playful sense. Abraham ibn Ezra did this with a prayer line once. He used it for the white neck and dark hair of a girl. A wrong pause can make a text a parody of itself. A green cantor once joined two lines of Genesis wrong. That made God speak absurd words to Noah in his ark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perahyah-aaron-:
Aaron ben Hayyim Peraḥyah was a rabbi of Salonica. He worked there in the seventeenth century as a legal writer. The Executive Committee and Lazarus Grünhut wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had studied under Hasdai Peraḥyah ha-Kohen.

Four books carry his name into print. The first holds his rulings from nearly fifty years of work. The second gives fresh readings of Talmud passages. Two more volumes came out long after his death. One gathers short rulings, and one gathers sermons. His son and grandson saw the books through the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philo-judus-121:
Philo Judaeus was a Jewish philosopher of Alexandria. He was born about 20 BCE and died after 40 CE. Three scholars shared his article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Crawford Howell Toy, Carl Siegfried, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach.

Philo sought to fuse Greek wisdom with Hebrew faith. Allegory, learned from the Stoics, was his tool for the task. In 40 he sailed to Rome on an embassy. Alexandria's Jews begged Caligula to shield them from Greek attacks. His own age in Judaism largely rejected him. The early Church preserved and prized his books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plymouth-12216:
Plymouth is a Devon seaport with a small old congregation. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A few Jewish families lived there in 1740. Deeds trace their burial ground to 1752. Its silver bells and brasswork are antique too.

In 1762 the town leased ground for a synagogue. Three hundred pounds finished the house of worship. The Catherine street synagogue keeps its ancient features still. A latticed gallery and carved Ark grace it. Jacob Nathan endowed a school for poor Jewish children. Some 300 Jews lived among 107,500 townsfolk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-potiphar-or-pot:
Potiphar is the name of an Egyptian officer in the book of Genesis. Emil G. Hirsch and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The form Potiphar is likely a short form of Potiphera. Greek translators treat the two names as one. In Egyptian the name means he whom Ra gave. Ra was the sun god of Egypt.

The name itself has not been found in Egyptian stone records. Names of like shape occur from an early dynasty, though. Potiphar was the officer to whom Joseph was sold. He is called a servant of Pharaoh in Genesis. The article weighs the name, its roots, and its forms. It then turns to the man's place in the Joseph story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-isaa:
Isaac Rabinowitz, called Ish Kovno, was a Russian poet in Hebrew. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Kovno in 1846. He died in New York in 1900. He made Hebrew songs from an early age. At fourteen he learned Hebrew grammar from Abraham Mapu.

At eighteen Rabinowitz entered the rabbinical school at Wilna. In 1867 he wed and settled at Telshi. There he won the friendship of two noted men. One was Mordecai Nathansohn, kin to his wife. The other was Leon Gordon, a teacher in that town. Gordon's verse left its mark on the young poet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rechabites-1261:
The Rechabites were a family group descended from Rechab. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, George A. Barton, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. They are also linked to the Kenites. Jeremiah tells their best known story.

The article says Jeremiah offered Rechabites wine in the Temple. They refused, citing a command from their ancestor Jehonadab. That command banned wine, houses, sowing, and vineyards. They were to live in tents all their days. Jeremiah used their loyalty to shame his own people. The writers see them as resisting settled life. They kept a nomad ideal in both kingdoms. The entry then turns to Talmud teaching on them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reverts-admissi:
Reverts are apostates who wish to return to Judaism. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Rabbinical law treats apostasy as a grave sum of sins. Yet an apostate never stops being an Israelite.

The article says he may repent and regain his standing. A saying ranks the repentant sinner very high. The truly righteous cannot reach that place, it claims. Maimonides lists twenty four classes of grave sinners. They include deniers of the Torah's divine source. They also include informers against fellow Israelites. Still, he says repentance opens the world to come. Even a lifelong denier who turns gains a share. The entry grounds welcome in law and Scripture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rowe-leo-s-1291:
Leo S. Rowe was an American economist born in McGregor, Iowa, on September 17, 1871. Cyrus Adler and J. H. Hollander wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at the Wharton School, then took his doctorate at Halle in 1892.

Rowe rose at the University of Pennsylvania to full professor of political science in 1904. President McKinley named him in 1900 to a commission revising Porto Rico's laws. He then chaired the Insular Code Commission for the island. In 1902 he became president of the American Academy of Political and Social Science. His 1904 book treats the United States and Porto Rico.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salamander-gree:
The salamander, in rabbinic lore, is a fabulous creature born of fire itself. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Ludwig Blau wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The Talmud elsewhere treats it as a kind of toad.

Glass-blowers who stoke a furnace seven days breed the creature, says the legend. Shaped like a mouse or spider, it perishes in open air. Smear its blood on a hand, and that spot is proof against fire. So Hezekiah's mother anointed him when Manasseh would sacrifice the child. Hell's fire, likewise, cannot harm the scribes, themselves all fire like Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jose:
Samuel ben Joseph of Verdun was a French tosafist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a disciple of Isaac ben Samuel the Elder of Dampierre.

Samuel corresponded with his master Isaac on learned questions of the day. The tosafot name him, as do Or Zarua and Haggahot Maimuniyyot. In those works he appears under the byname ha-Bahur, the Younger, to mark him off. He is sometimes confounded with Samuel ben Hayyim, also called Samuel of Verdun. The entry's care on that point saves readers a mix-up.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sasportas-13216:
Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, Isidore Singer, and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Sasportas family. They were Spanish rabbis and scholars. The earliest known members lived at Oran, in Algeria, late in the sixteenth century. The name may come from Seisportas, meaning six gates. The family stayed loyal to Spain against the Moors.

The family's giant is Jacob ben Aaron Sasportas. Born at Oran in 1610, he died at Amsterdam in 1698. He held rabbinates from Tlemçen to London and Hamburg. He also fought the false Messiah Shabbetai Ẓebi with great force. His son Isaac served the Portuguese community at Amsterdam. Isaac left decisions, poems, sermons, and letters in three languages. The entry traces a family that served synagogues across three continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiner-marti:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Martin Schreiner. He was a Hungarian rabbi. Schreiner was born at Grosswardein on July 8, 1863. He studied at Budapest's rabbinical seminary and university. He took his doctorate in 1885 and his rabbinical diploma in 1887. From 1887 to 1890 he served as rabbi at Somogy-Csurgó.

In 1893 Schreiner became a professor at Budapest's Jewish normal school. In 1894 Berlin's Lehranstalt called him to teach Jewish history. He also teaches the philosophy of religion there. His books treat the pronunciation of the Bible text. Others study Islam's movements in its first four centuries. He wrote on Kalam, the Muslim-style theology found in Jewish letters. He also published on the Jews of Egypt and a volume of Hungarian sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semitic-museum-:
Harvard's Semitic Museum was founded by Jacob H. Schiff of New York in 1889. Cyrus Adler and David Gordon Lyon wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Schiff gave money to buy objects that showed Semitic life, history, and thought. The first collection opened to the public in 1891.

In 1902 and 1903 the museum moved into its own building, also Schiff's gift. Its rooms held a library, lectures, and Assyrian, Babylonian, and Hittite exhibits. A Palestinian room displayed finds from the Holy Land. The entry shows how one donor built a home for studying the Semitic past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheba-kehillot-:
Sheba Kehillot means the Seven Communities, a name for seven Hungarian Jewish towns. Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The towns lay in the counties of Sopron and Mosony. They were Eisenstadt, Deutsch-Kreutz, Mattersdorf, and Lakenbach. Kobersdorf, Kittsee, and Frauenkirchen complete the seven.

These communities held special privileges under Hungarian rule. From the late seventeenth century they ranked among Hungary's richest Jewish towns. Their strength lasted into the early nineteenth century. The entry is brief, giving names in Hungarian, German, and Judeo-German forms. Even so, it marks a famed bloc of towns where Jewish life flourished under protection for over a century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shullam-samuel-:
Samuel Shullam was a Jewish physician and historian of the late sixteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He came from Spanish stock and lived an adventurous life. He ended at Constantinople under a powerful patron's care.

Kiera, called Esther, stood high in the sultan's favor. At her expense Shullam published Zacuto's Yuhasin in 1566. He cut much from that chronicle in his edition. He added an Arabic dynastic history and a Turkish one. The Turkish history was his own work entirely. He also issued Josephus against Apion in Hebrew. Sherira Gaon's letter and other old texts followed. Curiously, he dropped Zacuto's account of Spain's expulsion. He meant to write that sad history himself one day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-ha-s: Simeon ben ha-Segan was a tanna of the second generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Some of his legal sayings survive in the Mishnah. All of them were transmitted by Simeon ben Gamaliel. They appear in Shekalim, Ketubbot, and Menahot tractates. He may be the same man as Simeon ben Kahana. Simeon ben Gamaliel also transmits legal sayings in Kahana's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-snowman-isaac-1:
Isaac Snowman was an English artist born in London in 1874. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was educated at the City of London School. In 1890 he entered the Royal Academy School. There he won a free medal and then a scholarship. In 1897 he joined the Maccabean pilgrimage to Palestine.

His drawings often dealt with Jewish themes and scenes. They included A Difficult Passage in the Talmud. They also included The Blessing of Sabbath Lights. His painting Children's Voices drew much attention in 1901. The Bride, from 1904, became very popular with the public. He also painted The Wailing-Place at Jerusalem and other biblical scenes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-song-of-songs-t:
The Song of Songs, called The Song of Solomon in English Bibles, is a poem. Emil G Hirsch and Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It is one of the Five Megillot of the Bible. Its Hebrew title means the most excellent of songs. The title itself is later than the poem it heads.

The oldest reading of the Song was allegorical in kind. Midrash and Targum saw it as God and Israel in love. The Church read it as Christ and the Church instead. A literal reading sees it as praise of married love. That reading has now ousted the allegorical one almost fully. Scholars debate whether the groom is Solomon or a shepherd.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinheim-solom:
Solomon Ludwig Steinheim was a German physician, poet, and philosopher born in 1789. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinheim was born at Altona on August 6 of that year. He studied medicine at the University of Kiel. He died at Zurich on May 19, 1866.

Steinheim treated typhus patients when sickness struck Hamburg and Altona. Poor health ended his medical career in 1845, and he settled in Rome. He wrote on grasshoppers, animal instinct, and the pathology of tumors. His main work argued that revelation is a philosophic truth. Its first volume appeared in 1835 under a German title on revelation. He stressed creation from nothing and the unity of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sundeles-zebi-h:
Zebi Hirsch Sundeles was a Polish scholar of the sixteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He published prayer books with commentary for Polish Jews. His work served the rites of Poland, Bohemia, and Moravia. He often worked with a partner named Koppelmann.

His daily prayer book appeared at Lublin in 1571. A festival prayer book followed there in 1579. Both books carry his commentary on the prayers. In 1584 he issued penitential prayers at Cracow. That volume prints notes by his father-in-law, Mordecai Mardos. A 1592 book covers prayers for special Sabbaths. Later editions kept his books in use for decades. The entry preserves the record of a prayer-book editor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmudic-law-14:
Talmudic law is the legal system built on the Talmud. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its full history spans thousands of years of development. Joseph Caro's Shulhan Aruk states its later form. Three great epochs shape the code's growth.

The Pentateuch forms the first epoch and the base. The Talmud builds the second epoch upon it. Post-Talmudic literature forms the third and final epoch. Each age grew from the one before it. Yet each also stands as its own system. Changing material and spiritual life reshaped the law. Legal fictions link the stages across that change. Scholars thus speak of Mosaic, Talmudic, and rabbinic systems. The entry argues for evolution inside a constant frame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobacco-14416:
Tobacco use among Jews, and the rabbis' rulings on it, fill this article. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Jews traded widely in tobacco in some lands. One tradition credits a Jewish sailor with Columbus in 1492. Luis de Terres, it says, learned tobacco in Cuba.

Clergy fought tobacco as incense offered to Satan. Rabbis instead asked legal questions about its use. May one smoke on Sabbaths, holy days, and fasts? Does inhaling smoke require a blessing first? Gombiner doubted a blessing, since smoke has no substance. Benveniste banned smoking on the Ninth of Ab. He even excommunicated one man who smoked that day. Seventeenth-century debate shows the habit spreading fast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triest-14516:
Triest, a seaport at the head of the Adriatic, was Italian in culture but Austrian in rule. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews settled there even before Austrian control in 1382. One Jew, the city banker, lived in the great square. No full history of its Jews was ever written.

Triest's Jews enjoyed rare favor for their time. They could live in any part of the city. No badge was forced on them there. The first synagogue used the Ashkenazic ritual. Fire later destroyed that building and the old records. A grand new synagogue rose around 1787. Sephardic immigrants later built their own house of prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wihl-ludwig-149:
Ludwig Wihl was a German poet and philologist. He was born at Wevelingen, Prussia, on October 24, 1807. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Brussels on January 16, 1882. He studied at Bonn and Munich. He took his doctorate in 1830.

Wihl argued that Phoenician derived from Hebrew. He also traced Greek art to Phoenician roots. A university career closed when he refused baptism. He turned to journalism at Frankfort and Hamburg. His first poems appeared in 1837. His account of Heine made an enemy of the poet. Later he taught and edited in Holland and Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-asher-ans:
Asher Anshel Worms was a German doctor, math man, and Hebrew scholar. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Frankfort late in the 1600s, he died there in 1769. He took two degrees in 1723 and joined the Jewish hospital.

He served as a doctor at that hospital for forty-five years. Before his degree he wrote a book on algebra. It gives sums and their answers for the student. He also reworked an old chess book for new readers. He added a preface and a German poem to it. His chief work is a note set on the Torah text. It treats the Masoretic counts of the words and signs. Many more works of his stayed in draft form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ze-era-15216:
Zeera was a scholar of Palestine of the third rank of amoraim. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Babylon and spent his youth there. He sat with Hisda, Huna, and Judah in that land.

His love for the Holy Land drew him to leave home. He hid that plan from his teacher Judah in full. Judah held that no man should quit Babylon for the West. Ere he left, he spied on Judah at the bath house. The words he heard there he took as a dear gift. A dream told him his sins were wiped clean for the trip. He fasted one hundred days to shed the Babylon school way. That fast was to clear his mind for the new land.
journal-of-discourses-vol-16:
Volume Sixteen, from 1874, was preached as the legal noose tightened. Marshals raid homes while church leaders dodge arrest across Utah. The anti-polygamy drive turns from threat into daily, grinding fact.

Young's voice stays steady as the pressure mounts on his people. Sermons teach patience, secrecy where needed, and unbroken faith in God. Families learn to live with prison hanging over their fathers' heads. Faith practiced under the law's shadow fills these hard, brave pages. The Saints' resolve is tested here and, by their account, holds firm against the storm. Ordinary families, not just leaders, carry the volume's quiet heroism.
joyce-portrait-artist-1916:
James Joyce published A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in 1916, modernism's great coming-of-age novel in English. Stephen Dedalus forges his soul from Catholic Dublin toward exile, in a tale from Joyce's youth. Serialized in The Egoist, the book turned the autobiographical novel into a study of a mind's formation.

Stephen moves from Clongowes schoolboy through hellfire sermons to a university student's heresies on art, beauty, and the artist's calling in Dublin. A Christmas dinner fight over Parnell, a director's vocation talk, and a girl wading at Bull Island mark his road to refusal. He resolves on silence, exile, and cunning, to forge his race's uncreated conscience in art. Joyce's style grows with Stephen, from nursery babble to the aesthetic theory of the villanelle chapter. The book remains the model of the artist novel.
jung-collected-papers-long-1916:
C. G. Jung's Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology appeared in English in 1916, edited and translated by Constance E. Long. The papers show the early Jung after his break with Freud. Jung studies complexes, clusters of feeling that act like small selves within the psyche. Word association tests reveal these complexes at work.

Other papers treat dreams, hysteria, and the role of the unconscious in art and life. Jung already stresses that the unconscious compensates the conscious mind. The volume gave English readers their first full view of his method. It is a record of a new school being born. Readers of later Jung will find its roots here.
king-henry-iv-part-1-pg1516:
In this edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Fourth, Part One, the cast list names the whole divided kingdom. King Henry heads it, with his sons Henry, Prince of Wales, and John of Lancaster. The rebels follow: Northumberland, his son Hotspur, Worcester, Mortimer, and the Scottish Douglas. Sir John Falstaff and his tavern crew close the list.

The contents map the action: the king's palace, the Prince's apartment, an inn-yard at Rochester, and Gad's Hill. The Boar's Head Tavern in Eastcheap hosts the comedy. Warkworth Castle, the rebel camp, and Shrewsbury host the war. Reading the scene plan shows Shakespeare's design plainly: court, tavern, and battlefield in turn, until Hal and Hotspur meet at Shrewsbury.
lawrence-amores-1916:
Amores, published in 1916, is Lawrence's third book of poems and the first from the years of his marriage to Frieda. The love poems gathered here are fierce and tender by turns, written out of the couple's early life together.

Lawrence writes of desire, quarrels, longing, and the strange peace two people find in each other. The verse is looser than his apprentice work, feeling its way toward the free forms he would later master. Some poems still wear the dress of older lyric styles. Taken together, they show a poet remaking himself inside a marriage that changed his life and art.
lawrence-twilight-italy-1916:
Lawrence wrote these travel sketches after walking and staying around Lake Garda in the years before the First World War. Twilight in Italy, published in 1916, collects them into his first travel book.

He describes peasants, priests, dancers, and lemon gardens with a poet's eye and a prophet's temper. Again and again he sets the old, bodily life of Italy against the machine age creeping over it. The sketches wander, argue, and suddenly blaze into description of light and water. It is travel writing as thinking aloud, and it began a form Lawrence made his own.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The January 1876 Lippincott's opens a series on the century. Its fruits and its festival frame the American centennial year. Edward C. Bruce continues Up the Thames in a third paper. Frances Anne Kemble prints lines written at Venice in 1865.

Sketches of India begin with Lady Arthur Eildon's dying letter. Rebecca Harding Davis contributes The House on the Beach. Mrs. Linton's Atonement of Leam Dundas advances four chapters. Famishing Portugal and plantation papers round out the number. A dead love poem by Hillard and famishing Portugal reports follow. The old plantation papers begin their two-part run here.
lodge-raymond-1916:
Oliver Lodge sought his dead son in Raymond, his famed book of 1916. Raymond Lodge fell in the Great War in 1915. His sire, a chief of science, went to the dark room to test if the boy still lived in some form. The book gives the talks, word for word, as Lodge took them down.

Grief stricken homes seized on the book at once. It made Lodge's faith a mass hope in a land of loss. Doubts ran high too, and Lodge prints his checks. Few books show war grief so raw. Its fame still lasts.
lombard-sententiae-quaracchi-1916:
Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, compiled his Four Books of Sentences in the 1150s, and the work became the textbook of theology for the Latin West. Every master, from Aquinas to Luther, had to lecture on it. The text here is the critical edition of the College of Saint Bonaventure at Quaracchi, 1916, in two volumes and in Latin.

The books move from God and the Trinity to creation, then to Christ and the virtues, and last to the sacraments and the end of the world. Lombard weaves the church fathers into one ordered web of questions. No English version in the public domain exists. To read the Sentences is to read the syllabus of the medieval schools.
lvsvs-serivs-quo-hermes-sive-mercurius-r:
Lusus Serius, the Serious Game, is a Latin work by Michael Maier, printed in 1616. Maier was a German physician, alchemist, and count palatine. His long title tells the whole conceit of the book. All things under man debate which of them deserves the crown.

A council of eight hears the long dispute over worldly things. Rational man sits as judge over the rival claims. At last Hermes, or Mercury, is judged and made king of them all. Mercury stood for quicksilver, and for the secret art of alchemy. Maier hides deep doctrine inside this playful courtroom fable. The Getty Research Institute digitized this rare old copy.
mandelstam-stone-1916:
Osip Mandelstam called his first book of poems Stone, and the second Russian edition of 1916 gathers his early work. He wrote of buildings, music, and the old Greek and Roman world. Each poem is built with care, like a wall of cut stone.

Young Mandelstam rejected vague mystic moods in favor of clear, solid images. Cathedrals, domes, and ancient myths carry weight and order in his verse. The book announced a poet of rare skill and learning. Later readers would rank him among the finest Russian poets of the twentieth century, and Stone shows why.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-16: Last of the set in this slice, volume sixteen is etext 3566. Its file was changed in January 2003, later than its neighbours. A year label, 1821, stands in the head note with the title. Bourrienne's name stands there too, as author of the memoirs. The sample, however, ends with the license text and never reaches his prose. Contents cannot be grounded, so this entry reports the file facts and stops there.
openalex-w1680837216:
Kenneth Aamodt and the ALICE Collaboration reported this first measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in December 2010. The team studied lead-lead collisions at the CERN collider. It was the first such flow measurement at this energy. Particles were tracked near the central detector region.

Elliptic flow describes the oval pattern of emitted particles. The team used a four-particle correlation method for it. Flow rose by about a third versus older gold results. Some fluid models with viscosity matched that rise, they report. The signal probes the hot quark-gluon plasma directly. Strong flow hints the plasma flows like a liquid. The result opened a new energy frontier for the field.
openalex-w2115593216:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration searched for supersymmetric particles in LHC data. Their paper appeared in Journal of High Energy Physics in 2014. Supersymmetry predicts partner particles for known ones. Squarks and gluinos are among them. Finding none so far still teaches physicists where they cannot hide.

The search used proton collisions recorded in 2012. Events with strong jets and missing momentum were selected. No electrons or muons were allowed in the signal events. No excess over background appeared. The team set mass limits under several models. Gluinos below a set mass were excluded in one simple model. Squark limits depended on model assumptions. The results narrow the search space for supersymmetry.
openalex-w2127258416:
Neha Shah, Abigail Wright, Gill Han Bai, and colleagues published this survey in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2007. They documented the worldwide spread of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis, or XDR TB. These strains resist many of the backup drugs used when standard tuberculosis treatment already fails, leaving doctors with few options.

The authors surveyed a network of top reference laboratories for resistant isolates. Reports of near-untreatable cases had been anecdotal, and the survey tested whether they were isolated or a wider pattern. The study frames XDR TB as a growing global threat. Poor prescribing, weak drug supply, and missed doses drive resistance, and untreated patients can spread these hard strains.
openalex-w2140045216:
Ana Luisa Sosa, Emiliano Albanese, Martin Prince, and colleagues published this survey in BMC Neurology in 2009. They report reference scores for the 10/66 Dementia Research Group thinking tests. The battery helps diagnose dementia, but fair use needs norms for age, sex, and schooling in each population.

Household surveys ran in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico, China, and India. Only people free of dementia set the norms. Older people and those with less schooling scored worse on all four tests, while sex mattered little. Scores also differed much by site, with Chinese participants ahead and Indian participants behind Latin American ones, so norms travel poorly.
openalex-w2265611316:
Kenneth Stapleford, Gonzalo Moratorio, Rasmus Henningsson, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. They sequenced whole genomes of chikungunya virus from the Caribbean outbreak that began in late 2013. The mosquito-borne virus causes severe fever and joint pain, and this was its first major emergence in the Americas.

Twenty outbreak samples were sequenced in full and their consensus genomes deposited in a public archive. Comparing them with older strains let the team trace how the virus evolved as it spread. Their analysis reveals novel evolutionary elements in the viral genome. Such details help scientists follow emerging lineages and judge how outbreak strains differ from their ancestors.
openalex-w2529645216:
M. Tofazzal Islam, Daniel Croll, and Pierre Gladieux led this 2016 study in BMC Biology of a new wheat disease in Bangladesh. In February 2016, blast fungus appeared in wheat fields across eight districts. The outbreak covered an estimated fifteen thousand hectares and destroyed some harvests completely. Nobody yet knew where the fungus had come from.

Within weeks, the team sequenced RNA from diseased leaves gathered directly in the fields. They also re-infected seedlings with strains from infected grain, which caused blast on wheat but not rice. Family-tree analysis of the genomes pointed to a South American wheat-infecting lineage of Magnaporthe oryzae. The case shows genomic surveillance can be applied fast during an outbreak. It can reveal what a new plant pathogen is and where it likely originated.
openalex-w2898397916:
Artem Lysenko, Alok K. Sharma, and Keith A. Boroevich, with Tatsuhiko Tsunoda, proposed a machine learning method for drug safety in Life Science Alliance in 2018. Drug development costs keep climbing while approvals fall. Toxicity is a prime culprit: it causes about a fifth of clinical trial failures. Worse, it drives two-thirds of drug withdrawals after products reach the market.

Predicting toxic failures computationally could save years and fortunes. Earlier screening leaned on rule sets for druglikeness and simple absorption criteria. The authors propose an integrative machine learning approach instead. It aims to flag dangerous compounds before expensive trials begin. Every withdrawn drug represents patients exposed to harm that prediction might prevent. Better early warnings would also free resources for safer candidates. The paper positions learning-based screening as essential infrastructure for modern drug discovery.
openalex-w2953540816:
Nigel Arnell, Jason Lowe, Andrew Challinor, and Timothy Osborn published this study in Climatic Change in 2019. It estimates global and regional climate impacts at set levels of warming, up to five degrees above pre-industrial levels. Such estimates help governments debate how strict their climate targets should be.

The authors use more than thirty indicators, covering heatwaves, river floods, droughts, and likely effects on crop yields. At the global scale, every impact they judged was harmful, and risks grew with each added degree. The chance of a major heatwave rises steeply with warming, while other harms grow more steadily. They also stress that estimates carry wide uncertainty and differ strongly between regions.
openalex-w2981485716:
Marianna Vitaloni, Angie Botto-van Bemden, Rosa Sciortino Contreras, and colleagues published this systematic review in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2019. It gathers what is known about quality of life in people with knee osteoarthritis. The disease is a common chronic joint condition that brings pain and limits movement.

Searching four major databases up to early 2017, the team screened six hundred ten papers and kept sixty-two that met their rules. Every study found worse quality of life in patients than in control groups. Limits on activity cut social ties and mental wellbeing, not just physical function. The review also sorts the personal factors, such as age, sex, and other illnesses, that shape how strongly patients are affected.
openalex-w2997833216:
André Carrington, Paul Fieguth, Hammad Qazi, and colleagues published this methods paper in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2020. It proposes new scores for judging machine learning classifiers on skewed data. Standard scores can mislead when one class is far rarer than the other, as in disease screening.

The usual tool, the area under the ROC curve, mixes useful and useless parts of the curve on such data. Existing partial versions drop information about true negatives. The authors derive a concordant partial area and a matching partial c statistic, and prove the pair agree with each other and rebuild the full measures. They test the scores on classic examples and on two breast cancer datasets.
openalex-w3032034316:
Ryan Collins, Harrison Brand, Konrad Karczewski, and colleagues published this study in Nature in 2020. It builds a reference catalog of structural variation in human genomes for use in medicine and population genetics. Structural variants are rearrangements of DNA chunks at least fifty letters long.

Such variants include gains and losses of DNA, flips and swaps that keep the total amount balanced, and mobile elements that copy themselves around the genome. By sheer size and number, they shape how genomes evolve and work, and they contribute to inherited and acquired disease. A shared reference tells doctors and researchers which variants are common and harmless, and which deserve a closer look.
openalex-w4225700116:
Morten Dueholm, Marta Nierychlo, Kasper Andersen, and colleagues built MiDAS 4, a global catalogue of bacteria from wastewater treatment plants. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2022. Microbial communities do the real work of biological wastewater treatment, yet their diversity is still poorly known. Studies were hampered by missing standard methods and incomplete reference databases.

The team sequenced more than five million full-length marker gene sequences from seven hundred forty plants worldwide. From them they built a shared naming system and reference set, MiDAS 4. Earlier work had hinted at overwhelming diversity, with few types shared between plants. A common catalogue now lets engineers compare plants and track the microbes that matter for clean water.
openalex-w4293022516:
Pau Amaro-Seoane, Jeff Andrews, Manuel Arca Sedda, and colleagues review astrophysics with the future LISA observatory, in Living Reviews in Relativity in 2023. LISA will detect gravitational waves from space, opening a new window on the universe. Paired with light-based telescopes, it enables multi-messenger observations of the same events. The coming decade, the authors stress, must prepare scientists to read LISA's data stream.

The review covers the three main source classes LISA will hear. They are tight pairs of stellar remnants, merging massive black holes, and small objects spiralling into large ones. For each, the authors summarise the physics, the best models, and the open gaps. New data methods, mixing simulations with modern data science, run through the outlook.
openalex-w7133329016:
Hooriya Shafiq Butt, a dermatologist in Lahore, Pakistan, reported a 2026 case of lupoid cutaneous leishmaniasis, a rare skin disease caused by a parasite. Her patient was a 29-year-old man with a single plaque on his right cheek that had slowly grown for two years. The sore looked much like lupus vulgaris, a skin form of tuberculosis.

Tests gave mixed signals, with parasite bodies seen early on but not later, and tissue samples showing a pattern shared by several diseases. The team settled on leishmaniasis from the history, exam, and tissue findings. A month of injections into the muscle, then repeated injections into the sore itself, cured him completely. The case warns doctors not to miss this diagnosis on chronic face sores.
openalex-w7135012316:
Mone Mukai of Juntendo University in Tokyo wrote a 2026 mini review on polycythemia vera, a slow-growing blood cancer that makes too many red blood cells. Nearly all patients carry a change in the JAK2 gene. The review focuses on the heart and blood vessel problems that dominate illness and death in this disease, especially blood clots in arteries and veins.

Standard care uses blood removal, low-dose aspirin, and drugs that lower cell counts to cut clot risk. Yet some of these drugs may themselves harm the heart. Mukai describes a recent case where a newer interferon drug was tied to heart weakness that later reversed. The review urges structured heart monitoring for these patients.

The authors call for stronger surveillance and prevention aimed at pregnant adolescents, whose infection endangers their babies.
