Documenting when infections occurred inside the system grounds prevention policy in evidence rather than assumption. Seventeen years of records give the clearest picture available of prison transmission. Prisons hold men in close halls with poor air and much stress, a mix that breeds spread of all germs. So hard counts of spread there guard both the men held and the towns they return to.
plos-pone-0005516:
Karen Ruschke and co-authors studied fat tissue in special mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The links between nerves and fat in mammals are little explored. The mice in the study lack a nerve-related gene and grow obese as adults.

The team found that nerve growth into fat was faulty in these mice. Their fat tissue also had an abnormal build and burned energy in an unusual way. The work shows that nerves help shape how fat forms and works, not just how the brain controls appetite. The mouse gives workers a rare way to study nerve and fat links without changing diet or appetite first.
plos-pone-0005616:
Kim Monkhorst and co-authors studied how female cells choose an X chromosome to switch off, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Female mammals carry two X chromosomes but need only one active set, so one is shut down at random in each cell. Each X has a chance of being chosen.

The team showed that the balance between X chromosomes and the rest sets that chance. Properties of each X also weigh in. Knowing the rules helps explain diseases where the shutdown goes wrong or is skewed. Skewed shutdown in women can unmask gene faults on the active X, a known cause of some disorders.
plos-pone-0005716:
Kirstin Elgass and co-authors applied in 2009 a light-based method that times how long glow lasts, to watch plant cells in fine detail. To predict how cells behave, scientists need numbers, not just pictures, at very small scales. Fluorescence lifetime imaging gives those numbers from living cells.

The method tracks tiny changes inside plant cells as they happen. It can show where molecules meet and how their setting shifts. Pairing it with standard microscopy widened what the team could measure. Tools like this move plant science from still snapshots toward true moving accounts of cell life.
plos-pone-0005816:
Dapeng Zhang and co-authors profiled gene activity tied to breeding seasons in fish in 2009. Many vertebrates, goldfish included, breed on a yearly rhythm set by day length and internal hormones. The brain-pituitary-gonad axis runs that rhythm.

The team mapped which neuroendocrine genes rise and fall with the season. A broad pattern, rather than a few switches, seems to drive the cycle across the season. Fish farmers care because spawning time sets production schedules. Climate shifts may also disturb these rhythms. The gene list gives both farmers and ecologists markers to watch.
plos-pone-0005916:
Candace Mathiason and co-authors showed in 2009 that deer can catch chronic wasting disease from the environment alone, before showing any sign of illness. This prion disease of deer and elk spreads mysteriously among herds. The team had already found infectious prions in saliva and blood of infected deer.

Here, healthy deer exposed only to contaminated surroundings became infected. Shedding before symptoms makes control far harder, since apparently well animals seed pastures and pens. Environmental transmission explains the disease's stubborn spread in the wild. The findings press wildlife managers toward early, aggressive containment.
plos-pone-0006016:
A pain drug can, in some people, make pain worse instead of better. Karin Jensen, Tina Lonsdorf, Martin Schalling and colleagues studied that rebound after a single opiate dose in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper links the rise in heat pain sensitivity to a variant in the COMT gene, which helps break down key brain chemicals.

The variant, known as val158met, changes how active the COMT enzyme is. People who carry one form may thus feel the rebound more strongly. A gene that tunes an odd drug effect could one day guide dosing. The work also warns that added pain after opioids is not always a sign the drug has worn off.
plos-pone-0006116:
TB is the single largest killer of people living with HIV. Shahin Ranjbar, Helena Boshoff, Amara Mulder and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the strain of TB changes that grim partnership. Their PLOS ONE paper tests distinct clinical strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and measures how each one regulates HIV-1 replication when the two meet.

HIV replication was differentially regulated by strain, the title reports, so not all TB pushes HIV alike. A third to a half of all AIDS deaths have involved TB, which makes any strain effect a large-scale concern. The finding argues for reading co-infection by strain, not treating TB as one uniform partner to HIV.
plos-pone-0006216:
Staphylococcus aureus rides harmlessly in many noses, yet it can invade the blood and kill. Juan Fan and colleagues mapped the germ's global variety and harmfulness in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Much of the worldwide diversity of this staph species had never been charted, and strains differ in how readily they cause disease.

Combining geography with virulence data shows where dangerous lineages live and spread. That map helps hospitals and health agencies watch the riskiest strains. It also guides vaccine and drug planning toward the forms that matter most. A global picture replaces guesswork built on local samples alone.
plos-pone-0006316:
Growth signals inside a cell travel through space, not just through chemistry. Michelle Costa and colleagues simulated ErbB1 signalling with and without spatial detail in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. ErbB receptors control proliferation, growth, and survival, and their overexpression is often linked to cancer.

Coupled stochastic simulations showed that spatial organisation changes how the pathway behaves. Treating the cell as a well-mixed soup misses those effects. Receptor position and movement shape the signal's strength and timing. The study argues modellers and drug designers should keep the map, not just the wiring list.
plos-pone-0006416:
Sorting disease from health using gene expression means choosing the right few genes from thousands. Michael Gutkin, Ron Shamir, and Gideon Dror present SlimPLS, a feature selection method, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Classifiers are trained on labelled samples, cases versus controls, but bloated gene lists overfit and mislead.

SlimPLS selects lean feature sets for gene expression based disease classification. Leaner models generalise better to new patients. They are also easier to turn into practical tests. The method addresses a central challenge of biomedical data analysis. Lean gene sets also cost less to test, which helps clinics with small budgets.
plos-pone-0006516:
Hai-Feng Chen simulated a modified protein domain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The kinase-inducible domain, KID, is a transcriptional activator. It stimulates target gene expression in signal transduction by associating with a partner domain called KIX. Phosphorylation, the addition of a phosphate group, switches KID on. NMR studies had given partial views of its structure.

Using molecular dynamics simulation, the author modeled how phosphorylated KID behaves atom by atom. Simulations reveal motions too fast and small to watch directly. Understanding the switch helps explain how signals turn genes on. The work is a computational study, done entirely in silico.
plos-pone-0006616:
Séverine Hamann, Daniel Schorderet, and Sandra Cottet studied cell death in an inherited blindness in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pathogenesis in the Rpe65-deficient mouse model of Leber's congenital amaurosis is characterized by slow, progressive degeneration of rod photoreceptors. On the opposite schedule, cones die quickly. The team examined Bax-induced apoptosis in this dual pattern.

Bax is a protein that promotes programmed cell death. Their title highlights a dual role in rod and cone degeneration. One death protein acting differently in two cell types complicates therapy design. Saving both rods and cones may need separate strategies.
plos-pone-0006716:
Guilhem Ibos, Jean-René Duhamel, and Suliann Ben Hamed measured how voluntary attention moves across the visual field in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many studies ask how long attention takes to shift between places. Most estimates come from indirect comparisons. The authors designed a behavior task giving a more direct estimate. In one task they compared conditions needing shifts of different sizes.

Their setup estimates the time a voluntary shift actually takes. It also shows how attention spreads in space over time. Knowing true shift timing constrains theories of how the brain searches scenes. It matters for tasks like driving, reading, and scanning crowds. The method offers other attention researchers a cleaner measuring tool.
plos-pone-0006816:
Qing Ji and colleagues used a small RNA to attack pancreatic cancer's root cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs influence cancer by tuning genes for growth and death. The miR-34 family had recently been tied to the guardian protein p53. Tumor-initiating cells are the rare cells that seed a tumor. Pancreatic cancer is notoriously resistant to treatment.

MicroRNA miR-34 inhibited those tumor-initiating cells, as the title reports. Blocking the seed cells matters more than shrinking bulk tumor. If seeds are stopped, regrowth after treatment may fail. The result positions miR-34 as a candidate therapeutic RNA. It also supports the cancer stem cell view of pancreatic tumors.
plos-pone-0006916:
Run-Zhe Shu and colleagues deleted a cytoskeleton protein in mice and checked nerve growth in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is palladin, associated with the actin skeleton. It is crucial for cell shape change and movement. Earlier work placed palladin in the axonal growth cone of neurons. It seemed likely to help axons extend.

Deleting palladin did not impair neurite outgrowth in mice. The title reports that negative result plainly. Negative results rescue other laboratories from false trails. Palladin may act elsewhere, or other proteins may cover its absence. Either way, axon growth models must be revised without it at the center.
plos-pone-0007016:
Stefania Crispi, Raffaele Calogero, Mario Santini, and colleagues profiled a rare chest cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pleural mesothelioma grows in the lining around the lungs. The team wanted new markers for early diagnosis and new targets for treatment. They used microarrays to read gene activity across tumor samples.

Their profiling singled out one gene, MMP-14, as a possible tumor target. MMP enzymes help cells move through tissue, a step in cancer spread. A clear target matters in mesothelioma, which is usually found late. The gene list also offers candidate markers for catching the disease sooner.
plos-pone-0007116:
Florence Borot, Diane-Lore Vieu, Grazyna Faure, and colleagues studied inflammation signals in airway cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two proteins, annexin-1 and S100A10, restrain an enzyme that frees arachidonic acid from membranes. That acid is the raw material for eicosanoids, a family of inflammation messengers. The team used Calu-3 airway cells as their model.

They disturbed the membranes and blocked the CFTR channel. Eicosanoid release rose under both stresses. The result links membrane stability and CFTR to airway inflammation. That is relevant to cystic fibrosis, where CFTR fails and inflamed airways dominate the disease.
plos-pone-0007216:
Bisrat G. Debeb, Vasiliy Galat, Jessica Epple-Farmer, and colleagues isolated early embryo support cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The extraembryonic endoderm forms the yolk sac membranes. Those membranes give essential support to mammalian embryos during early development inside the womb.

Recent findings suggested committed precursors already sit inside the inner cell mass. The authors isolate cell lines that express Oct4 and act as those precursors. Their lines give developmental biologists a stable way to study how yolk sac tissue forms. Such work also clarifies how early cell fates are set.
plos-pone-0007316:
William A. Glover, Yanqin Yang, and Ying Zhang studied wall-less bacterial forms in Escherichia coli in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These forms, called L-forms, occur in many bacterial species. They are suspected in persistent infections that resist normal treatment, because many antibiotics target the cell wall that L-forms lack.

L-forms were discovered in 1935, and many studies described their shape and growth. Their molecular basis stayed unclear. The authors present insights into how E. coli L-forms form and survive. Their work may explain stubborn infections and suggest new ways to eliminate wall-less bacteria.
plos-pone-0007416:
Shinya Yamamoto, Tatyana Humle, and Masayuki Tanaka investigated helping behavior in chimpanzees in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Evolution of altruism has been explained mainly from ultimate, evolutionary perspectives. How and in which situations such social behavior is achieved, the proximate view, remained to be investigated in our closest relatives.

The authors study targeted helping in a tool transfer task. They report chimpanzees help each other upon request. A chimpanzee hands over a needed tool when a partner requests it. Their result shows helping can be responsive and specific, not just spontaneous, in chimpanzee social life.
plos-pone-0007516:
Matjaž Kuntner and Jonathan Coddington published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 announcing a new giant among orb-weaving spiders. The genus Nephila already included some of the largest web-building spiders known. The authors describe a species that exceeds them all. With the discovery in hand, they turned to the group's family tree. Their question was how such extreme size evolved within Nephila.

Tracing body size across the genus shows gigantism arising along particular branches. In these spiders, females grow huge while males stay small, an extreme split. The new species pushes that pattern to its known limit. Understanding the pressures behind it touches on predation, competition, and mating. The paper is both a species description and an evolutionary account. It gives arachnology a record holder, and a puzzle about how it got that way.
plos-pone-0007616:
Olivier Perrot and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the striatum, a part of the brain placed to shape how animals move. Its exact part in walking was not well known. The team harmed the striatum on one side in rats. Then they filmed the rats' walking in three dimensions. They measured plain gait and the harder task of stepping over blocks in the path, all in fine detail.

The data show how harm to the striatum changes both plain gait and hard steps. Plain steps and block steps did not suffer in the same way. That split shows the structure's finer job: tuning movement when the task gets hard. Such care counts for grasping diseases like Parkinson's, where this same structure fails. A rat's false step, closely measured, turns into facts about a human ill.
plos-pone-0007716:
Hannah Armer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows blood vessels in the act of joining inside a living zebrafish. Modern imaging can follow single cells in a whole animal. Yet fine detail often requires electron microscopy, which uses dead, fixed tissue.

The team combined both views of the same event. They filmed vessel fusion live, then captured the same site in three-dimensional electron images. This paired method is called correlative volume electron microscopy. It lets researchers match a moving process to its exact inner structure, a powerful step for cell biology.
plos-pone-0007816:
Emiliano Biasini and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It presents a cleaner way to isolate the rogue protein behind prion diseases. Prion diseases are fatal brain disorders that can arise by chance, inheritance or infection. Their key event is a normal protein folding into a harmful shape.

The bad form is rich in sheet-like structures and clumps together. To study it, researchers must pull the aggregates out of brain tissue. The authors describe immunopurification, using antibodies to fish the clumps out. Cleaner material should speed work on how prions form and spread.
plos-pone-0007916:
Sharon Pitteri and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It hunts for blood markers of ovarian cancer from three sources at once. Human plasma holds thousands of proteins, and that complexity blocks biomarker hunts. Cancer signals drown in the noise of normal blood proteins.

The team combined human cancer cells with plasma from tumor-bearing mice. Mouse models and isolated cells offer cleaner places to spot tumor proteins. Candidates found there were then checked in the human setting. The integrated design is a practical route around plasma's complexity. It aims at earlier detection of a cancer often found late.
plos-pone-0008016:
Lino Becerra and colleagues sought a brain sign that splits pain from mere heat in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pain reports rest on what a person says, which drugs and trials cannot easily verify. Their tool was diffuse optical tomography, a light-based scan of the outer brain.

Painful heat lit the touch cortex in a pattern that plain warm heat did not. A split that clear in brain activity is a step toward an objective pain gauge. Such a gauge could test pain drugs fairly and help patients who cannot speak for themselves.
plos-pone-0008116:
Shu-Hwa Chen and colleagues released a tool that builds family trees of species with less expert fuss in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tree building needs a model of how DNA changes, and picking the wrong model warps the tree. The pick used to demand deep training and long compute times.

Their framework, PALM, picks the model on its own and splits the work across many machines at once. Speed plus sound defaults opens careful tree building to more labs. Any field that reads kinship from DNA, from germ tracking to wildlife studies, stands to gain.
plos-pone-0008216:
Shoma Berkemeyer and colleagues studied bone scores and daily function in older Germans in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bone T-scores are the standard measure used to diagnose osteoporosis. The team suspected weak bones could limit what older people can do each day. Loss of function threatens independence in later life. They tested that link in community-dwelling elderly people.

Their cross-sectional study used data gathered in 2005 and 2006. It compared bone scores with functional status across participants. If bone health tracks daily ability, screening gains extra importance. The study speaks to keeping older adults independent for longer.
plos-pone-0008316:
Euiheon Chung and colleagues built a way to track spreading cancer in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Few techniques can quantify systemic metastases in preclinical models. Metastases are tumors that colonize distant organs. Sensitive, real-time detection of that spread is urgently needed. The team engineered tumor cells to secrete Gaussia luciferase, a glowing enzyme.

The secreted marker reports tumor burden from a blood sample. Researchers could monitor progression and treatment response over time. Repeated measures in the same animal improve experiment quality. The biomarker approach may speed testing of anti-metastatic drugs.
plos-pone-0008416:
Marta Codina and colleagues studied muscle building in zebrafish embryos in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. Making a myofibril requires folding and assembling sarcomeric proteins into ordered sarcomeres. The heat shock protein Hsp90 alpha1 acts as a myosin chaperone in that process. Knocking it down disrupts muscle fibers. Another protein, Smyhc1, is a myosin heavy chain itself.

Loss of Smyhc1 or Hsp90 alpha1 function had different effects on myofibril organization. Comparing the two separates chaperone failure from missing building blocks. The work clarifies how skeletal muscle assembles in embryos. It may inform research on muscle diseases.
plos-pone-0008516:
Songfa Zhong and co-authors link a gene to risk attitudes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. People often face longshot risks: a small chance of a large outcome. They tend to seek such risks for gains but avoid them for losses. That split is central to many models of choice. The team study monoamine oxidase A, or MAOA, a gene that affects brain chemicals. They test if MAOA variants track with longshot attitudes.

Their data associate MAOA with attitude toward longshot risks. The link suggests biology helps shape economic preferences. It does not by itself explain choice, but it adds a genetic layer. Such work bridges neuroscience, genetics, and decision science.
plos-pone-0008616:
Lei Phillip Wang and co-authors knock out a receptor in dopamine neurons in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Nicotine from tobacco produces one of the most common addictive behaviors. It has major societal and health consequences. Nicotine triggers addiction by activating receptors in midbrain dopamine pathways. NMDA receptors also shape learning in those pathways. The team conditionally delete NMDA receptors only in dopamine neurons of mice. They then test nicotine-conditioned place preference, a measure of reward learning.

Knockout prevents nicotine-conditioned place preference in the mice. Without NMDA receptors, dopamine neurons cannot encode nicotine reward normally. The result pinpoints a learning mechanism inside addiction circuitry. It may guide therapies that target reward learning, not just nicotine itself.
plos-pone-0008716:
Sandrine Daubeuf, Anne Aucher, Christine Bordier, and colleagues watched immune cells trade bits of surface. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study describes trogocytosis, a nibbling process. T and B cells bite off fragments from antigen-presenting cells. They wear the stolen bits on their own surface. Whether they grab all proteins equally was unknown.

Using mouse cells, the team tracked which membrane proteins moved across. Some proteins transferred readily while others stayed behind. That pickiness shapes what an immune cell displays afterward. Display choices affect how the cell talks to others and may steer later immune responses.
plos-pone-0008816:
Sandhya Vasan, Sarah Schlesinger, Zhiwei Chen, and colleagues ran a first-in-humans trial of an HIV vaccine. Their phase 1 report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vaccine, ADMVA, uses a weakened vaccinia virus as a carrier. It delivers five HIV genes from clades common in China. Dose-escalation trials in healthy volunteers test safety first. Immune responses hint whether the design deserves larger trials.

Volunteers received rising doses while the team watched reactions closely. The vaccine also had to prove it could wake immune defenses. Early safety and response data decide its future path. Multi-gene designs remain a leading hope against HIV diversity.
plos-pone-0008916:
Justyna Leja, Berith Nilsson, Di Yu, and colleagues tuned a cancer-killing virus to spare the liver. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oncolytic viruses infect and burst tumor cells while sparing healthy ones. Their virus targets neuroendocrine tumors, which often spread to the liver. A virus multiplying in liver tissue would be dangerous. Two detargeting tweaks were added to keep it out of liver cells while keeping its tumor aim.

The double-detargeted virus stalled its replication in liver cells. It kept its ability to kill neuroendocrine tumor cells. Safety and potency together are the whole challenge of virus therapy. The design moves this candidate closer to patient trials.
plos-pone-0009016:
S. Jyothi Prasanna and co-authors compared two sources of stem cells under inflammatory fire, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow are a staple of cell therapy research. Cells from Wharton's jelly, the cord tissue around umbilical vessels, are easier to get. Cord cells also grow faster and provoke less immune reaction.

The team exposed both cell types to two inflammatory signals, IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha. The sources reacted differently in their immune behaviour. Marrow and cord cells are therefore not interchangeable in therapy. Choosing between them should depend on the immune setting of the treatment.
plos-pone-0009116:
Sarah Kocher and co-authors compared worker honey bees that answer the queen's scent strongly or weakly, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Behaviour varies a lot between individuals inside any social group. Genes and the environment mix together to make those differences. The queen's pheromone normally keeps workers from raising eggs of their own.

Response strength to that scent differed from bee to bee in the tests. It tracked closely with each bee's own reproductive traits. Gene activity patterns in the brain matched the response levels too. One pheromone quietly divides a colony into responders and would-be rebels.
plos-pone-0009216:
Cira Daniela Rinaudo and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns group B Streptococcus, a bacterium that lives harmlessly in up to three in ten healthy women. During delivery it can infect newborns, causing sepsis and meningitis. Long-lasting colonization usually means the bacteria form biofilms, sticky layers that resist clearing.

Bacteria grow hair-like pili, and this species carries several pilus types. The team tested which type the biofilm depends on. They found that pilus type 2a is specifically involved in building the biofilm. That pinpoints a structure drug or vaccine designers could target to break colonization.
plos-pone-0009316:
Alice Yam and co-authors published this prion study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prion diseases, like mad cow disease, are fatal brain disorders. They begin when a normal brain protein, PrP, folds into a wrong shape and clumps. The wrong form, called PrP Sc, forces healthy copies to follow it, but its exact structure stayed elusive.

The team examined one stretch of the protein, the octarepeat region, named for its repeated blocks. They show that this region changes shape in the disease form. Pinpointing which parts rearrange is a step toward picturing the prion's structure. That picture is needed before anyone can design molecules to block the change.
plos-pone-0009416:
Jakob Hohwy and Bryan Paton published this perception study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the rubber hand illusion, a fake hand is stroked in time with your hidden real one. Soon the touch feels like it lands on the rubber hand. The brain projects feeling onto an object that is not part of the body.

The authors pushed the illusion further, testing touch felt on non-hand objects and even touches blamed on supernatural causes. They explored how far the body can be explained away by the brain. Mapping the limits of this projection shows how the sense of body ownership is built. It also informs work on prosthetics, where a fake limb must feel like one's own.
plos-pone-0009516:
Ofir Meir and co-authors studied how stressed cells decide to die in PLOS ONE in 2010. The endoplasmic reticulum folds new proteins. When it is overloaded, the cell first tries to cope. If stress lasts, the cell instead orders its own death. A protein called C/EBP-beta plays a part in that switch. The team tested its role in mouse and human cells.

They found that C/EBP-beta helps drive the death program once stress passes a point. Without it, the response changed in telling ways. Naming this switch matters for diseases where such stress harms tissue. Diabetes and brain diseases are among them, so the pathway is of wide interest.
plos-pone-0009616:
Donghwa Kim and co-authors mapped a tug of war inside cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. A kinase called MST2 pushes cells toward death and holds back growth. It is the mammal version of the fly protein Hippo, a known tumor guard. Growth signals from IGF1 run through a pathway led by Akt. The team tested how that growth pathway acts on MST2.

The IGF1 Akt pathway restrained MST2, easing its push toward cell death. So one pathway promotes survival by muting a death driver. When that balance breaks, cells may grow when they should die, a hallmark of cancer. The detail adds a control point that drug research can examine.
plos-pone-0009716:
Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that lives in the stomach and causes ulcers. Vittorio Necchi and colleagues looked inside infected cells for where its products end up. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Inside the cells, bacterial products piled up in a new kind of cytoplasmic structure. The same structure held NOD1, a sensor that detects bacteria, plus tagged proteins and the proteasome. The proteasome is the cell's disposal machine for worn proteins. The buildup was seen in living hosts, not just lab cells. It shows where the cell parks germ debris during infection.
plos-pone-0009816:
Learning to hear faint differences between sounds takes practice. Sygal Amitay and colleagues asked what makes some people improve faster at such listening tasks. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Auditory perceptual learning is the sharpening of hearing through repeated practice. Two traits drove the gains in their tests: motivation and intelligence. Learners who stayed engaged and scored higher on intelligence tests improved more. It also challenges the idea that practice alone explains progress. The result matters for training programs that rebuild listening skills. Listening tests are used in hearing clinics and classrooms alike.
plos-pone-0009916:
DNA in cells wraps around protein spools, and where the spools sit shapes gene activity. Hiromi Nishida and colleagues mapped those spools across the genome of a common mold. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The spools are nucleosomes, beads of DNA wrapped around histones. The team mapped mononucleosomes and dinucleosomes carrying hyperacetylated histones in Aspergillus fumigatus. Aspergillus fumigatus can cause serious lung infections in frail patients. Hyperacetylated means loaded with acetyl marks that usually loosen DNA. Genome-wide maps like this show where genes sit open or closed in the mold.
plos-pone-0010016:
The authors were Frank Odhiambo, Mary Hamel, John Williamson, and others. They ran a child health trial in rural western Kenya, reported in 2010. They tested preventive malaria treatment given to infants at set times, rather than waiting for illness. The drug pair used before, sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, was losing strength as resistance spread in the region.

Infants were assigned at random to treatment or a dummy drug, and neither families nor staff knew who got which. The trial judged whether the approach still prevented malaria and which drug mixes might work better. Results from such trials shape malaria policy for millions of young children in Africa.
plos-pone-0010116:
Richard Tunney, Gordon Fernie, and Duncan Astle studied how people sort things into categories in 2010. Two theories compete in psychology. One says we store each example we have met and compare new items to them. The other says we build an abstract prototype, a kind of average, and compare to that.

Using a prototype-distortion task, the team recorded brain signals during recognition and sorting decisions. Their PLOS ONE paper used those electrical patterns to weigh the two theories. Knowing how categories form in the mind shapes teaching, memory research, and models of learning.
plos-pone-0010216:
The authors were Cristina Viadas, María Rodríguez, Felix Sangari, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped gene control in Brucella abortus, a livestock bacterium. A two-component system, BvrR and BvrS, is essential for this germ's virulence. Faults in it changed outer membrane proteins and the pattern of fats on the cell surface in earlier work.

To find all genes the system regulates, the team analyzed the full transcriptome. That is the complete set of genes switched on under its control. A full list shows how one control system shapes this pathogen's ability to infect animals.
plos-pone-0010316:
Amit Khachane and Paul Harrison wrote a 2010 PLOS ONE study about long RNA strands that do not code for proteins. Such strands are called long non-coding RNAs. Scientists had grown curious about how these strands help control when genes switch on or off. Large sequencing projects in mice and humans had already listed huge numbers of copied RNA pieces.

Khachane and Harrison mined those existing data sets for useful clues. Their aim was to sort strands that likely do real work from strands that may be mere noise. Most copied pieces in a cell still have no known job. A careful filter could point lab workers toward the few worth testing first. That would save time in a field flooded with raw sequence data.
plos-pone-0010416:
Jan Beck and Andrea Sieber tested a famous claim about why societies differ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Writers such as Jared Diamond argued that climate and soil set the stage for human history. Farming began at different times in different regions, with huge effects. The authors asked whether climate and soil alone explain where basic economic traits appear. Those traits include farming itself and the growth that followed it.

Using worldwide data, they checked how far the two factors carry the explanation. If they fall short, culture and history must do more work. The debate shapes how we explain global inequality today. Careful tests keep grand theories honest. This study supplies one such test, with maps and numbers.
plos-pone-0010516:
Alice Laborte, Aileen Maunahan and Robert Hijmans showed how to improve satellite land maps by broadening their training data in PLOS ONE in 2010. Classifying satellite images usually trains on one image plus matching ground checks. Each land type gets a spectral signature, its fingerprint in light. Signatures from a single scene can fail elsewhere. The team compared that standard with methods using many images and wider signature sets.

Broader signatures classified new scenes more accurately. Better land maps feed farming, forestry, and disaster planning worldwide. Remote sensing is only as good as its ground truth and methods. This study offers a practical recipe for doing it better. It is a methods upgrade for a tool governments rely on.
plos-pone-0010616:
Mark McCormick and colleagues compared two groups of a sex-changing fish, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These fish start life female and some later become male. Males and females differ in size, but the size gap varied between the two reef groups.

The team traced the gap to different causes in each place. In one group, growth patterns drove the difference. In the other, survival and social rank mattered more. The contrast shows that the same body pattern can arise by different routes. Local conditions, not one fixed rule, shape the outcome.
plos-pone-0010716:
Juan Carlos Senar and colleagues tested food choice in great tits, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carotenoids are pigments birds must eat; they cannot make them. The pigments tint feathers yellow and red and also support health, so birds need a steady supply.

Given a choice, captive and wild great tits both picked food rich in carotenoids. The birds acted as if they had a specific appetite for the pigments. An appetite tuned to one nutrient class is strong design: it keeps a scarce, vital supply coming in. The result links diet choice directly to the bright colors used in courtship displays.
plos-pone-0010816:
Canchao Yang and colleagues documented an egg-color arms race between a cuckoo and its host, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brood parasites lay eggs in other birds' nests. Hosts that spot the odd egg can reject it, while parasites that mimic host eggs fool them. Both sides thus face pressure away from the common pattern, a force called disruptive selection.

Egg colors in the parasite and its host had split toward extremes. Matching and detection had sharpened together over generations. The split is visible proof of co-evolution at work in the wild. Few field studies catch the force itself, rather than its aftermath, this clearly.
plos-pone-0010916:
Julien Pansiot, Gauthier Loron, Paul Olivier and co-authors published this newborn brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inhaled nitric oxide is a promising treatment for newborns with breathing failure, but its effect on the developing brain was little known. The team tested it in rat pups facing excitotoxic injury, the kind of overexcitation damage that harms premature infants.

Pups breathed low-dose nitric oxide during their first week while a glutamate-like chemical was used to trigger brain lesions. Treated pups developed clearly smaller lesions in both white matter and cortex than untreated ones. Signs of inflammation and scarring were also reduced, and several glutamate receptor parts were turned down early. Pansiot and colleagues suggest the gas protects the newborn brain, a reassuring and potentially useful finding for neonatal care.
plos-pone-0011016:
Li Zhang, Michael Chopp, Rui Lan Zhang and co-authors published this stroke study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Erythropoietin, the blood hormone EPO, helps the brain recover from stroke by encouraging new neurons and blood vessels. The authors asked whether it also rebuilds white matter, the insulated wiring that stroke destroys, in a rat model of blockage stroke.

Rats received human EPO daily for a week starting a day after the stroke. Early on, EPO boosted dividing insulation precursor cells around the injury and in a brain stem cell niche, without sparing existing insulating cells. Weeks later, treated rats had significantly more mature insulating cells and myelinated fibers. Zhang and colleagues add white matter repair to EPO's recovery portfolio, relevant since reconnecting circuits is as important as saving neurons.
plos-pone-0011116:
Gelfand, Piro and Magnasco built a model of a gecko ear in PLOS ONE in 2010. The inner ear of the tokay gecko can emit faint sounds on its own. Those sounds come from hair cells, the tiny sensors that turn motion into nerve signals.

In the model, links between hair cells shaped the sounds the ear produced. Cells acting together behaved unlike cells acting alone. That points to self organization in hearing, where order arises from local links. The finding helps explain how ears can be both very sensitive and sharply tuned, a puzzle in hearing research.
plos-pone-0011216:
Renaudet, Dasgupta, Bettahi and colleagues compared vaccine shapes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their cancer vaccines combined sugar, fat and protein pieces in either straight or branched forms. The team tracked how the immune system presents each form to the killer cells that attack tumors.

The two shapes followed distinct presentation pathways. They also produced different strengths of anti tumor immunity. Shape, in other words, is itself a design choice in vaccines. Knowing which form does better helps optimize future cancer vaccine blueprints before costly human trials begin in patients with cancer.
plos-pone-0011316:
Kang, Chen, DeOliveira and colleagues boosted transplants in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Donor blood stem cells must settle, or engraft, in a recipient's marrow for a transplant to work. A drug that blocks a homing receptor was given in a mouse transplant model to see if settling could be improved.

The drug selectively enhanced donor cell engraftment in their tests. Better settling could make transplants succeed with fewer donor cells, widening who can be treated. It might also speed recovery of blood counts after transplant. The finding informs bone marrow transplantation practice with a repurposed, already known drug.
plos-pone-0011416:
Philip Grant and co-authors analyzed in 2010 who is most at risk of a dangerous flare when HIV treatment starts during another serious infection. As HIV drugs revive the immune system, the revived system can attack the existing infection so fiercely that the patient gets worse, a syndrome called IRIS. A trial had compared starting HIV treatment early versus waiting, and the flare struck some patients in both arms.

The team searched the trial data for starting traits that predicted the flare, such as immune cell counts and infection type. Knowing who carries the highest risk helps doctors time treatment and watch the right patients closely. Starting HIV drugs too late also carries real danger, so the goal is balance, not delay for all. The analysis turns a feared side effect into a risk that can be estimated before treatment begins.
plos-pone-0011516:
Simeon Kotchoni and co-authors mapped in 2010 the whole family of aldehyde-cleaning enzymes in rice. Aldehydes are reactive chemicals that damage cells, and the ALDH enzyme family neutralizes them. Rice carries many ALDH members, and knowing how they differ in shape and job helps explain how the crop handles drought, salt, and other stresses.

Using protein modeling across the superfamily, the team teased out distinct structural and functional features that separate the members into meaningful groups. A family-wide catalog replaces the old one-enzyme-at-a-time view. Crop scientists can now pick which members to breed for or engineer when they want hardier rice. In a crop that feeds half the world, a cleaner map of its stress defenses is a tool with very wide reach.
plos-pone-0011616:
Jacqueline Milet and colleagues searched Senegalese genomes for factors affecting malaria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People differ greatly in how they handle infection with the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Exposure, parasite strength, age and inherited traits all play a part, but the inherited share needed mapping in this population.

Using a dense map of DNA markers, the team linked regions of the genome to infection levels and to mild malaria attacks. The regions they pinpoint give researchers places to look for the actual protective or risky genes. That knowledge could eventually guide vaccines and care for children in high-risk areas.
plos-pone-0011716:
Morgan O'Hayre and co-authors charted a survival signal network in leukaemia cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, malignant B cells live far too long instead of dying on schedule. Signals from the cells' surroundings, including the CXCL12 and CXCR4 pair, are thought to protect them from spontaneous death.

The team read thousands of phosphate tags on proteins to map the signalling network downstream of that pair. Their wiring diagram shows which routes keep leukaemia cells alive. Those routes include points that future drugs might cut to strip the cancer of its protection.
plos-pone-0011816:
Yuichi Nakahara and co-authors traced blood cell lineages in silkworm larvae, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insects have multiple blood cell types with different functions, much like vertebrates. Their blood-forming lineages, however, were largely unexplored outside the fruit fly, leaving the silkworm Bombyx mori an open case.

Investigating the larval blood-forming organ, the team found two separate hemocyte lineages at work. A double production line reveals how insects build immune defences from distinct blueprints. The silkworm is also an industrial species, so its immunity bears directly on silk farming health.
plos-pone-0012016:
Kemar Brown and co-workers compared in 2010 the cell lines used to model the embryo's early support tissue. Before gastrulation in the mouse, all endoderm comes from the primitive endoderm of the blastocyst. Its descendants, called extra-embryonic endoderm, mostly build support structures rather than the embryo itself, and several cell lines claim to model them.

A comparative analysis asks how alike those lines really are and which embryo stage each one matches. Labs pick lines by habit, and a mismatch can quietly distort years of results. A careful side-by-side guide helps developmental biologists choose the right stand-in for early embryo support tissue.
plos-pone-0012116:
Masa Tsuchiya, Vincent Piras, Alessandro Giuliani, and co-authors studied how white blood cells mature, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A cell choosing its fate must coordinate thousands of genes at once, far too many to track one by one. The team looked at neutrophils, the most common white cells, and searched for groups of genes that switch together as the cells develop.

They found tight gene groups that act as units during this change, as if carried together through the process. Seeing the genome work in coordinated blocks, rather than as lone genes, changes how cell development can be studied. It may also help explain what goes wrong when blood cells mature badly, as in leukemia.
plos-pone-0012216:
Carlo Villa, Michele Caccia, Laura Sironi, and co-authors presented an image method for tracking tiny particles in living tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell biologists film glowing particles under powerful microscopes to follow molecules, vesicles, and pathogens, but picking moving specks out of noisy images is slow and error-prone. Their protocol stacks the differences between frames so real movers stand out from the background.

They tested the method in mouse lymph nodes, the immune organs where tracking cells matters most. A faster, more reliable way to follow particles turns shaky movies into measurements. Those measurements underpin research on how immune cells meet, how drugs reach targets, and how infections spread through tissue.
plos-pone-0012316:
Pan Wang, Hyoung-Woo Bai, and Bao Ting Zhu explained how some plant compounds supercharge inflammation enzymes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyclooxygenase enzymes, the targets of aspirin-like drugs, also drive inflammation and pain, and recent work had shown certain dietary bioflavonoids strongly boost their activity rather than blocking it. The boost seemed to come from helping the enzyme reactivate itself after each round of work.

The authors worked out the structural basis for which flavonoids can serve as the enzyme's reducing helpers. That knowledge cuts both ways: it warns that some supplement ingredients may amplify inflammation chemistry, and it teaches chemists new handles on a heavily drugged enzyme family. Diet-drug interactions start at exactly this molecular level.
plos-pone-0012416:
Christelle Mazuet, Julie Dano, Michel Popoff and colleagues built antibodies against botulinum toxin type A, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Botulinum toxins are among the most poisonous substances known, and botulism can paralyze and kill. Antibodies that neutralize the toxin are the main treatment, and how long they last in the body shapes how well they work.

The team characterized several neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and tested how their half-lives affected treatment success. Longer-lasting antibodies protected better in their tests. The work guides design of antibody therapies that can be stockpiled for outbreaks, whether natural, accidental, or deliberate, where rapid treatment saves lives.
plos-pone-0012516:
Nicola Gullick, Hayley Evans, Leigh Church and colleagues linked ultrasound images of arthritic joints to immune cells in the tissue, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Power Doppler ultrasound shows blood flow in the inflamed joint lining and is used to grade rheumatoid arthritis activity. Whether bright signals mean a particular immune cell type is present was unclear.

The team matched ultrasound scores with biopsy measures and found the signal linked to Th17 cells, an inflammation-driving T cell type. That link validates the scan as more than a pretty picture: it reflects specific biology. It may also help select patients for drugs that target the Th17 pathway.
plos-pone-0012616:
Van der Auwera, Yu, Suo and co-authors tried a chemical fingerprint to sort breast cancers into types. Breast tumours differ in how they grow and which drugs they answer, so sorting them well matters. Faulty DNA methylation, a chemical tag that can silence genes, helps drive many of these tumours.

Their 2010 work used array chips that read methylation at many sites across the genome at once. The tag patterns split tumours into subtypes, offering an option beside the usual gene activity tests. A second sorting method could help doctors match each patient to better care.
plos-pone-0012716:
Stridh, Hedreul, Beyeen and co-authors narrowed a rat gene region that controls nerve inflammation. They study a rat model of multiple sclerosis, the human disease where the immune system attacks nerve insulation. Their 2010 work took one known region, called Eae23, and split it into two separate effects.

One part pointed to ZEB1 as a candidate gene steering the inflammation. Splitting mixed regions is how gene hunts move from broad zones to single genes. A confirmed candidate could reveal a fresh control point in multiple sclerosis.  Rat models allow crosses that human studies cannot.
plos-pone-0012816:
Fu, Van Doorslaer, Chen and co-authors tested whether a cancer virus's power tracks its family tree or its record of harming p53. Human papillomaviruses use their E6 protein to destroy p53, the cell's main cancer guard. That destruction was long taken as the key step by which high-risk types drive cervical cancer.

Their 2010 comparison across many virus types found E6 strength follows the viruses' phylogeny more closely than their known cancer risk. The mismatch complicates a simple story of how these viruses cause cancer. It suggests other E6 jobs also shape risk.
plos-pone-0329716:
Ru-Gang An and seven colleagues examine delirium after heart surgery in children born with heart defects, in this 2026 PLOS ONE database study. Delirium — sudden confusion and disturbed awareness — is a recognised risk after major surgery, but its scale in these young patients was unclear. Records from a national United States hospital sample covering 2010 to 2019 held more than one hundred and eighty-seven thousand such operations.

About two children in every hundred were diagnosed with delirium afterwards. Those children carried more other illnesses, stayed longer, cost more, and died in hospital more often. Clotting disorders, fluid and salt imbalances, and pre-existing paralysis predicted it. Spotting high-risk children early could focus preventive care where it counts.
plos-pone-0330816:
Ri Nin and Kazuo Mori tested in 2026 whether old Japanese words for husband and wife still carry sexist weight in the mind. One term literally means master, the other inside the house, yet both are in everyday use.

University students took a paper based test that reveals hidden word associations, comparing the old terms with neutral ones. The old pair showed no stronger male dominant links than the neutral pair, suggesting the words have become plain labels for many speakers. A gap remained, though: men rated male linked terms more warmly, while women did not. Hidden bias, the authors note, can linger in speakers even as words fade.
plos-pone-0335116:
Stephen Mensah Arhin and colleagues surveyed more than two thousand doctors, nurses, and pharmacists across Ghana about medication errors and their reporting. Errors in prescribing and giving medicines cause preventable harm worldwide, and reporting systems in poorer countries are often patchy. The survey measured what professionals know about error types, what they actually do, and whether they know reporting channels exist.

Recognition was strongest for wrong-dose and wrong-patient errors, at over four in five respondents, but knowledge thinned for other categories, and awareness of reporting systems varied. Finding the exact gaps matters because a reporting system nobody knows about or trusts cannot catch mistakes. The multicenter snapshot gives Ghanaian health leaders a map for safety training.
plos-pone-0339016:
David Calderón Guzmán and seven colleagues test whether plant flavonoids can shield the brain and gut in a rat model of Huntington's disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Huntington's involves inflammation and oxidative damage; the model uses a toxin that produces both, layered on a bacterial challenge. Young rats received the toxin alone or with a mixture of three flavonoids, including rutin, while brain chemicals and damage markers were measured in cortex, cerebellum, and gut lining.

The toxin depressed dopamine in the cortex and left visible nerve-cell lesions. With flavonoids aboard, fat-damage markers in the cerebellum fell and several enzyme activities shifted toward normal. The results are early and mixed across brain regions, but they justify asking whether dietary flavonoids can blunt part of Huntington's damage.
plos-pone-0342616:
Bethsabe Romero and Amanda Burbage mine national survey data to profile first-generation medical school applicants in the United States, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These applicants — the first in their families to attend college — covered applications from 2017 to 2024, totalling over a quarter of a million people. About one applicant in eight was first-generation, and all who reported family finances came from low-income backgrounds.

Their motives leaned toward security, escaping career debt, and social change. Yet their acceptance rate lagged far behind other applicants', as did enrolment, with family obligations and older age among the drags. The authors map exactly where support — money, mentoring, time — would help most.
plos-pone-0343416:
Lisa J. Wallis and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on the welfare fallout of importing rescue dogs into the United Kingdom, a trade that has grown sharply. The title quotes a stakeholder's verdict that the practice sometimes just shifts a problem. The team interviewed and ran focus groups with over fifty people across the system, rescuers, transporters, trainers, vets, officials, fosterers, and owners, and read online forum threads too.

Seven themes emerged, covering dogs unfit to travel, transport welfare, infectious disease, and owner novelty, plus regulation and enforcement. New owners often met a dog unlike the one described, with costly health or behavior surprises, and some dogs were mismatched to their households. Rescue groups were seen as owing honest information and support around adoption, delivered inconsistently. Cross-border movement was hard to police, with gaps in compliance, resources, and communication between sectors.
plos-pone-0344916:
Bingbing Qian and co-authors borrowed the math of disease outbreaks to model how harm spreads through an ecosystem. In their 2026 study, species become nodes in a food web, and a disturbance, such as a pest outbreak, passes along feeding links much like an infection. Species can sit in one of three states: undisturbed, disturbed, or recovered.

The team derived a threshold number that decides the disturbance's fate. Below the threshold, the web settles back to a calm state, while above it the disturbance persists across the system. The threshold depends on the food web's shape, how easily harm spreads, and how fast species recover. Tests on a real New Zealand pine forest web, with eighty-five species, matched the theory. The framework also points to where protection efforts could slow a spreading disturbance.
plos-pone-0345916:
Rubeena Zakar and co-authors evaluated a year of community based teaching for public health students in Lahore, Pakistan, in 2026. The module aimed at mother and child health, sending undergraduates into a semi-urban community under supervision rather than keeping them in lecture halls.

Knowledge, skills, and practical competence were measured before and after with tests, observed exams, and surveys, while group talks and reflection logs added depth. Scores rose significantly across every mother and child health domain. The design shows community placement as the engine of the gain, a model other schools in similar settings could copy directly.
plos-pone-0348016:
Hamad Al-Ibrahim, Arokiasamy Perianayagam, and Noor Al Thani made a new scale to gauge how people in Qatar think about buying things. Qatar is rich, mixed, and changing fast. More than two thousand people, both Qataris and those who moved there, filled out a long form on buying, rank, thrift, and care for the earth.

Four clear themes came out: love of goods as a mark of rank, wasteful splurging, thrift, and care for the earth. Checks showed the scale reads the same for locals and newcomers, men and women, rich and poor, so group scores can be compared with trust. Fast growth sets goods and green aims at odds, and this tool can track that strain.
plos-pone-0348116:
Bin Chen and colleagues dated rocks that were baked by burning coal seams in China's Junggar Basin, hoping to time when the land was pushed upward and stripped bare. When rising ground brings coal near the surface, it can catch fire on its own, and the scorched rocks record the event. The team measured a helium-based clock in zircon crystals from these burnt rocks.

Three crystals agreed on a main burning episode in the middle Pleistocene, a few hundred thousand years ago, matching a period of uplift around the basin. Two older readings were judged leftovers from before the fire. The study shows burnt coal rocks can serve as rare clocks for recent mountain building.
plos-pone-0348216:
Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston, Emil Kendziorra, and Andrew McKenzie surveyed three hundred thirty-four American physicians about preserving the dead for possible future revival, through freezing or chemical fixation. The October 2025 poll ran on a verified physician platform. It asked how likely good preservation is to keep enough brain information for revival. It also asked what doctors think about helping procedures and the ethics around them.

The median doctor put the chance at about one in four under ideal conditions, and roughly twenty-eight percent found revival at least somewhat plausible. Views on steps like giving blood thinners before death, and on whether offering preservation fits patient-centered care, were also mapped. The results give the first broad read of medical opinion on a practice usually debated without data.
plos-pone-0348316:
Shoukat Ullah and colleagues built a hybrid computer model that judges products from online customer reviews. Instead of only sorting reviews into positive or negative, their system rates how easy a product seems to use and how well it works. They trained it on Amazon reviews labeled by hand using ideas from appraisal theory.

The model pairs a DistilRoBERTa reader, which grasps the meaning of review text, with a BiGRU network that follows word order. Explainable AI checks showed which words drove each rating. For shoppers and sellers, ratings split into ease of use and effectiveness carry more useful detail than a single sentiment score.
plos-pone-0348516:
Emmanuela Anele and colleagues surveyed clawed frogs and their worm parasites across Nigeria's ecological zones, identifying both hosts and parasites by shape and by DNA. Five frog species were found, one of them thriving across four different savanna zones. The frogs carried thirteen worm species from roundworm and flatworm lineages.

Roundworms proved the generalists, infecting several frog species across wide areas, while the flatworms were pickier about hosts, and every parasite specialized on a particular organ or a matching pair of organs. Frogs sit at the junction of water and land food webs, so their parasite communities read out ecosystem health. A mapped baseline for Nigeria lets later surveys detect ecological change through what lives inside the frogs.
plos-pone-0348616:
Jun Chen and colleagues tackled the seams and distortions that appear when drone photographs are stitched into one wide map. Tall buildings lean differently in overlapping shots, defeating many stitching tools or slowing them down. Their method reframes stitching as a pixel-by-pixel choice: for every spot in the overlap, pick which source photo shows it best, guided by a twin network that compares the candidates.

A second trick predicts the choices at low resolution and expands them, since the choices barely change across scales, avoiding retraining and heavy computation. Across four drone image sets the approach beat leading rivals on picture quality by wide margins while cutting processing time by up to nearly nine tenths. The authors pitch it for large mapping jobs where speed and clean joins both matter.
plos-pone-0348816:
Thomas V. Pollet and co-workers re-examine a widely used survey that measures how well new students settle into university life. The survey is usually scored as one single scale. Their 2026 study instead maps how its questions connect to each other, using answers from two hundred forty first-year students at a British university.

The questions grouped into four clusters rather than one. They covered happiness with university life and support, social connection, day-to-day adjustment, and motivation to keep going. The pattern looked much the same for students whose parents had not attended university. Treating the survey as four parts, the authors argue, gives advisers a clearer picture of where a struggling student actually needs help.
plos-pone-0349016:
Xiaonan Li and Lin Mao surveyed more than eighteen hundred Chinese college students about smartphone habits and sleep problems, then mapped how the symptoms connect to each other. Instead of treating each condition as a single score, they built networks showing which symptoms sit at the center and which ones bridge the two problems. A second method probed which symptoms may drive others.

Standard questionnaires measured phone addiction and sleep quality for every student. Network maps like these can show, for example, whether poor sleep fuels late-night phone use or the reverse. Finding the bridge symptoms matters because treating a bridge may loosen both problems at once. The authors also compared the networks of men and women for differences.
plos-pone-0349116:
Lauri Rapeli and Kim Backström ran a rare experiment on how to persuade politicians to join a research survey panel. Survey response is falling everywhere, and politicians are an especially reluctant group. Their 2026 study emailed more than seven thousand Finnish local politicians, randomly varying the invitation's appeal: helping others, personal benefit, or advancing science.

None of the three appeals worked better than the others. The authors conclude the altruism-versus-self-interest framing simply does not move politicians, and researchers need different tools to recruit them. Who did volunteer followed a pattern of its own: older politicians, those in urban municipalities, and those on the political left joined at higher rates. The study offers a sobering baseline for anyone surveying elected officials.
plos-pone-0349216:
Eman S El-Atfy and colleagues propose a new statistical test for whether waiting times follow the simplest random pattern, called exponential. Many fields, from medicine to machine life, need that check. Their test targets cases where average remaining life shrinks over time. Math built on a classic transform plus paired comparisons gives a test that keeps its scale and settles to a known shape in large samples.

Simulated trials with full and cut off data showed the test beating older checks at spotting the target pattern. Real examples included COVID death data and clinical survival data, where the test found clear departures. A bonus proof shows the logic still holds under a common shock model for failures.
plos-pone-0349416:
Yuki Yonekura and colleagues asked whether heavier Japanese adults being treated for diabetes cost the health system more, separating overweight from obesity and men from women. Japan's obesity rates are far below Western levels, so the cost question could not be answered from foreign data. Insurance records and national health checkup data from fiscal 2008 and 2009 were linked for the analysis.

Statistical models compared total, outpatient, and hospital spending across weight groups while adjusting for age, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar control, and smoking. They also tested the odds of crossing a high annual spending threshold. Diabetes already strains budgets; knowing how much extra weight adds, and for whom, helps insurers and clinics aim prevention where it pays.
plos-pone-0349516:
Susana Marquez Rosales and co-authors watched bacteria inside living zebrafish guts in 2026 to see how a meal changes their behaviour. Food shapes gut microbes, but behaviour inside a real intestine is hard to observe, and the see through larvae solve that.

Two gut strains were compared: one that clumps into large groups in unfed fish, and a mobile one that can damage tissue. The team fed larvae rotifers cleaned of most microbes by ultraviolet light, separating the effect of food itself from new germs arriving. Imaging then showed how feeding shifts clumping, movement, and place in the gut.
plos-pone-0350016:
Abdulsalam Al-Shami and co-authors measured blood ferritin, a marker tied to iron overload, in Yemeni teenagers and young adults with sickle cell anemia treated in Sana'a. Repeated transfusions load these patients with iron, yet ferritin also rises with inflammation, so reading it takes care. Their 2026 study enrolled eighty patients over six months and compared ferritin with blood counts and social factors.

About eighty-five percent of patients had elevated ferritin, with a typical value far above the normal ceiling. Ferritin tracked with white blood cell counts, hinting that inflammation inflates the numbers alongside true iron burden. Red cell measures and social factors showed no clear predictive power. The authors, noting their small sample, urge monitoring that separates iron overload from inflammation before treatment decisions are made.
plos-pone-0350116:
Noemi Cucurachi and co-authors tested live monitoring for a mishap in nuclear medicine in 2026: injected radioactive tracer leaking into tissue instead of the vein. Leaks distort scans and, in therapy, can burn the tissue they pool in.

Portable detectors watched nearly nine hundred diagnostic scans and a small set of therapies. Dozens of leaks were caught live and confirmed on images. Curves of dose over time yielded simple cut-offs that flag a leak, and correction factors linked to curve features. Catching leaks during injection lets staff act at once and fix scan numbers before reading.
plos-pone-0350416:
Arizona changed three rules in 2023 to get more children eating school meals, and Shreya Raval and colleagues tracked what happened across about seventeen hundred public and charter schools. Their 2026 PLOS One study used meal records over time, comparing periods before and after each change.

First the state dropped the small fee charged to lower-income families; participation by those students jumped about ten percent for breakfast and lunch alike. Two federal changes followed, widening automatic eligibility and letting more schools serve everyone free. After all three, participation rose across every group. The authors offer the sequence as evidence that paperwork and small fees, not appetite, were the barriers.
plos-pone-0350516:
Jingyuan Wu and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study teaching language models to spot harmful drug reactions. The clues hide in doctors' free-text notes. The team worked from a national benchmark dataset and a second set from Vanderbilt University Medical Center. They fine-tuned several transformer models. They compared two ways of chopping long notes into pieces the models can digest.

Cutting notes into structured chunks generally beat sliding a fixed word window across them. One long-document model, paired with chunking, gave the most balanced results across both datasets. Chunk size mattered even when notes fit within model limits. Scores fell on the real hospital data compared with the benchmark. The authors report that gap honestly, as they offer practical guidance for building such safety tools.
plos-pone-0350616:
Eun-Ji Lee and colleagues mined police crash records from Cheongju, a mid-sized South Korean city, to find which factors turn a crash severe. They ran the same data through classical logistic regression and through four machine learning models with explanation tools, trusting only the risk factors both families agreed on. Policy, not prediction alone, was the goal.

Three culprits topped both approaches: running signals, neglecting safe-driving duties, and missing median barriers on undivided roads. Because the methods converge, officials can act with more confidence than a single model would justify. The study is a template as much as a result: pairing an old statistical workhorse with explainable machine learning gives cities findings that are both modern and defensible in a council meeting.
plos-pone-0350816:
Ballerina X S Chong and colleagues studied work hours and well being. Data came from a New Zealand panel study. Close to twenty five thousand adults took part. Waves ran from 2020 to 2023. The method mimics a trial on the same people. It shifts hours up or down by ten per week.

Ten extra hours raised fatigue most clearly. Sleep fell too. Ten fewer hours lowered fatigue most clearly. Weight and felt health moved in hoped for ways. Those shifts hinged more on hidden factors. Most of twenty eight outcomes barely moved. Recovery is where long hours bite hardest.
plos-pone-0351116:
Ersan Arslan and colleagues tested how heat strains young soccer players during small training games. Sixteen players, about sixteen years old, played two against two and four against four games in low, moderate, and high heat. Heart rate, distance run, effort ratings, and ear temperature were tracked across repeated bouts in each condition.

Hotter conditions raised heart strain and felt effort step by step in both game sizes. Distance covered and ear temperature did not shift clearly with heat. Bout by bout patterns showed strain built unevenly as games repeated. Coaches should read heat load from heart and effort signals, the authors suggest, not from distance alone, and plan breaks accordingly in warm weather.
plos-pone-0351216:
Sepsis that starts outside the lungs often spreads damage to them, and magnesium levels in the blood may play a part. Taotao Peng and colleagues mined an American intensive care database covering more than four thousand eight hundred such patients, in this 2026 PLOS One analysis.

Patients who developed lung complications died more often within ninety days. Risk followed a U shape across magnesium levels: both the lowest and highest ranges fared worse, with the highest group worst of all. A middle band looked safest. The authors suggest magnesium deserves monitoring as an early warning sign, while cautioning that records alone cannot prove the mineral itself drives the harm.
plos-pone-0351316:
Xiongbao Zhang and seven coauthors link gut germs to stamina in this 2026 study. First they set young adults who train often against peers who sit most of the day. Surveys logged how much each group moved and ate. Stool tests then mapped each group's gut germs. The active group hosted a richer, more varied mix. Helpful kinds, such as Veillonella and Faecalibacterium, thrived there.

Then came the telling test. The team moved gut germs from human donors into mice. Mice given the active donors' germs ran with clearly better stamina. Germs from the sitting donors gave no such boost. The result hints that the germ mix of active people is no bystander. It can itself lift the power to keep going, which opens a path toward germ-based aids for sport and recovery.
plos-pone-0351416:
Defenders of an accused person sometimes flip the story. They call the accused the real victim. Stephen J Flusberg and colleagues tested how far that move travels. Five experiments involved nearly three thousand people. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026. Earlier work had shown the effect in one sexual assault setting.

Fictional news stories covered several kinds of assault claims. One story involved a police shooting of an unarmed civilian. Labeling one side the victim shifted support everywhere. Readers who credited the victim language showed the strongest shifts. Gender and politics changed little. The authors warn the tactic works broadly. It is not limited to headline cases.
plos-pone-0352016:
Lei Ren and Shixin Jin taught neural networks to solve a class of diffusion equations whose memory strength changes over time. Such equations, used for spread in messy materials where the past lingers, carry a fractional order that itself drifts, and normally both the solution and the order must be guessed separately. Their physics-informed design embeds the equation inside the network's training goal.

Two networks work as a pair: one sketches the spreading solution, the other learns the drifting order from the same data. In tests the pair recovered both with tiny errors, and kept working when the data were noisy or the order changed roughly. Inverse problems of this kind show up in groundwater flow, drug spread, and materials science, so a solver that also reads the hidden order off sparse data has wide use.
plos-pone-0352116:
Pan Gu and a team of psychologists ask how well people judge where another person is looking, and how that skill shifts with mental health traits. Reading gaze is a basic social skill that often falters in conditions marked by social trouble. In their 2026 study, just over one hundred adults viewed faces online with varied gaze angles, head turns, and added visual noise, and said whether each face seemed to look at them.

Noisier images and mismatched head and eye directions made judgments less exact and more self-focused for everyone. Higher autism traits linked to lower exactness, while higher social anxiety linked to sharper basic judgments but bigger drops under noise. Gu and colleagues say gaze reading rests on both raw sensing and self-related habits, which split differently across traits.
plos-pone-0352316:
Adooru L N Arunkumar led a team of six authors on this 2026 machining study of milling YXR-7, a hard tool steel used for dies. Twenty-seven experimental runs varied cutting depth, feed, speed, and a nano-particle cutting fluid, measuring surface smoothness, material removed, and tool wear. A fuzzy multi-criteria ranking method then weighed the trade-offs.

One run stood out, pairing a smooth finish and low tool wear with a high removal rate. The authors present their ranking method as a robust way to tune precision machining of hard steels with less waste.
plos-pone-0352416:
Amanda Chen, Martha Jeong, and Michele Rigolizzo study how luck distorts learning in this 2026 report. Learners often fail despite good strategies, through bad luck. They also succeed despite poor strategies, through good luck. Both moments could teach something, if read correctly. The authors ask whether people read them correctly. Pilot data hinted at an asymmetry worth chasing.

In the pilot, people assumed noise explained failure more readily than success. They therefore treated success as the more informative signal. The main research tests a sharper worry. An early lucky success may damage learning more than an early unlucky failure. Learners who over-trust a fluky win may stop improving a weak strategy. Those burned by bad luck at least keep searching. The work matters anywhere feedback is noisy, from classrooms to trading floors.
plos-pone-0353016:
Handley and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether giving birth at a hospital with a higher official level of maternity care protects mothers from severe complications. Guidelines sort hospitals into four levels, from basic to regional centers, so risky births can be steered to the right place. Evidence that the sorting itself helps was thin. The team studied more than three million births in four states.

Severe complications, counted without blood transfusion cases, actually rose with hospital level, which mostly reflects that sicker mothers are sent upward. After adjusting for risk, mothers at the most basic hospitals had slightly lower complication rates than those at top centers overall. Yet among mothers with common, treatable problems such as bleeding or infection, one middle level did worse than top centers. The authors read this as a warning: level labels alone do not guarantee safety.
plos-pone-0353116:
Xu and colleagues modeled earthquake protection for linked twin towers in a 2026 study. Connecting towers with bridges can worsen shaking, so the team placed special damping layers inside the towers. The layers use lead-core bearings that both isolate and absorb energy, a method meant to avoid the tipping risk of base isolation in tall buildings.

Models with damping on both sides shed more energy and shook less than single-sided designs. Smart placement of layers also limited dangerous bending. Vertical shaking, however, was barely reduced by either design. The work shows promise for sideways quakes while honestly flagging the vertical gap for future research.
plos-pone-0353216:
Yuan Zhao and colleagues tested how managing emotions affects focused problem solving when the mind is already loaded. Convergent thinking, narrowing to one right answer, underpins much study and work. Their 2026 experiment split ninety-three undergraduates into three groups: reframing feelings, suppressing their expression, or simply watching.

Everyone solved word-association puzzles under high and low mental load. Scores were higher under low load for all groups, and strategy made no clear difference to scores. Speed told another story. Under heavy load, reframing produced faster answers than free watching. Under light load, suppression was fastest. Zhao and colleagues say the best emotion strategy may depend on how busy the mind already is.
plos-pone-0353716:
Sikder and colleagues analyzed early breastfeeding in Bangladesh using a national health survey from 2022 in a 2026 paper. Starting breastfeeding within an hour of birth protects newborns, and mothers reported that timing for nearly five thousand births. About sixty-three in one hundred babies started within the hour.

Skin-to-skin contact right after birth stood out as a strong support for early starting. Rates varied by region and birth setting, with cesarean births a weak point. The authors urge focused help in hospitals and after surgical births. Closing the remaining gap could prevent newborn illness in a country where most births now occur in facilities.
plos-pone-0354016:
Chertemps and colleagues mapped the sense genes of deep-sea shrimp in a 2026 study. Four kinds of shrimp live near hot vents on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean, where water swings between scalding and cold and light never reaches. To survive there, the shrimp must smell chemicals and feel heat with great precision.

One vent shrimp carried the largest set of smell-related genes yet found in any shrimp-like animal. Many of those genes belong to one fast-growing family, which hints they help the animal read the mixed chemicals around vents. The team also found many heat-sensing genes, while other sense proteins seemed to serve wider jobs in the body.
plos-pone-0354516: Seid and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on cleaning dye from factory wastewater with bacteria. Some bacteria make laccase, an enzyme that can break down dyes. The team isolated such bacteria from dye-stained textile wastewater and tuned the conditions for their work. The goal is decolorizing the water. Living cleaners could offer textile towns a cheaper way to treat colored waste.
plos-pone-0354816:
Koichi Ohata led a team of eight authors on this 2026 chart review of an antifungal drug, isavuconazole, in Japanese patients with blood cancers. Forty-five patients treated between 2023 and 2025 had their lab values and heart rhythm intervals tracked over time.
