A subgroup also received a leukemia drug known to stretch the heart's electrical recovery.

Liver enzyme rises were uncommon and passed quickly, and no meaningful lab deterioration appeared. In the subgroup, the antifungal pairing actually showed shorter heart intervals than the leukemia drug alone. Ohata judges the antifungal reassuringly safe in this fragile group.
plos-pone-0354916:
Alnazzawi, in a 2026 study, asks whether free-text notes in patient records can help predict heart disease. Heart disease covers problems such as heart failure, heart attack, and stroke, and high blood pressure and diabetes raise the risk. Finding risk signs early in messy clinical notes could help doctors act sooner.

The approach maps words in written records onto structured traits, then feeds those traits into a boosting model that learns from many small decision trees. Training drew on both a corpus of clinical narratives and a classic structured heart disease data set. The model sorted patients by whether heart disease was present with solid accuracy in the low eighties, in percent terms. Alnazzawi presents the method as a way to flag high-risk patients from records that clinics already keep.
plos-pone-0355216:
Florian Vogt and colleagues try in 2026 to build a simple symptom rule for spotting chikungunya fever at basic clinics in Kinshasa, Congo. The mosquito borne illness looks like many other fevers in the region, and lab tests are scarce. Patients with suspected infection during an outbreak gave clinical details and blood for virus and antibody tests, plus a malaria check.

About two in five truly had acute infection. Pain in knees and shoulders showed some signal, but both a tree based rule and a regression model missed most cases or mislabelled many. The authors conclude that symptoms alone cannot guide care here and better test access is essential.
plos-pone-0355416:
Bo Gong and co-authors reanalyse a large surgical database in 2026. The patients were adults who had brain tumour surgery. The team asked one main question. Does long term steroid use before surgery raise clot risk? The clot of interest forms in the lungs after surgery. A blood cell ratio was tested as a link in the chain.

More than fifteen thousand patients were included in the study. Steroid users got lung clots more often than non users. The link stayed after other factors were counted. Part of the link ran through the blood cell ratio. The authors call for fresh studies to confirm the finding. They also want tests of whether the ratio can guide prevention.
plos-pone-0356816:
Nari Kim leads a team of eight giving veterinarians a ruler for bear hearts, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Heart disease is common in captive bears, but judging heart size on an X-ray needs a species specific reference. The method measures the heart against the spine's vertebrae. The team reviewed chest radiographs from forty-six healthy sanctuary bears, twenty-two Asiatic black bears and twenty-four sun bears, measuring the scale on two views and recording chest shape.

Both species centered near ten and two thirds vertebrae on the side view. The chest on the front view read slightly higher, especially in sun bears. The two species' heart scores did not differ significantly, though their chests did: black bears run deeper relative to width. Sex, age, weight, and condition showed no significant pull on the score. Sanctuary vets now have numbers to judge enlargement by, instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0356916:
CORRECTION: The PLOS One Editors issued this Correction in 2026 to a plan by Helena Pernice and colleagues. The plan covers a registry study of amyloidosis, a disease where misshapen proteins damage many organs. Care is split across clinics. The registry, based at Berlin's Charité center, is set up to follow patients across clinics in one shared record. Nerve, heart, and blood clinics are among them.

The fix is paperwork only. The author workplace listings printed with the plan were wrong. The notice reprints the full, correct list for all authors. It spans the amyloidosis center and its partner units. No methods, aims, or data change. Readers citing the plan should take author addresses and credits from the corrected version.
plos-pone-0357116:
Lee Rooney, Gerard McMahon, and Rodney Kennedy published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a small equipment question with practical consequences: where on the back should athletes wear a GPS tracker? Manufacturers recommend the upper back, between the shoulder blades, but units often slip. The team fitted players with two units at once, upper and mid-back, comparing both against measured ground truth during a team-sport circuit and sprint tests.

The upper-back unit matched the truth closely, with tiny bias for distance and low variability, and strong agreement for peak speed. The mid-back unit badly underestimated distance, varied more, and the two placements could not be treated as interchangeable for distance at all. A shift of only a hand's width down the back was enough to spoil the numbers. Teams, they advise, should enforce the recommended placement, because load decisions built on slipped sensors rest on sand.
plos-pone-0357816:
Debela Abdeta Efa, Megersa Akasa, and Yobsan Tamiru published a 2026 survey in PLOS ONE of parasites infecting fish in Lake Hawassa, Ethiopia. The lake supports a local fishing economy, yet its fish parasites had barely been documented. Over the 2023–2024 season the team examined three farmed and wild species, tilapia, catfish, and a local barb, checking skin, gills, and internal organs and recording each fish's size, sex, and weight.

Nearly nine in ten fish carried at least one parasite, and the team collected well over a thousand individual parasites in total. The haul spanned worm groups, single-celled parasites, small crustaceans, and leeches. Infection levels varied with the fish's sex, weight, and length. Because some of these parasites damage fish health and market value, the survey gives local fishery managers a first baseline for monitoring the lake's stocks.
plos-pone-0357916:
Van-Minh Nguyen and three colleagues ask whether a preliminary weld can save additively manufactured shafts from early fatigue death, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their hollow shafts are built by wire arc printing steel onto stacked rings. The print alone left a hairline unfused seam at each ring joint. Cyclic bending would find that seam. A designed experiment varied current, bead overlap, speed, and ring thickness over thirty runs to optimize the joined version.

The optimized pre joined shafts lasted about half again as long in rotating bending tests as print only shafts, roughly four hundred ninety thousand cycles against three hundred twenty-seven thousand. Scatter between specimens also narrowed. Microscopy explained the gain: the pre weld fused the ring wall completely, while the print only seam gaped slightly at the bore. The authors flag the small sample size, but the mechanism and the margin point the same way.
plos-pone-0359016:
Dongjin Yeo and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a nationwide cohort study from South Korea. The authors examine exposure to residential greenness, how much vegetation surrounds a person's home, and later diagnoses of common mental disorders among people who had COVID-19.

Following a national cohort over time lets the team link earlier surroundings to later diagnoses. Green neighborhoods are often tied to better mental health, and this study tests the link in people recovering from a disruptive illness. Urban planners and mental health researchers share the audience for this use of national health records.
plos-pone-0359316: Wolpold and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on where coral larvae choose to settle. Their computer model lets virtual larvae act as agents whose behavior evolves through a neuroevolution process. Where larvae land decides where new corals grow. A model that mimics real settlement can help reef teams pick sites where young corals are most likely to take hold.
plos-pone-0359416: Jeon and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a grave risk after colon or rectal cancer surgery. Sometimes the joined ends of the bowel leak, an event called anastomotic leakage. The team tracked long-term cancer outcomes for patients who had a major leak after curative surgery. They split the results by cancer stage and tumor site. The findings inform how closely such patients should be watched afterward.
plos-pone-0360216:
Chala Diriba Kenea and colleagues tested in 2026 a virtual reality system for arm rehabilitation after stroke, in a mixed-methods study set in Ethiopia. The system, called AdaptRehab VR, immerses patients in virtual tasks meant to retrain upper limb movement. The study asks three practical questions: can the system be used there, will patients and staff accept it, and does it show early signs of helping?

Mixed methods means the team combined measured outcomes with interviews and observation. Testing in Ethiopia matters because most rehabilitation technology is designed and proven in wealthy health systems, then assumed to travel. Evidence on cost, training, and patient response in a lower resource setting decides whether such tools can widen access to stroke therapy or remain a rich country extra.
pmc-13196916:
Salih Gürsoy and Aylin Zekioglu report a 2026 trial of peer teaching in school sport classes. They tested whether pupils learn hard wrestling moves better when classmates teach them. The work took place in middle school physical education lessons over eight weeks.

Thirty-six pupils split into a peer-teaching group and a group taught in the usual direct way. Trained raters scored four moves with set standards. The peer group did clearly better on the underarm pass and the double-leg takedown. The two groups tied on the arm drag and the single-leg takedown. The authors suggest peer teaching helps most where a move needs fine timing and joint body control.
pmc-13197116:
L Raymond Guo and Shuimei Liu mapped the research field on health data rules in the age of AI in 2026. AI tools in health care need vast patient data, which raises sharp debate on ownership and privacy. The pair asked what themes shape that debate and how they shift over time.

They screened three databases for studies from 2018 to mid 2025 and kept forty-three papers. A topic model sorted the work into five themes, from AI uses and ownership to ethics and law. Output has grown fast since 2018. Ethics and legal concerns grew most and now lead the field. The authors urge workable rules, not just debate.
pmc-13197416:
Mosa E Hosney and colleagues propose a 2026 search algorithm modeled on heart rate control. Optimization means finding the best option in a hard problem. Many search methods settle too fast on weak answers, so the team drew on how the heart speeds and slows to balance effort.

Their Heart Rate Optimizer mimics fast beats for wide searching and slow beats for fine local tuning. Random long jumps model irregular beats and help escape dead ends. A learning step keeps the search group diverse. On two standard test suites, it beat nine rival methods in accuracy, speed, and stability. It also solved three classic design problems, from welded beams to pressure vessels.
pmc-13197616:
Carly Malesky and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare tear sac growth causing bloody tears. The lacrimal sac drains tears from the eye. Growths there are rare, and a mixed growth pattern, part inward and part outward, had never been reported in this spot.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with two months of bloody tears and constant watering in one eye. Scans showed a small mass in the tear sac area. Surgeons from ear-nose-throat and eye plastics removed it together. Lab study confirmed the mixed growth type. The authors stress prompt, joint care, since such growths can return or, rarely, turn cancerous and need close follow-up.
pmc-13198516:
Bárbara A Rebelo and colleagues built a 2026 light-based tool to read pigments inside single plant cells. Carotenoids are yellow-to-red pigments prized for nutrition and industry. Growing them in plant cell factories could be greener, but checking each cell's pigment mix without killing it was hard.

Their platform pairs Raman imaging, a laser method that reads chemical fingerprints, with a neural network. Standard pigment tests set the key signal peaks. The network sorted tobacco cells by pigment content with high accuracy. Checks against standard liquid analysis backed the sorting. In engineered lines, pigments pooled in bubble-like stores near the nucleus. The tool could help pick top cells for biofactories.
pmc-13200916:
Khaled Al Tabaa and colleagues present a 2026 case report on saving a failed nose rebuild. Near-total nose loss from trauma is among the hardest rebuilds in facial surgery. The standard plan layers a forearm free flap for lining, rib cartilage for structure, and a forehead flap for cover, but no clear salvage path existed if the free flap died.

Their patient was a 43-year-old smoker who lost most of his nose in a human bite. The forearm flap partly died from a vein clot. Surgeons converted the first forehead flap into hinged lining, then used a second forehead flap from the other side for cover. Rib cartilage rebuilt the frame. At one year, airway, contour, and look were good.
pmc-13202916:
Betel nut chewing can reprogram mouth cancer cells through tiny vesicles, and a 2026 study by Hui-Hsin Ko traces that pathway. The research article examines how arecoline, the active agent in areca nut, drives methylation of the ZNF582 gene in oral squamous cell carcinoma through extracellular vesicles.

Working with two cancer cell lines, the team isolated vesicles and measured gene methylation, protein levels, and immune cell behavior. Silencing ZNF582 made cancer cells grow, migrate, and resist immune attack more strongly, partly by raising the PD-L1 shield protein through an interferon-related route. The authors propose blocking this vesicle pathway as a treatment strategy for exposed patients.
pmc-13210316:
Recommendation engines quietly learn users' politics, and a 2026 experiment headed by Tim Faverjon shows the learning happen step by step. The research article trains a model on real sharing behavior from a panel of nearly forty thousand X users, then generates synthetic recommendations to trace how ideology gets encoded.

Elementary recommendation rules, fed only on who shared what, built an internal left-right map of users inside the system. That map formed independently of age and gender signals in the authors' checks on the model. Tweaking the ideological representation shifted the political leaning, diversity, and relevance of what users were offered, exposing a trade-off platforms rarely discuss openly.
pmc-13213716:
Zhaoyan Li and colleagues map in 2026 the immune cells that crowd stomach tumours, hunting for markers that predict patient outcomes. Macrophages are the most abundant immune cells in that environment and can either fight or feed a tumour.

Merging single-cell, bulk, and spatial gene data, the team catalogued nine broad cell types and distinct macrophage subgroups that expand inside tumours. A machine-learning search built a seven-gene score from macrophage-linked genes, which predicted survival across several cohorts. Spatial maps showed one marker-heavy macrophage type sitting in its own metabolic niche and talking extensively to neighbours. The atlas offers both prognostic tools and possible treatment targets.
pmc-13214416:
Shaowei Fan leads a large team that pilots in 2026 a blood test for a diagnosis used in Chinese medicine. Doctors of that tradition sort a fast, uneven heartbeat by pattern, such as qi-yin deficiency. Past marker hunts for these patterns lacked sharp tools.

The team read a chemical mark on DNA from tiny sacs that float in blood. They did this for heart patients in two groups at one centre. Computer models sifted the marks and found nine that flag the deficiency pattern. A test built on those marks was trained and then checked on the second group. The work aims to give an old style of diagnosis a firm, measured base.
pmc-13215216:
Haodong Li leads a large team unveiling in 2026 a DNA-woven carbon nanotube mesh that drapes over living cells and lets gentle voltages steer their calcium signals. Biological signalling runs on ions, so electronics must couple softly to wet membranes without cooking or tearing them.

The mesh concentrates a sub-volt push into nanometre hotspots at the membrane, engaging the cell's own calcium channels. Sustained calcium entry followed across several cell types, without extra oxidative stress or lost viability. The focused field also slipped DNA cargo into cells gently and sharpened natural killer cells, which released more tumour-killing molecules. Gene programmes tied to calcium switched on as expected, confirming genuine biological activation.
pmc-13215516:
Mi Suk Noh and co-authors present a 2026 engineering evaluation of a warm-air circulation system fitted inside a vaporized hydrogen peroxide sterilizer. Residual moisture is a common cause of failed low-temperature sterilization for medical devices.

The system uses a fan and heater to keep chamber air moving and evenly warm. Sensors showed it held temperatures near 55 to 60 degrees Celsius and cleared added moisture during test cycles. Challenge devices, flexible and rigid lumens, and endoscope dummies all came through sterilized. The authors conclude that steady heat and drying make peroxide sterilization more reliable for complex instruments.
pmc-13216116:
Anna Rienmueller and co-authors present a 2026 clinical practice recommendation on planning spinal alignment in adult deformity surgery. Operating on a crooked adult spine works best when the target shape fits the individual patient, and several competing systems claim to define that target.

Written for the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Deformity, the review weighs four landmark papers that trace the field's path from shape descriptions to proportional and then continuous measures. The authors explain what the Roussouly types, the SRS-Schwab classification, the GAP score, and the T4-L1-hip axis each contribute, and they grade advice for using them together. Bone quality, stamina, and surgical goals should temper any numeric target.
pmc-13217016:
L. Damen and co-authors present a 2026 case series that ended three long diagnostic searches for inherited tumour syndromes. All three patients looked clinically affected, yet standard blood DNA testing found nothing, because each carried the fault in only a small fraction of cells.

The syndromes were von Hippel-Lindau disease and neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2. Sequencing several affected tissues from each patient exposed the same pathogenic variant recurring at low levels, and hindsight testing found it in blood at just 1 to 7 percent of reads. The authors argue that multi-tissue sequencing should be a routine next step when suspicion is strong and blood testing is blank, since a firm diagnosis changes surveillance and family counselling.
pmc-13219216:
Agda Costa Valério and colleagues describe the body measurements of Pantaneiro sheep and build simple trees for their visible traits in a 2026 study. The Pantaneiro is an adapted breed shaped by the Brazilian Pantanal's flooding, heat, and forage, and conserving it needs clear, field-friendly ways to describe the animals. Lab phenotyping will never reach remote floodplain farms.

The team measured twenty-three quantitative and ten qualitative traits in 211 ewes kept under semi-extensive grazing. Multivariate analysis distilled the measurements into four dimensions of body capacity, limb robustness, and head shape, together explaining about two thirds of the variation. Decision tree models predicted qualitative traits from a few tape measurements. Three traits, head profile, muzzle type, and wool colour, were predicted with accuracy above eighty percent, with leg circumferences doing the work. The authors present the approach as a cheap phenotyping kit for managing and conserving the floodplain breed.
pmc-13219516:
Xinlu Zhang and Yuemin Liu build a neural system recognizing themes of ancient Chinese poems in a 2026 paper. Digitizing classical culture needs machines to sort poems by theme, but ancient Chinese lacks corpora and language models adapt poorly to its allusive style. Their framework, BA-RILA, attacks it by listening to a poem on three channels.

The system extracts vectors from a BERT pre-trained on ancient Chinese, rhythm features for the metrical pattern in eleven dimensions, and seventy-five features for its symbols and scenes. Attention weighting blends the three streams before a two-layer bidirectional LSTM reads the fused sequence. A multi-head attention stage sharpens the telling elements, and a classifier assigns one of six themes. The method outperformed benchmark models and generalized across Tang and Song dynasty sets. The authors present feature fusion, rather than a language model, as the way forward for text tasks.
pmc-13219816:
Nuri Koray Ülgen and colleagues validate a bone measurement anyone can take from a chest X-ray as a hip fracture sign in a 2026 study. Hip fractures devastate older adults, and the bone density scan, DEXA, is unavailable in places. The deltoid tuberosity index measures the shoulder end of the arm bone, a region visible on chest films, and might stand in for a density workup.

The study covered 1,012 patients aged sixty and over who had surgery for hip fracture and seventy-five patients with normal bone density. Two observers could measure the index in three quarters of chest films, and their readings agreed perfectly. Fracture patients scored lower, and the index separated the groups with an accuracy of 0.903, with a cutoff that caught eighty-five percent of fracture patients while clearing eighty-seven percent of healthy ones. The authors propose it as opportunistic screening wherever chest films exist.
pmc-13222516:
Kağan Gökçe and co-authors report a giant benign ovarian cyst that looked like cancer, in a 2026 case report with a review of diagnostic challenges. The mass arose from the left ovary and required surgery. Imaging and blood markers often cannot separate benign, borderline, and malignant mucinous tumours, especially when they grow huge and complex.

Tissue examination after removal gave the answer: mucinous cystadenoma, a benign diagnosis. Giant benign masses have grown rarer as imaging improves, yet size alone still forces careful planning. The authors stress meticulous surgical technique and thorough pathology, since the final word on these tumours usually comes only after excision.
pmc-13222616:
Yunlei Cao, Yuqing Jiang, and Ding Ding compare conservative versus radical surgery for bowel endometriosis, in a 2026 prospective cohort study at a university hospital. Thirty-one patients completed follow-up after shaving, disc excision, or full segment removal of bowel lesions, chosen per patient. Symptoms, gut function, complications, and recurrence were tracked for two years.

Both strategies produced significant, comparable gains in pelvic symptoms and quality of life, and the benefits held steady across follow-up visits. Complication and recurrence rates stayed low in both groups. No clear superiority emerged for cutting out the bowel segment. The authors advise matching the operation to each lesion's character rather than defaulting to the bigger surgery.
pmc-13224716:
Jiang Ma and a large team set out a 2026 trial protocol for rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in the knee. Standard exercise programmes often leave weakness behind, partly because injury and surgery dull the nerve pathways that drive the leg muscles. The trial adds gentle electrical stimulation over the spine, delivered through the skin, alongside exercise.

Patients will be randomly assigned, without knowing their group, to real or sham stimulation during straight-leg raises. Sessions last twenty minutes at a fixed low current, stacked on top of routine rehabilitation for everyone. The main yardstick is a standard knee outcome score eighteen months after surgery, with safety tracked throughout the study.
pmc-13232416:
Jordan Mazzola and colleagues test in 2026 a copper peptide in aging mice, comparing a belly injection route with a nose route. The peptide, GHK-Cu, occurs naturally in the body and fades with age, while supporting repair and calm inflammation. Middle-aged mice near two years old received either five days of injections or eight weeks of nasal dosing.

Nasal dosing improved maze escape learning in both sexes across later trials, while injections helped males only briefly. Gene activity in the memory center split sharply by route, with nasal dosing quieting growth and energy pathways. Injections instead switched on repair and stress response programs. Better learning can arise from opposite cell states, so dose route and length shape any future therapy plan.
pmc-13232616:
Jaydeep Sharma and colleagues show in 2026 that a slow-twitch muscle protein also guards whole-body sugar control in mice. The protein, made by the Myh7 gene, powers the steady fibers used for posture and endurance. Mice bred without it in skeletal muscle let the team separate contraction from metabolism questions.

Young knockout mice grew oversized muscles that later wasted, with slow fibers dying back and strength falling. Sugar use faltered, insulin response dulled, and a key sugar doorway protein dropped in muscle, a pattern like type 2 diabetes. A protective pathway driven by the factor NRF2 had faded, letting harmful oxygen byproducts build up. A plant compound that switches that pathway back on rescued much of the damage.
pmc-13233316:
Long Chen and Ed Manley published a 2026 transport study on why goods vehicles speed in British cities. Using trajectory data from 3.2 million journeys across 13 cities, the pair examined speeding at several scales, from street-level engineering features to the shape of whole road networks. Most earlier work looked at single factors in isolation.

Road geometry and network connectivity showed associations with speeding comparable in strength to engineering interventions such as traffic calming. The authors argue that speed reduction plans gain credibility when they account for the surrounding network, not just the street where speeding occurs. They also urge analysts of local travel behavior to include measures of urban context. The findings speak to planners redesigning freight routes and residential streets alike.
pmc-13233916:
Melissa Hazen, Sharon L Cushing, and Karen A Gordon published a 2026 developmental study of children with cochlear implants in both ears. Ninety-six children aged about five to eighteen took part, sixty-six implant users and thirty peers with typical hearing. Standard tests measured language, working memory, reading, and math, while statistical modeling weighed hearing history, cause of deafness, balance function, and social disadvantage.

Implant users scored lower than peers on language, visual-spatial memory, math, and word reading. Balance and vestibular function were also clearly impaired in the implant group, though balance did not predict school outcomes. Only the richness of a child's auditory experience predicted results across every domain. Gaps ran deepest for children whose deafness came from congenital cytomegalovirus, inner ear malformations, or genetic causes, arguing for cause-aware, multidisciplinary support.
pmc-13234516:

pmc-13264816:

pmc-13264916:

pmc-13265016:

pmc-13266416:

pmc-13268116:

pmc-13269616:

pmc-13269816:

pmc-13271116:

pmc-13271316:

pmc-13271516:

pmc-13272716:

The authors suggest body mechanics alone do not explain men's worse outcomes.
pmc-13272816:

pmc-13274316:
Kazutoshi Masuda and Miho Yanagisawa present a 2026 journal article on programming the squishiness of synthetic cells. pmc-13274816:

pmc-13276616:
Sophie Schreiner and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a workflow for seeing overlapping pathologies inside single brain cells. Standard staining shows one marker at a time on thin slices, missing the three-dimensional picture.

pmc-13276816:

The notice replaces a wrong image in a supplementary figure. The clone formation image for T47D cells had been covered by mistake during figure preparation. The authors state the fix does not change the study's conclusions.
pmc-13279016:

pmc-13279416:

pmc-13279516:

pmc-13279916:

pmc-13280116:

Lab dish tests of diabetes related acts close the study.
pmc-13281416:

pmc-13281916:

pmc-13282216:

pmc-13282416:

pmc-13283916:

pmc-13284416:

pmc-13284516:

pmc-13285916:

pmc-13286216:

pmc-13286316:

pmc-13287316:

pmc-13288216:

pmc-13288716:

pmc-13289016:

pmc-13289216:

pmc-13289316:

pmc-13289416:

pmc-13290116:

pmc-13290616:

pmc-13290716:

pmc-13291616:

pmc-13291716:

Their patient was a 22-year-old woman with a ten-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and two weeks of upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Early blood tests and an ultrasound showed nothing unusual.

Endoscopy found an object stuck in the lower stomach, and a CT scan showed an abscess measuring 7 cm by 5.6 cm in the left liver lobe. Surgery confirmed the toothpick had pierced the stomach wall and entered the liver, so surgeons drained the abscess and repaired the stomach. She recovered well on antibiotics, and the authors urge suspicion when abdominal symptoms persist without explanation.
pmc-13292216:
Li-Yen Yang and co-authors introduce a 2026 benchmark called LiPP for testing how well software predicts lipid-protein binding poses. Predicting where lipids dock on proteins trails other complex types, partly for lack of shared ground-truth data. The team curated 311 nonredundant structures spanning many protein folds and lipid classes, then ran five modeling tools against them.

Three AI co-folding tools, one AI docking tool, and one physics-based docker were compared. AlphaFold 3 scored best, with 76.1 percent of poses under the accuracy cutoff, though that fell to 47.2 percent on structures outside its training data. Physics-based docking and some AI tools kept poses physically plausible, while others broke basic constraints. The authors offer LiPP as a standard test bed and call for better handling of lipid size and flexibility.
pmc-13292316:
Yunqin Sun's team reviews a 2026 field built on nanozymes, nanomaterials that act like enzymes. Their catalytic power, the authors stress, grows out of nanoscale traits such as surface defects and particle geometry. The review sorts mechanisms into pathways that generate reactive oxygen species and those that shuttle electrons.

Design progress runs from plain nanoparticles to single-atom and dual-atom designs that react far faster. Uses surveyed include lab diagnostics, combined tumor therapy, antibacterial treatment, and regenerative medicine. Translation still stalls on safety and manufacturing consistency, among other bottlenecks. The authors look to AI-guided design to rationalize the next generation and offer the review as a mechanistic roadmap for precision nanomedicine.
pmc-13292516:
Muthugounder Mohan and a large team deliver a 2026 data description: a chromosome-level genome for the Indian population of the legume pod borer, Maruca vitrata. The moth devastates grain and vegetable legumes worldwide, and Indian populations may be diverging into distinct races. PacBio HiFi sequencing plus Hi-C proximity mapping built the assembly, checked against microscope karyotyping.

The 459.3 megabase genome settled into 45 scaffolds, with 31 pseudochromosomes holding 99.73 percent of the sequence. Annotation predicted 21,586 protein-coding genes, and repeat content reached 36.67 percent of the genome. Completeness scoring captured 99.5 percent of expected insect genes. Chromosome counting in cells confirmed 31, matching the assembly. The authors say the resource sets up structural and functional studies and gene hunting for future pest control.
pmc-13292916:
Yuta Mine and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a scan method for spread of kidney cancer. A 76-year-old woman had part of one kidney removed for clear cell cancer, then later had a chest bone deposit removed as well.

Months later, a scan found a soft lump behind the breastbone. A PET scan with a tracer called 68Ga-DOTATOC showed no uptake there, yet lit up strongly at a spine bone, pointing to new spread. After focused radiation, uptake stayed, and surgery confirmed live tumor remained. The case suggests the tracer scan can help judge leftover disease and guide next steps.
pmc-13293416:
Sanjiv Rampal leads a 2026 chart review on what predicts major versus minor amputation in diabetic foot infection at a hospital in Central Malaysia. Foot infection is a grave diabetes complication, and major amputation above the ankle harms survival and quality of life.

Records covered 434 patients treated from January 2010 to December 2019, with minor cuts making up 70.7% of cases. Most patients arrived with advanced disease, and grade 4 wounds were most common. Older age and higher wound grade each raised the odds of major amputation on their own. Early care and strong limb-saving efforts for high-risk patients are stressed.
pmc-13293716:
Yohei Shimizu and colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, a rare abnormal vessel link near the skull base that appeared after head injury and was cured through an artery. A 60-year-old man had ringing in his right ear for two weeks after a blow to the right temple.

Detailed imaging showed a fistula in the posterior condylar canal fed by one branch of the occipital artery, draining to nearby veins without dangerous backflow to the brain. Glue and coils delivered through the artery closed the link fully, and ringing stopped at once. Later imaging showed the closure held with no return of the fistula.
pmc-13294116:
Emily A Schultz leads a 2026 effort to build fair care yardsticks for hand surgery. Social factors shape who gets care and how hands heal, yet clinics lack shared checks. A broad review pulled proof on gaps in care. Draft checks were then scored by 11 hand surgeons in the United States through two vote rounds with group talk.

Fourteen draft checks made the cut. Topics span wait time to surgery, ER use after surgery by plan type, and results by area need level. Judges scored each check on worth, ease of use, and sound base. Good checks could help clinics track gaps and test if fixes close them.
pmc-13294216:
Ghaith Abu-Zeinah and colleagues write a 2026 letter on switching interferon types for myeloproliferative neoplasms. Supply trouble with peginterferon alfa-2a, confirmed by regulators in January 2025, pushed many long-term patients toward ropeginterferon alfa-2b, yet no trial defines the right switch dose. The authors share center experience, where interferon use reaches 42% of polycythemia vera patients.

Their default switch starts ropeginterferon at 100 mcg every two weeks, rising by 50 mcg steps every 2 to 4 weeks to hold response. A faster high-dose route may suit patients in partial response on high old doses, but risks side effects and lab problems. No single conversion ratio fits all patients.
pmc-13294316:
Marc Maegele and colleagues report first hospital use of a blood test for mild brain injury in a 2026 study. Care in the ER leans on head scans that cost time and add radiation dose. Adults seen in Cologne from November 2023 to April 2024 had suspected mild injury and coma scores of 13 to 15. Each got a head scan plus blood tests for GFAP and UCH-L1 within 12 hours, for 320 patients in all.

Blood marks were high in 261 patients, or 82%, while scans found injury in only 29, or 9%, in the reported shares. Paired marks caught 97% of scan-proved injury and gave a 98% rate for ruling injury out when low. Safe scan cuts are the prize, pending wider checks.
pmc-13294416:
Lucas Fabian Polti and a large team stain and sequence rare jaw lesions for clues to cell identity in a 2026 study. Twenty-nine cases from two centers covered calcifying odontogenic cysts, ghost cell tumors, and two ameloblastoma types. Protein CK13 was mapped, and three exact mutations in the KRT13 and APC genes were hunted by PCR methods.

Cyst lining cells showed CK13 in 64% of cyst cases, and ghost cells stained in 54% in the reported shares. Tumor cases varied, with one adenoid case fully negative. None carried the hunted mutations, though common harmless variants and one new silent change appeared. Staining hints at squamous-style differentiation paths.
pmc-13295116:
Nuri Kim and colleagues build a self-boosting drug pair inside fat bubbles for cancer treatment in a 2026 study. Drug combinations often fail because the partners travel differently and arrive out of step. Their linked prodrug joins retinoic acid with a partner that drains a key cell protector, raising oxidative stress together.

The joined molecule forms cholesterol-free bubbles that gain a coating for longer circulation and tumour gathering. Inside tumour cells, an enzyme cut releases both partners at once, deepening stress and suppressing a cancer-linked protein called Pin1. Treated cells died more readily, and mouse tumours shrank strongly with little body-wide harm.
pmc-13295916:
Etienne Karl Duranté and colleagues map, in 2026, the trial landscape for app- and web-based talking therapies for depression. Such digital care could widen access, yet many past trials carry bias risks, so the team catalogue what newer trials are doing.

Across trial registries from 2018 to 2025 they found 681 studies, about half finished but only a third with results published. Most used cognitive behavioural therapy, many screened by self-report alone, and few recruited in poorer countries. The authors urge faster reporting, fairer comparison groups and broader populations in future trials.
pmc-13297016:
Maya Tang and Paul S.-H. Park review, in 2026, cone opsins, the light-catching proteins behind colour vision and sharp sight, and the inherited eye diseases their faults cause. Rod opsin faults are well mapped, but cone opsin gene clusters have drawn less attention.

Three cone opsin types tune the eye to different colours, and disruptions in their gene array cause conditions such as blue cone monochromacy and Bornholm eye disease, plus blue-yellow colour blindness. The authors survey known mutations and the mouse models used to probe how faulty cone opsins damage the retina.
pmc-13297416:
Fatty feeding changed not just mouse liver cells but the protein scaffold around them, shows a 2026 study from Roza Izgilov and co-authors. The group asked how high-fat eating, raised blood sugar, and fatty liver alter the liver extracellular matrix at very small scales.

Fed mice gained fat and deposited more matrix protein in the liver. After removing the cells, the team examined the bare scaffold with electron microscopy, cathodoluminescence imaging, and fluorescence measures. Sugar-driven damage products had accumulated, fibers looked thicker from extra crosslinking, and protein chemistry had shifted. Such scaffold changes may matter for regenerative medicine, since replacement tissue must grow on matrix that disease has already remodeled.
pmc-13298016:
Machine sight is entering the womb exam room, and Rafał Watrowski and his team take stock of it in a 2026 review. The exam, called hysteroscopy, is the gold way to see inside the uterus. Its reads rest on the eye of the doctor, and AI tools might make those reads more steady.

The team found 19 studies. Jobs ranged from sorting lesions and live spotting to image cutting, surgery help, and odds of later pregnancy. Top marks came in plain yes-or-no tasks and in big multi-site tools, one of which hit an AUC of 0.979 on home data. Wider class sets did worse. Most work was from one site and looked back in time, so the team see a support role for the tools for now.
pmc-13299516:
Pairing a human-derived peptide with ordinary antibiotics killed staph bacteria far faster than the antibiotics alone, show Eman Khalid Barahim and colleagues in a 2026 laboratory study. Their peptide, CaD23, targets Staphylococcus aureus, a leading cause of eye infection and resistance-linked deaths.

CaD23 alone stopped all six test strains, including resistant MRSA, at 16 to 32 μg/mL. Of twenty peptide-antibiotic combinations, nineteen interacted positively, a third of them truly synergistic. The peptide wiped out bacteria within fifteen minutes where two partner drugs needed eight to twenty-four hours, and it depolarized the bacterial membrane within seconds. The authors propose the combinations for drug-resistant eye and body infections.
pmc-13299816:
Diabetes damages the retina's neurons before its blood vessels, so eye drops that protect nerves could intervene earlier than current shots and lasers, argue Hugo Ramos and colleagues in a 2026 review. They survey neuroprotective therapies for early diabetic retinal disease delivered topically.

Ganglion cells die and synaptic signaling falters before vascular lesions become visible, a stage when invasive treatment cannot be justified. Eyedrops offer a non-invasive route, reaching the retina largely through the sclera. The review weighs the leading candidate compounds and the preclinical and clinical evidence behind them. The authors frame topical neuroprotection as the practical way to treat the disease's opening phase.
pmc-13300216:
Underground miners in South Africa's Mpumalanga Province breathe worse air and report worse lungs than surface crews, a 2026 survey by Masilu Daniel Masekameni and colleagues shows. The cross-sectional study covered 239 workers and compared dust exposure, ventilation, symptoms, and safety habits between the two settings.

High dust exposure was reported by 44.9 percent of underground miners versus 24.1 percent at the surface, with chronic cough at 45.7 against 25.9 percent. Adjusted models tied chronic cough to underground work, smoking, and heavy dust, and smoking multiplied the underground risk. Underground crews also knew less about protection and used it less, pointing to combined workplace and behavior programs.
pmc-13302216:
Students who feel ready for future careers also tend to score higher, and Ziluo Yan with colleagues trace the wiring in a 2026 three-wave study. Five hundred nineteen students at two general high schools in central China reported career adaptability first, then confidence and study strategies, with exam results collected at the start and end. Chinese, mathematics, and English scores carried the achievement measure.

Adaptability predicted later scores overall, yet its direct path vanished once the middle steps entered the model. Belief in one's academic ability and metacognitive strategy use each carried a real share of the effect. Expectations about outcomes, by contrast, mediated nothing. Schools aiming at grades, the authors imply, might train future-readiness and self-belief together.
pmc-13302716:
Clots still form in the heart's left appendage despite proper blood thinners, Kinga Gościńska-Bis and colleagues find in a 2026 prospective study. Five hundred ten patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, anticoagulated for at least three weeks before planned cardioversion, underwent both surface and transesophageal ultrasound. The team hunted factors behind appendage thrombus or dense spontaneous echo contrast.

Nearly thirty-eight percent of patients carried one or the other finding. Weak pumping on either side of the heart, a stretched left atrium, and female sex raised the odds, while significant mitral leakage lowered them. The standard CHA2DS2-VASc score and device leads predicted nothing. Ultrasound markers, the authors argue, should guide the pre-shock check.
pmc-13302816:
Etching a pattern into a light sensor's skin boosts its output while slowing its reflexes, Gailing Tian and colleagues find in a 2026 device study. Silver selenide photothermoelectric detectors, which turn light into heat and then voltage, received periodic microstructure arrays through photolithography. The team varied the pattern's pitch and measured responses across wavelengths from 405 to 950 nanometers.

Structures trapped more light and sharpened local heating, raising output voltage, but heat also had farther to travel, damping response speed. A pitch of 6.7 micrometers balanced the trade-off best. At 950 nanometers the device reached a voltage sensitivity of 0.14 millivolts per watt, guiding room-temperature detector design.
pmc-13303216:
A stacked learning model using routine blood tests can flag hidden spread of thyroid cancer, Li Zhou and colleagues report in a 2026 study of 1,697 patients with papillary thyroid cancer. Spread to central neck lymph nodes, found in 30.4 percent, is hard to spot on scans before surgery. The team fed twenty-nine chosen features, mixing clinical facts with ratios from standard blood counts, into eight competing models.

The stacked model scored near perfect in training and stayed strong in testing, far ahead of plain logistic regression. Tumor size mattered most, then a lymphocyte-monocyte ratio, age, VEGF, and an immune-inflammation index. The authors pitch the model, whose reasoning can be inspected, as an aid for planning neck surgery.
pmc-13303616:
Mohammed Amjed Alsaegh and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of bent needle tips during numbing injections in the upper jaw. Tip damage can affect how safe and effective dental anesthesia is, yet rates by injection route were unclear.

A total of 180 needles were studied, half used in patients and half kept as controls. Used needles covered cheek-side, palate-side, and combined approaches. Under a strong microscope, more than half of used needles showed tip bending, compared with almost none of the controls. Rates were similar for students and interns and across approaches, while feeling bone contact differed by route.
pmc-13303716:
Bin Li and colleagues use a 2026 modeling study to explain how silicon shapes carry electric current in aluminum-silicon alloys. These light alloys serve cars and communications gear, but tangled silicon features make cause and effect hard to separate.

Cast alloys with three silicon levels were cooled at varied rates and imaged by electron microscopy. A principal component regression sorted overlapping silicon traits into two main drivers. Silicon amount set the baseline by shortening electron paths, while shape mattered most within one alloy mix. Longer, flatter silicon forced electrons into detours and lowered conductivity, guiding design of motor housings.
pmc-13304116:
Falk Gerrik Verhees and colleagues present clickBrick, a 2026 prompt-building method that helps language models read psychiatric records. Well-built prompts can raise model accuracy on clinical tasks, but gains in mental health records were untested.

Charts for 100 patients were scored by experts on 12 cross-diagnosis mental state features, then two local models tried the same task with prompts of growing structure. Balanced accuracy ranged widely across features, and structured prompts lifted the most responsive model a great deal. Features pulled with the best prompts also predicted final diagnoses in a past group of 1,692 patients.
pmc-13304216:
Jia Chyi Tay and colleagues report a 2026 surgical case where two rare hernia types and a hidden lymphoma met in one patient. A 62-year-old man carried a giant groin hernia plus a deep belly mass that scans could not clearly explain.

During surgery the hernia sac held the appendix and a Meckel's pouch, confirming both an Amyand and a Littre hernia at once. A separate deep mass was removed as well. Tissue testing showed a cyst with dead tissue and, unexpectedly, mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma in a lymph node. Careful tissue checks after complex hernia surgery can reveal major hidden disease.
pmc-13304516:
Ivie Maneschy and co-authors trace how eating behavior forms from infancy through the teen years in a 2026 narrative review. Habits set early can steer diet quality and chronic disease risk for decades.

Long-term studies, trials, and policy reviews were favored in the synthesis. Breastfeeding, gentle first-food steps, and calm self-guided parenting tied to better hunger awareness and healthier food likes. Forceful feeding, early rich-tasting foods, and marketing pushed impulse eating instead. Stressed or food-short homes raised teen emotional eating risk. Parent help, school lessons, marketing limits, and healthier food settings are urged together.
pmc-13305316:
Xueyin Fei and co-authors test combined aerobic and strength training in young adults with obesity in a 2026 study. Some people with obesity stay metabolically healthy while others do not, and exercise may move people between those states.

Eighty-four young adults were classed as metabolically healthy or unhealthy at entry, then all trained under supervision for eight weeks. Body measures, fitness, and heart-risk markers improved across the group, and some unhealthy participants shifted to the healthy class. Chemical profiling of blood found exercise-linked shifts in building blocks tied to arginine and histidine pathways in both followed groups.
pmc-13305916:
Kutlwano Moeketsi asked whether voluntary drinking in young rats shifts immune signalling balance in a 2026 animal study. Twenty male Sprague-Dawley rats aged 25 days were split evenly, with one group choosing alcohol for 30 days.

Blood taken at the end showed higher white cell and lymphocyte counts in drinkers, yet lower platelet counts in the reported results. Several signalling proteins fell, including interleukin-2 and interferon-gamma from one helper family and interleukin-5, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 from the other. The authors conclude that drinking did not push the response toward one helper pattern alone.
pmc-13307416:
Yiming Cui and co-authors write a 2026 letter about a study that used microbes in saliva, stomach fluid, and stomach lining to detect stomach cancer. That study paired machine learning with samples from three sites and built models that scored well in training and in outside data sets.

The letter praises the joint oral and stomach view, then raises two main gaps for future work. All who took part shared one ethnic group and a like diet, so tests in more varied groups are needed to check broad use. The gene based hints about what the microbes do also need direct proof through deeper lab methods before clinical use.
pmc-13307616:
Masoumeh Taghizadeh and co-authors run in 2026 a double blind trial of ostrich oil for chronic anal fissure, a lasting tear that causes sharp pain. A total of 150 patients were split at random between glyceryl trinitrate ointment alone and the same ointment mixed with ostrich oil.

Pain scores fell more in the oil group at every check after care began in the trial. Early healing and bleeding looked alike, yet at two and four months the oil group had fewer severe ulcers, less bleeding, and fewer returns of the tear. Easy home use and a good safety record make the oil a plausible add on for ongoing care.
pmc-13309016:
Ashley L Taylor and Tyler N Starr map in 2026 how nearly every single letter change alters the spike grip part of the fresh SARS-CoV-2 variant KP.3.1.1 and a second new variant. Their yeast display scans weighed fold shape and grip on the human ACE2 entry point for each change in turn.

Three sites, 455, 456, and 493 in the chain, kept shifting which letters they would bear as variants rolled on. Those hot spots have flipped again and again since early Omicron, and they still show no settled pick in the new maps. One change, H505W, may favour a shut spike shape that hides from antibodies. Watch lists must track joint effects, not lone changes.
pmc-13309616:
Hymavathi Reddy Vari and colleagues look for a controlled cell-death route in Down syndrome brains in a 2026 study. The route, called necroptosis, is tied to neuron loss in Alzheimer disease. Down syndrome also brings neuron loss, but the routes behind it stay unclear.

Brain tissue from people with the condition, and from a mouse model of it, was checked for necroptosis markers, covering two kinases, an executor protein, and a long RNA. Young model mice showed no gap from normal mice, while old model mice showed clearly higher marker levels. Post-mortem human brains showed the same rise. The authors say this death route deserves study as a drug target in Down syndrome.
pmc-13311016:
Frank Phasha and co-authors test seed soaking tricks on a leafy medicinal plant in a 2026 early study. Soaking seeds in water, a growth chemical, a plastic polymer, or iron salt can prime later plant chemistry. The team asked which prime lifts helpful compounds and germ killing power in Corchorus trilocularis leaves.

Leaf extracts were checked at young and flowering stages. Both prime type and stage shaped compound levels, with flowering leaves richer overall. Iron salt priming gave the largest gains in flavonoids, phenolics, and tannins. Polymer primed plants killed Staphylococcus aureus best. No prime worked at the young stage or against a hardier germ.
pmc-13311116:
Ziang Li and colleagues build a simple ratio score for death risk in septic shock in a 2026 study. Lactate alone can understate risk when its rise is modest, so lactate was paired with diastolic pressure into one ratio. Past records from two intensive care groups were used to build and test the score.

The build group held 320 patients and the test group held 962 patients from a large database. Death at 28 days neared three in ten in both groups. The ratio sorted risk in both groups and beat lactate alone by a small margin. Gains in the gray zone were modest, so the score should aid, not replace, lactate.
pmc-13311216:
Mamadou Dioulde Balde and co-authors offer a 2026 before-and-after study from Guinea on staff training to cut mistreatment of women in gynecology and obstetrics care. Client reports were used to judge change.

Women were asked about their care before and after providers were trained, and the results were adjusted for other factors. The risk of violence or mistreatment fell by 43 percent in gynecology and 44 percent in obstetrics after training. Blows and harsh words both dropped by roughly a quarter to a third. The team argues that steady staff training plus community outreach can make maternity care safer.
pmc-13311616:
Merita Neziraj, Christine Kumlien, and Malin Axelsson describe a 2026 pilot trial of a staff learning program in Swedish nursing homes. The STAIR OF KNOWLEDGE program targets pressure ulcers, malnutrition, poor mouth health, and falls.

Eight nursing homes joined the pilot, with four assigned to the program and four to comparison care. Registry data covered 309 residents aged 65 to 102. The pilot tests whether homes can be recruited, assigned, and kept in a trial, and which outcome measure suits a full trial. The staged approach follows national guidance for building complex care programs step by step.
pmc-13311816:
Revathy Sampath-Kumar and co-authors, in 2026, analyze a two-country registry study on how heart pumping strength changes after a heart attack treated with artery opening. The path of recovery, not just one reading, is the focus.

The study covered 13,439 patients in Swedish and San Diego registries from 2007 to 2022 who had repeat heart scans. Groups with always-low, recovered, always-kept, and newly-dropped pumping strength were compared over six years. Heart failure hospital stays ran highest in the always-low group, at 40.0 percent in this cohort. Even recovered patients kept triple the risk of the always-kept group, urging lasting follow-up.
pmc-13311916:
Wen Huang and colleagues present a 2026 study building a CT scan model to predict three-year disease worsening in lung cancer patients on anti-PD-1 therapy. Scan texture features, called radiomics, supply the raw material.

The study drew 173 patients with non-small-cell lung cancer on such therapy. Features from target tumors joined clinical traits in the model. COPD and tumor stage stood out among clinical predictors. The combined model scored accuracy values of 0.802 in training and 0.836 in testing in this study. A chart form of the model beat single-source versions on clinical benefit measures.
pmc-13312016:
David S Kennedy and co-authors examine, in a 2026 article, what physical therapists who treat people with persistent pain see as their main challenges and priorities. Persistent pain is a heavy burden in Australia, where its cost was estimated at $80 billion in 2018, topping heart disease, cancer, and diabetes combined.

The authors argue that pain care needs a joined-up approach that runs from the single patient to society as a whole. Therapists need better training and mentoring to deliver care that takes mental health into account, and funding models need to give them enough time and resources with each patient. Rather than leaving change to individual clinics, the profession itself should push for reform in training, resources, and payment.
pmc-13312116:
Khloud Adel Mohamed Elshaitany and colleagues report a 2026 trial testing two feed supplements against drug-induced immune suppression in broiler chickens. Intensive poultry production suffers when birds' immune systems are weakened, so the team examined Spirulina platensis algae and beta-glucan as diet additions.

Two hundred forty Sasso chicks were divided into six groups, including a healthy control, a group given the immune-suppressing drug cyclophosphamide, and groups receiving each supplement either before or after the drug. Cyclophosphamide cut growth, shrank lymphoid organs, and raised oxidative stress. Both supplements softened these harms, restoring growth, antioxidant defenses, and lymphoid tissue structure, with preventive use showing the stronger effect. The authors credit shifts in oxidation and inflammation pathways for the protection.
pmc-13312816:
Andrew R. LeBlanc and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study simplifying the aogacillins, natural products that make aminoglycoside antibiotics work far better against resistant bacteria. The original pair of compounds, isolated from a fungus, showed striking synergy, but their complexity slowed study, so the team set out to reach working analogs in just a few steps.

Their shortened routes delivered analogs in three to four steps. Testing showed the molecules permanently trap cysteine nucleophiles at a reactive enone warhead, the likely source of their power. The same warhead also leaves them open to unwanted cycloaddition side reactions. The authors therefore built redesigned analogs that quiet that side reactivity while keeping the sensitizing effect. The tuned compounds made MRSA respond to aminoglycosides at concentrations below the drugs' usual minimum inhibitory levels.
pmc-13314916:
Carolin Kurz and colleagues run two blood test platforms head to head in Alzheimer disease, in their 2026 study. Blood markers are fast joining clinic and research use for this disease, yet results from unlike machines may not swap cleanly.

The team tested 86 patients with the disease and 56 healthy controls, as counted in the report, on both Roche and Fujirebio systems. Markers included two forms of phosphorylated tau, at spots 217 and 181, and two amyloid fragments, as listed in the report. They checked how well the machines agreed and which marker held up best against clinical state. A clear winner on agreement would let clinics trust blood tests more and mix data across sites with less fear of drift.
pmc-13315116:
Zhipeng Liu and colleagues dissect why older Haimen goats marble better, in a study appearing in 2026. Fat threaded through muscle marks high-grade meat with richer taste and nutrition, and its build with age in this breed was not mapped.

The team tracked meat traits in goats slaughtered at set ages, then split high-fat and low-fat meat for lipid and amino acid profiling. Marbling grew in a straight line with age, as the authors report. High-fat meat held more of each fat class and more of the key and flavor amino acids. Protein scans flagged control genes such as ECI1, HADH, and ACO2, named in the report, with two energy hubs at the core of fat handling. The maps can guide feeding and slaughter timing for premium goat meat.
pmc-13316216:
Seyedeh Zalfa Modarresi and co-authors report in 2026 the first known child case of xanthomatous pleuritis, a rare benign inflammation where fat-filled macrophages gather in the pleura. Only three adult cases had been described worldwide, tied to long pleural inflammation or infection.

Their patient was a 3.5-year-old girl with repeated pneumonia, chronic breathing symptoms, and failure to thrive. Scans showed an enlarged heart, nodules under the pleura, patchy consolidation, mild pleural thickening, and trapped fluid. A guided biopsy of a pleural nodule found many foamy macrophages and scattered giant cells, with no granuloma or cancer.
pmc-13316616:
Isabella Vu and co-authors describe a 2026 imaging case of an 89-year-old woman with heavy vaginal bleeding caused by lymphoma of the cervix that grew into the womb body. Cervical lymphoma is rare and can look exactly like the far more common cervical cancer on scans.

Combined CT, MRI, and PET imaging showed a large, active cervical mass with spread to glands in the pelvis, chest, and above the collarbone. Certain MRI signs, such as a smooth outer surface and a preserved canal, pointed toward lymphoma over cancer. Tissue proof mattered, since treatment differs sharply. Gentle radiation stopped the bleeding, then a reduced chemotherapy mix brought a strong response despite her age and frailty.
pmc-13316816:
Md Saleh Uddin and co-authors adapted, in a 2026 study, the Mental Health Literacy Scale into Bangla for use in Bangladesh. No checked tool existed there to gauge how well people understand mental illness and its care. Their test group was undergraduate nursing students.

Translation, back-translation, expert review, and pretesting shaped 35 items across illness knowledge, health promotion, help seeking, and stigma. Face-to-face surveys in three teaching hospitals gathered 224 students, whose average score was 19.78 out of 35 in the reported tally. Factor checks supported four themes and scoring consistency was acceptable, though the sample was too small for a final structural test. Wider validation is the next step.
pmc-13319516:
Jingyi Zhu and co-authors set safe light limits for a sound based microscope in a 2026 study of blood oxygen mapping. The tool can map oxygen in tiny vessels in the brain and other organs with fine detail. Fast scans fire many light pulses on one spot, and heat can build up and skew the oxygen readout even when total power looks safe.

Tests in live mice and in a blood model were paired with math to find the top safe dose for true readings. The safe cap fell as pulse count rose, and a short rule links the two for two common light colors. Long scans held steady under the rule. Labs can use the cap to pick scan settings that keep readings true.
pmc-13319716:
Tareq Al-Ahdal and co-authors set out a step by step method in a 2026 protocol for linking climate strain to dark mood in social media posts. Heat, storms, and other climate shocks track with worse mental well being at group level, yet shared workflows to test that link are scarce. Their plan joins place tagged posts with weather and health data across Europe.

Posts from the X platform are cleaned, then scored for negative feeling with a word count tool that works across languages. Climate and health signs are merged by place and time, and a math model that respects both space and time weighs the links. Care steps for privacy and data rights are built into the plan for reuse by other teams.
pmc-13319916:
Rezhat Abbas and co-authors gather all past case reports on a very rare birth condition in a 2026 review of Hallermann-Streiff syndrome. The condition shapes the face and skull, clouds the eyes, thins the hair, and shrinks the lower jaw, which can also block the airway. No past review had weighed airway, eye, and face traits together, so the team swept four databases for cases.

Fifteen studies with 32 cases in total met the rules. Airway trouble showed in more than half the cases, at times severe enough to need a neck breathing tube. Eye faults were common, with birth cataracts in about three in four cases and a small jaw in most. Care took many specialists at once, and most cases improved in part.
pmc-13320116:
Lan Yang and co-authors pool trials of two breathing aids for adults whose lungs fail to clear carbon dioxide in a 2026 review. A high flow nose tube gives warm moist oxygen at speed, while a tight mask system pushes air in with each breath. Which aid saves more lives or spares more tubes down the throat was still unsettled.

The nose tube cut hospital and intensive care stays by near a day, cut sore skin on the nose by a wide margin, and felt more comfortable to wear. Larger trials across wider groups are still called for.
pmc-13320316:
Marieta Mateva-Mladenova and co-authors count radiation load from repeat scans in hospital COVID care in a 2026 records study. Chest scans guided care for sick lung patients, yet each scan adds dose and stacked scans in one stay can reach high totals. Whether that load matters was the question for a group scanned again and again.

Records covered 69 adults who each had three or more scans in one stay, totaling 296 scans in all. Median total dose sat near fifty units on the scale used, and near half the group passed that mark while near a quarter passed double it. Dose tracked more with the count of scan phases than with scan count alone. The team urges firm grounds for each repeat scan and leaner phase counts.
pmc-13320416:
Hayato Tada and co-authors check whether a strong cholesterol drug drains a key cell fuel in a 2026 small study of inherited high cholesterol. Muscle aches on statin drugs have been blamed in part on low levels of that fuel, which statins can cut. A newer shot drug that blocks a cholesterol control protein is used when statins fail or hurt, yet its effect on the fuel was unknown.

Bad cholesterol fell by about half in the counts reported, and a second harmful fat fell too, while fuel levels held flat. Fuel shifts also showed no tie to fat drops. pmc-13320816:
Steven D Hicks and colleagues test whether spit samples can flag severe COVID illness in children in a 2026 study. Small RNA pieces in saliva, called miRNAs, shift with infection, but their value for predicting severe disease in children was unknown. The team followed children with SARS-CoV-2 infection at two United States children's hospitals.

Saliva from 395 children, of whom 105 became severely ill, was tested for three chosen miRNAs. Children whose illness turned severe showed lower amounts of one piece, miR-296-5p, with a fold difference of 0.361 reported in the study. After checks for age, health, and symptoms, higher levels still meant lower odds of severe illness. The signal could aid early triage if larger studies confirm it.
pmc-13321316:
Eleonora Dolcher and colleagues study how iron based cancer drug candidates break down in water in a 2026 chemistry report. The diiron aminocarbyne complexes act inside cells by falling apart and releasing reactive iron. The team made water soluble nitrate salts on a gram scale and tracked decay in water and cell medium at body temperature.

Breakdown followed steady zero-order kinetics at higher strengths over 72 hours, partly forming simple amines and cyclopentadiene. Slow brown solids proved to be iron(III) oxyhydroxide materials with minor organic parts. Tests of oxygen, light, heat, and acidity clarified the path, and a trapping agent caught a mid-step form. Computer models mapped the full loss of the metal framework.
pmc-13322816:
Vladislavs Sokaļskis leads a Latvian hospital study, published in 2026, on blood-thinning drugs and stroke linked to atrial fibrillation. The team reviewed 2,610 people with cardioembolic stroke admitted to two large university hospitals between January 2022 and December 2024.

The largest share, described as 43.4 percent of the group, knew they had atrial fibrillation but were not taking anticoagulant drugs before the stroke. In a matched comparison of 352 people per group, those already taking direct oral anticoagulants arrived with milder strokes on the NIHSS scale. They also had larger left atria. The authors link missed treatment to a large part of this stroke burden.
pmc-13323016:
Yazed Alruthia leads a survey of caregivers of people with Duchenne muscular dystrophy in Saudi Arabia, published in 2026, on emotional and financial strain. Forty informal caregivers, mostly fathers with a mean age near 42 years, answered a telephone survey through a Riyadh neurology clinic over one year.

Validated Arabic tools measured out-of-pocket costs, depression, anxiety and quality of life. Most families lacked private insurance, and mean yearly out-of-pocket spending reached about US dollars 12,400 per family in their figures, led by medicines and medical travel. The authors call for stronger financial and mental health support for these caregivers, whose burden is rarely counted in Saudi data.
pmc-13323816:
Yingying Fang and co-authors run a first-in-human trial of an anti-C5a antibody called STSA-1002, in a 2026 phase I study in healthy adults in China. C5a drives inflammation in virus-linked acute respiratory distress, and the antibody blocks C5a-triggered oxygen radical release in lab tests.

Side effects were frequent in both arms, mostly mild, with a few moderate drug-linked events such as lowered white cell counts and raised liver enzymes. Blood levels rose roughly in step with dose, and free C5a fell below detection after the first dose for weeks. Anti-drug antibodies were also tracked for safety planning.
pmc-13324316:
Moti Zwilling and co-authors survey digital media habits during wartime among Israeli adults, in a 2026 cross-sectional study from early January 2024. Their sample held 512 adults aged 18 to 65 years, who rated how ten media activities had grown since the war began.

Cluster analysis split respondents into a low engagement group of about a quarter and a high engagement group of about three quarters. The high group reported clearly higher stress on standard scales, while well-being and resilience were scored with short validated tools. Factor work separated active, passive and institutional media use. Path models then linked those patterns to stress and resilience, guiding advice on healthy media diets in conflict.
pmc-13325316:
Sophia Ehrström and colleagues hunt risk factors for opioid prescriptions after benign hysterectomy in a 2026 Swedish register study. Cutting needless opioid exposure matters, yet dispensing has kept rising.

The cohort covered 50,601 hysterectomies with linked drug and patient records. Older age lowered risk, as did surgery for prolapse. Pre-surgery use of calming psycholeptic drugs raised risk most among patient traits, with an adjusted risk ratio of 1.65 for dispensing. Endometriosis, open surgery, and complications also raised risk. Region towered over all, with Stockholm patients at more than double the risk of others. Dispensing grew 8 percent a year from 2005 to 2022 despite gentler surgical methods.
pmc-13327516:
Gen Xu and co-authors uncover a control switch for enzyme production in the fungus Trichoderma reesei in a 2026 study. The fungus makes cellulase enzymes prized by industry, but a repressor named Cre1 blocks their genes when easy carbon is around. How that block lifts when cellulose appears was largely unknown.

When marking at one site, K361, failed, Cre1 clung to enzyme gene promoters and shut out the activator Xyr1, even under inducing conditions. Restoring the mark freed the promoters, showing how protein tagging times enzyme output in industrial fungi.
pmc-13329716:
Hosouk Joung and Hyunju Liu test a SUMO-blocking drug on womb muscle cancer cells in a 2026 study. Uterine leiomyosarcoma is fast-growing with few treatment options. The drug TAK-981, also called subasumstat, blocks enzymes that attach SUMO tags to proteins and has shown action in other cancers.

It also raised harmful oxygen species and weakened cell power units. Death was partly tied to those species. SUMO tagging fell and death markers rose, while self-eating markers stayed flat.
pmc-13330516:
Ying Zhang and colleagues build a method to count living probiotic bacteria in animal feed in a 2026 study. Enterococcus faecium loses viability during pelleting, which weakens its benefit. Their method pairs a dye that enters dead cells with gene counting, so only living cells register.

Checks showed high accuracy and no cross-reaction with seven feed bacteria in the reported validation. Simulated gut fluid freed most cells from coatings for testing. During making, survival fell as conditioning heat rose from 65 to 85 degrees, from 72.4 percent to 12.2 percent in the overall counts given. Bacteria coated before processing survived best at every step. The method can guide coating choices.
pmc-13330716:
Jingting Liu and colleagues review links between nerves and immunity in cancer in a 2026 article. Tumours sit inside host networks, not apart from them, and nerve signals can shape immune cell action in the tumour setting. Peripheral, central, and gut nerve routes all take part in that cross-talk.

Messengers covered include neurotransmitters, cytokines, and nerve growth factors. The review sorts pathways by which nerves tune tumour immunity, then turns to care ideas: blocking neural inputs, pairing nerve-immune tuning with immunotherapy, and gene-control effects on the shared setting. Gaps and next steps are mapped. Harnessing the axis could open fresh cancer care routes, the authors argue.
pmc-13332116:
Huijun Guo and colleagues review how retuning the metabolism of macrophages, the immune cells that drive heart disease inflammation, could become a treatment strategy, in a 2026 survey. Heart and vessel diseases remain the top global killer, largely through chronic inflammation and poor repair after injury.

Macrophages that burn sugar quickly tend to fan inflammation, while those relying on oxygen-based energy and fat burning tend to calm it and repair tissue. Signals such as mTOR, NF-κB, PPAR-γ, and NRF2 steer these states, and chemical marks on DNA can lock them in as a kind of memory. The review weighs drugs and gene approaches against these switches, with special weight on nanoparticle carriers that deliver treatment precisely to macrophages. The authors frame the approach as a route to settle plaque inflammation, limit heart damage, and support repair.
pmc-13332816:
Gustavo Oliveira Campos and co-authors put five reciprocating root canal file systems under a multimethod laboratory examination in 2026. The nickel-titanium instruments share similar cross-section shapes, letting the team separate how much of their behavior comes from geometry and how much from metal treatment.

Reciproc Blue, ProDesign R, V File, V+ File, and Univy One were checked by microscopy, elemental analysis, heat scanning, X-ray diffraction, bending, and twisting tests. Most files were dominated by the R-phase crystal form, while Univy One mixed martensite with R-phase. ProDesign R bent most easily, whereas Reciproc Blue and V File resisted twisting best. Wider cross-sections raised stiffness, but metal phase also shaped flexibility, with martensite-rich files bending more freely. The authors caution that the tests were static and did not include the repeated flexing that tires files in real canals.
pmc-13333316:
Laura Carrera-Faja and colleagues checked migrating birds in northeastern Spain for hitchhiking ticks that carry Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus, in a 2026 field study. The tick Hyalomma rufipes rides birds from Africa into Europe and could settle in the warming south.
