Only 0.5 percent carried ticks, but 77 percent of those ticks were H. rufipes, and every tick tested negative for the virus. Birds that feed on the ground or in shrubs, and those wintering in open country or wetlands, were most likely to carry the tick. Gene reads from 88 ticks showed wide diversity with no single origin pattern, pointing mostly to Central-West Africa. A few birds carried genetically distinct ticks at the same time, which could let pathogens swap between them. The authors urge continued watch on this entry route.
pmc-13333416:
Andreas Holstein and co-authors report a diagnosis made under pressure in a 2026 case report: a rare inherited fat-loss disorder unmasked by pregnancy. Familial partial lipodystrophy strips fat from some body regions while driving metabolic trouble, and pregnancy with it is high risk, little documented.

At 18 weeks pregnant, the woman arrived with extreme blood triglycerides complicated by pancreas inflammation. Her history held young-onset diabetes, high blood pressure, polycystic ovary syndrome, high triglycerides, and the telltale missing fat over her buttocks and legs. Gene panel testing found a new variant in the PPARG gene, c.380A>C, judged likely disease-causing and fitting type 3 of the disorder, plus a second uncertain variant in ABCC8. Insulin therapy with metformin and omega-3 fatty acids cut her triglycerides sharply, normalized her glucose through delivery, and prevented pancreas attacks. The authors stress early recognition and team-based metabolic control in such pregnancies.
pmc-13333516:
Xingyin Yang and co-authors review rosacea treatments in 2026 through the lens of nerves, blood vessels, and immunity. The chronic facial condition, with its flushing, redness, bumps, and eye symptoms, often brings anxiety and poor sleep. The reviewers argue its engine is an over-activated neuro-vascular-immune triad that creams partly reach.

The review walks through drug families aimed at each leg of the triad. These include GABA derivatives and antidepressants to quiet nerve signalling, anti-CGRP agents borrowed from migraine care, beta-blockers to tame flushing, and botulinum toxin injections. It also covers neuromodulation such as vagus nerve stimulation and magnetic brain stimulation. For each it sets out the rationale, the evidence, and the gaps. The recurring weakness is proof: large randomized trials are scarce and nobody knows the best doses or durations. The authors call for stronger basic work, combinations, and personalized plans for long-term control.
pmc-13333716:
Preeta Rajandran and co-authors asked what shapes daily television time in young children with and without autism in a 2026 questionnaire study. Caregivers of 225 children aged 3 to 6, including 65 with autism, reported home conditions and screen habits.

Regression analysis found that time on other electronic devices and the availability of indoor play space were the clearest factors tied to television time. Family income level and holiday family interaction showed weaker, marginal links. Children with autism watched slightly less television than typically developing peers, at 1.88 hours against 2.03 hours per day on average. More holiday family interaction went with less viewing in the autism group, which supports guidance to limit early screen exposure.
pmc-13334316:
Grace Y. Wang, Jian-Ming Hao, and Joe G. Chen reviewed how artificial intelligence strains pharmaceutical patent law in a 2026 legal analysis. AI now speeds drug design and personalizes medicine, but patent systems built for human inventors must decide who, if anyone, invents AI-generated output.

The review centers on inventorship, the issue that most directly threatens drug patents. In the United States, the Supreme Court's March 2026 denial of review in Thaler v. Perlmutter settled whether an AI can count as an inventor under US law. The authors set that outcome beside approaches in Germany and China, drawing targeted lessons rather than urging wholesale reform. Their guidance aims at companies and counsel trying to protect AI-assisted drug discoveries across jurisdictions.
pmc-13335116:
Yiran Wang and co-authors uncovered a storage role for the transcription factor TEAD1 in cancer cells in a 2026 molecular study. TEAD1, a Hippo pathway factor, is usually discussed as a gene switch, but in kidney cancer cells it also gathers into droplets that stay silent.

Using high-resolution imaging, ChIP sequencing, RNA sequencing, and proximity proteomics in patient-derived renal cell carcinoma cells, the team showed TEAD1 forms micrometer-sized condensates on pericentromeric heterochromatin. Specific MCAT motifs cluster there and seed the droplets through TEAD1's DNA-binding domain. These condensates activate nothing; they warehouse surplus TEAD1. Breaking them up raised expression of YAP and TEAD target genes. Elsewhere in the genome TEAD1 behaved normally, joining active transcription, which makes the storage depots a distinct regulatory trick.
pmc-13336416:
Hao Yu and co-authors combined capture and destruction to eliminate short-chain PFAS from water in a 2026 environmental engineering study. These smaller forever chemicals move fast and resist the adsorption and breakdown methods that work, partially, on their longer cousins.

Their sorbent coats carbon felt with a polypyrrole nanostructure tuned at the interface. It grabbed short-chain PFAS and the replacement chemical GenX within 300 seconds, with capacities of 283.2 to 572.1 milligrams per gram in the reported range, beating granular activated carbon more than twenty-fold. Column tests quintupled breakthrough volume past 4,000 bed volumes. Solvent washing regenerated the felt, and a copper-mediated light-driven step then fully defluorinated the concentrated PFAS in the wash liquid, closing the loop the title promises.
pmc-13336916:
Dominika Wilczok and colleagues borrow drug discovery lessons for designing better freezing protectants in a 2026 perspective. Cryopreservation stores cells, tissues, and someday organs at extreme cold for banking, fertility care, and transplants. Protective agents prevent ice damage but turn toxic at the high doses deep freezing needs.

The authors argue protectant design should copy that multiparameter balancing act, judging candidates on a broad profile from the start. Systematic design could yield safer agents for ever more delicate tissues and whole organs.
pmc-13337416:
Afsona Parveen and co-authors review how the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus causes disease in a 2026 article. This common mold threatens people with weak immunity or chronic lung disease, causing allergy, chronic lung infection, or invasive spread. The review sets out to gather molecular mechanisms, better diagnostics, and current therapies in one place.

Virulence factors let the fungus harm airway cells, dodge immunity, and thrive at temperatures up to 50 °C while releasing tissue-damaging toxins. Biofilms, slimy cell communities, shelter infections and raise drug resistance. The authors survey new antifungals, personalized care, prevention through environmental control, and vaccine hopes for high-risk groups. Understanding host-fungus interplay is cast as the route to better outcomes.
pmc-13337816:
Hai-Hong Lin and a large team compare safety profiles for three related heart and kidney drugs in a 2026 analysis. Spironolactone, eplerenone, and finerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor and anchor modern care. No large head-to-head safety comparison from real-world reports had been done.

Spironolactone showed the widest harm pattern, including hormone-related effects, while eplerenone centered on heart and organ failure signals. Finerenone stayed narrowest, mostly kidney and metabolic issues. High potassium appeared for all three drugs.
pmc-13339816:

pmc-13341416:

pmc-13341616:
Extracellular vesicles as windows into rare brain diseases are reviewed by Nathan D. Phan and colleagues in a 2026 paper. Rare neurological diseases are hard to study because few patients exist, symptoms vary widely, and mechanisms stay tangled, delaying both diagnosis and treatment.

Source differences and patchy validation still limit clinical use.
pmc-13341816:
Weights training eases stiff arteries in at-risk adults, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis by Yanhao Wang and colleagues. For patients often steered only toward cardio, the results put strength work on the vascular prescription pad.
pmc-13342416:

pmc-13342616:

pmc-13342816:

The original article has been updated to match the corrected figures.
pmc-13343316:

pmc-13347616:

Genes and environment must be read together here.
pmc-13349916:

pmc-13351916:

pmc-13353216:

pmc-13354016:

pmc-13355216:

pmc-13355916:

pmc-13356716:

The authors call for randomized trials to confirm the gains.
pmc-13356816:
Dhruvi R Patel and co-authors surveyed general dental practitioners in 2026 on how well they grasp the role of mental factors in gum disease. The authors urge adding behavioral science and mental screening skills to dental training.
pmc-13358516:

Tests on spinal fluid grew a germ called Globicatella sanguinis, which labs seldom see and can easily mistake for a more common germ.

It warns labs and doctors that this rare germ can cause severe infection in infants and can hide behind routine tests.
pmc-13358816:

pmc-13359516:

Radiation shares several of these effects, such as hampering DNA repair. Mapping the overlap could guide smart pairings of the fields with radiation, immune drugs, and targeted drugs.
pmc-13360316:

A bioreactor is a tank system that feeds plant cells or roots under clean, set conditions. The review covers the main tank types and how each one works.

Their guide aims to help growers produce steady, high-grade plant material without draining wild stocks. It also points to where the field may head next, toward greener large-scale production.
pmc-13362616:
Jian Liu and colleagues present a 2026 case study of a smart road grid that both strengthens asphalt and senses strain while the road is built. The grid is a woven mesh with fiber optic sensors knitted in, laid to stop cracks from spreading up through new pavement. Lab pull tests checked the sensors, and crews then tracked the grid through each paving stage on a real road job.

The weaving left the sensors intact, and their readings tracked grid strain in a clean, straight-line match. Big strain came during the lower layer work, and machines pressed about 22 centimeters deep. The reinforced stretch sagged about two fifths less under load than plain road. The trial supports grids that report road health from day one.
pmc-13362916:
Jisun Paik and colleagues present a 2026 mouse study of a drug that blocks ALDH1A1, an enzyme that makes retinoic acid, a signal tied to body weight. Mice that lack the enzyme resist diet-driven obesity, and the drug, called N42, had already curbed weight gain in males. This study asked whether it works the same way in females, using two feeding trials with high-fat and moderate-fat diets.

N42 curbed weight gain in females kept on the high-fat diet, matching the male results. When obese females switched to a leaner diet, the diet alone drove strong weight loss and the drug added nothing more. The authors suggest the drug's role may be in preventing gain rather than speeding loss once calories drop.
pmc-13363416:
Q R D S Moreira and colleagues present a 2026 theoretical physics study of a quantum system where a particle's mass changes with its position. The system sits inside a fractal-style trap that mimics a semiconductor well. Using a fractal momentum operator and a standard ordering rule, they solved for the exact energy levels and wave shapes. They then tracked how three dials steer the states: the fractal index, the lattice scale, and the trap strength.

Information measures told the same story from another side. Entropy and Fisher information shifted in step as the states spread or tightened, and the checks against known uncertainty rules passed. The team also derived exact heat behavior, from free energy to specific heat. The closed-form results give a reference for quantum dots and other tiny confined systems.
pmc-13364016:
Nikolay Kiktev and colleagues present a 2026 review on precision livestock farming, where sensors and machine learning watch feed, health, and behavior on farms. One thread covers feed plants: camera and neural checks on vitamin and mineral premix quality, dosing, and mixing evenness. A second covers animals in the barn, with vision systems that track lying, feeding, and aggression, plus tags and leg sensors that pinpoint position and spot lameness or play.

A third thread brings learning models to veterinary diagnosis, reading X-rays, ultrasound, and MRI for heart, cancer, and bone problems in farm and pet animals, and flagging disease early. The authors organize this fast field into a clear map and stress non-destructive, on-line quality control.
pmc-13365116:
Jiu-Yan Zhao and co-workers read in 2026 the gene range of 144 pea lines drawn from many lands, a core set kept for breed use. Pea gives rich plant protein, yet its gene pool maps were thin. The team reads short repeat marks in the DNA to split the set by kin.

Marks show rich range in the set, with most split held in each group, not between them. Two big kin groups stand out, with a third of lines of mixed blood. Maps and tree charts match that split. Breeders can pick cross pairs and guard rare lines from this base.
pmc-13366216:
Ming Li and co-workers run in 2026 a blind test of two big chat tools on breast cancer care plans, next to past plans by top cancer docs. They use charts of 213 patients, from stage one to four, all stripped of names. Three blind pros grade each plan for right fit and stead.

Both tools beat the past doc plans on grades and vary less. One tool tops the grades with a near full score. Still, tool and doc plans drift far part as stage climbs, most at stage four. The tools may aid care talks, but late stage calls stay a pro job.
pmc-13373516:
Weam Mohammed Ahmed Mohammed and co-authors summed up smart computer forecasts of dialysis access faults in a 2026 review. The access point, a joined artery and vein in the arm, is the top choice for blood cleaning. It often blocks, thins, or fails, which cuts care short.

The team searched four data banks for peer-read work from 2021 to 2025 in English. Each study taught a computer to flag who would have access trouble. Old score ways miss the web of causes, the team notes. Smart tools may flag risk in time for a fix, but proof is still young and needs checks in real clinics.
pmc-13374016:
Dávid Mester and Mihály Kállay built a fast way to sum electron loss costs in large molecules in a 2026 study. Such sums help read photo tests and build new stuff, but they grow slow and dear as molecules grow. Their way cuts the work to small zones picked by the sum itself.

The zones shape on their own, with no hand tuning for each case. Tests on three kin sums found slips of just a few parts in a hundred of a unit. At the same time the hard steps ran much faster. The black-box style means bench staff can use it with no deep craft in the math.
pmc-13375416:
Zhou and colleagues connect a blood microRNA, miR-342-3p, to smoking-related kidney cancer and test small molecules that reverse its tumor-promoting effect, in 2026 oncology research. Smoking is a major risk factor for clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the commonest kidney cancer. The team measured two microRNAs in tumors and blood of patients and healthy controls. They then traced the molecule's target genes and challenged cancer cells with a cocktail of neurogenic small molecules, compounds used to steer cell identity.

Both microRNAs were significantly upregulated in the cancer group, and miR-342-3p tracked with smoking status, peaking in current smokers. Combined blood levels distinguished patients from controls with an accuracy score of 0.767, sensitivity of 81.6 percent, and specificity of 69.4 percent in testing. The molecule's 178 targets clustered in lipid metabolism and nerve development. Raising miR-342-3p sped cell proliferation, but the four-compound cocktail blunted that growth in lab cells.
pmc-13376916:
Prabhjot Singh and co-authors put waste sands to work in green concrete in a 2026 study. The concrete binds with ash and slag waked by a salt bath, with no cement at all. Fine sand from burnt brick dust and from mold shops swapped for river sand, in steps to full swap.

Brick dust cut crush strength, by near one fourth at full swap and late age, since it drinks water and is full of holes. Mold sand did the reverse and beat plain at half swap. Cold-warm rounds and leak tests were also run. Waste picks are not all peers: sort first, the team shows.
pmc-13379316:
Páez Fajardo and colleagues settle a debate about where the charge goes inside lithium battery cathodes, in 2026 energy research. Whether electrons leave the metal atoms or the oxygen atoms during charging, a process called oxygen redox, has confused battery design, because the two routes wear batteries differently. Using X-ray resonance photoemission spectroscopy, which fingerprints which atoms change state, plus theory, the team examined two cathodes during operation at sub-nanoscale resolution.

In the iron-manganese phosphate cathode, weak metal-oxygen hybridization meant capacity came from emptying metal states, standard redox. In the nickel-rich LiNiO2 cathode, negative charge transfer dominated: redox ran through ligand-hole states on oxygen, formed and removed as it cycled. The results explain capacity in highly covalent cathodes without invoking oxygen pairing, once a favored idea. Páez Fajardo offers the framework to guide cathode design, clarifying when oxygen participates and when it spectates.
pmc-13382116:
Vivien Chan and colleagues present a 2026 study of harms linked to donor blood transfusion in children's spine surgery for scoliosis, where the spine curves sideways without a known cause. Such surgery can involve heavy blood loss. Transfusion of donated blood is sometimes needed, but it carries its own risks.

Using a national paediatric surgical database covering 2016 to 2022, the team studied more than twenty-three thousand patients who had fusion of at least seven spine levels. About one in eight received donated blood. Rates of problems within thirty days were compared between groups, with statistical adjustment for other factors. The study quantifies how much extra risk transfusion adds in this setting.
pmc-13384516:
Bedirhan B. Bayıcı and Fatih Kızılyel question how a heart surgery study reads early creatinine rises in a 2026 letter. The study tracked kidney and thumb muscle oxygen in 55 bypass patients and found oxygen drops predicted later creatinine gains. A rise occurred in 43.6 percent of patients after surgery.

The letter writers caution that bypass itself dilutes blood and shifts fluids, which can move creatinine without true kidney damage. Without a standard injury grading system, early changes may reflect passing shifts rather than lasting harm. They urge care in treating a small rise as the main endpoint for judging the sensors' worth.
pmc-13390016:
Aixin Liu and colleagues investigate, in 2026, a protein called UBTD1 that may drive ovarian cancer growth. Ovarian cancer is often found late, spreads readily, and resists platinum drugs, so new drivers of the disease are urgently sought.

The team blends single-cell gene data, mutation analysis, and immune environment checks from public databases such as The Cancer Genome Atlas. They link UBTD1 to mutation-related change and to reshaping of the tissue around tumours. A TNF and AP-1 signalling route is also implicated. Laboratory checks support the database findings. Cancer researchers gain a candidate target with a mapped mechanism, plus a worked example of joining public data with bench tests to judge a gene's role.
pmc-13390616:
Jia-Yi Wang and a large team review, in 2026, the sirtuin family of proteins as both biological regulators and possible drug targets. Sirtuins, numbered one to seven, sense the cell's energy state through a key molecule and adjust chromatin, mitochondria, and stress responses.

Faulty sirtuin activity has been tied to ageing, metabolic syndrome, heart disease, brain degeneration, cancer, and immune disorders, yet firm human proof and working sirtuin drugs are still missing. The review draws heavily on transgenic mouse models for each family member, covering metabolism, genome protection, stress resistance, immunity, and cell recycling. Drug developers gain a model-by-model guide to where sirtuin targeting looks most promising.
pmc-13390816:
Kim Ellis and a large team examine, in 2026, COVID-19 vaccine confidence among adults in Pima County through a health gaps lens. Vaccination is among the most effective ways to stop infectious spread, yet hesitancy has grown and must be understood community by community.

Using the national minority health and disparities framework, the interview-based analysis sorts what shapes confidence at three levels. Those levels are the person, the town, and the wider system. Old inequities still shape uptake too. Public health workers gain a clear account of why confidence varies within one county. It can guide outreach that meets named local barriers. That beats airing the same broad pro-vaccine lines at all. Trust sits at the heart of the work, and past wrongs still shape what many adults hear.
pmc-13392216:
Jeana M Holt and colleagues explore, in 2026, joy in the family lives of autistic teens and young adults. Joy is a side of life that autism research rarely looks at. Most family research centres on stress and burden, leaving shared happiness undocumented.

Six families, seventeen people in all including siblings and caregivers, kept family joy journals for two weeks. The journals frame joy as a shared act. It weaves through daily routines, art and play, and time spent as one. Themes span small daily treats, joy felt as one, and joy with mixed shades. Family researchers gain a fresh lens. Joy here is not luck. It is a thing that kin make as a team, day by day.
pmc-13392316:
Daniel John Murray argues, in 2026, that hormesis, the beneficial response to low doses of stressors, follows necessarily from the geometry of bounded adaptive systems. Instead of fitting curves to dose data, he derives the biphasic pattern from first principles.

Bounded responses are recast in rapidity coordinates, with repair activation and damage accumulation treated as opposing bounded steps with separately measurable thresholds. The resulting predictions are compared with published dose-response data for hydrogen peroxide, cadmium chloride, and heat shock. Readers gain a theory with numbers, one that can be put to the test. The low-dose gain zone has long been told from data alone. Here its place is worked out in advance, from the shape of the system.
pmc-13392416:
Niccolò Garofalo leads a team reporting hip bone infection caused by Granulicatella adiacens, a mouth bacterium almost never linked to osteomyelitis. Their patient was a 59-year-old man who first complained of low back pain. The authors present the case as the first of its kind for the hip, alongside a review of earlier reports.

Standard cultures can miss this organism, so identification relied on sequencing of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene. Care combined repeated surgical cleaning, a cement spacer carrying antibiotics that was later renewed, and finally a hip prosthesis, with doxycycline and cotrimoxazole given throughout. Infection cleared by final follow-up, although hip function remained poor, and the authors note that missed diagnosis may explain why such cases seem so rare.
pmc-13392516:
Ania Mezouari leads a report on a uterine muscle tumour that came back widely after the uterus had already been removed. The growth belongs to a rare group whose behaviour sits between clearly benign and clearly malignant, often shortened to STUMP. The patient was a 61-year-old woman who had passed menopause.

Eighteen months after surgery for what were thought to be ordinary fibroids, lumps appeared in the abdominal wall muscle, the vaginal cuff, the belly lining, the small bowel, and the abdominal wall. Reviewing the original specimen then revealed features of the uncertain group that had been missed first time round. One returning lump had lost a protein called MTAP, a finding the authors present cautiously as a clue for study rather than proof, while urging long-term checks even after full removal surgery.
pmc-13392616:
Justin Gainor interviews Stevan Bradford, a steel mill worker from the Mobile area of Alabama. Bradford is living with lung cancer at stage four, of the non-small cell type, carrying a rare NTRK gene fusion. Their recorded conversation forms the heart of the piece, published in 2026. Gainor is a thoracic oncologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and Bradford tells his story in his own words.

Bradford recounts learning his diagnosis in January, starting treatment, and later moving from chemotherapy to a drug aimed at the fusion. He speaks about side effects, the strain of hunting down information on a rare change by himself, waits for testing and treatment, and the emotional weight of the diagnosis. Both men press for faster biomarker testing and clearer talk about timelines, so patients with rare changes face less uncertainty.
pmc-13392816:
Naoko Nambu and five colleagues reviewed eighty-six adults operated on for a burst intestine. They hunted for cases caused by a missing stretch of gut muscle rather than by infection or blocked blood flow. Diverticular disease led the list of causes, followed by poor blood supply, with the muscle-gap condition third. Five patients in total had the rare defect, called segmental absence of intestinal musculature.

Four of the five bursts sat in the sigmoid colon and one in the caecum, and most patients were older women. Under the microscope the muscle layer stopped abruptly or thinned to nothing at the hole, without the deep infection or dead tissue that would suggest another cause. Because the condition appeared commoner than textbooks imply, the authors urge generous tissue sampling after such surgery so the diagnosis is not missed.
pmc-13392916:
Manar Foura-Matar, Hazem Melad, Mohammed Taha, and Hannah Wesley ran a split-mouth trial testing whether painting a bone-promoting mix onto fresh dental implants speeds their grip in the jaw. Each of eighteen healthy adults received two implants in the same jaw, one treated with a sponge soaked in dexamethasone, vitamin C, and a phosphate compound, the other with a plain sponge. Neither patients nor the measuring examiner knew which side got which.

Stability scores, measured on a standard quotient scale, ran clearly higher for treated implants at four weeks, the early healing window the mix targets. By eight and sixteen weeks the two sides had converged, although both grew steadily firmer over time. The authors, reporting the first human test of the blend, present it as a short-term healing booster rather than a lasting advantage.
pmc-13393516:
Yu Zong, Yuxin Wang, and Liang Qiao present DeepGPO, a deep learning system that predicts the fragmentation fingerprints of sugar-carrying peptides so researchers can identify them in mass spectrometry data. Mapping O-linked glycosylation, sugars attached at oxygen sites, is among the hardest problems in protein analysis because sites and sugar shapes vary enormously. Models existed for the nitrogen-linked cousin, but the oxygen-linked version resisted prediction and training data are scarce.

The framework pairs a Transformer with two graph networks built to handle branched sugar trees. Weighting schemes for uneven spectra and pretraining helped it learn from limited examples. Predicted spectra can pinpoint attachment sites even when the decisive ions are missing from real data. The system currently handles peptides carrying one or two such sugars, and the authors report promise in clinical human samples.
pmc-13393716:
Caroline Skovsbo Clausen and four colleagues interviewed twelve premenopausal Danish women living with recurrent urinary tract infections to learn how the condition feels and how general practice care lands. Recurrence is common and known to strain quality of life, mental health, and relationships, but the consultation room experience was under-explored. The interviews were read for themes.

Three themes emerged. Set practice routines clashed with women's own sense of their illness, leaving them wanting clearer pathways and more person-centred care. Many felt dismissed or unacknowledged by their doctor, a lack of backing that damaged trust. Those experiences fed gendered self-images, tipping into self-blame, stoic acceptance, or feeling wronged. The authors urge practices to treat recurrence as a continuing condition needing a plan, not a loop of repeat tests and scripts.
pmc-13395816:
Jingyi Chen and co-authors study, in 2026, team eye care by video link in far western Australia. Towns sat more than 1,500 kilometres from the capital, Perth. Optometrists examined patients in person, then joined a video call with an eye surgeon for joint decisions. Records from 2023 covered three settings: hospital, community clinic, and outreach visits.

More than half of all non-surgical eye care ran through the video model. Only a small share of video cases needed a later in-person surgeon visit. Attendance odds ran well over three times higher for video visits than face-to-face ones. Cataracts and lid growths often went straight to surgery booking. The authors urge wider use of the model.
pmc-13396216:
Hasan Abdel Aziz Mohamed and co-authors built a compact hardware version of ASCON, the cipher chosen for lightweight cryptography, and describe it in a 2026 paper. Small internet-connected devices need strong encryption but have little power or chip space to spare.

Their design processes data in a serial stream rather than in wide parallel blocks, which trims the logic needed. On a low-power Lattice iCE40 chip it reached a top speed of 228.8 megahertz using only 582 lookup tables and 418 flip-flops, and drew 2.28 milliwatts at a lower test speed. The chip runs ASCON-128 in its authenticated mode, which both hides data and proves it was not altered.
pmc-13396616:
Amanda Drury and co-authors mapped what nurses actually do in precision oncology, where cancer care is matched to a tumor's genetic profile, in a 2026 scoping review. Nurses guide patients through genomic testing and targeted drugs, yet the skills that work demands, and whether training supplies them, had not been charted.

Five databases were searched in July 2025 following the JBI method for scoping reviews. The team also hunted postgraduate and continuing courses aimed at nurses, using an artificial intelligence search of grey sources. The result is an inventory of roles, from consent talks to side effect coaching, set against the education on offer, and it shows where preparation lags behind practice.
pmc-13397116:
Tae Jung Oh and co-authors hunted for teamwork between the two genomes every cell carries, the main nuclear set and the small mitochondrial one, in shaping diabetes risk. Their 2026 study uses 7,047 non-Hispanic White participants in the Health and Retirement Study, Americans aged 50 and over.

First, the team scanned a gene called Klotho, tied to ageing and sugar handling, for variants linked to diabetes. Then a purpose-built interaction test crossed the winning Klotho variant against 85 mitochondrial variants. Effects split by sex, the title reports, meaning a mitochondrial variant mattered only alongside a particular Klotho version, and differently in men and women.
pmc-13397516:
Steven Zeng and fellow authors compare wound dressings used after breast reduction surgery, hunting for the option that heals best. Their 2026 review covers one hospital's cases from July 2023 to July 2025. Choices on the market range from skin glues to adhesive strips, yet no study had crowned a clear winner.

Patients were grouped by what covered their wounds: two glue brands, a glue-and-mesh pairing, a silk dressing, simple strips or a mix of products. The team tracked big problems such as a return to theatre and smaller ones like skin reactions, fluid build-up, infection and poor scars. Fair tests then weighed whether dressing choice tracked with how often each problem showed up.
pmc-13397916:
Lauryn Rudin and co-authors measure what mouth sores from cancer treatment cost hospitals and patients with oral cavity cancer. Their 2026 study mines the 2019 National Inpatient Sample, a large United States hospital database, covering about 59,710 weighted admissions. Ulcerative mucositis, a raw and painful mouth lining breakdown, follows both chemotherapy and radiation aimed at lip, mouth and throat cancers.

Cases were split by whether the sores came from drugs or radiation, then compared on hospital stay length and total charges. Models adjusted for age, other illnesses, insurance, income and type of admission, and also probed gaps between patient groups. Pinpointing the cost drivers, the authors argue, can guide support care and fairer resource planning.
pmc-13398616:
Tianyi Liu, Rou Meng, Shufen Zhang and Suli Wu pack three kinds of light into a single tiny sphere. Their 2026 study coats zinc sulfide spheres with a silica nanoarmor so they survive a 1,000 degree firing without losing their round shape. Structural colour, glow and afterglow usually fight each other, since glow needs hot crystallisation that melts fine structure.

Alternating oxygen and nitrogen during heating burned off carbon at low heat, then flipped the crystal to its wurtzite form with 91 percent conversion in the figures reported. Doped metals (silver, copper or manganese) tune the glow, while the perfect spheres give angle-free structural colour by Mie resonance. One particle thus carries colour, light emission and a fading afterglow together.
pmc-13399116:
Sharma and co-authors search for a drug target that stays present across every stage of prostate cancer. Their 2026 paper combines a single-cell atlas of roughly one million cells from 213 patients with animal models and protein checks on patient tissue. The goal was a surface protein that treatment-resistant cancers, including hormone-insensitive forms, cannot easily shed.

One candidate stood out: B7-H3 was the most uniformly expressed target across the whole disease continuum, with little variation between or within tumours. The androgen receptor normally suppresses it, and blocking that receptor while targeting B7-H3 inhibited tumour growth more than either approach's expected effect alone. The authors also rank partner targets, including TROP-2 and NECTIN4, for two-target antibody designs. They propose B7-H3 as a broad-spectrum anchor for combination therapy.
pmc-13399616:
Vrgoč Goran and co-authors describe a surgical technique they call Biobridge for massive rotator cuff tears that cannot be repaired directly, in a 2026 technique paper. Their reconstruction uses the patient's own long head of biceps tendon, still attached at the glenoid, as living graft material. That avoids donor tissue harvest and its complications. The whole procedure is done through the arthroscope.

The surgeons free the biceps tendon, cut the transverse humeral ligament that tethers it, and swing the tendon onto the supraspinatus footprint on the humeral head. Anchors fix it there with a lasso-loop stitch, and a shoelace side-to-side pattern joins it to the remaining cuff tissue, finishing with double-row fixation. The transferred tendon shrinks the tear and rebuilds the superior restraint with vascularized tissue. They offer the method as a reproducible, biologically sound alternative to graft-based reconstruction.
pmc-13399816:
Beas and colleagues warn, in 2026, that a class of leukemia-driving NOTCH1 mutations is being missed by routine genetic testing. In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, juxtamembrane internal tandem duplications in NOTCH1 activate the gene. They carry favorable prognostic meaning when RAS and PTEN are normal, but their size and sequence make them hard for short-read sequencing pipelines to call. An index case whose variant was detected discordantly by software prompted a systematic check.

In that patient, the caller VarDict found a 51-base-pair duplication that VarScan2 missed, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Reanalyzing seven confirmed cases, Mutect2 and VarDict detected every duplication, 100 percent, Pindel caught six of seven at 85.7 percent, and VarScan2 found only three, 42.8 percent of the set. Haplotype-based callers that use soft-clipped and split reads succeeded where pileup-based callers discarded evidence. The authors urge combining calling strategies for this variant class.
pmc-13400716:
Dominic Bertram and colleagues report, in 2026, a case of stubborn nerve pain after shingles that eased with botulinum toxin injections. Postherpetic neuralgia can persist for years, especially in older people, and standard drugs often fail or cause side effects. Their patient had severe chest pain resistant to usual care.

Doctors injected the toxin across forty points in the painful area, with one corner receiving saline instead, blinded, as an internal comparison. Pain in the treated zone fell from peaks at the top of the scale to mid-range, while the saline corner barely changed. A top-up injection shrank the remaining painful patch to coin size. Benefits lasted about three months per round, and repeat treatment held gains for nearly a year.
pmc-13401316:
Kemal Ozan Lüle wrote a 2026 cross-sectional study of health literacy among preclinical medical students in Türkiye, asking how well future doctors can find, understand. Use health information before their clinical training begins. Those skills underpin clear communication with patients.

At Gaziantep University Faculty of Medicine, 305 students in years one to three completed the Turkish Health Literacy Scale-32 during the 2025-2026 academic year. The scale yields an overall index plus domain and competence scores. Lüle compared years with standard statistical tests. He then used correlation and multivariable regression to check whether academic year predicted literacy on its own, after accounting for sex and body mass index. Age was added in sensitivity checks. The study maps where early training leaves literacy gaps.
pmc-13401616:
Zhong and colleagues built two aging clocks for the musculoskeletal system from blood proteins. They mapped what speeds them up, in a 2026 study of more than twenty-one thousand UK Biobank records. Existing protein clocks track aging but miss decline in organs and its causes. The team assembled a pool of 39 musculoskeletal proteins from gene readouts, protein function, and studies.

Zhong trained one clock to estimate age and a second, mortality-tuned clock that tracked age more tightly, especially in women. People whose muscle-and-bone age ran ahead of their actual age faced higher risks of death, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, back pain, and diseases of aging. Speeding up was tied to air pollutants, mental strain, and lifestyles, while genome scans found thirteen variants and seventy-one genes clustered in gene-control and tissue-setting pathways. A screen named zinc as a protective agent.
pmc-13401716:
Thang Dinh Nguyen, Huong Tu Lam, and Thong Duy Vo tested two blood-based scores for predicting oesophageal varices in people with liver cirrhosis, in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Vietnam. Swollen veins in the gullet can bleed catastrophically, but the standard check, endoscopy, is invasive and resource-hungry.

At Cho Ray Hospital between November 2022 and May 2023, 152 cirrhotic patients, mean age 56 and about two-thirds male, underwent screening endoscopy. Their albumin-bilirubin score and its platelet-augmented version were calculated from routine labs. Varices were present in 56 percent. Both scores performed moderately, with discrimination values just under four-fifths for varices overall and for varices needing treatment. At one suggested cutoff, about a fifth of patients could skip endoscopy, at the price of missing roughly a tenth of varices needing treatment.
pmc-13402016:
Chunli Zeng and co-authors used UK Biobank data to ask whether a diet rich in antioxidants relates to overlap syndrome, where asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease occur together. They split participants into thirds by composite dietary antioxidant index and built three Cox models with growing levels of adjustment. Survival curves, spline curves, and subgroup checks filled out the analysis.

After full adjustment, the overall link was flat, with a hazard estimate of 1.01 and a confidence interval from 0.94 to 1.09 that crossed no effect. Spline curves told a different story: the link bent, running downward before an inflection point and upward after it. That bent pattern held only in women, in people aged 60 or older, and in those with body mass index below 30, a nuance a single average figure hides.
pmc-13402316:
Sarin Segev-Nakar and Itay Koren uncover a cleanup route in which mitochondria dispose of membrane proteins meant for peroxisomes when peroxisomes are missing. Peroxisomes handle fat and reactive oxygen chemistry, and their membrane proteins drop sharply in cells lacking working peroxisomes, for reasons that were unclear. Using protein and RNA counts in deficient cells, the pair traced the drop to faster destruction, not slower production.

A CRISPR screen pointed at two mitochondrial outer membrane enzymes, MUL1 and MARCH5, which tag the stray proteins for proteasome disposal and can cover for each other. The membrane-spanning part of a protein alone was enough to send it down this route. Cells missing both peroxisomes and these enzymes grew very poorly, showing the pathway is essential backup. The finding reframes mitochondria as watchdogs for proteins orphaned by a failed organelle.
pmc-13402716:
Jiawei Lu and colleagues show how lymphoid clusters that form in inflamed gums become hubs for the bone loss of periodontitis. These tertiary lymphoid structures gather B cells, the main local source of RANKL, the signal that orders bone-eating cells into action. Staining of gum tissue showed the clusters grow and mature as inflammation worsens, and patients with them fared worse after surgery.

Gene-level work traced the trigger: mouth bacteria fire the type I interferon pathway in gum fibroblasts, which then mature into CXCL13-making organizers that assemble the clusters. Inside them, activated B cells poured out RANKL and drove bone resorption in a mouse model of the disease. Blocking interferon signaling broke the chain, shrinking clusters and sparing bone. The authors nominate that pathway as a drug target for gum disease.
pmc-13403016:
Pablo Alvarez-Aguilar and the TRAQUEOSCR Group describe how percutaneous tracheostomy, a bedside airway opening for long ventilation, is practiced across eight public hospitals in Costa Rica. Their prospective cohort from 2019 to 2022 covered 516 adults, mean age 53.2 years, two-thirds male. Expected long ventilation, neurological deficits, and ventilation past ten days were the leading reasons, and two techniques, Ciaglia and Griggs, split the cases almost evenly.

First-attempt success reached 85.1 percent. Acute complications touched 28.3 percent of patients, mostly minor bleeding at 25.4 percent, while serious events such as airway loss stayed rare at 3.9 percent and no death was tied to the procedure. Blood thinners, obesity, clotting disorders, prior neck surgery, neck immobilization, and technical difficulty each predicted trouble. Monitoring aids were unevenly used, capnography in 74.2 percent but ultrasound in only 17.7 percent.
pmc-13403416:
Victoria Tsvetkova and colleagues compared hormone and sugar control across three groups in a 2026 study tied to COVID-19. One group had active infection, one had lasting metabolic trouble after infection, and one had metabolic syndrome without COVID. The team rated insulin-making cell output and thyroid hormone levels in each group.

Cell output was lowest during active infection and middling in the post-COVID group. One active thyroid hormone and its ratio to a second hormone were also low during illness. In the post-COVID group, higher levels of that hormone tracked with better cell output. Much of the thyroid gap seemed to reflect prior illness, not new gland damage.
pmc-13403716:
Qing Zhang and a large team built a gene catalog in 2026 for microbes that live in the human airway. Healthy breathing depends partly on these germ communities, yet no fine map of their genes existed. The team mined gene data from 12,273 airway samples across body sites and regions.

Their catalog holds more than 24 million distinct microbial genes, each tagged by job where known. It flags drug resistance genes, harm factors, and germ-fighting peptides, plus the germs that carry them. Patterns shift by airway site and by world region. The open catalog gives lung researchers a shared base for work on health and disease.
pmc-13404416:
Vuyelwa Zandile Peter, Mershen Pillay, and Yougan Saman explored in 2026 what caregivers and preschool staff in Durban believe about children's communication disorders. Poor families often struggle to reach therapy services, and home beliefs shape whether they try. Thirty people joined group talks and interviews for the study.

Nineteen were early childhood center staff, and eleven were caregivers of varied kinds. Two themes stood out in their accounts. Views of cause mixed social and spiritual threads into one knot. Care choices grew just as tangled, with families weighing many paths at once. Services that ignore those beliefs risk low uptake and weak follow-through.
pmc-13404616:
Md Fuad Al Fidah leads a 2026 effort to predict shigellosis in young children without waiting for lab results. Shigella causes much diarrhoea and many deaths in children under five in poorer countries. Labs are often out of reach there, and treating by visible blood in stool misses many cases.

Data came from 3,356 children with diarrhoea in the Global Enteric Multicentre Study, after removing mixed infections and controls. Several machine learning models learned from 32 predictors and were checked with ten-fold cross-validation. A support vector machine caught the most true cases, with recall of 0.64 in the reported metric, though overall accuracy stayed modest. A trimmed ten-predictor version was built into a prototype web tool for clinic decision support.
pmc-13405116:
Phornthip Ploensil and colleagues test a worm protein against leukaemia cells in 2026 laboratory work. Stefin-1, taken from the liver fluke Fasciola gigantica, normally helps the parasite handle its host. Whether it could harm cancer cells was unexplored.

Human U937 leukaemia cells exposed to the protein lost viability as dose and time rose, with half killed near 11 micromolar at 48 hours in the reported assays. Normal blood cells from donors barely changed under the same treatment. Treated cancer cells showed signs of programmed death, including a shifted BAX to BCL-2 balance and activated caspase-3. The authors propose the parasite protein as a selective lead worth further study.
pmc-13405316:
Rosinete Maria dos Santos Guimarães and co-authors count tuberculosis cases among Brazilians on biologic drugs, in a 2026 ten-year study. The drugs treat immune diseases well but raise infection risk, a serious issue in high-burden Pernambuco. Records cover 2013 to 2023 across rheumatology, gut and skin clinics.

Of 8,623 patients, overall tuberculosis incidence was 2.1 percent in the reported figures. Gut patients carried the highest rate at 4.7 percent, with a risk ratio of 2.4 against other groups. Timing comparisons found no clear rise during treatment versus before it. Infliximab showed a slightly higher rate than other drug classes, at 2.6 percent in the reported data.
pmc-13406016:
Xu Jiang, Shannon M Testa and Marissa F Mulvey test how beliefs about stress shape teenagers' positive behaviour, in a 2026 survey of 620 high school students. Ages ran from 14 to 19, with data gathered online in spring 2022 across United States regions. Two outcomes were tracked: taking initiative for personal growth and using one's strengths.

A stress mindset helped or hindered depending on social support and sex together, a three-way pattern. For boys, the link between a helpful stress mindset and strengths use weakened as support rose. For girls the same link strengthened with high support, the opposite trend. Single-moderator models missed the effect entirely, showing context and mindset must be read together.
pmc-13407016:
Katsuhito Iikura and co-authors follow a 13-year-old girl with diffuse panbronchiolitis, a chronic lung inflammation rarely seen in children, in this 2026 case report. The condition usually affects middle-aged adults and brings chronic sinus trouble, a productive cough, and breathlessness on exertion.

Her breath sounds were recorded with an electronic stethoscope across the whole course of low-dose erythromycin treatment. As symptoms and lung function improved, abnormal sounds faded in a clear order: coarse crackles vanished first, then continuous sounds eased from the outer airways inward. The pattern suggested at least six months of treatment were needed. Recording breath sounds, the authors argue, gives an objective window on recovery in this rare disease.
pmc-13407516:
Carrie Sailer, Kellie Littlefield, and Michael Hendricks describe, in 2026, a short billing course that raised hospital doctors' confidence and their hospital's revenue. Hospitalists spend long hours documenting care, yet weak coding quietly loses money, and newer rules letting visit level rest on decision complexity or total time were going unused for lack of training.

Fifty-six hospitalists joined five 15-minute virtual sessions spread over six months, mixing mini-lectures, case rounds, a record-system phrase shortcut, a cheat sheet, and feedback aimed at the lowest performers. Confidence in billing discharge summaries as very or completely confident jumped from 46 to 95 percent, with similar leaps for admission and progress notes. Coding improved measurably, work units rose 77 percent, and added revenue passed 150,000 dollars.
pmc-13407716:
Tonthoza Uganja, Eefke Mollee, and James Gibbons check, in 2026, whether global satellite land-cover maps can track Malawi's pledge to restore 4.5 million hectares of forest by 2030. Malawi loses tree cover fast, and three popular ten-metre global products promise cheap monitoring, so the team scored them against more than 5,000 national forest inventory points.

Esri Land Cover scored highest overall at 65.6 percent accuracy, followed by ESA WorldCover at 61.9 percent, while Dynamic World trailed at 46.9 percent. Tree cover itself was detected reliably by all three, but cropland and built-up areas were systematically missed and rangeland was over-predicted, a serious flaw in smallholder farming mosaics. The authors recommend blending global maps with national inventories and community data rather than trusting satellites alone.
pmc-13408116:
Zhijian Zhu and co-authors trace, in 2026, how two near-identical RNA-binding proteins keep antibody factories running. Germinal centres are where B cells multiply and refine antibodies during immune responses. Deleting the genes for hnRNP A1 and A2B1 in mouse B cells crippled that reaction. Proliferation fell, and high-affinity antibody output dropped.

The mechanism is splicing control: the proteins grip UAG-rich motifs in the Ezh2 gene's raw transcript and force inclusion of exon 14, keeping the EZH2 enzyme catalytically active. Without them, exon skipping yields a dead enzyme, a cell-cycle brake protein accumulates, and B cells stall. Deleting that brake partly rescued the defect. An axis linking splicing to epigenetic control of immunity is the authors' formulation.
pmc-13408216:
Joseph Sliepka, Nyaluma Wagala, and Brian Feeley set out a 2026 surgical technique for rebuilding a torn shoulder labrum. The labrum is the cartilage rim that keeps the ball of the shoulder seated, and repeated dislocations can leave it too damaged to stitch back. Moderate bone loss makes the repair decision harder still.

Their approach reconstructs the rim using a donated hamstring tendon graft fixed with knotless anchors, aiming for a repair that other surgeons can reproduce reliably. The article reviews why standard repairs fail in a sizeable share of patients and where bone-block operations fit instead. For sports-medicine surgeons, the value lies in a step-by-step option for the awkward middle ground between simple repair and major bone surgery.
pmc-13409016:
Indrani Sarma and colleagues pool the human trial evidence in 2026 on whether diabetes drugs that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1 can also treat addiction. Animal work had hinted these drugs dampen reward-seeking across substances, raising hopes of repurposing. Five randomised trials covering 764 adults with substance use disorders met the review's criteria, with follow-ups from six weeks to a year.

Combined analysis found no significant effect on days free of alcohol, cigarettes smoked per day, or nicotine dependence scores. Certainty ranged only from low to moderate, and results for alcohol varied widely between trials. Three trials were judged low risk of bias and two raised some concerns. A possible benefit signal in one patient subgroup is flagged for future testing. For now, the authors conclude, enthusiasm from animal studies remains unconfirmed in people.
pmc-13409416:
Muhammad Usman and colleagues report in 2026 a thirty-eight-year-old man whose month of spiking fevers and right-sided abdominal pain defeated an extensive infection hunt. He had recently travelled to Mexico, inflammatory markers ran high, yet his liver enzymes stayed stubbornly normal, a combination that pointed away from ordinary hepatitis. Imaging finally showed multiple cystic widenings of the bile ducts inside the liver.

A liver biopsy confirmed inborn scarring, sealing the diagnosis of Caroli syndrome, a one-in-a-million congenital disorder in which the bile ducts balloon and bacteria stagnate. Broad-spectrum antibiotics settled his fever quickly once the anatomy was understood. The authors urge clinicians to keep the syndrome in mind when recurrent unexplained fever meets any biliary abnormality. Spotting it early triggers watching for the syndrome's long-term troubles. Those include returning infection and malignant change.
pmc-13410416:
Jiaying Wu and Xuwen Mao report in 2026 that an extract of the plant Artemisia rupestris eases gut inflammation in mice. Bowel inflammation is linked to disturbed gut microbes and faulty metabolism. The plant holds compounds known to calm inflammation, yet its effect on colitis had not been tested.

Mice were given a chemical that triggers colitis, plus varied doses of the water extract. Treated mice showed lower levels of three inflammation signals and less gut leakiness. Two receptor proteins tied to inflammation fell, while two proteins that seal the gut wall recovered. Gut microbe mixes shifted toward helpful groups, and disturbed chemical pathways in the gut moved back toward normal.
pmc-13410616:
Ying Dai and co-workers hunt in 2026 for a peptide that can break up a protein pair driving lung cancer growth. The pair, METTL3 and METTL14, tag RNA in ways that help tumors progress. Blocking their join is a possible drug strategy, though no such drug is in routine use.

Computer screening of a peptide library, followed by docking tests, produced four candidates. The lead peptide bound METTL3 most tightly in lab measures and held a fitting shape in simulations. In lung cancer cells it slowed growth while sparing normal lung cells more. Treated cells showed less of the pair's RNA tagging and lower output of a growth-linked gene. Removing METTL3 blunted the peptide's effect, supporting its aim.
pmc-13411716:
Chunfeng Xiao and a large team describe in 2026 a program to build and test personal music therapy for common mental disorders. Drugs for depression, anxiety, and insomnia often bring side effects or faltering adherence. Music listening is gentle and popular, yet standard playlists help unevenly and the brain mechanisms stay fuzzy.

Four linked studies at a Beijing hospital move from groundwork to validation. Early phases profile patients and test fixed playlists, then a 300-person trial compares standard listening with AI-composed tracks tuned to weekly preferences over eight weeks. A final study validates a model that predicts who responds. Brain wave measures run alongside symptoms to expose how the therapy works.
pmc-13415416:
Si Liu and colleagues tune the liquid inside a zinc organic battery so two kinds of ions can store charge together, in 2026. Adding potassium chloride to a zinc chloride electrolyte pushes the organic cathode material, called PTCDA, out of solution instead of letting it dissolve away. That salting out effect protects the cathode during cycling.

Zinc and potassium ions were shown to enter and leave the cathode together in a reversible way. The built battery delivered about 125 milliamp hours per gram at a fast rate, reaching over ninety percent of its theoretical capacity. Fast charging plus long life are the twin goals for this safer water based battery family.
pmc-13415716:
Li and co-authors show, in 2026, that remote ischemic preconditioning, briefly restricting blood flow in a limb to protect distant tissue, improves skin flap survival after transplant surgery in rats. They trace the mechanism through gene expression. Flaps starved of blood during transfer often die at the edges. Preconditioning boosted new blood vessel growth and shrank the necrotic area in their model, where rats were anesthetized with ketamine at 75 milligrams per kilogram.

Transcriptome analysis flagged genes, including NCOA1, SDF1, VHL, and ZNF667, several known for roles in vessel formation and tissue repair. The pathway centers on ZNF667 driving SDF1, a signal that recruits endothelial progenitor cells, the builders of new vessels, to the flap. Animals were monitored with pain relief and excluded for distress or blood pressure collapse under rules. The authors position preconditioning, a cheap, drug-free maneuver, as a shield against ischemia-reperfusion injury in reconstructive surgery.
pmc-13415916:
Ashlyn Conant and co-authors review type 1 interferons made by cancer cells themselves, focusing on cancers that mainly affect women, in 2026. Interferons alpha and beta are best known for antiviral defense and immune activation. Within tumor cells they can act without immune help, shaping responses to standard therapies and tumor growth.

Signal strength and duration decide direction: these interferons sometimes suppress tumors and sometimes help them. Ovarian, breast, cervical, and endometrial cancers anchor the discussion. Mechanisms cover production triggers, signaling chains, and downstream outcomes. Sex bias in these diseases adds a further layer the authors keep in view throughout.
pmc-13416016:
Martina Tosi and co-authors pilot a slow release microtablet protein substitute for children with phenylketonuria, in 2026. In this inherited condition, the amino acid phenylalanine must stay low, so medical protein substitutes fill the diet. Taste, volume, and fatigue make children skip doses. Tiny coated tablets release amino acids over about three hours.

Ten participants aged three and up swapped at least one daily dose for seven days. Adherence hit eighty percent, above the seventy percent for their usual substitute. Stomach symptoms were mild or absent by day seven for everyone. Four teenagers continued for twenty-eight more days, keeping tolerance and reporting less aftertaste.
pmc-13418416:
Sharma and colleagues reviewed in 2026 modern ways to make dithiocarbamates, a family of sulfur-containing chemicals. These compounds are used in medicines, farm chemicals, materials, and chemical catalysis, meaning speeding up reactions. It also covers methods that need no catalyst, methods with catalyst help, greener routes, and routes with no solvent at all.

For each route, the authors weigh which starting materials work, how well reactions run, and which chemical groups survive the process. They highlight a shift toward cleaner methods that cut waste and avoid harsh solvents. Open problems include reusing catalysts, hitting one product among several possible ones, and scaling methods up safely. The review closes with directions for making these useful compounds in ways that are both efficient and sustainable.
pmc-13418516:
Miaomiao Yu and colleagues make magnetic imprinted polymers to pull geosmin, a musty water contaminant, out of water samples, in a 2026 study. Geosmin spoils drinking water taste at tiny levels. Their particles have a magnetic iron oxide core, a silica shell, and an imprinted layer shaped using a stand in template, so the real target is not consumed during making.

The sorbent loaded well, reached balance in 75 minutes, and could be fished out magnetically in 30 seconds. It preferred geosmin over a similar odorant and kept most capacity after six reuses. Paired with chromatography, it recovered most spiked geosmin from real water samples reliably.
pmc-13418616:
Liang and colleagues report a 2026 field study on how offshore wind farms change the flight of breeding seabirds. The team tracked Bridled Terns near a colony close to turbines, using satellite tags that logged position every second on some flights. They measured path bends, turns, speed, and flight height.

Birds bent their routes more and flew lower when a flight pointed toward the turbines from the colony. That pattern points to local route shifts on turbine-facing trips. Yet flight traits showed no clear link to how close a bird came to a turbine, and birds acted much the same inside and outside the farm. Farms seem to reshape flight by direction near colonies rather than by distance alone. Planners can use that pattern to judge the extra flight cost birds pay on feeding trips.
pmc-13418716:
Yixin Jiang and co-authors argue that physical forces are active drivers of bacterial virulence, in a 2026 review. Bacteria in the body face shear from fluids, tight confinement, and tissues of varying stiffness. Sensors in their envelopes, tails, and hairs translate those forces into chemical signals that reprogram behaviour, from sticking under flow to building biofilms.

Force landscapes differ by tissue, which may explain why strains favour certain organs better than chemistry alone can. The authors propose attacking force sensing nodes or exploiting biofilm mechanical weak points. Such physical disruption could sidestep antibiotic resistance rather than fight it chemically.
pmc-13418816:
Annabell Hüsken and colleagues track how parasites returned to snails after a large stream system was restored. Heavy damage had left few water creatures alive, so free-living species and their parasites had to recolonize from scratch. That rare reset let the team watch the first steps of community rebuilding in fresh water.

Seasonal sampling during the early years after restoration caught trematode worms living inside their first snail hosts. Species were named by shape and by gene checks, giving firmer counts than either route alone. Both snail and worm communities differed sharply from site to site, with strong turnover along the stream. The patchy pattern shows that recovery after restoration follows local conditions closely, not one smooth shared path.
pmc-13420316:
Yue Zhao and colleagues copy the papery husk of the golden berry to build a spray-on food wrap that fights germs without plastic. The husk stretches the berry's room-temperature shelf life from 11 to 24 days in the study they cite, a striking natural trick. Foodborne illness and plastic waste are the twin targets of the design.

The sprayable coating aims to match the husk's protection in a form farms and packers can apply at scale. The paper weighs strength against function, since active packaging often trades one for the other. Full life cycle thinking runs through the design choices, from ingredients to disposal. A wrap that composts after keeping food safe longer would cut both food waste and plastic in one move.
pmc-13420716:
Tomoya Hamashoji and colleagues ask whether low blood chloride at enrollment predicts death in patients on peritoneal dialysis, using a registry from Fukuoka, Japan. The registry enrolled patients from 20 centers between 2011 and 2020 for home-based dialysis care. Low chloride had already been linked to death in kidney disease and in center-based dialysis, yet home dialysis proof was thin.

In the fullest adjusted model, the lowest chloride third carried more than double the death risk of the highest third, with a hazard ratio of 2.59 in the reported figure, and heart-related death ran higher still at 3.33 in the same model. Chloride was measured once, at entry, a limit the authors flag. A cheap salt value may still help clinics flag fragile patients early.
pmc-13421116:
Irina Kolobova and colleagues review the literature on HIV-related stigma and its drag on treatment and quality of life. Their search ran from January 2021 to June 2023 across journals, conferences, and reference lists. A prior pooled analysis had found stigma reported by 44 percent of people with HIV across 13 countries in the figures cited.

Higher stigma tracked with poorer clinic engagement in 8 of 11 studies and with weaker drug adherence in 16 of 20 studies in the counts reported. Unsuppressed virus and poor mental health showed the same pattern across most of their study sets. Stigma behaves here like a clinical variable, not a soft concern: it predicts missed doses and lost follow-up. Programs that fund only pills, the review implies, leave a main driver of failure untouched.
pmc-13421216:
Jack Doyle and five colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of shoulder injuries in rugby union, covering how often they occur, how they happen and how they are treated. Searching three databases up to June 2025, they screened 1,099 abstracts and included 37 studies.

The pooled match rate was about 11 injuries per 1,000 player-hours. Studies differed so widely, though, that the authors warn against reading it as one true rate. They call it an average across unlike groups of players. Rates were highest in elite men and in school and university players, while training injuries were far rarer. Tackling caused most injuries, usually hurting the tackler. Surgical options such as Bankart and Latarjet repairs feature in the treatment evidence reviewed.
pmc-13421316:
S. Rinaldetti leads a large international team reporting, in 2026, molecular findings from the EURO-SKI trial, which tested whether people with chronic myeloid leukaemia can safely stop their kinase inhibitor drugs. Many patients stay in remission off treatment, yet the biology separating them from those who relapse is poorly understood.

The team profiled gene activity in blood cells from 240 patients on their final day of drug intake, with healthy controls and untreated patients for comparison. Patients who stayed in remission showed active blood-forming gene programmes and healthy-style communication between innate and adaptive immune cells, a pattern lost in relapsers. A threshold in one gene, FLT3, also separated groups with different relapse risk. The authors suggest reinforcing these mechanisms could widen treatment-free remission.
pmc-13421616:
Souza and colleagues sequenced in 2026 Escherichia coli germs taken from cows with mastitis, an udder infection that costs dairy farms dearly. Many such germs resist several antibiotics, so the team also tested plant extracts and a synthetic polymer as alternative killers. Eight isolates from sick cows plus a standard strain were genome-sequenced and checked for resistance and virulence genes.

Of the plant products, only Amburana cearensis extract killed the germs, and only at a high dose. The polymer, highly soluble polypyrrole, killed at a far lower dose and was the only agent with true bactericidal action. All isolates carried efflux pump genes, but only three actually used the mechanism in the lab. The authors present the polymer as a candidate alternative against resistant mastitis germs.
pmc-13421916:
Vélez-Esperilla and co-authors trace in 2026 how two groups of Talipariti, tropical trees and shrubs in the mallow family, spread across Malesia, the island region between Asia and Australia. One group lives worldwide on coasts; the other is confined to Papua.

Combining genome-wide nuclear data with plastid genomes, the team dated the group's origin in Malesia to about 20 million years ago. The Papuan group separated along Lydekker's Line about 8 million years ago. The coastal group then radiated rapidly from about 1.4 million years ago onward in their dated tree. Model comparisons told two stories. The coastal group's range fits rare long-distance dispersal, with new populations founding far away, while the Papuan group fits slow stepping-stone spread between islands.
pmc-13423816:

During infection by phage T7, its protein Gp0.4 grabs FtsZ, the host's cell-division protein, freezing division. That trapped pair is exactly what CapRelEbc senses, switching on its toxin. Structural modelling and exchange measurements show all three proteins locked in one complex. The authors liken the logic to plant and animal immunity, where damage to host machinery, rather than the invader itself, raises the alarm.
pmc-13424116:
Zhang, Qiu, and Shang build an automated pain reader in this 2026 study for the patients least able to report pain: newborns in intensive care. Training drew on 9,485 annotated facial images from 153 neonates, expanded past 25,000 samples with augmentation. On held-out test data the system reached 94.3 percent accuracy and an AUC of 0.978 against the study's labels, beating larger standard networks. A prospective hospital validation across 62 neonates and 287 painful procedures agreed substantially with expert nurse consensus, at a kappa of 0.84 in the reported analysis, while scoring each frame in about 0.3 seconds. Nurses rated it usable as a monitoring aid, not a replacement for judgment.
pmc-13424516:
Narjes Abshorshori and six colleagues measure how well surgical patients in southern Iran know their rights, and how well they think care teams honour them. Five hospital systems contributed 582 surgical inpatients, who completed two validated scales, one on rights awareness and one on perceived compliance by the healthcare team.

Most patients scored in the middle range for awareness, with wide differences between topics; privacy and confidentiality knowledge was weakest. Patients generally rated team compliance as high, yet privacy protection and access to their own records still showed gaps. Age, education, operation type, and hospital setting all shaped the scores. The authors call for targeted teaching of patients and staff, above all in hectic emergency settings.
pmc-13425616:
Ahmadi and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how the microbial communities of the mouth and gut may start and steer rheumatoid arthritis, and how changing them could become treatment. The disease is an autoimmune attack on joints, shaped by genes and environment. Mouth and gut microbes differ clearly between patients and healthy people, and some of the shifts look causal rather than incidental.

Certain mouth bacteria can alter the body's own proteins so the immune system reads them as foreign, a mimicry route to autoimmunity. Other helpful species that calm immune responses run low in patients. The review weighs the tools now being tried to reset the balance: probiotics, stool transplants, antibiotics, and tailored nutrition.
pmc-13425816:
Chandrashekar and collaborators built a brain-wide targeting atlas for transcranial magnetic stimulation. That is a magnetic brain treatment done without surgery. So the team sought treatment sites picked from each brain's wiring, rather than fixed scalp landmarks.

They combined clinical, structural, and resting-state scans from 350 veterans with and without PTSD. Math models linked patterns of functional connectivity to symptom severity. Functional connectivity means activity in two brain regions rising and falling together. The team then ran computer models of electric fields at 200 random sites on each person's brain surface. That let them predict which sites would shift wiring toward relief. The atlas flagged two opposite patterns. Boosting left prefrontal connectivity should reduce symptoms. So should dampening parietal and occipital connectivity, in the side and back regions.
pmc-13426716:
De Guzman and colleagues report a 2026 case of a stomach that burst from internal pressure in a 27-year-old non-verbal man with a complex medical history. His background included repaired esophageal atresia, severe gastroparesis, where the stomach barely empties, a prior anti-reflux operation that wraps the stomach top, and feeding tube dependence.

He arrived with a swollen belly and failing breathing, fast heart and breathing rates, and deranged blood chemistry. Scans showed free air and a perforation. Emergency surgery found a large tear, about eight to ten centimeters, in the back wall of the stomach with heavy contamination. Surgeons removed part of the stomach and managed the abdomen in stages, adding a venting tube and a feeding tube into the intestine at a second operation. He recovered with critical care.
pmc-13427416:
Nabil Ziani and coauthors report a cirrhosis-like liver change from metastatic breast cancer in a 2026 case study. Their patient was a 65-year-old woman with triple-negative disease, an extremely rare pairing for this liver pattern, followed over twelve months by CT and MRI.

Despite chemotherapy, her liver developed marked lobulation, capsular retraction, and segmental shrinkage without any cirrhosis risk factors. Recognizing this pseudocirrhosis prevents mislabeling metastatic change as ordinary liver failure. Scans month by month let the team watch the liver warp in slow steps, a rare chance to learn how this odd state forms in a sick woman.
pmc-13427516:
Yohei Mikami and coauthors used data-driven clustering to find a relapse-prone ulcerative colitis subtype in Japan in a 2026 prospective multicenter cohort study. Symptoms often mismatch true disease activity in ulcerative colitis, and whether patient-reported quality-of-life measures reveal meaningful subphenotypes during remission was unknown. Data came from the YOURS registry of Japanese patients, collected between December 2018 and June 2022 across centers.

Clustering combined laboratory values with reported symptoms, fatigue, anxiety, and disease-specific quality of life to define groups. One identified subtype carried high relapse risk, suggesting routine patient questionnaires could flag patients needing closer monitoring while they feel well. A man or woman who feels well may still sit in the high risk set, and a short form they fill in could be the flag that brings them back in time.
pmc-13427716:
Polese and colleagues published a 2026 set of reflections on engineering research in the real world. Five teams revisit papers they published in Communications Engineering in 2022.
