One team showed wireless networks and weather satellites can share high airwaves. Their live test rig sensed passing satellites and yielded the band in seconds. Policy bodies now treat such sharing as a real option in filings. Other cases trace gains for research groups and wider communities alike. Together, the pieces argue that impact grows slowly and rarely in straight lines. The cases span work first shared with readers four years earlier.
pmc-13427916:
Mayanne Karla da Silva and colleagues review the coloured fungi that live in the world's hottest and coldest deserts, from the Atacama to polar ice fields. These fungi make pigments, natural colour chemicals, that help them survive fierce sun, dryness, and cold.

The review gathers what is known of their naming, family relations, and genes, and the uses their pigments may serve. Most records belong to two big fungal groups, which produce colours classed as melanins, carotenoids, and polyketides. Uses span farming, food, cosmetics, and medicine, and even space research, where hardy fungi model life in harsh worlds. Sequenced strains carry genes for making pigments and for coping with stress, da Silva notes.
pmc-13428116:
Bywater and colleagues report a 2026 case, with a literature review, of a 48-year-old kidney transplant patient who also had primary myelofibrosis, a bone marrow scarring disease. Balancing the two conditions was delicate: transplant drugs suppress the immune system, and the marrow disease later needed a JAK inhibitor, a drug that further dampens immunity.

After his living-donor transplant, worsening marrow disease led to the JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib. BK polyomavirus, a normally quiet virus that attacks transplanted kidneys, then appeared in his blood, forcing dose cuts. His course was further complicated by graft rejection. Switching to a second-generation JAK inhibitor, fedratinib, improved the marrow measures while graft function and virus levels stabilized. The authors stress close monitoring of total immune suppression in such layered cases.
pmc-13429116:
Juanjuan Xiong and colleagues trace, in a 2026 study, the hidden paths between how lung-hypertension patients see their illness and how well they live with it. Pulmonary hypertension strains the heart by raising pressure in the lung arteries. The team surveyed 185 patients at two campuses of one Chinese hospital between mid-2025 and early 2026. Validated scales measured illness perception, confidence in self-care, fear of movement, and quality of life.

Statistical mediation tests showed that a harsher view of the illness lowered quality of life partly by raising fear of movement. Self-confidence carried a smaller share of the effect on its own. A chain ran through both: fear first, then confidence, accounting for a small slice of the total. The authors suggest therapy that calms movement fears and builds self-care confidence together, rather than treating the body alone.
pmc-13430216:
Lacouture and colleagues test an asthma drug against skin reactions caused by cancer therapy. Their 2026 phase II trial enrols 47 patients whose systemic cancer treatments triggered eosinophil-related cutaneous adverse events, rashes driven by a white blood cell type called eosinophils. Patients received benralizumab, an antibody that depletes eosinophils, on its approved dosing schedule at a single centre.

Of 42 patients evaluable at the main checkpoint, 76 percent responded by week four, with reactions dropping to mild or better. Median rash grade halved, quality of life improved, the affected skin area shrank, and blood eosinophil counts fell. Every patient whose rash followed two specific cancer drugs, alpelisib and enfortumab vedotin, responded by week four. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate and likely unrelated to the study drug, and the authors call for larger controlled trials.
pmc-13436116:
Vibol Iem and a large team ask clinics and patients in seven countries whether pooled sputum testing for tuberculosis feels workable in 2026. Pooling runs several spit samples in one gene test to save cost. Thirty eight expert interviews and eighteen group talks span Bangladesh to Viet Nam.

Stakeholders called pooling workable in clinics and in community drives. Trust ran higher where teams had pooled before. Fit with test routines, safety steps, training, and clear manuals decided the verdict. The World Health Organization backed pooling in 2026, yet field proof was thin until now. Rollout guides can build on the terms staff named here.
pmc-13437316:
Limin Wang and colleagues surveyed Chinese college students about knee trouble and how it relates to their activity habits. Knee pain is rising among young adults, not just older people. Their 2026 study gathered valid answers from 1,111 students between June and November 2022. About seventeen percent reported knee symptoms, and more than a third said their knees made sounds after sitting or standing for a long time.

Strong exercise carried a mixed message. Students with moderate to high levels of vigorous activity had notably higher odds of knee symptoms, and so did those who climbed more than twenty floors a day. pmc-13479816:

pmc-13483616:

pmc-13483716:

pmc-13484916:

pmc-13486516:

pmc-13486716:

pmc-13488316:

pmc-13490416:

pmc-13491616:

pmc-13493216:

pmc-13493816:

pmc-13495116:

pmc-13495216:

pmc-13495416:

pmc-13499416:

pmc-13507216:

pmc-13512616:

Days later, still ill with climbing markers and new skin nodules, she was rechecked. An antibody titer more than three times the normal ceiling proved a recent streptococcal infection, and the Jones criteria were met. Antibiotics plus high-dose aspirin brought fast improvement, and monthly depot penicillin began to guard her heart.
pmc-13513816:
Camargo García and colleagues compared five fruit and vegetable residue mixtures as feed for black soldier fly larvae under tropical conditions. The larvae are widely used to convert organic leftovers into protein-rich material, but performance depends heavily on what they are fed. Coffee husk was added to some mixes as a structural bulking material.

Camargo García found the all-fruit mixture produced the most total fresh and dry larval biomass per rearing unit. The all-vegetable and half-and-half mixtures looked better once results were adjusted for the estimated number of viable larvae and the dry feed offered. A vegetable-heavy mix performed worst across several measures. Harvested biomass differed in protein, fat, energy, and mineral content by mixture. Safety screening found no Salmonella in the pooled sample, supporting local residue valorization while flagging density standardization for future work.
pmc-13514216:
Rawan Budair and five co-authors describe a cluster of yeast bloodstream infections in children with cancer at a Jordanian center, in 2026 work. Seven confirmed cases appeared between June and September 2025, against a background of one case in the prior six months. Five more children were treated for suspected fungal invasion without positive blood cultures. Most confirmed patients had leukemia, and every one carried a central line and recent broad antibiotic exposure.

The main species was Candida tropicalis, and azole drug resistance appeared in a large share of tested isolates. The cluster coincided with a plumbing failure and linked water event inside the hospital, which the team flags as a putative source. A multi-field infection control response followed. The authors stress that candidemia kills more than thirty percent of such children in lower-income settings, so fast source hunting matters.
pmc-13516116:
Silvia Gabriela Ionescu leads a twelve-author team mapping Candida yeast species across pregnancy-related samples in a 2026 retrospective study from Iași, Romania. Positive cultures turn up often in obstetric care, yet species patterns by sample type were little charted. The team reviewed a single centre's Candida-positive results from 2024: 242 amniotic fluid isolates, 2,020 from vaginal discharge, and 827 from lochia, the discharge after birth.

Candida albicans led everywhere, taking about seventy percent of amniotic and lochial finds and fifty-five percent of vaginal ones. Non-albicans species, chiefly Pichia kudriavzevii, filled most of the rest. Vaginal samples carried the richest links to maternal and pregnancy factors, while the other two types showed few. Older maternal age was the one steady correlate of non-albicans finds. The authors back routine species-level naming for surveillance, while drawing no treatment lessons, since drug sensitivity and baby outcomes went unmeasured.
pmc-13517616:
Guillermo Cortés-Roco leads a seven-author trial of jump-style training in boulder climbers in a 2026 exploratory paper. Bouldering demands force in split seconds, so plyometric work, explosive push-offs and catches, might transfer. Eighteen trained male climbers split into two groups of nine. One added two plyometric sessions weekly for ten weeks; the other trained as usual. Lab tests covered finger strength, pull-up power, push-up power, and jump height.

The training group gained about four extra pull-ups and clearly faster force in the early pull-up phase. Push-up power rose as well. Finger strength, finger speed, top pull-up strength, and jump height showed no clear group difference. Cortés-Roco's team stresses the small numbers and shaky reliability of speed measures. They offer the gains as early, movement-specific hints, worth a bigger and stricter trial before coaches rewrite programmes around them.
pmc-13518316:
Suryakanta Mondal leads a eighteen-author team switching a magnet with electricity alone in a 2026 study. Spintronics wants magnetic states flipped by current for leaner memory, but flipping between two wholly different magnetic phases, not just nudging one, is largely untested. Their stage is a thin film of a strontium-doped samarium manganite, a strongly interacting oxide.

Past a threshold current, the film snapped from a low-resistance ferromagnetic state into a high-resistance antiferromagnetic-like one, and the switch reversed on command. Built into nanoscale tunnel devices a quarter micron square, the effect gave stable two-state resistance with magnetoresistance above two hundred percent, tunable by current, heat, and field. Mondal's team presents phase-transition switching as a fresh device route, beyond the torque tricks that dominate spintronics today, with potential for dense, low-power information hardware.
pmc-13518916:
Shuai Xia leads a ten-author team making acetamide directly from carbon dioxide and nitrate with electricity in 2026. Amides appear in a quarter of marketed drugs, yet factory synthesis needs high heat and emits carbon. Electrochemical routes stall because carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds compete during formation.

Their catalyst places single nickel atoms beside copper nanoclusters on nitrogen-doped carbon. Nickel sites turn carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide, while copper neighbors couple carbons and reduce nitrate toward an amine fragment, and the pair then joins the pieces. Acetamide formed at a high yield rate under industrial-level current and ran stably for 160 hours. Spectroscopy and theory traced the boost to strong nickel-copper electronic coupling.
pmc-13519016:
M. V. Suryanarayana, Dipjyoti Balo Majumder, and M. Sankari model a laser route in 2026 for enriching erbium-169, a medical isotope whose decay profile resembles the cancer therapy workhorse lutetium-177. Lutetium supply is squeezed because its parent isotopes are hard to enrich. Erbium-169's longer half-life also eases shipping to remote hospitals.

Their three-step laser isotope separation analysis, built on density matrix math, varied atomic, laser, and beam settings to tune yield. The math suggests making 30 to 300 daily doses at 7.4 gigabecquerels each, with very high specific activity. The scheme works with medium-flux reactors, giving hospitals a backup supply line without scarce high-flux plants.
pmc-13520316:
Dilek Kurnaz and colleagues ask in 2026 whether vitamin D levels in preterm infants relate to inflammation scores calculated from a routine blood count. Such scores combine white-cell and platelet counts and are cheap to obtain in intensive care.

Charts for 212 infants born at or before 34 weeks were reviewed. Vitamin D was low in many infants, with deficiency in about four in ten. Blood-count scores and standard infection markers differed little across vitamin D groups in the opening results. Readers get a careful check on whether a common vitamin measure adds information beyond tests already taken on the first day of life.
pmc-13520416:
Wei Zhang leads a large team reporting in 2026 a blood test approach that combines protein and metabolite profiling to detect early breast cancer without imaging. Standard scans miss cancers in dense breast tissue, a common issue for Asian women, so a biology-based blood route is attractive.

A prospective study across nine centres enrolled 662 participants, profiling thousands of proteins and hundreds of metabolites. Patterns involved cell-structure proteins and altered fat metabolism, grouped into modules tied to malignancy. A combined model named ProMeta-BC was built from those features, with separate groups used for validation. Node spread risk scoring is also addressed in the full analysis.
pmc-13521016:
Haixuan Deng and colleagues compare in 2026 housing systems for slow-growing broiler chickens, testing free-range access and enrichment items against net-floor rearing. Consumer interest in welfare-friendly poultry has grown, while tailored systems for slow breeds remain under-studied.

A total of 1,350 female chickens were split across four systems with sand baths, perches, ramps, platforms and hide houses as enrichment. Net-floor birds finished heavier, while free-range birds gave higher dressed yield with less belly fat and richer breast colour. Fat profiles also shifted with range access. Results help producers balance growth speed against carcass traits and welfare features.
pmc-13522516:
M Andrea Pisauro, Daniele Pollicino, Lucy Fisher, and Matthew A J Apps investigate how deadline pressure changes willingness to work hard in a 2026 study combining behavior, modeling, and brain imaging. Their framework defines pressure as work remaining divided by time remaining. Across four studies, people made effortful choices that advanced longer-term goals rather than earning immediate reward.

Rising pressure shifted people from avoiding effort toward seeking the progress effort brings. Brain scans at very high field strength showed connected areas in the putamen and midcingulate tracking and updating pressure estimates. Separate subregions handled effort itself, whether it was being avoided or sought. The results explain, in neural and computational terms, how looming deadlines keep people on track toward distant goals.
pmc-13522616:
Haihui Shen, Hu Han, Jianli Liu, and Dong Yang model signal loss in optical fibers bent inside hot, deep wells in a 2026 simulation study. Temperatures in such wells can range from near room level to very high, and tiny bends leak light in ways that heat complicates. A combined model linked thermal, mechanical, and optical effects so that temperature entered the bend-loss calculation directly.

Multimode fiber showed oscillating loss driven by interactions between modes, with a non-steady response to temperature. Single-mode fiber stayed stable until a threshold near the top of the range, where loss surged, while its phase remained continuous. Longer wavelengths made single-mode fiber more bend-sensitive. The results give engineers criteria for choosing fiber and compensating loss in extreme downhole telemetry.
pmc-13523216:
Chunyan Yang and co-authors profile fear of disease progression in glaucoma patients in a 2026 questionnaire study. Glaucoma slowly damages vision, and fear that it will worsen can erode quality of life. Two hundred twenty-seven patients completed scales on fear of progression, eye symptoms, and illness perception, alongside clinical and social information. Statistical profiling grouped patients by their fear patterns.

Three groups emerged: a low-fear supported group covering about one fifth, a moderate-fear stable group near half, and a high-fear uncertain group near one third. Middle age, unemployment, being married, worse visual field loss in the poorer eye, and a heavier perceived illness burden each raised the odds of higher fear. The authors urge clinicians to identify high-fear patients and tailor psychological support to their needs.
pmc-13523316:
Hossein Pourahmadiyan-Nadiki and colleagues apply deep learning to sharpen dental X-rays in a 2026 study. One thousand bitewing and periapical radiographs were divided into training and test sets. High-resolution images were deliberately downscaled to create low-resolution versions, and three super-resolution approaches were trained to reconstruct the originals. The best design was then tested against simple interpolation methods on six quality metrics.

After repeated training runs, the chosen model scored strongly across all metrics, including a high structural similarity score and a solid signal quality value. Every metric beat the conventional interpolation methods. The authors conclude that the deep learning approach can meaningfully enhance dental radiograph resolution, which could support more accurate diagnosis where original image quality is limited by anatomy, noise, or equipment.
pmc-13525016:
Sheer A. Joodi and others review, in a 2026 paper, research and treatment frontiers in fibromyalgia, a chronic syndrome of widespread pain, fatigue, broken sleep, and trouble thinking. Few drugs are cleared for it, and they mainly ease symptoms, often not enough or with harsh side effects. The review joins disease mechanisms with new uses for old drugs.

Topics covered include altered neurochemistry, central sensitization where pain signaling grows louder, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial problems, gut microbe upset, and autoimmunity. Drug classes reused this way range from antidepressants and antiepileptics to cannabinoids, melatonin agonists, and antidiabetic agents, most still in lab or early human testing. The authors urge work on several fronts: stronger descending pain inhibition, a calmer specific inflammasome, and repair of oxidative and mitochondrial dysfunction.
pmc-13526716:
Elena Shipitsyna and others pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, what microbes live in amniotic fluid sludge, an ultrasound finding tied to infection inside the womb and early preterm birth. Its microbial makeup was poorly characterized. Three databases were searched through February 2026 for studies with at least ten cases diagnosed by transvaginal ultrasound.

Only four studies with 85 women qualified. The pooled share carrying any microorganism was thirty-five percent, and Ureaplasma species were the most common finding at 17 percent. Sampling route explained much of the variation. Removing the single study that sampled through the vagina dropped prevalence to twenty-eight percent and erased heterogeneity, while vaginal samples showed more diverse microbes including normal vaginal residents, suggesting contamination. Abdominal sampling is recommended as more trustworthy.
pmc-13527116:
Amaogu and colleagues published a 2026 study on shrubs and trees creeping north across Canada. Taller growth in the boreal-tundra zone is widely expected to warm the land. Dark plants absorb more sunlight, the usual story goes, speeding thaw. The team checked 38 years of satellite and surface-energy records against that story.

About 70 percent of ecozones showed net surface cooling, not warming, trends. Shifts toward mixedwood and broadleaf growth drove the strongest cooling measured. Those landscapes warmed far less each year than shrub or conifer zones. Moisture and plant type decided each zone's direction of change overall. Northern greening may thus brake, not boost, some surface warming. Climate models may need to split greening by plant type.
pmc-13529616:
Tamás Faragó and five colleagues test whether dogs hear their own kind's voices as special in a 2026 study. Dogs first heard plain noise until they tuned it out. New sounds then probed their attention. Test sounds covered dog calls, human voices, chimpanzee calls, and violin music. None used distress cries, which can swamp subtle effects.

Dogs perked up for every new sound. Responses to dog, human, and music sounds beat chance. Chimpanzee calls did not clear that bar. Dog voices drew the strongest rebound of all. Human and chimpanzee voices tied with each other. Voice as such beat no category by itself. The authors read this as a biological relevance effect. Being the same species matters more than being social or merely vocal, at least for dogs.
pmc-13529716:
Leon Wang, Sara Knox, Andrew B. Lawson, and Abe Mollalo map farm pesticide patterns against Alzheimer's rates across United States counties in a 2026 study. Instead of single chemicals, they grouped use into exposure regimes. Over four hundred pesticides were screened. A stability method kept 112 and sorted them into twenty-five clusters. County dementia rates were then compared.

Twenty clusters tied significantly with Alzheimer's prevalence. The strongest positive ties came from soil fumigation mixes, herbicide-heavy weed control, and nerve-active insecticide systems. Herbicide families of two other kinds leaned the other way. The full model explained fifty-nine percent of county-to-county spread. The authors stress this is an area-level snapshot, not proof of personal risk. They ask for finer, longer tracking of real exposures. The mixture view, they argue, matches how farms actually spray.
pmc-13530716:
Youn and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 160, a new mouse model of exercise-induced muscle injury. This is the fatigue-driven damage athletes suffer from relentless repetition rather than one violent strain. No animal model had reproduced that slow-burn condition.

Nine young male mice received five daily sets of one hundred electrically triggered isometric contractions of the calf muscles for six straight days. Strength fell significantly from the second day, measured as a drop in maximum torque, and weight-bearing on the hind paw declined in parallel, signaling pain. Muscle harvested on day seven and stained with a dye that enters only damaged fibers confirmed fiber injury. The remaining mice recovered fully by week four, when their tissue was checked. A separate four-mouse group sacrificed on day four captured the early stage of damage.
pmc-13530816:
Knapik and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 181, the largest injury census of National Hockey League players. It was built from the league's own medical record system rather than public reports. It covers nine seasons between 2012 and 2023, skipping the pandemic-shortened ones.

The system logged 24,776 injuries. Injury density ran highest in the playoffs, at about 68 per thousand athlete exposures, against about 51 in the regular season. Forwards were hurt most often, the first period produced the largest share of injuries, and pucks caused about a quarter of them. The head and the hand were the commonest sites. An average injury cost about two man-games, but knee and shoulder injuries cost the most time each. Knee injuries, abdominal injuries, body checks, and the goaltender position predicted absences of five games or more.
pmc-13531816:
Fang Zhang and colleagues document a 2026 prenatal puzzle where a fetus carried two copies of chromosome 3 from the father alone. Screening in a 19-year-old mother first flagged a duplication on that chromosome, while the baby grew slowly in the womb. Fluid testing combined chromosome counting, microarray, and family gene sequencing.

The chromosome count looked normal, yet a long identical stretch revealed the double paternal copy, with no harmful recessive variants found. Placenta tissue later showed leftover three-copy cells, evidence of an early rescue event. The boy was born at 38 weeks and developed normally to age two and a half.
pmc-13532816:
Daniel Pecher and colleagues report in 2026 a very sensitive urine test for testosterone esters, the lab-made forms used in doping. Natural and added testosterone share the same structure, which makes proof hard. Esters are not made by the body, so finding them gives clear proof of doping.

The new method uses a chemical tag to boost signal and reach levels below one picogram per millilitre. Applied to doping control urine, it found esters in cases with raised hormone ratios. Readers gain a urine-based tool that adds to blood tests for catching banned hormone use.
pmc-13532916:
Severine Lannoy and colleagues use Swedish records in 2026 to study family genetic risk for suicidal acts. Many studies tie such acts to mental disorders, yet a large share occur with no prior diagnosis. The cohort held 926,040 people born from 1980 to 1990, with family risk scores built from relatives.

Only about 30 percent of people with an attempt or death had a prior mental diagnosis. All studied disorders raised risk a lot, and family genetic risk ran higher in those with a diagnosis. Genetic effects looked stronger in people with no prior disorder, so screening should reach beyond clinics.
pmc-13534416:
Anya S Plotnikova and colleagues compare in 2026 viral vectors that reach dopamine cells in the substantia nigra of rhesus monkeys from a distance. Tools for targeted gene delivery work well in rodents yet lag in primates, where dopamine cells sit deep and are hard to reach cleanly. Injecting a larger, easier region lets viruses travel backward along cell fibres.

The comparison highlights one vector that efficiently marked dopamine neurons through this backward route. Such targeting could pair with cell-specific switches for precise studies of reward and movement circuits. Readers gain a base for gene therapy models in primate brains.
pmc-13534716:
Caio Sberni Pinheiro Souza and colleagues study in 2026 awake teeth grinding habits in esports players in Sao Paulo, Brazil. The habit has barely been explored in this group, despite long, tense play sessions. A total of 447 players completed self-report questionnaires drawn from standard bruxism tools.

About 35 percent met the mark for frequent awake grinding. Frequent grinders reported far more clenching and daily jaw pain than low-frequency peers. Past grinding history, mental distress, and reflux symptoms each linked independently in adjusted models, supporting prevention and education for players. The findings point to joint care across dental, mental health, and gut clinics for this group.
pmc-13536616:
Xiao-Fei Wu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether mismatch between remnant cholesterol and LDL cholesterol predicts new hypertension in Chinese adults. Remnant cholesterol is the fat-rich leftover part of blood lipids, and its role apart from LDL was unclear. Records followed 4,508 adults aged 45 and over with normal pressure for nine years.

About four in ten developed hypertension during follow-up, and mismatch was common across the group. Higher remnant levels meant higher risk even after full adjustment. People with high remnants but low LDL faced more risk than those low on both measures.
pmc-13536816:
Syed Abul Faraz, Imtiaz Ahmed, and Syed Jaffar Abbas Zaidi validate dental age methods for forensic use in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Tooth growth on X-rays offers a reliable age clue where birth records are missing. The team reviewed 700 panoramic X-rays for people aged about 4 to 18 years, estimating dental age with two atlas methods and comparing each estimate with true age. A Pakistan-specific reference chart was also developed.

Both atlases tracked true age closely, yet the London Atlas showed smaller bias, tighter agreement, and higher accuracy within one year. Early tooth growth ran slightly late in the local group, limiting direct transfer of outside charts. The new local atlas is offered as a closer reference for legal age decisions in Pakistan.
pmc-13539716:
Yan Wang and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of how people with cancer who struggle to swallow decide about a feeding tube placed through the abdomen into the stomach. The work drew on interviews at two large hospitals in Fujian Province, China, where family views carry real weight in medical choices.

Eighteen patients who had faced the tube decision spoke in depth with the researchers. Their accounts grouped into hopes for survival and clear advice from clinicians, worries where feelings pulled against reason, and gaps in the information they received. The authors argue for plain, open information, better talks with care teams, and stronger backing from relatives and fellow patients.
pmc-13543216:
Felix Bolinski's team ran a 2026 experiment on how Dutch railway delay notices after a collision affect listeners' thoughts about suicide. Earlier research found that saying a delay followed a collision with a person raised thoughts of suicide and negative feelings. In 2021 the railway switched to simply saying a collision had occurred. The team randomly assigned 346 railway panel members to hear one of several wordings, crossed with whether the delay affected them personally.

The new wording gave fewer thoughts of suicide than the old person-naming phrasing, yet more than an announcement blaming emergency services, which listeners liked least. Reactions did not differ much between wordings. Delays hitting the listener personally raised thoughts of suicide and negative emotions, while also raising willingness to help fellow passengers. The authors judge the collision wording, or the emergency-services wording, better than naming a person.
pmc-13543416:
Samuel Coleman and colleagues published a 2026 software paper presenting CRISPRessoSea, a tool for analysing pooled CRISPR editing experiments. CRISPR editing can also cut at unintended sites resembling the target. Pooled amplicon sequencing, which reads many edited regions at once, is a standard way to check both intended and off-target changes. Comparing results across many samples and experiments, however, has lacked a standard workflow.

The new package processes, compares, and visualises editing rates from such pooled experiments in a uniform way. It covers both classic nuclease editing and base editing, where single letters are changed without cutting both strands. Outputs are standardised, data-rich summaries meant to make editing specificity easier to judge and reproduce across laboratories. The software is freely available, and the authors position it as shared infrastructure for a field where transparent off-target reporting matters for clinical translation.
pmc-13546516:
Qimei Chen and colleagues investigated in 2026 whether exosomes from human umbilical cord stem cells can treat pattern hair loss, and how. Exosomes are small parcels cells use to pass molecular messages. In a mouse model of the condition, the parcels reached the cells at the base of hair follicles, nudged resting follicles back into growth, and reduced follicle shrinkage.

Sequencing showed the parcels were rich in Let-7 family microRNAs. One of them, Let-7b-5p, tags a helper protein for destruction, which lowers the androgen receptor that drives follicle damage and switches on a growth pathway. A second microRNA damped a pathway that promotes follicle cell death. An early clinical test also found higher hair density and thicker hairs after treatment.
pmc-13546716:
Ade Sukma and co-authors tested in 2026 a probiotic bacterium taken from Dadiah, a traditional Indonesian fermented buffalo milk, against diarrhea caused by Staphylococcus aureus in mice. Twenty-five mice were divided among healthy controls, untreated diarrhea controls, an antibiotic group, and two probiotic dosing schedules. The bacterium, Lactococcus lactis D4, was given by mouth for seven days after infection.

Mice on the twice-daily probiotic schedule fared best, losing little body weight and passing firmer stools than untreated animals. The authors describe the strain as a promising ecological alternative to antibiotics, which face growing resistance in this bacterium. They also frame the work as support for developing local fermented foods into health products.
pmc-13547216:
Cedric E. Beogo, Wepari C. Yaguibou, and Luc T. Bambara measured in 2026 radon gas levels inside 21 homes in the village of Villy, alongside temperature, humidity, and other indoor conditions. Radon seeps from the ground through cracks and is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Each home was monitored for 48 hours with a detector that also logged weather variables and movement.

Radon concentrations spread widely between homes, averaging about 45 becquerels per cubic meter, with the highest reading near 122 in the reported range. Indoor air was hot, averaging about 36 degrees, and dry. The authors set out the variation across homes and over time so that local exposure can be judged against health guidance and linked to the conditions that let radon build up.
pmc-13548616:
Danyang Xu and colleagues test whether a calming protein released by stem cells can ease bone cancer pain, in a 2026 rat and cell study. The protein works by quieting an inflammatory alarm in the spinal cord. Bone marrow stem cells injected near the spine were already known to relieve such pain, and they release extra TSG-6 when inflamed. Rats received cancer cells in the shin bone to model the pain, then stem cells or pure TSG-6 near the spine.

Both treatments improved pain behavior, lowered the NLRP3 inflammasome machinery in spinal microglia, and cut inflammatory factor release. In dishes, the same treatments stopped microglial cells from undergoing fiery death after a bacterial trigger. Stem cells stripped of TSG-6 lost much of that power, fingering the protein as a key messenger. The authors propose TSG-6 delivery as a candidate therapy for cancer bone pain.
pmc-13548716:
Ruikun Jia and colleagues study how carrying several heart and metabolic conditions at once affects people after a rhythm-correcting procedure for atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 three-cohort analysis. Over three thousand patients in the main group underwent catheter ablation, and about one in five had cardiometabolic multimorbidity, meaning at least two such conditions together. The team tracked rhythm relapse and deaths, then asked which body changes carried the effect.

Multimorbidity independently raised the risks of relapse, death from any cause, and heart-related death, with risk climbing as conditions stacked up. An enlarged left atrium carried nearly half of the effect on relapse, with insulin resistance and two other measures sharing the rest. Machine learning beat standard risk scores at forecasting relapse, especially a model that also used early post-procedure relapse.
pmc-13549216:
Valenziano and colleagues reviewed research on predicting difficult laryngeal exposure during microlaryngoscopy, a surgery performed through the mouth with a microscope. Difficult exposure means the surgeon cannot see the voice box well. Poor exposure can lengthen operations or leave tumor surgery incomplete. Their 2026 scoping review searched two large databases for tests that forecast this problem before patients are put to sleep.

Valenziano analyzed sixteen studies and found the same predictors coming up again. They were body mass index, neck size, the gap between the front teeth when the mouth opens, jaw-to-throat distance, dental condition, and a standard mouth-opening score. Two combined scoring tools, the Laryngoscore and its shorter mini version, looked promising but did unevenly when tested at new centers. The authors conclude that no single measure works reliably yet and call for large studies at many centers with shared definitions to build a reliable prediction tool.
pmc-13551916:
Sangwoo Cho, leading seven colleagues, published a 2026 imaging study asking whether a PET scan tracer for prostate cancer beats MRI at finding tumor left after hormone therapy. Twenty patients treated with androgen deprivation before prostate removal had MRI before and after therapy plus a PSMA-targeted PET scan, and lesion findings were compared against surgical pathology.

The PET scan's sensitivity and accuracy were far higher than post-therapy MRI in the reported figures, catching most residual lesions that MRI missed. Standard MRI measures shifted with therapy yet no longer separated tumor from benign enlargement afterward, and tracer uptake levels also overlapped after therapy. The authors call the PET approach feasible and promising for planning further management, while labeling the findings preliminary.
pmc-13553616:
Carl-Eric Aubin leads a thirteen-author team adding three-dimensional detail to the grading of curved spines in teens. Their 2026 study covers 162 young people with the common Lenke 1 pattern of adolescent scoliosis. Standard grading uses flat X-ray views, which miss twist and sideways shift at the curve's peak. The team rebuilt each spine in three dimensions from paired X-ray images.

Twist and shift varied widely even among teens whose flat views looked much alike. Links between curve size on flat views and the new measures changed by spine region. In the lower curve, several links were firm, while higher up they were weak or absent. The authors argue the added measures give surgeons facts that flat grading cannot supply on its own.
pmc-13554216:
Josef Huemer leads a nine-author team tracking heart and stroke risk after sudden retinal artery blockage in a 2026 London study. Such blockages blind an eye by cutting its blood supply, much like a stroke. The matched study followed 566 patients at a specialist eye hospital, linked to national health records. Full blockage of the central retinal artery stood out sharply from lesser events.

Those patients faced nearly triple the risk of later stroke or heart attack versus matched peers. Branch blockages and brief passing vision loss showed no such rise. New cases of a quivering heart rhythm appeared in six percent within a year after central blockage. The authors urge quick treatment, long heart monitoring, and strict prevention for these patients.
pmc-13556016:
Sherine Loyidcy Mariyanayagam and five colleagues surveyed in 2026 how health students in Sri Lanka know, view, and use artificial intelligence. Formal teaching about AI remains rare in health courses, especially in lower income countries. Their team questioned students at five state universities between March and June 2025, using an online questionnaire checked by experts before use.

Of 430 respondents, nearly all had heard of AI and most already used AI tools for study work. Yet very few had received formal training, and only about a fifth had met AI in clinical settings. Students whose courses included AI teaching were far more likely to use the tools and to have seen them in practice, and workshop attendance also helped. The authors argue that adding AI to the curriculum, not leaving it to chance, is what closes the gap.
pmc-13559416:
Shuyang Chen and colleagues test whether two blood-based scores can predict both survival and radiation side effects in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy. Their 2026 study followed 126 patients at Harbin Medical University Cancer Hospital treated between March 2019 and December 2022. The CONUT score and the Naples prognostic score both blend nutrition and inflammation markers from routine blood work.

Median follow-up reached 53 months. High scores on either measure independently predicted shorter progression-free and overall survival in adjusted models. Their accuracy for survival at two to five years sat in a similar range, with areas under the curve around 0.8 in several of the reported checks. High scores also flagged patients more likely to suffer grade 2 or worse lung or esophagus inflammation from radiation. The authors propose the pair as cheap dual-purpose tools for planning treatment and counseling patients.
pmc-13560116:
Qinxiang Shant Sin, Hun Yi Koh, and Kumaran Rasappan evaluate 3D-printed models as a teaching aid for musculoskeletal oncology anatomy. Their 2026 study enrolled 75 clinical-year students from two medical schools rotating through one teaching hospital's orthopaedic department. Students first answered a fifteen-question test using CT images of a large pelvic bone sarcoma, then repeated it with a printed model of the same tumor.

Scores rose after the model arrived, from a mean of 8.15 to 9.49 on the questionnaire. Final-year students improved most, and students who started weakest gained far more than strong starters. Most students, 91 percent in the feedback survey, said the model deepened their understanding of the tumor's anatomy. Nearly as many wanted printed models woven into anatomy teaching. The authors recommend 3D printing as an adjunct for surgical anatomy teaching, based on this self-controlled series.
pmc-13560216:
Maaweya Jabareen and colleagues survey e-cigarette use, knowledge, and attitudes among Palestinian medical students and physicians. Their 2026 cross-sectional study gathered 433 respondents from West Bank universities and teaching hospitals during November and December 2025. A set survey form, adapted from a proven tool, covered smoking habits plus knowledge and attitude scores.

About a third of participants currently used some tobacco or nicotine product, and 11.8 percent used e-cigarettes in the reported figures. Use ran far higher in men than women. Three quarters showed high knowledge, yet a quarter held positive attitudes toward vaping. Positive attitude strongly predicted current use in adjusted models, as did having close friends who smoke and spending long days at college. Half the vapers also smoked combustible products. The authors find the pattern worrying in future health professionals who should anchor tobacco control.
pmc-13563816:
Liming Zhao and four colleagues compare two ways to rescue a failed heart valve: threading a valve inside the old one by catheter, or reopening the chest for surgical replacement. Tissue valves wear out, and redo surgery is heavy going. Their 2026 study found patients treated between 2011 and 2021 in a readmissions database, then weighted the groups to balance them. Use of the catheter route, valve-in-valve TAVI, climbed across the decade while its patients grew younger.

The catheter patients died in hospital at half the odds of the surgical group and kept a survival edge at thirty days. Stroke, kidney failure, and major bleeding ran lower. The trade came later: readmissions ran higher at thirty days and six months. Days alive and out of hospital favoured the catheter route at both marks. Age changed some effects, so the authors ask which ages gain most from each path.
pmc-13563916:
Koji Nozaka, Shuichi Chida, and Naohisa Miyakoshi report a 2026 case of rebuilding a badly infected shin bone in a 20-year-old man after severe injury and several failed operations. The wedge-shaped gap measured 90 millimeters, the bone was infected with a drug-resistant staph bacterium, and the foot was fixed in a deformed position.

Instead of cutting away healthy slanted bone to make a flat join, the surgeons moved bone so the remaining cortex overlapped and locked against the transported segment. Overlap grew greatly by docking, preserving living bone. The case offers limb reconstruction surgeons a selective option for wedge-shaped defects rather than a general rule.
pmc-13573416:
Paula Corominas, with six colleagues, details a 2026 study of a parasite in dogs seen at two Barcelona animal hospitals. Leishmania infantum spreads by sand fly bites, and dogs are the main home reservoir for human infection. Barcelona was long seen as low risk, yet city and fringe growth may change that.

From September 2022 to September 2023, 189 owned dogs gave blood and eye swabs for antibody and gene tests. Infection showed in 10.6 percent of dogs, and every positive dog was sick, none merely in for a check-up. Both tests agreed at the same overall rate. All gene-positive dogs came from the fringe hospital, where the rate hit 15.2 percent against 3.9 percent at the city site. The authors read this as active spread, stronger at the city edge.
pmc-13574916:
Aida Kapic Lunder leads a 2026 study comparing MRI scans with tissue checks for a warning sign in rectal cancer. The sign, called EMVI, means tumour growth into veins just outside the bowel wall. Finding it before surgery can shape how strong treatment should be.

The team followed 150 patients with confirmed rectal cancer and read both scan and tissue results. MRI flagged the sign in 52.7 percent of cases and two readers agreed well on the scans. Scan-positive patients faced much higher risks of recurrence and death over time. Tissue-based readings showed no clear link to outcomes. The authors argue the scan result is the more useful guide for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13575216:
A I González, Pedro A Orellana, and Vladimir Juričić study exotic bound states in a triple quantum dot device in a 2026 physics paper. Quantum dots are tiny islands that hold single electrons. Bound states in the continuum are trapped states that sit inside a range of free energies yet stay localised, a rare interference effect.

Their device couples a central dot to normal leads, with side dots touching superconducting electrodes. An applied voltage reveals interference between the direct path through the centre and indirect paths via the side dots. In the balanced case a true bound state of Andreev type appears. Shifting the side dot energies softens it into a near-bound state. Current dips to near zero at the matching voltages, and side dot charges shift in step, giving an internal check on the effect.
pmc-13575716:
Anne Snelson leads a 2026 audit study of dietitian staffing and malnutrition in dialysis patients in Victoria, Australia. Good nutrition support matters in kidney dialysis care, and guidelines set a target of one full-time dietitian per 143 patients. The team tracked whether staffing kept pace over a decade.

Nine point-in-time audits ran between 2009 and 2024 across centre-based, home, and peritoneal dialysis. Between 2014 and 2024 staffing grew with patient numbers, holding ratios between one dietitian per 126 and per 157 patients. Assessment coverage in home dialysis rose from 25 to 96 percent. Malnutrition fell from 25 to 18 percent in centre patients and from 22 to 11 percent in home patients. Rates stayed higher in older adults, women, and people in their first dialysis year.
pmc-13576116:
Scovia Nalugo Mbalinda leads a 2026 study of HPV vaccine uptake among young Ugandans living with HIV. HPV infection and its diseases hit this group hard, and the vaccine can prevent much of that harm. Uganda's uptake, though, has stayed patchy, with many starting the doses yet few finishing them.

The survey covered 274 clinic patients aged 15 to 24 in 2024, and their ages averaged 20.3 years. Starting the vaccine was reported by 68.2 percent, while only 24.1 percent had completed two or more doses. Starting linked strongly to school teaching about the vaccine, living within five kilometres of the clinic, vaccine stock on site, and younger age. Completion linked to the older age band. The authors urge priority for this group and fixes aimed at finishing the course.
pmc-13580316:
Julio Fernández-Fernández and colleagues show that how charges are arranged, not just how many there are, steers droplets formed by floppy protein polymers, in a 2026 study. Such polymers mimic the shapeless proteins that gather into drops inside cells. Single chains carrying one charge sign refused to clump under body like conditions. Mixing a positive and a negative chain brought clumping back as the charges balanced each other.

Linking the same two chains into one molecule changed the game again. The linked version paired charges inside itself more, leaving the dense drop with different leftover charge and feel. Drops either blended into one phase or split into layers depending on that wiring. Acidity inside the drops shifted too. The team frames wiring as a design dial for building tiny compartments.
pmc-13582216:
Thakshani Wimalanathan and colleagues link heart muscle scarring to weaker, less synced squeezing in older adults, in a 2026 study from Norway. The group scanned 200 people born in 1950. None had known artery disease. The scans graded both scar tissue and the spread of fluid in the muscle, a sign of fine scarring. Motion tracking then measured how much the main chamber shortens and how evenly its walls pull together.

Visible scars tied to weaker shortening and to a larger share of segments falling below the healthy strain line. Scarred hearts also pulled less evenly across segments. A fluid spread score above a set line tied to weaker motion on both axes. The authors read silent scarring as an early drag on heart mechanics in the general older population.
pmc-13586316:
Yingwei Zhu and colleagues uncover how bowel cancer that has spread learns to shrug off the drug cetuximab. The drug blocks a growth receptor called EGFR, yet most patients' tumors resist it in time. Their 2026 study found a metabolic enzyme, GDH1, piling up in treated tumor samples. They traced a chain that starts when the drug blocks a normal tagging step, one that would send that enzyme for disposal.

With the enzyme spared, cells made more of a chemical called alpha-ketoglutarate. That chemical woke a second enzyme that rewired tumor metabolism, quieted immune attack, and fed a growth pathway that drives spread to the liver. Pairing cetuximab with a blocker of the first enzyme undid those shifts in their models. The authors suggest watching the chemical in blood to pick patients who might gain from the pairing.
pmc-13591316:
Nirasha Jayawardhana and three colleagues coat cotton cloth with sulfur nanoparticles to stop fungal growth. Cotton soaks up moisture, which invites fungi that stain, weaken, and soil the fabric. The team made tiny sulfur particles by a simple chemical route and soaked woven cotton in them so the particles spread through the fibers. Treated cloth then faced a common mold in a standard test.

Growth of the mold was strongly curbed compared with plain cotton. After five and ten wash cycles the cloth still fought the fungus, showing the particles cling well to the fibers. Jayawardhana and the team pitch sulfur as a low poison, metal free finish for health care cloth and protective gear, where lasting hygiene matters.
pmc-13591716:
Bing Han leads a 2026 study scanning blood plasma for chemical clues to schizophrenia, a severe mental illness whose roots stay unclear. The team compared 30 patients with 30 healthy controls using untargeted metabolomics, a method that measures over a thousand small molecules at once. Statistical sorting pulled out 237 molecules that differed clearly between the groups.

Most of the differing molecules were fats, organic acids, and amino acid kin, which made up near 70 percent of the set. Pathway checks pointed to amino acid handling, energy production, and brain signal systems. Han and the team stress that larger groups and fresh validation must come before any of these molecules can serve as a test marker.
pmc-13592316:
Simon H Rüdisser leads a 2026 team unveiling an open library and workflow for fragment based drug hunting by NMR. Fragment hunting tests tiny molecules for weak grips on a target, then grows the best into drugs. Their library, OpenFL600, was built for fluorine NMR reading and screened against eleven targets spanning RNA, receptors, kinases, and proteases. Clean hits emerged for each class, with no sticky false friends.

Ranking hits by grip strength usually eats weeks, so the team paired the library with a fast method based on fluorine signal behavior. Each fragment ships with the values that method needs. Rüdisser and colleagues present the free package as a full road from first screen to a ranked lead list.
pmc-13592616:
Qiu Zhu leads a team mapping what symptom network analysis has shown in stomach cancer care. Network methods treat each symptom as a node and its links to other symptoms as edges, exposing which symptoms sit at the center and which bridge separate clusters. Their scoping review searched nine databases in two languages and kept nine studies of patients around surgery or chemotherapy. Tools, central symptoms, bridges, and time patterns were charted.

Six symptom scales appeared, one Chinese stomach cancer module dominating. Fatigue was the most common core symptom, named in five studies, while bridge symptoms varied widely between papers. One time ordered study tied a body constitution type to later taste change, and taste change to later appetite loss. Zhu and the team call for standard tools and larger, longer studies.
pmc-13594616:
Ran Bao and colleagues pooled the research on the International Fitness Scale, a short questionnaire that lets people rate their own fitness instead of taking laboratory tests. Self-ratings promise a practical option for large population surveys, and their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered thirteen studies covering more than nine thousand six hundred participants.

When people answered the scale twice, their overall fitness ratings agreed substantially, and the same held for each part: heart and lung fitness, muscle fitness, speed and agility, and flexibility. Studies checking the ratings against other measures generally supported the scale's validity, though results varied a great deal between studies. Quality checks using a standard bias tool were part of the review. The authors conclude the scale is dependable enough for monitoring fitness in big groups where direct testing is out of reach.
pmc-13597516:
Suellen Almeida-Correa leads a ten-author team refining a rodent test of effort-based choice, the decision to work harder for a better reward, whose failure sits at the heart of depression and schizophrenia. Their 2026 modified task raises the effort bar, stretches the waits between trials, and preserves free choice, aiming to catch drug effects in both directions within one assay.

The refined task did exactly that, registering both impairments and boosts from dopamine-modulating drugs where older paradigms usually catch only one direction. Animals also revealed drug-sensitive anticipatory behavior during the waiting intervals, a window onto timing and motivational vigor. Chemical and light-based brain measurements tied performance to dopamine signals on several timescales, with a ceiling beyond which behavior stopped responding. Species differences tracked baseline dopamine tone. The authors offer the task for screening treatments aimed at motivational symptoms.
pmc-13598116:
P. R. Guaita and P. Crippa release a two-thousand-year climate reconstruction for North America at monthly resolution, built for ecological and impact models that need slow, local detail. Earth system models supply the raw past, yet their grids are coarse and biased; their 2026 dataset statistically downscales one such model against weather station records from 1875 to 2014.

The result gives temperature and precipitation on a fine grid with explicit uncertainty attached, a rare honesty about reconstruction error. Careful model selection guarded against overfitting, and leftover error patterns were modeled in space and time rather than ignored. The reconstruction sharpens the raw model output substantially while keeping its long-term trends and swings. The authors aim it at researchers validating impact assessments and modeling ecological processes that unfold over centuries.
pmc-13606716:
Ahmed Hassan Shujaa, Ahmad M. Rayani, and John H. Foster survey how psychiatric nurses in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, cope with a demanding job. Psychiatric nursing brings constant emotional strain, and coping habits shape how nurses weather it. The team handed a structured questionnaire, including the Brief COPE inventory, to 225 nurses in person over four months in 2024, then compared coping styles across demographic groups.

The most used strategies were constructive: positive reframing scored highest, followed by instrumental support, active coping, and planning. Behavioral disengagement and humor sat at the bottom. Two apparent group differences, self-blame by nationality and venting by experience, appeared in simple tests but vanished after correction for multiple comparisons. Gender, education, and department showed no differences at all. The authors present a descriptive map of coping in this workforce, useful for designing support and aiming future research, not for judging which strategies work best.
pmc-13607916:
Giuseppe Sberna leads a sixteen-author team putting a four-in-one virus test through its paces. Dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and West Nile viruses circulate together in many regions and cause look-alike fevers, so sorting them quickly matters. The Novaplex assay detects all four at once by real-time PCR. The team measured its detection limits with diluted virus stocks and probit analysis, then compared it against single-target tests on stored clinical samples.

Detection limits ranged from 2.04 to 4.79 log copies per milliliter across buffer and spiked plasma or urine, depending on the virus. The assay showed no cross-reaction with the related Usutu virus. On 34 clinical specimens, agreement with singleplex testing was highest for West Nile, substantial for chikungunya, and limited for dengue. The authors position the kit as a complement for arbovirus diagnosis and surveillance, not a replacement, and call for fuller clinical evaluation.
pmc-13613816:
Jiabin Xu and colleagues ask in 2026 what shapes older Chinese adults' willingness to use a medical visit companion service, where a hired helper goes with a patient to hospital visits. Digital booking systems and smaller families have made solo hospital trips harder for older people, so such services are growing. The team surveyed 494 older adults in Zhejiang Province between January and May 2024.

Willingness scored an average of 3.27 on their scale. Using a health behaviour model, the authors sorted causes into need, enabling, and personal factors, then ranked each factor's share and mapped how they stack on each other. Need factors carried the most weight. Service providers and local planners can see which levers, from price to trust to family support, are most likely to turn hesitation into use.
pmc-13615016:
Ahmed Mohammed Abdelghany and colleagues report a 2026 study from Benha University Hospitals in Egypt. It covers hearing damage in patients with a long-running infected ear condition. Patients with cholesteatoma, a skin growth inside the ear that can destroy bone, were compared with patients without it. The study covered 62 patients with the condition in one ear, 30 with the growth and 32 without, treated between April 2024 and April 2025.

Each patient had hearing tests covering tones, speech thresholds, and word understanding, plus a scan of the ear bone. The growth group had been ill for clearly longer. The team used the bone-conduction hearing score as a stand-in for damage to the inner ear itself and modelled which traits predicted mixed hearing loss. Their results help ear surgeons judge which patients risk permanent hearing harm and need closer watch.
pmc-13616416:
Xavier L. Pinheiro leads a team shielding nearly the whole rear face of ultra-thin solar cells to rescue the performance lost when the light-absorbing layer is thinned down. Thin absorbers cut cost and save scarce indium and gallium, yet they leak light and lose charge at the rear contact. The team coated the back of silver-and-copper indium gallium selenide cells with a porous silica layer only 8 nanometres thick, covering everything.

Full coverage beat a patterned coat covering about 70 percent, and both beat no coat at all, reaching 16.4 percent efficiency, a gain of two points over the bare reference. Standard current and light-response tests confirmed the order. Near-total rear passivation borrowed from silicon practice gives thin-film makers a cheap lever: use less rare material without paying for it in output.
pmc-13617216:
Yucong Sun and five colleagues tackle inverse design of non-rigid origami, where the goal is to work backward from a wanted behavior to the crease pattern that produces it. Non-rigid origami lets panels bend as they fold, which widens what designers can build, from metamaterials to robots. Full simulations are accurate but too slow to search huge design spaces, while simple models can silently fail.

Their framework first runs a geometry-mechanics compatibility test to check whether a design family can honestly be represented by a single-degree-of-freedom motion model. Families that pass get explored quickly with that simple model, and families that fail stay with detailed analysis. Demonstrations include origami materials with programmable multistability and layered force responses, shape-morphing targets, and task-specific robot motions. The authors say turning model choice into an explicit test makes origami design faster without hiding its assumptions.
pmc-13617316:
Ingrid Lorena da Silva Gomes and nine colleagues describe an adult-onset case of dystonia caused by mutations in the PRKRA gene, a rare inherited form labeled DYT16. Dystonia twists muscles into sustained abnormal postures, and this genetic type usually begins in youth as generalized dystonia with parkinson-like features. Drug options are limited, and who benefits from deep brain stimulation has been unclear.

Their patient, a forty-seven-year-old Brazilian man, developed abnormal upper-limb postures at thirty-five that spread to his neck and back muscles, wrecking his walking and causing frequent falls. Stimulation of the globus pallidus, a deep brain target, gave him sustained benefit. Placing his course beside previously reported cases, the authors argue that adult onset may predict a favorable stimulation outcome, while younger, more complex presentations respond less predictably. They say onset age deserves weight when teams select candidates for surgery.
pmc-13618916:
Guido Schröder and fourteen colleagues chart how the spongy inner bone of the human spine thins with age. They used CT scans of seventy-one spines spanning vertebrae from the neck to the lower back and ages four to one hundred two. Density in Hounsfield units was read at mid-vertebra, with bone mineral density and micro-CT bone volume measures in subsets. Such lifespan data have been scarce.

Density fell with age and head-to-tail in both sexes, with a marked drop at the thoracolumbar junction after sixty. Loss came in two phases, and the second phase arrived later in women, after sixty-four, than in men, after fifty-six. CT density correlated strongly with bone mineral density and moderately with bone volume fraction. The authors argue for sex-specific timing in osteoporosis assessment and prevention, since one age means different bone loss by sex.
pmc-13619716:
Amy S Wong and four colleagues asked whether MRI alone can identify the most common benign parotid gland tumor well enough to skip a needle biopsy, in a 2026 study. They reviewed 155 patients whose parotid tumors were confirmed by final pathology and who had MRI, needle sampling, or both before surgery between 2015 and 2020. Two senior radiologists re-read one hundred scans without knowing the answers.

Needle sampling and MRI performed closely overall, with MRI slightly ahead on sensitivity and slightly behind on accuracy. Statistical tests found no firm difference between the two methods. The team also built an MRI assessment tool based on clinical points and scan features typical of this tumor. They suggest the tool could help surgeons plan and could spare some patients an invasive biopsy, though final decisions still rest on the whole clinical picture.
pmc-13621816:
Enos Moyo and colleagues examine sexually transmitted infections among teenage girls and young women in Namibia who took part in the DREAMS programme, a health effort supported by Project HOPE Namibia. Infections were judged by symptoms rather than lab tests, a common approach where testing is limited. The study looks for patterns that mark higher or lower risk.

Records from 2018 to 2024 covered 27,992 sexually active participants aged fifteen to twenty-four, and roughly one in nine received a syndromic infection diagnosis. Diagnosis was less likely among younger teens, those who were pregnant or breastfeeding, and those using family planning. Risk ran higher among repeat users of preventive medicine after exposure and among those who had sex while using alcohol or drugs. The authors call for stronger teaching on safe sex and steady condom use for the highest-risk groups.
pmc-13624016:
Daphne Wrobel Goldberg leads a veterinary case report of a stranded olive ridley sea turtle that died carrying three infections at once. The adult turtle washed up in southeastern Brazil thin, dehydrated, and lethargic, and died six days after admission despite antibiotics and supportive care. Sea turtles weakened by illness often fall prey to germs that healthy animals shrug off.

The post-mortem found widespread small lumps across the inner body surfaces, plus pneumonia, liver and bladder inflammation, and severe gut infection. Lab work named the players: Mycobacterium fortuitum, a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis bacterium, spread through the body. An uncommon environmental fungus, Epicoccum, inflamed the body cavity, and coccidian parasites wrecked the gut lining. The authors argue that long debilitation and gut damage opened the door to the bacterial invasion. They flag the mycobacterium as a growing threat in marine wildlife.
pmc-13624416:
Li Zhu and co-authors ask why a gene called AFF4 matters when jaw bone heals after tooth removal. Their work centers on orofacial mesenchymal stem cells, the repair cells of the mouth and face. Mice bred so AFF4 could be switched off healed the empty tooth socket more slowly than normal mice did.

Cells lacking AFF4 made fewer bone-building markers and formed less new mineral in dishes. The loss also weakened a cleanup process in which worn-out cell power plants are recycled, a step tied to the energy sensor AMPK. A drug that turns AMPK on restored both cleanup and bone building, unless a blocking drug was added, which pins the effect on that pathway.
pmc-13625216:
Yao Ning Zhuang and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, trial a new training loop for intensive care nurses in a Chinese teaching hospital. The model cycles nurses through subspecialty study, mind mapping, and rolling quizzes, grounded in cognitive load theory, which holds that learning sticks when mental effort is well paced. In a cluster trial, 196 nurses in four units were assigned by unit to the new loop or to standard training, from January to September 2025.

The loop group scored higher on clinical judgment, exams, confidence, and critical thinking, and they kept more knowledge three months later. Interviews with sixteen nurses surfaced themes of rebuilt mental frameworks and a shift in how they saw themselves as learners. Structured cycles may beat one-off lectures for ward skills.
pmc-13627216:
Werner Seitz, Artyom Zinchenko, Hermann J Müller, and Thomas Geyer test a lean idea about how people get faster at searching cluttered scenes. In the classic contextual cueing effect, a repeated display speeds the hunt for a hidden target, and older models explained it by memorizing each layout. Their connectionist model learns no layouts at all; it only practices the search procedure itself, weakly guided, until the routine sharpens.

Remarkably, procedure practice alone reproduced the human pattern. It matched the key measures better than memory models. It even grew a central bias, the pull toward the middle of a scene, as a side effect of practice. Mastering the how, the authors argue, can mimic memorizing the what. That trims the supervision artificial systems need and reframes what practice does to attention.
pmc-13627616:
Shuaijie Wang and co-authors cook maize stalks into glowing carbon dots and spray them on maize seedlings to feed the plants more light. The dots, about two nanometers wide with a graphene heart, soak up light and re-emit it at wavelengths leaves love. Seedlings were sprayed at several strengths for a week, and the team measured growth, leaf traits, and the chemistry of photosynthesis against unsprayed controls.

A mid-strength spray won. Treated seedlings grew over forty percent taller, with larger, greener leaves, and their photosynthetic machinery ran markedly faster on every gauge, from chlorophyll content to the net rate of carbon capture. Turning crop waste into a light-harvesting spray closes a neat loop, though the authors frame the gains as early-stage results under controlled conditions.
pmc-13627716:
Johann Fritzen and co-authors build a fake nucleus out of DNA to watch a disease-linked protein misbehave in realistic crowding. Proteins such as FUS, tied to nerve degeneration, clump into droplets inside cells, and those droplets can harden into harmful solids, yet test tubes miss the nucleus's tight, sticky environment. Their programmable protonuclei are DNA compartments whose sequence, squeeze, and springiness can be dialed, letting the team watch FUS partition and condense under near-nuclear conditions.

FUS behavior swung sharply with each dial, and simple binding tests in tubes failed to forecast what happened inside. Tuning the DNA mesh also slowed the dreaded hardening of droplets. Environment, the study shows, is not background for phase separation; it is a main author of it, and these compartments give it a laboratory.
pmc-13630716:
The GBD 2023 ASEAN Causes of Death Collaborators chart how the leading killers change across life in Southeast Asia. The study covers the region's ten member states. It draws on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023. The span runs from 1990 to 2023. It estimates life expectancy and cause-specific death from birth to age seventy for each land.

In 2023 regional life expectancy reached roughly seventy years for men. For women it reached seventy-six. The range stretched from Singapore's highs to Myanmar's lows. Newborn disorders led infant deaths. Road injuries dominated male deaths from the teen years into early adulthood. Maternal disorders led for women in their late twenties and early thirties. Then heart disease and stroke took over in midlife. Tobacco ruled male risk factors. High blood pressure ruled female ones.
pmc-13635616:
Atefeh Allahbakhshian and five colleagues studied why empowered heart patients do or do not take their drugs. Empowerment programs teach patients with heart artery disease about their condition and choices. Knowledge alone may not change habits, the team argued. Adults at a heart clinic filled in standard scales for empowerment, cardiac self-efficacy, meaning confidence in handling their heart condition, and how faithfully they took their drugs. Path analysis tested how the three connect.

All three scores rose. Yet empowerment by itself did not predict adherence in the adjusted models. Confidence did, and the path analysis confirmed it as the bridge: empowerment raised adherence only by first building confidence. Within empowerment, the self-rule part, feeling in charge of one's own choices, built confidence most strongly, while a sense of personal skill added little. The authors advise nurse-led programs to favor motivation-building coaching over plain information.
pmc-13636216:
Quazi Noor E Sabrina and five colleagues published this 2026 review of how computing, printing, and artificial intelligence meet in heart failure care. Routine measures often miss the uneven mechanical strain inside a failing heart that drives decline. The review gathers work from 2015 to 2026 on three tools. Finite-element models simulate heart mechanics from scans. Printed heart replicas serve bench testing and rehearsal. AI pipelines segment images and predict risk.

Each tool contributes something the others lack. Models estimate wall stress and remodeling paths, printed replicas let teams test devices physically, and AI speeds image work and pattern finding. Yet support rests mostly on backward-looking studies, bench work, and small groups, with little proof on real patient outcomes. The authors propose digital-physical twin workflows where the three tools check each other. Better reporting standards and multi-center outcome studies must come first, they say.
pmc-13637916:
Vishal Pendse and six colleagues ask whether simple math can predict the shape of an upper-limb prosthetic socket from the shape of the limb itself. Socket fit decides whether a prosthesis works, yet design leans on clinician craft. Fourteen people with below-elbow limb absence contributed digitized limb and socket pairs, aligned by a new spline method. The team fit basic linear models linking limb measurements to socket measurements, overall and at three heights along the limb.

Overall size predicted beautifully: socket volume, surface area, and length followed the limb with little error. Cross-sections behaved unevenly, strongest mid-limb and weaker near the ends, exactly where trimlines, suspension choices, and end clearance reflect individual clinician judgment. Prediction errors stayed modest overall. The authors frame the models as a preliminary scaffold for digital design tools: software can draft the broad shape while skilled hands finish the details.
pmc-13641716:
Kavita Singh and twenty-one colleagues report the C-QIP feasibility trial, testing a bundled quality improvement program for chronic heart and vessel disease care in India. Care quality for these long-term conditions remains uneven worldwide.

Four hospitals randomized 410 adults with heart disease, stroke, or heart failure to usual care or the bundle, which combined decision support, care coordinators, patient education, text reminders, and feedback. Retention stayed above ninety percent, and guideline-directed drug use rose sharply for heart disease and stroke, though not heart failure. Patients also reported better adherence and habits. A larger trial is needed to test effects on illness and death.
pmc-13645516:
Yierfan Yilihaer and four colleagues present a ten-year retrospective study of risk factors for lymph node spread in hepatic alveolar echinococcosis, a parasitic liver disease that grows like a cancer. Whether surgeons should remove nearby nodes preventively is debated because spread is hard to spot beforehand.

From 623 admitted patients between 2012 and 2022, the team studied 191 who had radical liver surgery, fifty-five of whom proved to have node spread. Female sex, existing distant organ spread, and disease in both liver lobes each independently raised the odds. The authors suggest preventive node removal for patients carrying those features.
pmc-13645716:
Margarida Tavares writes a commentary arguing that protecting public confidence in vaccines should count as a core duty of national immunization programs. She opens with a 2026 case in Palermo, Italy, where a four-year-old girl died of diphtheria after her family refused vaccination over a feared link with autism. A vaccinated cousin with the same infection stayed only mildly ill. Tavares uses the case to shift blame away from one family's choice alone.

For two decades, she notes, programs have framed low uptake as individual hesitancy, which explains how people decide yet says little about what health systems owe families beforehand. She argues that confidence should be tracked like coverage, with early monitoring of public concerns and real dialogue before doubts harden. The COVID-19 years showed that louder messaging alone does not rebuild trust. Programs, she concludes, should treat confidence work as standing infrastructure, not a crisis add-on.
pmc-13646016:
Yogev Peri and three colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, whether a heart ultrasound ratio can predict death in people with a leaky tricuspid valve. The ratio compares how well the right side of the heart pumps against the pressure it pumps into. Records covered 247 patients of any leak severity, with a median age of eighty and a majority of women. The team also tried a combined index that folds in a second motion measure.

Patients with a low ratio died far more often within a year than those with a preserved ratio, and the link held after other factors were counted. The same held in the subgroup with moderate to severe leaks. The combined index sorted risk only slightly better than the simple ratio. The authors call the simple measure a practical warning sign, while labeling the combined version exploratory until other hospitals confirm it.
pmc-13649516:
Shan Cong studied one Oroqen family in China to see how ethnic identity is built across three generations. The Oroqen are among China's smallest ethnic groups, with just over nine thousand people, and they moved from forest hunting to digital life in about eighty years. Five family members shared deep interviews sparked by old family photos.

For the grandparents, identity rested on lived memories of hunting and gathering. The middle generation centred theirs on saving fading traditions. The youngest rebuilt identity from chosen symbols and online talk, with a looser tie to the native tongue. Each age group also carried its own emotional load. The study shows how fast change squeezes and reshapes identity in a small culture.
pmc-13649716:
Zheying Xiao and five colleagues surveyed 353 Chinese students in Kazakhstan on how felt support from their school links to fitting into local life. Adapting abroad drains time, funds, and spirit, so the team treated support as a resource and exercise as a way students invest it.

Felt support tied strongly to more exercise, and more exercise tied to smoother adaptation. Once exercise was in the model, support showed no direct link left: the whole path ran through activity. A type-based split found four groups, from low support to high support, and both exercise and adaptation split clearly across them. The authors back school support that gets students moving.
pmc-13650116:
Clara Bodelon and thirteen colleagues, publishing in 2026, ask whether known breast cancer risk factors leave marks on the tissue around tumors. That surrounding tissue, called the tumor microenvironment, helps shape how a cancer grows and how patients fare, yet little is known about which life and hormone factors change it.

The team used deep learning to measure 110 tissue features covering tumor cells, supporting stroma, and immune cells across thousands of slides from three long-running cohort studies. Age, race, hormone use, and lifestyle factors each lined up with particular features. Hormone therapy after menopause matched features seen in less aggressive tumors, while higher body weight matched two features tied to worse outcomes. Those features also carried part of the link between body weight and death from breast cancer, suggesting prevention could work partly through tissue change.
pmc-13650316:
Thomas Davergne and eight colleagues, publishing in 2026, map the outside-the-person factors that help or hinder physical activity in people with rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases.
