Staying active clearly benefits these patients, yet programs often fail because reviews have focused on personal motivation while daily surroundings quietly decide what is possible.

The scoping review gathered 42 studies with 3,084 participants across 17 countries and coded what patients themselves reported. The team sorted 233 separate factors into 25 themes spanning social, environmental, and system-level conditions. Support from others, cost, weather, access to adapted programs, and work or family duties could each cut either way depending on context. Less-studied factors included pet ownership, family habits, nearby nature, and patient groups. The authors argue that lasting change needs strategies aimed at surroundings, not only at the patient.
pmc-13650916:
Maria Munch-Menzer and one colleague review the puzzling link between narcolepsy and chronic pain. People with this sleep disorder report far more long-term pain than expected, and the obvious suspect, loss of the wakefulness chemical orexin in type 1 disease, does not explain the pattern.

Registry and self-report data show high pain prevalence in type 1 narcolepsy, yet laboratory pain tests often find no difference from healthy controls, which points toward secondary mechanisms that simple testing misses. Type 2 patients, whose orexin levels stay normal, report just as much pain, further weakening the single-cause story. The authors discuss altered dopamine signaling downstream of orexin as a shared pathway, plus activating autoantibodies found in type 1 disease as a possible immune contribution for some patients. They recommend holistic treatment and better-matched, larger studies that compare the two types directly.
pmc-13651516:
Nikolaos Vagkidis and two co-authors open a new route into the benzoin reaction, a polarity-reversing coupling known since 1832, by taming hydroxycarbenes. These fleeting intermediates normally snap into aldehydes almost at once through quantum tunneling, which kept them out of practical synthesis.

The team extended a pyridine probe method to catch the carbenes the moment they formed, freezing them as lasting zwitterionic intermediates, charged but overall neutral species. Those trapped intermediates then reacted with many aldehydes to give cross-benzoin products in high yields, strongly favoring the desired pairing. Mass spectrometry gave the first full picture of such intermediates, and calculations backed how they form and react. The authors present nucleophilic trapping as a general tool for putting hydroxycarbene reactivity to work rather than watching it vanish.
pmc-4868116:
Huerta-Cepas, Serra, and Bork presented ETE version three in 2016. ETE, the Environment for Tree Exploration, is a framework that simplifies work with phylogenetic trees and sequence alignments. Such trees show how species and genes are related through evolution.

Version three brought many improvements to the underlying methods library. Users can reconstruct, analyze, and visualize trees in one Python environment, including publication-quality figures. Phylogenomic data, drawn from whole genomes, need tools that scale and automate. ETE is used in comparative genomics to trace gene families, species history, and the spread of traits.
pmc-4890616:
Shin, Roth, Gao, and their colleagues reviewed deep neural networks for computer-aided detection in 2016. Remarkable progress in image recognition had come from large labeled datasets and deep convolutional neural networks. These networks learn layered image features directly from training data.

The review covers network architectures, the traits of medical image datasets, and transfer learning, where a network trained on one task is adapted to another. Computer-aided detection helps radiologists spot lesions in scans. Medical data are smaller and more specialized than web images, so adaptation is key. The paper guided medical imaging teams adopting deep learning.
pmc-5395016:
Kawahara, de la Bastide, Hamilton, and their team improved the rice reference genome in 2013. Rice research had been enabled by the high-quality reference genome produced in 2005 through a global project to sequence the rice genome. That reference covers the Nipponbare variety, the standard for rice genetics.

Using next generation sequencing and optical map data, the team rebuilt the assembly and checked the sequence anew. A better reference sharpens every study built on it, from gene discovery to breeding. Rice feeds more people than any other crop, so gains in its genetics carry global weight. The improved assembly became the base for rice genomic research.
pmc-6030816:
Enis Afgan, Dannon Baker, Berenice Batut, and many colleagues gave the 2018 update on the Galaxy platform. Galaxy is a web system that lets scientists run large biomedical analyses in a browser. Tens of thousands use its public servers for genomics and related work.

The update reports new tools, training materials, and ways to share exact analysis histories. Sharing matters because a result is only useful if others can repeat it. Galaxy hides computing details so bench scientists can work unaided. The paper shows how the project keeps pace as data sets grow larger and methods multiply.
pmc-6522516:
Jan Meier-Kolthoff and Markus Göker introduced TYGS, a web platform for genome-based taxonomy, in 2019. Naming microbes increasingly rests on whole genomes rather than lab traits. Such analyses are complex and once needed expert hands.

TYGS automates the full workflow for prokaryote genomes sent in by users. It finds close type strains, computes genome similarity, and builds trees with standard methods. Results arrive as a report ready to support a species call. The service lets small labs apply the same rigorous taxonomy as genome centers. Results come back with plain-language explanations, not only taxonomic labels and trees.
pmc-7488116:
Jian-Jun Jin and co-authors presented in 2020 a software toolkit called GetOrganelle, built to assemble organelle genomes from ordinary sequencing data. Organelles such as chloroplasts and mitochondria carry their own small genomes, which scientists use to trace species relationships. Pulling those small genomes cleanly out of a whole genome sequencing run is a fiddly step that often slows projects down.

The toolkit fishes out the reads that belong to organelles, builds the genome from scratch, and untangles the tangled assembly paths that result. The authors report that it is fast and flexible enough for many kinds of samples and organelles. Tools like this quietly power thousands of studies in plant and animal evolution.
poems-pg10216:
Marietta Holley, who wrote famous comic prose as Josiah Allen's Wife. Gathered her serious verse in this volume of Poems and dedicated it to the memory of her mother, whose eyes once brightened over these lines. Holley was one of America's best-selling humorists, a feminist voice disguised as a country wife, yet the dedication reveals a private, earnest poet behind the dialect comedy.

Contents run to ballads and story poems: the Brothers, a Rich Man's Reverie, the Deacon's Daughter, the Coquette, Little Nell, and the Fisher's Wife. Titles like the Land of Long Ago, Sometime, and Waiting show her sentimental register, while the Haunted Castle and the Knight of Normandy try romance. Readers who know only Samantha Allen's lectures to her husband Josiah will be surprised by the tenderness here, the same moral seriousness without the jokes.
pound-gaudier-brzeska-1916:
Henri Gaudier-Brzeska was a French sculptor working in London, a leader of the vorticist movement, who was killed in the trenches in 1915 at twenty-three. Ezra Pound, his friend and champion, published this memoir and manifesto in 1916.

Pound prints Gaudier's letters from the front, his statements on art, and his own fierce defense of the young sculptor's work. The book is part biography, part battle cry for the new art of hard, clear form. Grief drives it: Pound is building a monument in print for a friend the war erased. It remains vorticism's founding document.
pound-lustra-1916:
Ezra Pound published Lustra in 1916, in the middle of the First World War. The title is a Latin word for ritual purifications, and also a sly joke about luster and wandering. The collection gathers the satires and epigrams of his London years, at his sharpest and most quotable.

Short poems skewer dull critics, timid editors, and the whole apparatus of polite letters. Others turn tender: versions from the Chinese, through Ernest Fenollosa's notes, sit beside love songs and street scenes. Pound's lines are cut to the bone, with no wasted syllable. Lustra is the clearest single display of his pre-war modernism, funny and fierce by turns.
proclus-theology-plato-taylor-1816:
Proclus was the last great head of the Platonic school at Athens. His Theology of Plato sums up the late Greek scheme of the gods. Thomas Taylor gave the six books English dress in 1816. Taylor was the great voice for Plato in the tongue of his day.

Rank on rank of gods flows from the One in Proclus's scheme. He sorts them by their place in the chain of being. Hard Greek terms fill the text, but the sweep is grand. The book stands at the peak of Greek thought on the divine, late and full.
procopius-wars-gothic-1-dewing-1916:
The Gothic War of Procopius opens in books five and six, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1916. Justinian sent Belisarius to take Italy back from the Ostrogoths, and Procopius went with him as his secretary. This first half of the war runs through the great siege of Rome.

Naples falls, Rome is taken, lost in siege, and held against the Gothic king Vitiges in a year of sorties and starvation. Procopius gives the war street by street and wall by wall. He also pauses for the plague winds and the strange signs of the age. The volume is the fullest battle narrative to survive from the ancient world.
procopius-wars-vandalic-dewing-1916:
Books three and four of the History of the Wars of Procopius tell how Belisarius won North Africa back from the Vandals. H. B. Dewing's Loeb translation of 1916 carries the text. Procopius sailed with the fleet in 533 and saw the campaign himself. His post as the general's secretary gave him the council tent view.

The fleet lands, the Vandals fall at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, and Carthage opens its gates. Then the hard part starts: Moorish wars, mutinies, and a province that would not stay won. Procopius tells it with a soldier's eye for ground and luck. The Vandal kingdom, a century old, vanishes in a year of his telling.
prose-edda-brodeur-1916:
Snorri Sturluson's handbook of Norse myth and poetry reaches English readers here in the version by Rasmus B. Anderson, printed at Chicago in 1901 from a translation first copyrighted in 1879. The book is called the Younger Edda, or Snorre's Edda.

It gives the Foreword, the Fooling of Gylfe, Brage's Talk, and key passages from the Poetical Diction, with notes, a word list, and an index. The preface begins before heaven and earth, with the great empty gulf called Ginungagap. Readers get the main storehouse of the old northern gods and their tales.
ristretto-prezioso-d-arcani-nel-quale-si: Ristretto prezioso d'arcani, 1716. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.

A dedication page in Italian, its old long letters misread by the scan, opens this book of secrets. A stamp of the Surgeon General's Office stands at its head. The writer lays his book at an Excellency's feet, hoping to show a wish to serve. The book, he says, holds a summary of his choice and precious secrets. Some he learned from famed masters while travelling in Europe. Others he found himself, by twenty-five years of study. No author's name is legible, and no other page is shown.
roberts-treatise-of-witchcraft-english-1:
Alexander Roberts, a minister, published his Treatise of Witchcraft in 1616, the same year as Cotta's skeptical Triall. Roberts takes the other road. His treatise lays down propositions on witchcraft, point by careful point, building an orderly rulebook for Jacobean readers.

Scripture anchors each proposition, and English cases fill out the doctrine. Roberts writes for the parish pulpit, clear and systematic. His book was meant to be preached from on Sundays. Set beside Cotta, it shows two English churchmen of one year facing opposite ways on evidence. Roberts represents the settled teaching that most Jacobean congregations actually heard about witches.
robinson-man-against-sky-1916:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Man Against the Sky in 1916, his narrative poems of New England failure and dignity. The haunting title poem crowns a collection that fixed Robinson's fame as America's poet of quiet, ruined lives in verse. He wrote of Tilbury Town, his mask for Gardiner, Maine, and its clerks, drunks, and disappointed gentlemen.

Richard Cory, who glittered and shot himself, and Miniver Cheevy, who coughed and called it fate, appear in companion earlier work. Here, Flammonde, Cassandre, and the title's lone figure against a flaming sky carry his studies of pride and defeat. The title poem ends in affirmation hard won from a parade of suicides, skeptics, and broken believers. Robinson's plain diction and strict forms hide an irony as dry as his native Maine coast. Three Pulitzers later confirmed what this volume's readers already knew.
royce-hope-great-community-1916:
The Hope of the Great Community, published in 1916, gathers Royce's wartime addresses on the hope of a world community beyond nationalism. Dying that year, he spent his last public efforts arguing that the war's horror might teach mankind its interdependence.

Royce proposes that the duties of loyalty, learned in small communities, can extend to a great community of mankind, bound by interpretation and mutual understanding. He addresses America's role with both pride and warning. The addresses are brief and valedictory in feeling. The book stands as the final word of a philosopher who made community his life's theme.
russell-social-reconstruction-1916:
Principles of Social Reconstruction, published in 1916, is Russell's wartime program for rebuilding society, and it cost him his Cambridge lectureship. Written as Britain conscripted its young men, the book asks what a good society would actually protect.

Russell sets impulse, the urge to grow and create, against the dead hand of possession and power. He applies the test to the state, war, property, marriage, and schooling. His standard is simple: institutions are good when they help human beings grow. The book made him a hero to reformers and a marked man to the authorities of his day.
ruysbroeck-adornment-1916: The Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage by the Flemish mystic Jan van Ruysbroeck, in a 1916 translation. It describes the soul's union with God through love. This book preserves that medieval mystical classic. The file is now open to the public.
ruysbroeck-adornment-spiritual-marriage-: John of Ruysbroeck, whose life dates are given as 1293 to 1381, wrote The Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage, shown here in a print basis of 1916. C. A. Wynschenk translated the work from the Flemish, and Evelyn Underhill edited it with an introduction and notes. The same title page groups it with The Sparkling Stone and The Book of Supreme Truth. A Latin line from St. Bernard heads the work, to the effect that God is known in so far as he is loved.
sandburg-chicago-poems-1916:
Carl Sandburg published Chicago Poems in 1916, his raw celebration of industrial Chicago in Whitman's long shadow. Many call the book the birth of modern American city poetry in the United States of that age. Sandburg, a reporter and prairie socialist, wrote the poems out of stockyards, rail yards, and street life there.

Chicago, the title poem, hails the city as hog butcher, tool maker, and stacker of wheat. Fog, cinders, and the laughter of the poor fill verses built on catalogues and plain American speech rhythms. Poems on labor, war, and the IWW's dead stand beside tender sketches of girls, grass, and passersby in Chicago. The book scandalized genteel readers and made Sandburg the voice of the industrial Midwest in verse for decades. Its roughness is the point: the city's own energy forced into print.
scientific-character-analysis-practicall: Dr. Charles F. Boger wrote Scientific Character Analysis Practically Applied, issued in 1916 at Detroit, Michigan, by Wm. Cornehl and Sons. Boger is named, in worn title page type, as late assistant editor of Human Culture in Chicago. He was president of the Boger Institute of Mental Functions at Detroit. He was also psychologist and job expert of the Packard Motor Car Company at Detroit. A foreword begins with the observation that most people are interested in the study, and breaks off in the portion shown here.
shaker-testimonies-mother-ann-lee-1816:
Those who knew Mother Ann Lee best set down their memories in the Testimonies of 1816, reprinted here in the 1888 edition. Elders and sisters recall the Shaker foundress's life, sayings, sufferings, and revelations. Their witness accounts form the movement's first hagiography, written within living memory of its subject.

Hardship in England, passage to America, and the first hard years of the community pass through these pages. The speakers testify rather than argue, swearing to what they saw and heard. For anyone studying Shaker beginnings, this stands as the primary source, the foundress preserved by her own people.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5016:
Andrew Jackson gives eight yearly addresses, from December 8, 1829, to December 5, 1836, parted by three stars. The first tenders friendly greetings to Congress met at the seat of government. Under the Constitution, Jackson must lay before the federal law body of twenty-four sovereign states and twelve million happy people a view of the nation's affairs.

For the first time in that office, he voices true joy, calling for joint cheer and devout thanks. The states are at peace with all mankind, and the country shows the most cheering signs of broad welfare and steady gain. Looking at other nations, he voices a great wish: to see all men held fast in the same blessings, and moving on in knowledge, freedom, and social joy. Ties abroad stay mild and friendly in the main, though points of difference of deep weight remain.
sushruta-samhita-vol-3-1916:
The Sushruta Samhita is the great old text of surgery in India. Kaviraj Kunjalal Bhishagratna gave it English dress in three books. Book Three, from 1916, holds the Uttara-Tantra. That part is the last great head of the whole work.

The Uttara-Tantra deals with ills of the eyes, ears, head, and mind. It adds fevers, fits, and the care of babes to the surgical core. Sushruta is held the sire of surgery in the lore of India. The three books give the whole text in English for the use of all.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Cupid governs both tales in the sixteenth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Amorous Courtesan and Nicaise, two verse tales of love's transformations. Cupid governs both, in the poet's gayest and most myth-making mood.

The first opens on Dan Cupid, god of soft love. He works miracles in every age. He can change Catos into coquets. He can make fools into oracles. He can turn wolves to sheep. Nothing of the former shape remains. Hercules spinning for love and Polyphemus singing to the winds stand as the god's trophies. Nicaise, the companion piece, is the tale of a simpleton whose very name became a byword, sent on an errand of love he is too innocent to understand.
the-apologie-or-defence-of-a-verity-here: A much-garbled title page can still be read in parts. It names Anthony and an apologie, or defence, of a truth put out before. Its subject is a medicine called Aurum Potabile. The medicine is the pure substance of gold, made drinkable and fit for healing without corrosives. It is said to help in most diseases. Above all, it is said to strengthen the heart and the vital spirits. The writer calls it a universal medicine. The scan is badly broken, and no place or date can be read.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-16:
Part XVI of The Caxtons brings Pisistratus a mysterious note, in a tale he tells in his own person. The family picture format holds: a son's chronicle of his house. His scholar father's quiet world stands behind the intrigue that now enters it.

A waiter hands the narrator a note addressed in a hand he knows but does not at first place. The writing was once cramped, stiff, and upright, like a feigned hand. Now it runs hasty and rough, with scarce a letter finished, yet still plain to read. The note tells him the writer watched all morning and saw her go.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated February 25, 1897, No. 16 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and one offer. A year cost $2.50, and a copy five cents. The offer is headed School Books Wanted. Used school books will be taken in exchange for subscriptions, at named prices. Readers by Barnes, Appleton, and Cyr are listed. McGuffey's Revised readers are listed too.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Miguel de Cervantes' Don Quixote, rendered by John Ormsby, stands at Volume 1, Part 16 here. Chapter forty-seven tells of the strange manner in which Don Quixote of La Mancha was carried away enchanted, with other remarkable incidents. The knight finds himself caged and hoisted on a cart.

Seeing himself caged in that way, Don Quixote reflects that he has read many grave histories of knights-errant, yet never one in which a knight was borne off in such a fashion. Enchantment becomes his ready explanation for a humbling ride home. Cervantes turns the rescue into a slow, public undoing of the knight's dignity.
the-journal-of-negro-history-volume-1-ja:
Carter G. Woodson edited the first issue of this quarterly. Volume one, number one, is dated January 1916. The Association for the Study of Negro Life and History published it. A copy cost twenty-five cents, or a dollar a year. The contents show the founding program. Woodson writes on Cincinnati's Negroes before the Civil War. W. B. Hartgrove treats two Black teachers of Michigan. Monroe N. Work covers the passing tradition and African culture. A. O. Stafford reads the African mind in its proverbs.

A documents section prints eighteenth-century Black thought. Letters trace early Negro churches in Georgia and the West Indies. Reviews treat several works on Black history. Woodson's own Education of the Negro Prior to 1861 is among them. The first article opens with a claim. Cincinnati's annals show that colored people thrive when given a chance. The journal was founded to document that thesis.
the-love-letters-of-dorothy-osborne-to-s:
Edward Abbott Parry edited The Love Letters of Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple, 1652–54, in a New York edition of 1901, dedicated to his daughter Helen. The contents divide the letters by season and place. Early letters cover winter and spring 1652–53 and life at Chicksands in 1653. Later ones treat despondency at Christmas and visiting in the summer of 1654. An appendix on Lady Temple closes the volume. Parry's opening chapter explains that the letters begin with a long letter from Chicksands in the autumn of 1652, after Temple returned to England from a long absence.

Dorothy mentions an engagement her parents were forcing on her. Parry guesses that only after her London visit in March 1653, when she met Temple again, did the friendship pass its original limits, and he leaves readers to judge from the letters.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Saturday, July 11, 1829, brings the Mirror's No. 380, which illustrates Mercers' Hall and Cheapside as the metropolis's seventeenth-century architecture. Trades once congregated street by street, and the mercers assembled in West Cheap, called the Mercery. Lines from Lydgate's London Lyckpenny show a penniless narrator offered velvet, silk, and lawn there. Pennant's history of the spot follows.

On Cheapside's north side stood the Hospital of St. Thomas of Acon, founded by Thomas Fitz-Theobald de Helles and his wife Agnes. Agnes was sister to Thomas Becket, who was born on this spot in his father Gilbert's house. The hospital rose within twenty years of Becket's murder, dedicated to him without waiting for canonization. Its master and brethren professed St. Austin's rule. Readers see a shopping street excavated into saints, hospitals, and silk merchants.

Volume 19, No. 552, dated June 16, 1832, introduces the Brahmin bull kept in the Zoological Gardens, Regent's Park. The society owned several zebus, or Indian oxen. Zoologists quoted here, including Mr. Bennett, treat the zebu as a variety of the common ox rather than a separate species.

Only the shoulder hump and slimmer legs mark the zebu out, since its anatomy matches the common ox exactly. Larger zebus stayed at the society's farm at Kingston Hill, where an improved breed was the goal. The bull shown had come from India and ranked among the largest seen in Europe. Grey-bodied, cream-legged, short-horned, and long-eared, he was also perfectly quiet and friendly with strangers.
the-part-borne-by-the-dutch-in-the-disco: J. E. Heeres, a professor at the Dutch Colonial Institute at Delft, wrote The Part Borne by the Dutch in the Discovery of Australia, 1606 to 1765. The Royal Dutch Geographical Society published it in London in 1899 for its twenty-fifth anniversary. Only the front matter and lists are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The lists name maps by Hessel Gerritsz and others, including a chart of the Land of Eendracht from 1627.
the-tragical-history-of-doctor-faustus-f: Christopher Marlowe's Tragical History of Doctor Faustus is given here from the quarto of 1604, edited by the Rev. Alexander Dyce. The pages present carry the old title page and the full list of persons. They also carry Dyce's short note on his editing. He amended the text from the later quartos of 1616, 1624, and 1631, while ignoring 1663. That list runs from the Pope and the Emperor of Germany to Faustus, Wagner, Lucifer, Mephistophilis, the Good and Evil Angels, and the Seven Deadly Sins. The play's own first scene begins beyond these leaves.
the-voyage-of-captain-popanilla-pg7816:
Benjamin Disraeli begins his imaginary voyage on an island in the Indian Ocean that no discovery ship or missionary society has yet visited. A note dates the tale's first publication to 1827. The island overflows with flowers, fruit, and perpetual summer under a cloudless purple sky, ringed by a calm blue lagoon behind coral rocks.

Heat and perfume hide all animal life by day, but near sunset mermaids float on the rosy sea and sing from their shells. Answering choruses rise from the island, and crowds rush from the woods to the shore. The men combine a faun's vivacity with a Hercules' strength and an Adonis' beauty. A companion record of the same tale preserves only its contents list.
thompson-narrative-1916:
David Thompson mapped more of western North America than most men of his age. His tale of travel from 1784 to 1812 came out in print in 1916. J. B. Tyrrell edited the book for the Champlain Society. Thompson writes of fur trade posts, rivers, and Native peoples.

One brief note draws much note today. In January 1811, near the Rocky Mountains, Thompson saw huge tracks in the snow. He took them for the marks of a great beast, a mammoth as he put it. Fans of wild-man lore cite the note as an early track report.
tob-0116:
Albert Pike's Morals and Dogma appears here in its plain Gutenberg text: thirty-two lectures on the degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. Pike weaves Egyptian myth, Kabbalah, Zoroastrianism, and comparative religion into Masonic moral teaching, degree by degree. Each lecture expands a ritual's symbols into philosophy and history.

Conspiracy theorists love quoting Pike, usually in fragments, while Masons themselves often shelve the massive book unread. V1 evidence gives the sound advice: read the whole thing before judging it. Taken entire, Morals and Dogma is a nineteenth-century comparative-religion course wearing Masonic dress, tolerant in aim and relentless in digression.
tob-10816:
Maurice H. Harris edited a selection, published as Hebraic Literature, drawing striking passages from the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the Kabbalah. Harris chose for interest as much as importance. Parables, proverbs, legal debates, and mystical visions sit side by side in short, digestible portions.

Rabbinic literature can intimidate newcomers with its size and argument style; an anthology lowers the door. Harris aimed at Jewish and Gentile readers alike, offering a first taste of rabbinic wit and depth. Readers meet sages arguing law, telling stories to explain Scripture, and speculating on hidden things, in extracts short enough to read one at a sitting.
tob-3016:
Plutarch, a Greek writer living under Roman rule around 100 AD, paired Greek and Roman greats in his Parallel Lives. Alexander stands beside Caesar, Demosthenes beside Cicero, each pair closing with a comparison of virtues and flaws. Plutarch states openly that he writes lives, not histories, hunting character in small acts and sayings.

Statesmen, generals, lawgivers, and orators receive the treatment, from Athens and Sparta to republican and imperial Rome. The Renaissance learned what character meant partly from these biographies. Shakespeare mined them, through translation, for his Roman plays. Readers still use Plutarch as the ancient world's most humane portrait gallery.
tob-4016:
Volume two of Vasari's Lives marches through the fifteenth century, the middle act of his Renaissance story. Brunelleschi's dome over Florence Cathedral, Donatello's bronze, and Botticelli's grace headline a crowded cast of painters, sculptors, and architects. Vasari knew many of his subjects' workshops and pupils firsthand, and his judgments carry that closeness.

Biography here works as foundation myth: each master adds a technique or a freedom, preparing the perfection Vasari sees coming in the next generation. This is where the modern idea of artistic genius takes recognizable shape. Readers get both reliable workshop detail and legend in the making, sorted only partly by Vasari himself.
tob-4116:
Kunjlal Bhishagratna gave English readers the Sushruta Samhita, ancient India's great manual of surgery, beginning with volume one in 1907. Sushruta, the reputed father of Indian surgery, teaches the healer's training, tools, and operations in detail. The text claims roots more than two thousand years old.

Students learn to cut, stitch, set bones, and couch cataracts, with drills on gourds and leather before touching a patient. Herbs, diet, and the care of wounds fill the supporting chapters. Bhishagratna's early English is rough in places but bold in scope. Checked from the 1919 printing, the volume preserves surgery of startling ambition.
tob-4216:
Edward Carpenter, an English writer who preached simple living and social reform, collected The Art of Creation in 1905. His essays treat the self and its powers: consciousness, desire, heredity, and the creative force that shapes a life from within. Carpenter wrote as a disciple of Whitman, and the warmth shows.

He urges readers to trust the deeper self over custom and fear, in work, love, and art alike. The prose moves between philosophy and plain confession. Verified from the 1919 edition, the collection catches Carpenter at his most characteristic: mystical, democratic, and quietly radical about how people might live if they dared.
tob-9416:
Origen, a Christian teacher in Alexandria in the third century, wrote De Principiis to set out his faith in an ordered way. It is often called the first full work of Christian theology. The copy here comes from a 1919 edition.

Origen works through God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, the soul, and the end of all things. He argues that souls existed before birth and that, in the end, God may restore all creation. Some of his bold ideas were condemned centuries later, but the book still shows a sharp mind trying to hold faith and reason together.
trotter-herd-instinct-1916:
Wilfred Trotter was a British surgeon who wrote on crowd behavior while Europe was deep in the First World War. His 1916 book Instincts of the Herd in Peace and War argues that humans, like herd animals, crave the group's voice. He first printed the core essays before the war began.

Trotter claims the herd instinct explains fashion, panic, loyalty, and the pull of leaders in wartime. A person alone may doubt, but the herd's agreement feels like truth itself. His medical, unsparing look at mass feeling became a classic of crowd psychology. He hoped that naming the instinct might help nations resist its worst effects.
un-ga-res-16: Money questions got their own expert panel in Resolution 16, passed on 13 February 1946. The General Assembly names ten men to the Committee on Contributions, among them Paul H. Appleby and Sir Cecil Kisch. Four of them draw two-year terms. The panel's first big task: work out a fair scale for how member states should split the costs of the UN, in time for the next part of the session.
un-ga-res-a-69-16:
Ten years for people of African descent were proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2013, and Resolution A/69/16 sets that decade in motion. The span runs from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2024. Its theme is named in full: people of African descent, with the watchwords of respect, justice, and growth. The start of the decade falls right after the main debate of the Assembly's sixty-ninth session.

The text recalls the world year for people of African descent, kept in 2011. Gains won in that year form the base for the decade's work. Joint force is the aim: the decade should add fresh weight to the fight against racism in all its forms, and to the pledges of the Durban meeting of 2001.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: On 13 February 1946, at the thirty-first plenary meeting, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 16. It is an election record. The Assembly named the ten members of the new Committee on Contributions. It set four of them to serve two-year terms. It pointed the committee to the Preparatory Commission's guidance on money matters. It asked the committee to bring a detailed plan for sharing United Nations costs. The plan was for the second part of the first session.

General Assembly resolution 69/16 was adopted on 18 November 2014. It adopts the programme of activities for the International Decade for People of African Descent. The Decade runs from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2024. Its theme is 'recognition, justice and development.' The annexed programme, built on the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, is the resolution's real substance.

The programme asks states to remove legal and practical obstacles to equality. It asks them to strengthen anti-discrimination law. It asks them to widen access to education, health, housing, and justice for people of African descent. All this is in full consultation with them. The Assembly appoints the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights as coordinator of the Decade. It requests annual progress reports and regular budget funding. It plans a midterm review and a final high-level assessment. The Decade gave the fight against racism a ten-year, program-shaped framework.
un-sc-res-1316:
The Congo mission received a short technical extension on 23 August 2000. The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement was in place, and summits of the Southern African Development Community and of the cease-fire parties had met in August. Yet poor access, weak security, and low cooperation kept the United Nations mission, MONUC, from deploying to its authorized strength. The Secretary-General had written to the Council on 14 August.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate to 15 October 2000. It stressed that this was a technical extension, not a change of course. The government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the other parties were called to lift every obstacle to the mission's deployment and work. All parties bore duty for the safety of United Nations and linked staff across the country. The Secretary-General had to report by 21 September 2000. The Council praised the mission's staff for strong work in hard conditions.
un-sc-res-1416: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 1416 is catalogued here as dating from 2002. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1516:
Resolution 1516 came in November 2003, days after truck bombs struck synagogues and British targets in Istanbul, Turkey. The Security Council used it to condemn those attacks in the strongest terms. Dozens of people had been killed and hundreds hurt in the blasts.

Beyond the condemnation, the members call on all states to help find and punish those behind the bombings. They also repeat that terrorism threatens world peace and must be fought under the UN Charter. Short as it is, the text shows the Council's standard response to a major terror attack in those years.
un-sc-res-1616: Formal output of the Security Council, Resolution 1616 survives in this collection in official-record wording from Wikisource. Many resolutions adjust running machinery: a mission renewed, a sanctions list updated, a deadline moved. The text here follows the usual architecture for such acts, and its exact terms are what officials on the ground would have followed.
un-sc-res-1716:
Georgia and its breakaway region of Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1716. The Council adopted it on 13 October 2006. A Georgian move into the upper Kodori Valley that July had raised tensions and strained the 1994 cease-fire.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 15 April 2007. It urges Georgia to keep the Kodori Valley in line with the cease-fire deal. It urges Abkhaz leaders to let displaced people return home with safety and dignity. Both sides are pressed to sign papers on no violence and on refugee returns.
un-sc-res-1816:
Piracy off Somalia met a naval answer on 2 June 2008. Pirate attacks and armed robbery at sea threatened aid deliveries to Somalia and the safety of trade routes. Maritime reports since 2005 showed the attacks going on. Somalia's transitional government lacked the means to stop pirates or to patrol its own waters. The Law of the Sea Convention supplied the legal frame.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned all piracy and armed robbery against ships off Somalia. For six months, states working with the transitional government, and named by it in advance to the Secretary-General, could enter Somalia's territorial waters. They could use all necessary means to repress piracy, in line with the law for the high seas. States were urged to share information, help crews, and bring suspects to trial. The step opened the door to the foreign naval patrols that followed off the Horn of Africa.
un-sc-res-1916:
Somalia and Eritrea are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1916, adopted on 19 March 2010. Weapons kept flowing to both countries in breach of the arms embargoes. Armed groups also stole or misused aid meant for hungry people. The monitors doing this work faced threats and interference.

The text extends the Monitoring Group for twelve months and adds three experts. The group will track money, ships, and routes used to break the embargoes. It will also draft lists of offenders for possible future action. For one year, the asset freeze will not block funds needed to deliver urgent aid in Somalia. The aid coordinator must report every 120 days on how that carve-out works.
un-sc-res-2016: Under number 2016, a Security Council decision is preserved in this collection through a Wikisource copy of the UN record. The text observes the genre's discipline: the preamble argues, the operative part acts, and neither does the other's job. Keeping both parts together and complete is what makes the entry a faithful piece of the record.
un-sc-res-216:
Southern Rhodesia's white minority government declared independence from Britain on its own on 11 November 1965. The Council answered the very next day. Resolution 216, adopted on 12 November 1965, is short, with only two decisions. Both of them are firm.

The Council condemned the unilateral declaration of independence. The declaration had been made by a racist minority, and the regime it created was illegal. All states were called on not to recognize that regime. They also had to refrain from giving it any assistance at all. The text was the Council's first word on Rhodesia's breakaway. Stronger measures, including the sanctions of later years, all built on this refusal to accept the minority regime as lawful.
un-sc-res-316:
Israeli raids into Lebanon brought a sharp rebuke in June 1972. Israeli forces had seized Syrian and Lebanese personnel on Lebanese soil on 21 June. On 26 June 1972 the Council condemned the repeated attacks. It deplored all acts of violence in the exchange. The attacks, it said, broke the Charter and Israel's duties under it. Truce reports covering April to June fed the debate.

Israel had to obey past resolutions and stop all military acts against Lebanon. The Council voiced a strong desire for the captives' quick release. If they were not freed, or if Israel defied the text, the Council would meet again fast. Panama and the United States abstained in the vote.
un-sc-res-416:
The Sinai emergency force was renewed for a full year on 21 October 1977. The Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Emergency Force guided the Council. He warned that letting the search for a full settlement relax could prove dangerous. He advised one more year for the force. The force had stood between Egypt and Israel since the 1973 war.

The Council called on all parties to carry out resolution 338 (1973) at once. It renewed the Emergency Force's mandate for one year, until 24 October 1978. The Secretary-General had to report at the end of the period on events and on the steps taken toward resolution 338. That text demanded a cease-fire and talks for a just and durable peace. The Council voiced its confidence that the force would be kept with the greatest efficiency and economy.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Tunisia ended its time as a French protectorate in March 1956. Independence brought an application to join the United Nations. The paperwork reached the Council as document S/3622. Resolution 116 was adopted unanimously on 26 July 1956. It was the second meeting in two days on North African admissions, following Morocco's case.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit Tunisia. The Assembly welcomed it that November. Tunisia took its seat during a season of rapid decolonization. Its first UN years made it a bridge between the Arab world and the West. This brief resolution records the formal recommendation that opened the door.

Resolution 1316, adopted on 23 August 2000, deals with a peacekeeping mission that cannot get onto the ground. MONUC, the UN mission for Congo, had been authorized to grow, but poor access, weak security, and limited cooperation from the parties kept it below strength. Two August summits of the Lusaka ceasefire parties had just been held.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate briefly, into October 2000, while it worked with the ceasefire parties and potential troop contributors to create conditions for fuller deployment. It reaffirmed support for the Lusaka agreement and thanked states that had offered troops. Congo's government was called on in particular to remove the obstacles blocking the mission's work.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 13 June 2002, to 15 December 2002. The island's government agreed the force was still needed. The Secretary-General's report had also urged urgent work on the humanitarian issue of missing persons from the island's conflict.

The mandate is renewed and a report is due by 1 December 2002. The Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces are urged to lift restrictions placed on UNFICYP in June 2000. The military position at Strovilia is to return to what it had been before those restrictions. The force's long watch over the island's ceasefire lines thus continues.

Bomb attacks in Istanbul, Turkey, on 15 and 20 November 2003 are condemned in this text of 20 November. The two rounds of blasts killed and injured many people within one week. Other terrorist acts in various countries are cited in the same statement.

Deepest sympathy goes to the people and governments of Turkey and the United Kingdom and to the victims and their families. All states are urged, as resolution 1373 requires, to cooperate in finding and bringing to justice those who carried out, organized, and sponsored the attacks. The text closes by restating a strengthened resolve to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Trieste's fate as a free city under UN guard starts with this act of 1947. On 10 January, the Council adopted Resolution 16. The peace treaty with Italy was then being finished. It carved the port city and its hinterland out of both Italy and Yugoslavia. A Free Territory would stand under direct UN care. An open free port formed part of the design.

The Council records its backing for three treaty texts. They cover the land's first regime, its lasting statute, and the free port. It accepts the duties the treaty lays on it. Naming a governor sat among those duties. The Free Territory never took full shape in the end. Trieste was split between Italy and Yugoslavia in 1954.

Weapons still flowed to militias in Ituri and the Kivus, and on 29 July 2005 the arms embargo and related measures on armed groups in eastern Congo are renewed. The ban had been set in 2003 and widened in April 2005. The arms trade is linked to the illegal exploitation of Congo's natural resources.

The parties had again failed to meet the Council's demands, so the embargo measures are renewed for a further period. The group of experts that tracks violations is re-established, and the plan to enforce penalties against people and bodies breaking the ban is restated. States and the Congolese government are pressed to cooperate with the experts and the sanctions committee.

Fresh tension in Georgia's Kodori Valley shapes Resolution 1716, adopted on 13 October 2006. A Georgian special operation in the upper valley that July had raised Abkhaz fears and breached the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal. Joint patrols by the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, and the CIS peacekeeping force had just resumed there.

The Council extends UNOMIG until 15 April 2007. It voices concern at Georgia's moves in the Kodori Valley and urges Tbilisi to keep the valley in line with the Moscow agreement, with no unauthorized troops present. It urges the Abkhaz leadership to take the return of displaced people seriously and to reassure residents of the Gali district about their rights. Both sides are pressed to finish draft papers on non-use of violence and refugee return and to restart talks at the highest level.

Sea piracy off Somalia meets a new legal tool in Resolution 1816, passed on 2 June 2008. Pirate raids put food aid for Somalia at risk. They also scared off trade ships and made sea lanes unsafe. World sea reports had charted the raids since 2005. The Council based its reply on the law of the sea pact. It also had the nod of Somalia's own interim rulers.

For six months, states that worked with those rulers could enter Somalia's own waters. They could use all needed force to crush piracy and armed theft at sea, as on the high seas. The grant was fenced with care. It held for Somalia's coast alone, and set no rule for any other shore.

Weapon flows into Somalia and Eritrea are targeted by Resolution 1916, adopted on 19 March 2010. The Monitoring Group's March 2010 report documented embargo violations, and the Group itself faced intimidation. Eritrea had been placed under its own arms embargo and sanctions by Resolution 1907 (2009). The Djibouti peace process remained the Council's path for Somalia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Monitoring Group for 12 months, adding three experts so it can cover both embargoes. The Group must trace the money and transport routes behind violations, keep draft lists of violators for both countries, brief the Sanctions Committee monthly, and report finally before its mandate ends. For 12 months, the asset freeze does not block funds needed for urgent humanitarian aid in Somalia, with reviews every 120 days. All states, Eritrea included, must cooperate with the Group and guarantee its safety and access.

Libya's civil war had just ended when the Council adopted Resolution 2016 on 27 October 2011. Four days earlier, the National Transitional Council had declared the country liberated. The resolution closes the military chapter of the international intervention in Libya.

The Council ended the main powers granted by Resolution 1973 earlier that year. That text had allowed member states to protect civilians and enforce a no-fly zone over Libya. Those powers, and the related ban on flights, would end at the close of 31 October 2011, Libyan time. The Council welcomed the change of power. It urged Libya's new authorities to stop revenge attacks and arrests without legal basis. It also looked ahead to a government that included all parts of society.

One day after Rhodesia's white rulers broke from Britain, the Council condemned the move. On 12 November 1965, it adopted Resolution 216. Ten members voted yes and none voted no. France held back. The minority regime had declared itself free rather than accept majority rule.

The text condemns the break, made by a racist minority. It calls on all states to refuse the regime any standing. No state should grant it aid of any kind. That refusal, set within a day of the break, fixed world policy toward Rhodesia. It held for fifteen years, until majority-rule Zimbabwe emerged in 1980.

A grab of Arab troops on Lebanese soil lit this 1972 clash. Israeli men had seized Syrian and Lebanese staff on 21 June. Cross-border raids had run for years by then. Truce staff sent sheaves of fresh word. Resolution 316 passed on 26 June 1972 by thirteen votes to none. Panama and the United States held back.

Israel was told to heed the whole chain of past texts. All raids on Lebanon had to cease. The Council damned the fresh strikes by name. It voiced grief at deaths from raids and counter-raids alike. One sharp wish stood out: the seized men must be freed, and fast. If they were not, or if Israel balked, the Council would meet at once to weigh next steps. The words had a hard edge rare for the day.

Resolution 416, adopted on 21 October 1977, concerns the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East. The force had been set up after the 1973 war to keep Egypt and Israel apart while a wider peace was sought. The Secretary-General reported on the force and warned that letting the search for a full settlement fade could be dangerous.

The Council calls on all parties to carry out Resolution 338, the 1973 call for a ceasefire and peace talks, without delay. It renews the Emergency Force mandate for one more year, until 24 October 1978. It also asks the Secretary-General to report at the end of that year on events in the area and on steps taken toward the settlement the Council wanted.
woman-and-super-woman-a-trumpet-call-to-: Pages present here hold a long scanner's notice about public domain books, then the start of a title page. The title reads Woman and Super-Woman, with a subtitle calling women of the present generation to come out. The subtitle breaks off mid-phrase in these pages. No author's name, date, chapter list, or body text appears here. Nothing beyond the partial title can be described from what is present.
yeats-reveries-1916:
Yeats looked back at his own beginnings in this 1916 autobiography, covering his childhood in Sligo and his youth in London. It is the first of his prose memoirs and the root of much of his later myth-making about himself.

He recalls his grandfather's house by the sea, the servants' tales of fairies, and the Sligo landscape that filled his imagination. In London he meets the poets and occultists who formed his early circle. The writing is tender and exact, already shaping memory into symbol. Readers of the poems will find here the places and people behind them, in the poet's own prose.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol16:
By 1874 the Journal of Discourses reached Volume XVI, still printed at Liverpool from shorthand reports. Brigham Young and the senior elders address the Saints on doctrine and the duties of their gathered life. The sermons preserve not just what was taught, but how it sounded from the pulpit.

Sixteen volumes in, the set had become the movement's memory of its own mind. A reader can watch themes return year after year, each time fitted to new needs. Volume XVI holds that pattern steady, one more link in the running doctrinal record of the Latter-day Saints.
